## Khuddaka Nikāya
## Sutta Nipāta Commentary
## (Volume 1)
## Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.
## Introduction to the Text

Having paid homage to the Triple Gem, the most excellent among those worthy of worship, I shall compose the explanation of the meaning of the Sutta Nipāta, which was taught in the Khuddaka Nikāya by the Protector of the World, who sought liberation from the round of suffering and who has abandoned all unwholesome conduct.

This Sutta Nipāta is included solely within the Khuddaka Nikāya; therefore, I shall also compose the explanation of the meaning of this Sutta Nipāta Pāḷi.

If it is asked: "Why is this text, which is well-interspersed with hundreds of verses and marked by Geyya (prose-verse) and Byākaraṇa (expositions), called the Sutta Nipāta?"

It is called "Sutta" because it is well-spoken (suvutta), because it is to be heard (savana), because it well-protects (tāṇa) the meanings, because it indicates (sūcanā) the meanings, and because it yields (sūdana) the meanings.

Because such suttas have been brought forth from various contexts and gathered together, this text has come to be known as the "Sutta Nipāta".

All these suttas are also similar in measure; therefore, this is the collection (nipāta) of those suttas.

Since there are no other specific reasons for naming it otherwise, it has rightly acquired the name "Sutta Nipāta".
2:
## 1. Uragavagga
## 1. Commentary on the Uraga Sutta

This text, having thus acquired its name, consists of five chapters (vaggas): the Uragavagga, Cūḷavagga, Mahāvagga, Aṭṭhakavagga, and Pārāyanavagga. Among these five, the Uragavagga is the first. In terms of the number of suttas, there are 12 suttas in the Uragavagga, 14 in the Cūḷavagga, 12 in the Mahāvagga, 16 in the Aṭṭhakavagga, and 16 in the Pārāyanavagga, making a total of seventy suttas. Among these, the Uraga Sutta is the first. In terms of the extent of the scriptures (pariyatti), it consists of eight recitation sections (bhāṇavāras). The beginning of this text, which is thus structured by chapters, suttas, and scriptural extent, is as follows:

"The bhikkhu who subdues arisen anger, as one subdues spreading snake-venom with medicines; that bhikkhu leaves behind the hither and the further shores, as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin."

This verse is the beginning. Therefore, to provide the explanation of the meaning starting from this verse, it is said:

"By whom, where, when, and for what reason was this verse spoken? Having revealed this context, we shall provide the explanation of its meaning."

Who spoke this verse? Where, when, and why was it spoken? It was spoken by the Blessed One, the Self-Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), the Self-Existent One (Sayambhū) who had no teacher. He received the prophecy (byādita) in the presence of twenty-four Buddhas, fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) until the Vessantara Jātaka, was reborn in the Tusita heaven, and then, passing away from there, took rebirth in the Sakyan royal clan. In due course, he made the Great Renunciation (Mahābhinikkhamana), realized the Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi) at the foot of the Bodhi tree, turned the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka), and taught the Dhamma for the benefit of devas and humans. He spoke this verse in the city of Āḷavī. It was spoken for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to those who had gathered there at the time when the training rule concerning vegetation (bhūtagāma-sikkhāpada) was being laid down. This is the brief answer here. In detail, it should be understood through the Distant Origin (Dūrenidāna), the Intermediate Origin (Avidūrenidāna), and the Proximate Origin (Santikenidāna). Among these, the Distant Origin is...
3:
The account from the time of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara until the present story is called the Distant Origin (Dūrenidāna). The account from the Tusita heaven until the present story is called the Intermediate Origin (Avidūrenidāna). The account from the seat of enlightenment (Bodhimanda) until the present story is called the Proximate Origin (Santikenidāna).

Among these three origins, the Intermediate and Proximate Origins are merged within the Distant Origin. Therefore, in this context, the detailed answer should be understood by way of the Distant Origin. Since that detailed answer has already been taught in the Jātaka Commentary, it is not expanded upon here. It should be understood exactly as detailed in that Jātaka Commentary. However, there is this distinction: while the story of the first verse in that Jātaka Commentary occurred in Sāvatthī, in this Sutta Nipāta, it occurred in Āḷavī.

As it was said: At one time, the Blessed One was staying at the Aggāḷava Shrine in Āḷavī. At that time, the monks of Āḷavī, while performing construction work (navakamma), were themselves cutting trees and also having others cut them. A certain monk of Āḷavī was cutting a tree. A deity dwelling in that tree said to the monk: "Venerable sir, do not cut down my dwelling place in your desire to build a dwelling for yourself." That monk, disregarding the deity's words, continued to cut and struck the arm of the deity's young son. Then the deity thought: "What if I were to deprive this monk of his life right here?" Then she thought again: "It would not be proper for me to deprive this monk of his life right here. What if I were to report this matter to the Blessed One?"

Then that deity approached the Blessed One and reported the matter. The Blessed One said: "Excellent, excellent, deity! It is good, deity, that you did not deprive that monk of his life. If you had deprived that monk of his life today, deity, you would have produced much demerit. Go, deity, there is a secluded tree in such-and-such a place; go and stay there."

Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, in order to dispel the anger that had arisen in that deity, spoke this verse:
"He who restrains arisen anger, as a charioteer restrains a swaying chariot..."
4:
He spoke this verse. Thereafter, hearing the people's criticism, "How can these recluses, sons of the Sakyans, cut down trees and have them cut down? These recluses, sons of the Sakyans, are harming life which has a single faculty (ekindriya)," the monks reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then prescribed this training rule: "For the destruction of vegetable growth, there is an offence of expiation (pācittiya)." Then, for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to those who had gathered there, He spoke this verse:

"He who subdues arisen anger, as one subdues spreading snake-venom with medicines."

In this way, this single story is included in three places: the Vinaya, the Dhammapada, and the Sutta Nipāta. By this much, the outline (mātikā) that was set forth—"By whom, where, when, and for what reason this verse was spoken; having revealed this method, I shall perform the commentary on the meaning"—has been shown both in brief and in detail, except for the commentary on the meaning.

Now, here is the commentary on the meaning. "Yo" (whoever) refers to such a person as one who has gone forth from a khattiya family, or from a brahmin family, or a new monk, a monk of middle standing, or an elder. "Uppatitaṃ" means that which has gone or fallen upwards; the meaning is "occurred." It means "uppanna" (arisen).

That which is called "arisen" (uppanna) has many divisions by way of: presently arisen (vattamānuppanna), arisen and passed away (bhūtvāpagatuppanna), arisen by way of opportunity (okāsakatuppanna), and arisen by way of obtaining a plane (bhūmiladdhuppanna). Among these, all conditioned things (saṅkhata) endowed with the moment of arising (uppāda), etc., are called "presently arisen." Referring to these, it was said: "Arisen states, unarisen states, states about to arise."

Wholesome and unwholesome states that have ceased after experiencing the flavor of an object, and other conditioned things that have ceased after reaching the three moments of arising, etc., are called "arisen and passed away."

This should be understood in such suttas as: "Such an evil wrong view has arisen," and "Thus there is the fulfillment of the development of the arisen enlightenment factor of mindfulness." Kamma spoken of in the manner of "Those were his previously performed kammas," even though it is past, is called "arisen by way of opportunity" (okāsakatuppanna) because it remains having blocked the results of other kammas and having made an opportunity for its own result; and also because the result for which such an opportunity has been made, though not yet arisen, will inevitably arise when the opportunity is thus gained. Wholesome and unwholesome states obtained in various planes are called "arisen by way of obtaining a plane" (bhūmiladdhuppanna). Thus, the difference between the plane (bhūmi) and that which is obtained in the plane (bhūmiladdha) should be understood. Herein, the difference is as follows: What is the difference? The "plane" refers to the five aggregates of the three planes which are the objects of insight (vipassanā). "Bhūmiladdha" is...
5:
...arisen by way of opportunity (okāsakatuppanna). The unabandoned unwholesome states in those various planes are called "arisen by way of obtaining a plane" (bhūmiladdhuppanna). In this context, the difference between the plane (bhūmi) and that which is obtained in the plane (bhūmiladdha) should be understood. To wit: the "plane" refers to the five aggregates of the three planes which are the objects of insight (vipassanā). "Bhūmiladdha" refers to the collection of defilements (kilesa) that are liable to arise in those five aggregates. Because of those defilements, that plane (the aggregates) is called "obtained in the plane" (bhūmiladdha). Therefore, it is called "bhūmiladdha."

Furthermore, this is not by way of the object (ārammaṇa). For if it were by way of the object, defilements would arise even towards all past aggregates, etc., and even towards the aggregates of Arahants which have been fully understood, as defilements arose in Soreyya the treasurer's son and Nanda the youth towards the aggregates of Mahākaccāyana and Uppalavaṇṇā respectively. If this were called "bhūmiladdha" merely by being an object, then because those defilements could not be abandoned, no one would be able to give up the root of existence. However, "bhūmiladdha" should be understood by way of the basis (vatthu). For wherever aggregates not fully understood by insight arise, from the moment of their arising, the collection of defilements which are the root of the round of rebirth lie latent (anuseti) in them. This should be understood as "arisen by way of obtaining a plane" (bhūmiladdhuppanna) in the sense of being unabandoned.

In that case, for whomsoever there are unabandoned latent defilements in the aggregates, those very aggregates of his are the basis (vatthu) for those defilements, not the aggregates of others. Regarding his past aggregates, only the past aggregates are the basis for the unabandoned latent defilements, not other aggregates. This same method applies to the future, etc. Likewise, for defilements unabandoned in the sensual-sphere aggregates, only the sensual-sphere aggregates are the basis, not others. This method applies to the fine-material and immaterial spheres.

However, for Noble Persons (ariya-puggala) such as Stream-enterers (sotāpanna), for whomsoever the collection of defilements that are the root of the round have been abandoned in those respective aggregates by those respective paths (magga), those respective aggregates of theirs no longer receive the designation of "plane" (bhūmi) because they are no longer the basis for those abandoned root-defilements of the round. But for the worldling (puthujjana), because the root-defilements of the round are not abandoned in any way, whatever kamma is performed, whether wholesome or unwholesome, the round of rebirth increases for him due to the condition of defilements. It should not be said that his root of the round (defilement) exists only in the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) and not in the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha), etc., or only in the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha) and not in the aggregate of form, etc. Why? Because they lie latent in all five aggregates without distinction.

How? Just as the essence of earth and water exists in a tree. For a great tree, standing on the ground and depending on the essence of earth and water, increases by way of that cause through its roots, trunk, main branches, minor branches, leaves, shoots, bark, flowers, and fruits, filling the sky and continuing the lineage of the tree through a succession of seeds until the end of the aeon...
6:
When a tree exists, one should not say, "That tree's earth-essence and so forth exist only in the roots, not in the trunk, etc.," or "It exists only in the fruit, not in the roots, etc." Why? Because it pervades all parts such as the roots without distinction. Likewise, it should not be said that the five aggregates are separate, as they follow a continuous process.

For example, a man who is weary of the flowers and fruits of that tree might apply a poison called "frog-thorn" (maṇḍūka-kaṇṭaka) to the tree from the four directions. Then, that tree, touched by the contact of that poison, becomes unable to produce further growth because the earth-essence and water-essence are exhausted. Similarly, a noble son (kulaputta) who is weary of the occurrence of the aggregates begins the development of the Four Paths (catu-magga-bhāvanā) in his own continuum, just as that man applied poison to the tree.

Then, his continuum of aggregates, being touched by the contact of the poison of the Four Paths, and because the defilements (kilesa) which are the root of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) are exhausted, all types of karma such as bodily karma, which have reached the state of mere functional action (kiriya), are no longer able to produce a continuum in another existence by way of the nature of future rebirth. Indeed, with the cessation of the final consciousness (carima-viññāṇa), he attains Parinibbāna without fuel, like a fire that has gone out. Thus, the difference between the ground (bhūmi) and the latent tendencies (anusaya) that have gained ground (bhūmiladdha) should be understood.

Furthermore, "arisen" (uppanna) is fourfold by way of: Samudācāra (active), Ārammaṇādhiggahita (grasped by the object), Vikkhambhita (suppressed), and Asamūhata (not yet uprooted). Among these, the previously mentioned "presently arisen" (vattamanuppanna) is indeed Samudācāra-uppanna. Even if defilements have not yet arisen in the initial stage when an object comes into the range of the eye-faculty, etc., because the object is grasped, they will inevitably arise in the subsequent stage; this is called Ārammaṇādhiggahita-uppanna. The defilements that arose in the Elder Mahātissa while he was wandering for alms in Kalyāṇī village upon seeing a disagreeable (visabhāga) form are an illustration here. His effort (payoga) should be understood in such passages as "arisen sensual thought" (uppannaṃ kāma-vitakkaṃ), etc.

Defilements that have not yet been suppressed by either serenity (samatha) or insight (vipassanā), though they have not yet entered the mental continuum, are called Avikkhambhita-uppanna because there is no cause—namely, the supramundane path—to prevent their occurrence. This Avikkhambhita-uppanna should be understood in such passages as: "Monks, this concentration on mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati-samādhi), when developed and cultivated, is peaceful and sublime, an unadulterated and pleasant dwelling, and it causes evil unwholesome states that have arisen to disappear instantly."

Defilements that have been suppressed by serenity and insight but have not yet been uprooted by the Noble Path are called Asamūhata-uppanna, as they have not yet transcended the nature of arising. An illustration of this Asamūhata is the arising of defilements in an Elder who possessed the eight attainments (samāpatti) and could travel through the air, upon hearing the song of a woman gathering flowers in a forest grove. To that person, by the Noble Path...
7:
The defilement that arises in an Elder who hears the song of a woman singing with a sweet voice is an illustration of this asamūhatuppanna (arisen but not uprooted). In such a person, the application (payoga) should be noted in passages such as: "When one frequently develops the Noble Eightfold Path, it causes the evil unwholesome states that have arisen to disappear right in the middle." These three (ārammaṇādhiggahita, vikkhambhita, and asamūhatuppanna) should be understood as being included only within the bhūmiladdha (gained ground).

Among the various types of arisen (uppanna) states mentioned above, it should be understood that this anger has arisen by way of bhūmiladdha, ārammaṇādhiggahita, vikkhambhita, and asamūhatuppanna. Why? Because anger of such a nature is to be disciplined. Only anger of such a nature can be disciplined by any kind of Vinaya (discipline). However, regarding the arisen states called vattamanuppanna (presently arisen), bhūtvāpagatuppanna (arisen and gone), okāsakatuppanna (arisen by opportunity), and samudācāruppanna (arisen through active manifestation), effort is fruitless and impossible. Indeed, effort is fruitless regarding anger that has already arisen and ceased (bhūtvāpagata), because that anger has already vanished before any other effort could be made. Likewise, it is fruitless in the case of okāsakatuppanna. Regarding the anger called vattamanuppanna and samudācāruppanna, effort is impossible because the occurrence of defilement and purification cannot happen simultaneously.

Regarding the word "vineti" (he disciplines):
"Discipline is of two kinds; each of these is fivefold.
Among those (ten), it is said that this person disciplines by eight ways."

To explain this further—discipline is of two kinds: saṃvara-vinaya (discipline of restraint) and pahāna-vinaya (discipline of abandonment). In these two kinds of discipline, each is further divided into five. Saṃvara-vinaya is fivefold: sīla-saṃvara (restraint by virtue), sati-saṃvara (restraint by mindfulness), ñāṇa-saṃvara (restraint by knowledge), khanti-saṃvara (restraint by patience), and vīriya-saṃvara (restraint by energy). Pahāna-vinaya is also fivefold: tadaṅga-pahāna (abandonment by substitution of opposites), vikkhambhana-pahāna (abandonment by suppression), samuccheda-pahāna (abandonment by eradication), paṭippassaddhi-pahāna (abandonment by tranquilization), and nissaraṇa-pahāna (abandonment by escape).

Among those ten, sīla-saṃvara should be understood as discipline in passages such as: "He is endowed, fully endowed with this Pātimokkha restraint." Sati-saṃvara should be understood as discipline in passages such as: "He guards the eye-faculty, he attains restraint in the eye-faculty."

"Whatever streams (of defilements) there are in the world, (O Ajita, said the Blessed One)
Mindfulness is the dam for those streams.
I declare the restraint of the streams;
They are blocked by wisdom."
8:
Restraint by knowledge (ñāṇasaṃvara) should be understood in such passages as the beginning [of the list]; restraint by patience (khantisaṃvara) in such passages as 'He is one who forbears cold and heat'; and restraint by energy (vīriyasaṃvara) in such passages as 'He does not tolerate an arisen sensual thought, he abandons it, dispels it.' All these forms of restraint are called 'restraint' (saṃvara) because they restrain, and 'discipline' (vinaya) because they discipline, the bodily and vocal misconduct and so forth that ought to be restrained and disciplined according to their respective natures. Thus, it should be understood that the discipline of restraint (saṃvaravinaya) is divided into five kinds.

Furthermore, in the factors of insight such as the defining of mentality-materiality, as long as they proceed by way of one's own non-decline, there is the abandoning of various successions of misfortune by means of those respective knowledges. To wit: the abandoning of personality belief (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) by the defining of mentality-materiality; the abandoning of the views of no-cause and wrong-cause by the grasping of conditions; the abandoning of the state of doubt by the overcoming of doubt which is the subsequent part of that same knowledge; the abandoning of the grasping of 'I' and 'mine' by the comprehension of groups; the abandoning of the perception of the path in what is not the path by the defining of path and non-path; the abandoning of annihilationism (ucchedadiṭṭhi) by the vision of arising; the abandoning of eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi) by the vision of passing away; the abandoning of the perception of fearlessness in fearful things by the vision of fear; the abandoning of the perception of gratification by the vision of danger; the abandoning of the perception of delight by the contemplation of disenchantment; the abandoning of the desire not to be delivered by the knowledge of the desire for deliverance; the abandoning of the lack of equanimity by the knowledge of equanimity; the abandoning of the state of opposition to the stability of Dhamma and to Nibbāna by conformity knowledge (anuloma); and the abandoning of the grasping of the sign of formations by change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhu). This is called abandonment by substitution of opposites (tadaṅgapahāna).

As long as concentration, consisting of access and absorption, proceeds without its own decline, there is the abandoning, in the sense of non-occurrence, of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and their respective opposing factors such as applied thought, which are suppressed by that concentration. This is called abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhanapahāna).

Because the four noble paths have been developed, there is the abandoning, in the sense of eradication so that they never occur again, of the thicket of defilements belonging to the side of origination (samudaya), as described in the method beginning with 'for the abandoning of views' for one who possesses those respective paths. This is called abandonment by eradication (samucchedapahāna).

The abandoning of defilements which is their tranquilization at the moment of fruition (phala) is called abandonment by tranquilization (paṭippassaddhipahāna).

Nibbāna, in which all conditioned things are abandoned because it is the escape from all conditioned things, is called abandonment by escape (nissaraṇapahāna).

All these forms of abandonment are called 'abandonment' (pahāna) in the sense of relinquishment, and 'discipline' (vinaya) in the sense of disciplining. Therefore, they are called 'discipline of abandonment' (pahānavinaya). Alternatively, they are so called because that respective discipline occurs for the person who possesses that respective abandonment.
9:
It is called 'discipline of abandonment' (pahānavinaya). Thus, it should be understood that the discipline of abandonment is also divided into five kinds. Since each of these is fivefold, there are ten kinds of discipline.

Among those ten kinds of discipline, excluding the discipline of tranquilization and the discipline of escape, it is said that this person disciplines by means of the remaining eight kinds of discipline through various methods. How? A person who disciplines bodily and vocal misconduct through restraint by virtue (sīlasaṃvara) also disciplines the anger associated with that misconduct. A person who disciplines covetousness, displeasure, and so forth through restraint by mindfulness and restraint by knowledge also disciplines the anger associated with displeasure. A person who forbears cold and so forth through restraint by patience also disciplines the anger arising from those various bases of resentment (āghātavatthu). A person who disciplines thoughts of ill-will through restraint by energy also disciplines the anger associated with those thoughts of ill-will. A person who abandons various unwholesome states by producing in his own continuity those wholesome states by which abandonment by substitution, suppression, and eradication occur, also disciplines the anger that is to be abandoned by substitution, suppressed, or eradicated. Although in this context disciplining by the discipline of abandonment might not [literally] occur, a person who disciplines by means of those states through which abandonment occurs is said, by way of method, to 'discipline by the discipline of abandonment.' However, at the time of abandonment by tranquilization, because there is no state left to be disciplined, and because abandonment by escape is not something to be [further] produced, it is not said that one disciplines anything by those. Thus, among those ten kinds of discipline, excluding the discipline of tranquilization and the discipline of escape, it is said that one disciplines this [anger] by the remaining eight kinds of discipline through various methods.

Alternatively— "Monks, there are these five ways of removing resentment, whereby resentment arisen in a monk should be entirely removed. What five? Monks, in whatever person resentment should arise, loving-kindness (mettā) should be developed toward that person... compassion (karuṇā)... equanimity (upekkhā)... non-attention and lack of reflection should be practiced toward that person. In this way, resentment toward that person should be removed. Or else, the fact that kamma is one's own (kammassakatā) should be resolved upon toward that person: 'This venerable one is the owner of his kamma... he will be the heir of his kamma.'" Thus, these five ways of removing resentment are stated.

And those five which are— "Friends, there are these five ways of removing resentment, whereby resentment arisen in a monk should be entirely removed. What five?"
10:
“Friends, in this Dispensation, a certain person is of impure bodily conduct but of pure verbal conduct. Friends, in such a person as well, resentment should be removed.” (A. Ni. 5.162)

By this and other methods, the five ways of removing resentment are taught. Among those methods, a person who removes resentment by any one of them is said to be one who “removes [anger].” Furthermore, because it is said:

“Monks, even if bandits were to sever you limb by limb with a double-handled saw, if anyone among you should give way to a mind of hate, he would not be a follower of my teaching.” (M. Ni. 1.232)

Thus is the advice of the Teacher, and also:

“He who returns anger to one who is angry is, for that very reason, worse than the other.
He who does not return anger to one who is angry wins a battle hard to win.
He who, knowing the other is angry, remains mindful and calm, acts for the benefit of both—himself and the other.” (Saṃ. Ni. 1.188)

“Monks, these seven things, which are pleasing to an enemy and bring about an enemy’s purpose, come upon an angry woman or man. What are the seven? Here, monks, an enemy wishes for an enemy: ‘Oh, may this person be ugly!’ Why is that? Monks, an enemy does not rejoice in an enemy’s beauty. Monks, this person who is angry, being conquered by anger and overwhelmed by anger, even if he is well-bathed, well-anointed, with hair and beard trimmed, and dressed in white clothes, he is still ugly because he is conquered by anger. Monks, this is the first thing pleasing to an enemy and bringing about an enemy’s purpose that comes upon an angry woman or man.” (A. Ni. 7.64)

“Furthermore, monks, an enemy wishes for an enemy: ‘Oh, may this person sleep in suffering!’ ... ‘May he have no great benefit!’ ... ‘May he have no wealth!’ ... ‘May he have no fame!’ ... ‘May he have no friends!’ ... ‘May he, after the breaking up of the body, after death, reach a state of loss, a bad destination, ruin, and hell.’”
11:
“‘May he reach a state of loss, a bad destination, and hell,’ [the enemy] wishes. Why is that? Monks, an enemy does not rejoice in an enemy’s going to a happy destination. Monks, this person who is angry, being conquered by anger and overwhelmed by anger, commits misconduct by body, misconduct by speech... misconduct by mind. Having committed misconduct by body... by speech... by mind, after the breaking up of the body, after death... being conquered by anger, he reaches hell.” (A. Ni. 7.64)

“An angry person does not know the benefit; an angry person does not see the Dhamma...” (A. Ni. 7.64, Mahāni. 5)

“Those beings who, being angry, go to a bad destination because of that anger—those of insight, having rightly understood that anger, abandon it.” (Itivu. 4)

“One should abandon anger, one should give up conceit, one should transcend all fetters.” (Dha. Pa. 221)

“Anger gives rise to harm; anger disturbs the mind.” (A. Ni. 7.64, Itivu. 88)

“O one of great wisdom, forgive this one fault; the wise do not have anger as their strength.” (Jā. 1.15.19)

By such methods, for one who contemplates the danger in anger, anger comes under restraint. Therefore, a person who restrains anger by contemplating in this way is also said to be one who “restrains anger.”

“Kodha” (Anger) refers to resentment arising from any of the nineteen grounds for resentment (āghātavatthu): the nine grounds taught in the Suttas such as “He has done me harm,” etc.; the nine grounds that are established as their opposites such as “He has not done me a benefit,” etc., totaling eighteen; and together with the groundless instances such as [stumbling over] a stump or a thorn, making nineteen.

“Visaṭaṃ” means spread out. “Sappavisaṃ” means snake venom. The word “iva” is a term of comparison, and it is stated as “va” after dropping the “i” sound. “Osadhehi” means with medicines.

This is the meaning: Just as a physician who can cure poison quickly removes the spread-out snake venom that has pervaded the entire body after a snake bite, using various medicines formulated from roots, trunks, bark, leaves, flowers, and so on.
12:
Just as a physician quickly dispels with various medicines—compounded from roots, stems, bark, leaves, flowers, and so forth—the potent snake venom that has spread and settled throughout the entire body; in the same way, whoever dispels, through any of the aforementioned methods of discipline, the anger that has arisen and overwhelmed the mind-stream, and does not tolerate it but abandons it, removes it, and eliminates it.

That monk is said to abandon the hither and farther shores because, since anger is entirely abandoned by the Third Path, he abandons the five lower fetters (pañcorambhāgiya-saṃyojana) known as the hither and farther shores. In truth, 'pāra' is a name for a shore. Therefore, because they are both of this side and constitute the shores of the ocean of saṃsāra, they are called 'ora-pāra' (hither and farther shores). Alternatively, just as one dispels spreading snake venom with medicines, that monk who dispels the arisen anger, having entirely abandoned anger through the Third Path and established in the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmiphala), abandons the hither and farther (ora-pāra). In this context, 'ora' (hither) refers to one's own personality (sakat-tabhāva), and 'pāra' (farther) refers to another's personality (parattabhāva). Or, 'ora' refers to the six internal sense bases, and 'pāra' refers to the six external sense bases. Likewise, 'ora' is the human world, and 'pāra' is the celestial world. 'ora' is the sense sphere (kāma-dhātu), and 'pāra' is the fine-material and immaterial spheres (rūpārūpa-dhātu). 'ora' is the sense-sphere existence and fine-material existence, and 'pāra' is the immaterial existence. 'ora' is the personality, and 'pāra' is the requisites for the happiness of the personality. Thus, one who abandons desire and lust (chanda-rāga) for these hither and farther shores through the Fourth Path is said to 'abandon the hither and farther shores.' Here, although an Anāgāmī (Non-returner) has already abandoned sensual lust and thus has no desire and lust for this personality and so forth, this is stated—encompassing all the divisions of hither and farther—to clarify the excellence of the Fourth Path, just as the excellence of the Third Path and others were shown, by the abandonment of desire and lust therein.

Now, to clarify that meaning, he spoke the simile: 'as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin.' In that context, it is called 'uraga' because it goes on its breast; this is a designation for a snake. That snake is of two kinds: those capable of taking forms at will (kāmarūpī) and those not capable (akāmarūpī). The form-assuming kind is also of two types: water-born and land-born. The water-born kind can only assume forms in water, not on land, like the Naga King Saṅkhapāla in the Saṅkhapāla Jātaka. The land-born kind can only do so on land, not in water. That snake abandons the skin which is called 'old' (jiṇṇa) due to its decayed state and 'worn-out' (purāṇa) due to the long passage of time. It abandons it through four causes: (1) remaining in its own species, (2) loathing, (3) dependence, and (4) strength. 'Sajātī' (own species) refers to the long-bodied personality that is the nature of a snake. Snakes do not transcend their own nature in five situations: at birth, at death, when falling into a deep sleep, when mating with their own kind, and when shedding their old skin.
13:
(Nagas) do not abandon their own nature when mating with their own species, nor when shedding their old skin. When a snake sheds its skin, it does so while remaining in its own species. Even while remaining in its species, it sheds the skin out of loathing. Loathing means that when the skin is released in half the places but not in the other half and remains hanging, the snake sheds it out of weariness and disgust. Being thus disgusted, it sheds it by depending on the space between branches, roots, or stones. Even when shedding by depending on such support, it does so by generating strength, making an effort, curling its tail with energy, and raising its hood while breathing heavily. Having shed it in this way, it goes wherever it desires.

In the same way, when this monk desires to abandon the states called the hither and farther shores (internal and external), he abandons them through four modes: remaining in his own nature, loathing, dependence, and strength. The monk's 'own nature' (sajātī) is virtue (sīla), according to the words: 'born of the Noble birth.' Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'A wise man, established in virtue.' Thus, the monk established in his own nature of virtue, loathing the hither and farther shores consisting of his own personality and so forth—seeing them as causing suffering like old, worn-out skin—by perceiving the danger (ādīnava) in various aspects, relies on good friends (kalyāṇamitta) and generates strength consisting of supreme effort. Following the method stated as: 'By walking and sitting during the day, he purifies his mind from obstructive states,' he divides the day and night into six parts and strives. Like the snake curling its tail and sitting cross-legged, like the snake breathing heavily, he strives with unflagging effort; like the snake raising its hood, he generates the expansion of wisdom; and like the snake shedding its skin, he abandons the hither and farther shores. Having abandoned them, just as the snake that has cast off its skin goes wherever it desires, this monk, having laid down the burden (ohitabhāro), goes towards the region of the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). Therefore, the Blessed One said:

'The monk who dispels the arisen anger,
As one dispels spreading snake venom with medicines,
That monk abandons the hither and farther shores,
As a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin.'

Thus, the Blessed One taught this first verse, culminating it in Arahatship. Now, the sequence for the explanation of the meaning of the second verse has arrived. In that second verse also—
14: ## "I shall explain the meaning of this verse, having revealed the sequence—by whom, where, when, and for what reason it was spoken." This is merely the table of contents (mātikā). Hereafter, fearing excessive detail, I shall not set out the table of contents separately for all verses, but shall perform the commentary by showing the meaning of each verse through the method of showing its origin (uppatti). This is the second verse beginning with "Yo rāgamudacchidā asesaṃ." The origin of that verse is as follows: At one time, the Blessed One was staying at Jetavana Monastery, the park of Anāthapiṇḍika, in Sāvatthī. At that time, a certain son of a goldsmith, who was an attendant of the Venerable Sāriputta Thera, went forth (ordained) in the presence of the Thera. The Thera, thinking "The meditation on foulness (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna) is suitable for young monks," gave him the meditation on foulness to dispel lust (rāga). That monk did not gain even a hint of mental cultivation in that meditation. The monk informed the Thera, "This meditation is of no benefit to me." The Thera, thinking "This is suitable for young monks," taught him that same meditation again. In this way, four months passed, yet the monk did not achieve even the slightest distinction. Then the Thera took him to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "Sāriputta, it is not your province to know the suitable meditation for this monk; he is one who should be tamed by a Buddha (Buddha-veneyya)." Having said this, He created a lotus flower of radiant color by His psychic power and gave it into the monk's hand, saying, "Come, monk, go and fix this lotus with its stalk in a mound of sand in the shade of the monastery. Sit cross-legged in front of it and contemplate, 'Red, red' (lohitaka)." It is said that this monk had been a goldsmith for five hundred births. Therefore, knowing that a red object was suitable for him, the Blessed One gave him the meditation on the color red (lohitaka-kammaṭṭhāna). By doing as instructed, the monk attained the four jhānas in due order in a mere moment and began to practice the play of jhānas (jhāna-kīḷā) through the methods of direct and reverse order (anuloma-paṭiloma). Then the Blessed One resolved, "Let that lotus wither." When the monk emerged from jhāna and saw the lotus withered and dark in color, he gained the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā), thinking, "This radiant form has been crushed by old age." Then he applied that perception of impermanence to his own body. Furthermore, he saw the three realms of existence as if they were ablaze, realizing, "Whatever is impermanent is suffering; whatever is suffering is non-self." While he was contemplating thus, there was a lotus pond not far from him. There, children went down, plucked the lotuses, and made a pile of them. To that monk, those lotuses in the water appeared like flames of fire in a reed forest; the falling petals appeared as if falling into an abyss; and the withered tips of the lotuses placed on the ground appeared as if burnt by fire.
15: ...appeared as if [burnt by fire]. Then, as he closely contemplated all phenomena following that method, the three realms of existence appeared to that monk more and more as a burning house without refuge. At that time, the Blessed One, while seated in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), emitted a ray of light from His body towards the monk. That light enveloped the monk's face. Then the monk, wondering "What is this?", saw the Blessed One as if He had come and stood near him; he rose from his seat and paid homage with joined palms. Then the Blessed One, knowing the teaching suitable for him and wishing to preach the Dhamma, spoke this Verse of Radiance (obhāsa-gāthā): "Yo rāgamudacchidā asesaṃ." In that verse, "rāga" (lust) is the name for the lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure, which occurs by way of attachment. "Udacchidā" means cuts off, breaks, or destroys. Experts in grammar (akkharacintaka) also desire the past tense suffix to have the meaning of the present tense. "Asesaṃ" (without remainder) means lust together with its latent tendencies (anusaya). "Bhisa-pupphaṃva saroruhaṃ" means like a lotus flower growing in a lake. "Vigayha" means having descended or entered. The remaining words are just the same as in the previous verse. What is meant is this: Just as those children descend into a lake and cut the lotus flower growing in the lake, even so, whatever monk enters this world-dwelling of the three realms— "There is no fire like lust," (Dhp. 202), "I burn with sensual lust, my mind is consumed," (Saṃ. Ni. 1.212), "Those obsessed with lust fall into the stream, like a spider into its own web," (Dhp. 347), "Friends, one who is lustful, overcome by lust, with a mind completely possessed, even kills living beings," (A. Ni. 3.56, 72)— following such methods, by contemplating the danger of lust, by the restraints such as the restraint of virtue (sīla-saṃvara) mentioned before, and by the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā) regarding animate and inanimate objects, he cuts off lust little by little. He cuts off the remainder with the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmi-magga) and cuts it off without remainder with the Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga). In the manner previously described, that monk abandons the near shore and the far shore, just as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin. Thus, the Blessed One preached this verse, culminating it in Arahantship. At the conclusion of the teaching, that monk was established in Arahantship.
16:
What is the origin of the verse: "He who has cut off craving entirely"? The Buddha was staying in Sāvatthī. A certain monk, while staying on the bank of the Gaggarā pond, was thinking unwholesome thoughts under the influence of craving. The Buddha, knowing that monk's intention, spoke this verse of illumination.

In that verse, it is called "taṇhā" (craving) because of the nature of thirsting, expressed as "tasati." It means not reaching satisfaction with sense objects. This is a designation for sensual craving (kāma-taṇhā), craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā), and craving for non-existence (vibhava-taṇhā). "Saritaṃ" means that which has arisen and remains pervading up to the peak of existence (bhavagga). "Sīghasaraṃ" means that which moves swiftly; it refers to craving that is capable of reaching other world-systems or the peak of existence in a mere moment, without considering the dangers of the present or the future. Thus, regarding this craving that pervades up to the peak of existence, moves swiftly, and is of all kinds:

"There is a desire (craving) that is wide at the top, difficult to fill, and moves pervasively. Those who are infatuated with that craving are those who are oppressed by the wheel of saṃsāra."

"A man with craving as his companion wanders for a long time in saṃsāra; he does not transcend saṃsāra, which has the nature of changing from this state to another state."

"Great King, the world is unsatisfied, it is a slave to craving and is always deficient."

By contemplating such faults and through the aforementioned restraint of virtue (sīla-saṃvara) and so forth, a monk dries it up bit by bit and cuts it off entirely with the Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga). At that very moment, that monk abandons the passion (craving) of all kinds that has arisen within his internal continuity. At the conclusion of the teaching, that monk was established in the Fruit of Arahantship.

What is the origin of the verse: "He who has destroyed conceit entirely"? The Buddha was staying in Sāvatthī. A certain monk, while staying on the bank of the Ganges river, saw a reed bridge (naḷasetu) built in a shallow stream during the summer being swept away by a powerful flood (mahogha) that came later. Seeing this, he stood struck with emotion (saṃvega), thinking, "Conditioned things are impermanent." Knowing that monk's intention, the Buddha spoke this verse of illumination: "He who has destroyed conceit entirely... he leaves behind this shore and the far shore, as a snake sheds its old skin."

Just as a powerful flood entirely destroys a very weak reed bridge, similarly, if one entirely destroys the nine types of conceit, that monk at that very moment abandons the lower (orambhāgiya) and upper (uddhambhāgiya) fetters, just as a snake sheds its old, aged skin. In that verse, "māna" (conceit) is the elevated nature of the mind that arises based on birth and so forth. It is of three kinds: "I am better," "I am equal," and "I am inferior." Again, it is of nine kinds: for one who is better, thinking "I am better," "I am equal," or "I am inferior"; for one who is equal, thinking "I am better," "I am equal," or "I am inferior"; for one who is inferior, thinking "I am better," "I am equal"...
17:
In that verse, conceit (māna) is the elevation and arrogance of the mind that arises based on birth and so forth. That conceit is of three kinds: the conceit "I am better," the conceit "I am equal," and the conceit "I am inferior." Again, it is of nine kinds: "I am better than the better, I am equal to the better, I am inferior to the better; I am better than the equal, I am equal to the equal, I am inferior to the equal; I am better than the inferior, I am equal to the inferior, I am inferior to the inferior."

Regarding all that conceit:

"Intoxicated by which conceit,
beings go to a miserable state (duggati)."

By contemplating the faults in that conceit through such methods, and by destroying it bit by bit through the aforementioned restraint of virtue and so forth, the defilements become weak and are like a reed bridge. Because the supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma) are exceedingly powerful, one destroys that conceit entirely with the Path of Arahantship, which is like a powerful flood. It means one kills and destroys it by cutting it off through abandonment without remainder. At that very moment, that monk abandons all kinds of lower and upper fetters. At the conclusion of the teaching, that monk was established in the Fruit of Arahantship.

What is the origin of this verse? The origin of this verse and the twelve verses following it is one and the same. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Sāvatthī. At that time, a certain Brahmin, when the time came for his daughter's marriage, thought: "I will adorn my daughter with flowers that have never been used by any low-born person and send her to her husband's house." While searching inside and outside the city of Sāvatthī, he did not see even a blade of grass-flower that had not been used by people. Then, seeing many Brahmin youths of a harsh nature gathered together, he thought, "I will ask these youths; among so many, someone will surely know," and he approached and asked them.

Those youths, wishing to mock the Brahmin, said: "Brahmin, in this world, the flower called the Udumbara flower is one that has never been used by anyone. Adorn your daughter with that flower and give her in marriage." On the second day, the Brahmin rose early, and after finishing his meal, went to the Udumbara grove on the bank of the Aciravatī river. Searching tree by tree, he did not see even the stalk of a flower. While searching thus, when midday had passed, he went to the other bank. There, he saw a certain monk sitting for his day-rest under a pleasant tree...
18:
He attends to the meditation subject. That Brahmin approached where the monk was and, without paying attention [to the monk's activity], sat down once, crouched once, and stood once, searching among all the branches, twigs, and leaves of that fig tree, becoming exhausted. Then that monk asked, "Brahmin, what are you searching for?" "Sir, I am searching for a fig flower (udumbara flower)," he replied. "Brahmin, there is no such thing as a fig flower in the world; these words are untrue. Do not exhaust yourself," said the monk. Then the Blessed One, knowing the monk's inclination, emitted a radiance and, to that monk who was filled with mindfulness and great respect, spoke all these verses of radiance beginning with: "He who found no essence in the realms of existence."

Among those verses, in the first verse, "nājjhagamā" means did not find, or cannot find. "Bhavesu" refers to the realms of existence: the sense realm (kāma-bhava), the fine-material realm (rūpa-bhava), the immaterial realm (arūpa-bhava), the realm of percipient beings (saññī-bhava), the realm of non-percipient beings (asaññī-bhava), the realm of neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient beings (nevasaññīnāsaññī-bhava), the one-constituent realm (ekavokāra-bhava), the four-constituent realm (catuvokāra-bhava), and the five-constituent realm (pañcavokāra-bhava). "Sāraṃ" means the nature of permanence (nicca-bhāva) or the nature of self (atta-bhāva). "Vicinaṃ" means searching with wisdom. "Pupphamiva udumbaresu" means just as this Brahmin searching for a flower among fig trees could not find one, so too any practitioner searching with wisdom cannot find any essence in any realm of existence. When that person, seeing those things in the three planes as impermanent and non-self in the sense of being without essence, gradually attains the supramundane states, he abandons this shore and the further shore (saṃsāra) just as a snake sheds its old skin—this is the meaning and the construction (yojanā). In the remaining verses, I shall state only the specific meanings without mentioning the construction.

In the passage "Yassantarato na santi kopā, itibhavābhavatañca vītivatto," first, this word "antara" is used:
In the sense of "cause" (or "interval") in the passage: "On riverbanks, in gathering places, in assemblies, and on roads, people meet and deliberate: what is the 'antara' (reason/matter) between me and you?"
In the sense of "middle" in the passage: "By attaining a slight distinction, he reached the end in the 'antarā' (middle/interim)."
In the sense of "internal (mind)" in the passage: "Anger gives birth to harm; anger corrupts the mind. People do not realize the danger born from 'antarato' (within)."
Thus, it is found in many senses such as cause, middle, and mind. In this verse, however, it should be taken as "in the mind" (internally). Therefore, "yassantarato na santi kopā" means that anger does not exist within the mind of that person, having been eradicated by the third path (anāgāmi-magga). This is the meaning. "Bhava" means success (sampatti); "vibhava" means failure (vipatti). Similarly, "bhava" is growth (vuddhi); "vibhava" is decline (hāni). "Bhava" is the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi); "vibhava" is the annihilationist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi). "Bhava" is merit (puñña); "vibhava" is demerit (pāpa). "Vibhava" and "abhava" are the same in meaning. Therefore, in this term "itibhavābhavatañca vītivatto," it refers to the state of various kinds of existence (bhavābhava) through the power of success and failure, growth and decline, eternalism and annihilationism, merit and demerit. That state of existence has been transcended in various ways as appropriate by the four paths. Thus the meaning should be understood.
19:
Thus, it is found in many senses such as cause, middle, and mind. In this verse, however, it refers to the mind. Therefore, "yassantarato na santi kopā" means that anger does not exist in the mind of that person, having been eradicated by the third path. Because "bhava" is success (sampatti) and "vibhava" is failure (vipatti). Furthermore, "bhava" is growth (vuddhi) and "vibhava" is decline (hāni). "Bhava" is the eternalist view; "vibhava" is the annihilationist view. "Bhava" is merit; "vibhava" is demerit. "Vibhava" and "abhava" are also the same in meaning. Therefore, in this term "itibhavābhavatañca vītivatto," the state of various kinds of existence (bhavābhava) is spoken of through the power of success and failure, growth and decline, eternalism and annihilationism, merit and demerit. It should be understood that one has transcended that state of existence in various ways as appropriate by the four paths.

In the phrase "yassa vitakkā," for that monk, the nine types of thoughts—namely, the three thoughts of sensuality (kāma), ill-will (byāpāda), and cruelty (vihiṃsā); the three thoughts of relatives (ñāti), country (janapada), and immortality (amara); and the three thoughts connected with compassion for others, gain, honor, and fame, and not being despised—have been destroyed, thoroughly dispelled, tormented, and burnt away by the three lower paths which are capable of abandoning those respective thoughts by contemplating the danger in each case and establishing the opposite states, as described in the Samantabhaddaka. Having been destroyed in this way, they are completely and well-cut within the internal continuity. They have been cut without remainder by the path of Arahantship in such a way that they cannot arise again in one's own continuity of aggregates, which is internal, and in the mind, which is the innermost. What is cut is called "kappita." It is like saying, "The hair and beard are shorn (kappita-kesamassu)." Thus the meaning should be seen here.

Now, in the phrase "yo nāccasārī," "yo nāccasārī" means that person does not over-exert (does not run ahead); "na paccasārī" means he does not slacken his energy (does not lag behind). What does this mean? If one falls into restlessness (uddhacca) due to excessive energy, it is called "overshooting" (accasārati). If one falls into sloth (kosajja) due to excessive laxity, it is called "lagging behind" (paccasārati). Similarly, if one torments oneself through craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā), it is called overshooting; if one indulges in sensual pleasure through craving for sensuality (kāma-taṇhā), it is called lagging behind. One overshoots through the eternalist view and lags behind through the annihilationist view. One overshoots by grieving over the past and lags behind by longing for the future. One overshoots through the view of the past (pubbantānudiṭṭhi) and lags behind through the view of the future (aparantānudiṭṭhi). Therefore, the meaning is that one who avoids these two extremes and practices the middle way (majjhima-paṭipadā) neither over-exerts nor under-exerts his effort.
20:
“He has transcended all this proliferation” means that through the Middle Way (majjhimā paṭipadā) which culminates in the Path of Arahantship, he has transcended and completely overcome all this threefold proliferation (papañca) consisting of craving (taṇhā), conceit (māna), and views (diṭṭhi), which are preceded by feeling (vedanā), perception (saññā), and thought (vitakka).

In the verse immediately following that, the phrase “knowing that everything in this world is false” is the distinct feature. Its meaning is: “Everything” (sabbaṃ) means all without exception. Even so, what is intended here is only the conditioned (saṅkhata) categorized as aggregates (khandha), sense bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu), which are the objects of insight (vipassanā). “False” (vitathaṃ) means departing from the state of truth (tatha). Fools, under the influence of defilements, grasp things as permanent (nicca), pleasant (sukha), beautiful (subha), or as a self (atta); because things are not as they are grasped, they are called “false.” By the word “this” (idaṃ), he points to all those things as being directly present. “Knowing” (ñatvā) means knowing with path-wisdom (maggapaññā); such knowing is by way of non-delusion and by way of the object. “In the world” (loke) means in the world of opportunities (okāsaloka); it should be connected as “knowing that all these phenomena (dhamma) categorized as aggregates and so forth are false.”

10-13. Now, in the four verses following this, there are these distinctions: “one free from greed, one free from lust, one free from hatred, and one free from delusion.” Therein, “greed” (lobha) is so-called by way of desiring. This is a designation for the first unwholesome root in its entirety, or for unrighteous greed (visamalobha). That greed is described thus: “Sometimes greed arises even for those who are like a mother, for those who are like a sister, or for those who are like a daughter.” “Lust” (rāga) is so-called by way of attachment; it is a designation for lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure. “Hatred” (dosa) is so-called by way of corruption; it is a designation for the anger (kodha) mentioned previously. “Delusion” (moha) is so-called by way of bewilderment; it is a designation for ignorance (aññāṇa) regarding the Four Noble Truths. In this context, because this monk, loathing greed, began insight practice thinking, “When shall I live free from greed, having abandoned it?”, the Buddha spoke this verse to show him the way to abandon greed—by seeing the falsity of all conditioned things—and the benefit of abandoning greed, which is the abandoning of the “near and the far shore.” This method should also be understood for the subsequent verses. Some teachers, however, say: “A single verse was spoken for each of those monks who, loathing those states in the manner described, began insight practice.” One may accept whichever view one prefers. This method applies to the next four verses as well.
21:
The explanation of the meaning here is as follows: They are called “underlying tendencies” (anusaya) because they lie latent in the mental continuum in the sense of not being abandoned. This term “underlying tendency” is a designation for sensual lust (kāmarāga), aversion (paṭigha), conceit (māna), views (diṭṭhi), doubt (vicikicchā), lust for existence (bhavarāga), and ignorance (avijjā). They are called “roots” (mūla) because they act in accordance with the modes of their associated states. They are called “unwholesome” (akusala) in the sense of being unsafe. They are also called “roots” because they are the foundation for phenomena. They are called “unwholesome” because they are blameworthy and have painful results. These two names (root and unwholesome) are designations for greed (lobha), hatred (dosa), and delusion (moha). Indeed, these states are described in this way: “Monks, greed is unwholesome and it is an unwholesome root,” and so on.

Thus, because these underlying tendencies have been abandoned by the respective paths, they do not exist for a certain person; likewise, those unwholesome roots are uprooted. “Samūhatāse” means “they are uprooted.” Those skilled in grammar desire the appearance of the letter “se” at the end of the nominative plural. However, the teachers of the Commentaries explain that “se” is an indeclinable (nipāta). One should accept whichever view one prefers. In this context, it is said: “Although such a monk is one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), an Arahant neither takes up nor gives up; he remains having already given up.” Nevertheless, because it is close to the present time, it is said using the present tense: “He abandons the near and the far shore.” Alternatively, it should be understood that one who attains final Nibbāna through the Nibbāna-element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu) abandons the “near and the far shore” known as the internal and external sense bases.

In that statement, the absence of underlying tendencies should be understood in two ways: by the sequence of defilements and by the sequence of the paths. By the sequence of defilements, the absence of the underlying tendencies of sensual lust and aversion occurs through the third path; conceit through the fourth path; views and doubt through the first path; and lust for existence and ignorance through the fourth path itself. By the sequence of the paths, however, the absence of the underlying tendencies of views and doubt occurs through the first path. Through the second path, there is the thinning of sensual lust and aversion. Through the third path, there is their total absence. Through the fourth path, there is the absence of conceit, lust for existence, and ignorance.

In that context, it is because not all underlying tendencies are unwholesome roots. Indeed, only the underlying tendencies of sensual lust and lust for existence are included in the unwholesome root of greed. The underlying tendencies of aversion and ignorance are reckoned as “hatred is an unwholesome root” and “delusion is an unwholesome root.” The underlying tendencies of views, conceit, and doubt, however, are not any kind of unwholesome root. Alternatively, because he began the teaching on the abandonment of defilements by way of the absence of underlying tendencies and the uprooting of unwholesome roots—
22:
The Blessed One said: "He in whom no latent tendencies exist at all, and in whom the roots of unwholesomeness have been uprooted."

Regarding the phrase "Yassa darathajā": Here, the defilements that arise first are called "daratha" (distress) because of their nature of causing burning. The defilements that arise subsequently are called "darathaja" (born of distress) because they are born from those distresses. "Oraṃ" (the near shore) refers to the view of self (sakkāya-diṭṭhi). As it was said: "Monk, 'the near shore' is a designation for the view of self." "Āgamanāya" means for the purpose of arising. "Paccayāse" means just conditions. What is meant is this: For the person in whom the defilements known as "darathaja"—which are the conditions for grasping the aggregates of clinging—have been abandoned by the Noble Path and no longer exist at all, that monk abandons the near and the far shore (orapāraṃ) in the same manner as previously mentioned.

Regarding the phrase "Yassa vanathajā": Here too, "vanathaja" should be understood in the same way as "darathaja". However, in terms of word-meaning (vacanattha), there is this distinction: It is called "vana" because it clusters around or resorts to objects. It means longing, indulging, or associating. This is a designation for craving (taṇhā). That craving is called "vana" because of its longing for and indulging in sense objects. It is called "vanatha" (thicket) because, through the power of obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna), it overspreads and expands the "vana" (craving). This is a designation for the latent tendency of craving (taṇhā-anusaya). It is called "vanathaja" because it is born from "vanatha". Some teachers, however, say: "All defilements are called 'vanatha' because of their nature of being a thicket; those that arise subsequently are called 'vanathaja'." In this Uraga Sutta, this latter meaning is intended. The other meaning is intended in the Dhammapada verse. "Vinibandhāya bhavāya" means for the purpose of binding to existence. Alternatively, it means for the purpose of binding the mind to sense objects and for future arising. "Hetukappa" means simply because of a cause.

Regarding the phrase "Yo nīvaraṇe": They are called "nīvaraṇa" (hindrances) because they obstruct the mind or the beneficial practice (hita-paṭipatti). It means they cover or shroud. "Pahāya" means having abandoned. "Pañca" is the word that delimits their number. He is called "anīgha" because of the absence of suffering (īgha). He is called "tiṇṇakathaṃkatho" because he has crossed over doubt (kathaṃkathā). He is called "visallo" because he is free from darts (salla). What is meant is this: That monk who, having seen the danger in the hindrances—both generally and specifically as mentioned in the Samantabhaddaka verse—abandons the five hindrances such as sensual desire (kāmacchanda) by means of the respective paths, is called "anīgha" because he is free from the suffering (īgha) known as the misery of defilements (kilesa-dukkha) precisely because of having abandoned them. He is called "tiṇṇakathaṃkatho" because he has crossed over the doubt that arises in such ways as "Was I in the past?". In that context, what are the five darts? They are: the dart of lust (rāga), the dart of hatred (dosa), the dart of delusion (moha), the dart of pride (māna), and the dart of views (diṭṭhi). He is called "visallo" because he is free from these five aforementioned darts. That monk abandons the near and the far shore in the same manner as previously mentioned.
23:
He is called anīgha because of the absence of suffering (īgha). He is called tiṇṇakathaṃkatha because he has crossed over doubt (kathaṃkathā) that occurs in such ways as: "Was I in the past?" He is called visalla because the five darts have been removed, as it is said: "In that context, what are the five darts? They are the dart of lust, the dart of hatred, the dart of delusion, the dart of pride, and the dart of views." That monk abandons the near and the far shores (orapāra) in the same manner as previously described.

In this sutta, the abandonment of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) should be understood in two ways: by the sequence of defilements (kilesapaṭipāṭi) and by the sequence of the paths (maggapaṭipāṭi). By the sequence of defilements, the abandonment of the hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa) and the hindrance of ill will (byāpāda-nīvaraṇa) occurs through the third path. The abandonment of the hindrance of sloth and torpor (thina-middha-nīvaraṇa) and the hindrance of restlessness (uddhacca-nīvaraṇa) occurs through the fourth path. The abandonment of the hindrance of remorse (kukkucca-nīvaraṇa), which is the state of regret (vippaṭisāra) occurring in such ways as "Alas, I have not done what is wholesome," and the hindrance of doubt (vicikicchā-nīvaraṇa) occurs through the first path. By the sequence of the paths, the abandonment of the hindrance of remorse and the hindrance of doubt occurs through the first path. The hindrance of sensual desire and the hindrance of ill will are weakened by the second path and abandoned without remainder by the third path. The hindrance of sloth and torpor and the hindrance of restlessness are abandoned by the fourth path. Thus:

"The monk who, having abandoned the five hindrances, is free from suffering, has crossed over doubt, and is free from darts,
Abandons the near and the far shores, just as a snake sheds its worn-out old skin."

In this way, the Blessed One concluded the teaching with Arahantship as the culmination. At the conclusion of the teaching, that monk was established in the fruit of Arahantship. Some teachers say: "Whichever verse was taught to those respective monks, at the conclusion of that respective verse, that respective monk was established in the fruit of Arahantship."

## In the Khuddaka Commentary named Paramatthajotikā,
## the explanation of the Uraga Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is finished.
24:
## 2. Commentary on the Dhaniya Sutta

'Pakkodano' is the Dhaniya Sutta. For what reason did it arise? The Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī. At that time, a herdsman named Dhaniya lived on the bank of the Mahī River. This was his past merit (pubbayoga): during the dispensation of Kassapa Buddha, while it was flourishing, he gave twenty food-tickets (salāka-bhatta) daily to the Saṅgha for twenty thousand years. Passing away from that life, he was reborn among the devas. Having thus spent one interval between Buddhas (buddhantara) in the deva world, in the time of our Buddha, he was reborn as the son of a merchant in the city of Dhammakoraṇḍa in the Pabbata region, in the midst of the Videha country, and lived depending on a herd of cattle. He possessed about thirty thousand cattle, of which twenty-seven thousand were cows that were milked. Herdsmen do not live in one place permanently. During the four months of the rainy season, they live on high ground; during the remaining eight months, they live where grass and water are easily obtained. Such a place is usually a riverbank or the shore of a large lake.

At that time, this Dhaniya also left his home village during the rainy season to find a place where the cattle could live comfortably. The Great Mahī River split, becoming known as the Kālamahī on one side and the Mahāmahī on the other, and after flowing separately, they reunited near the ocean. He entered the island (antaradīpa) formed between these two rivers, built pens for the calves and a dwelling for himself, and lived there. He had seven sons, seven daughters, seven daughters-in-law, and many workers. Herdsmen know the signs of rain. When birds build their nests at the tops of trees and crabs close their holes near the water and use the holes near the land, they understand that there will be good rain. But when birds build their nests in low places near the water's surface and crabs close their holes near the land and use the holes near the water, they understand that there will be a drought.

Then, Dhaniya, noticing the signs of good rain, as the rainy season approached, left the island between the rivers and made a dwelling place on the other bank of the Mahāmahī River, in a spot that would not be submerged by water even if it rained for seven weeks. He built calf-pens all around and lived there. Then, having completed the collection of firewood, grass, and so on, and when all...
25:
...when his wife, children, slaves, and workers had gathered together, and various kinds of food had been prepared, clouds rose up from all four directions. Dhaniya had the cows milked, the calves properly settled in their pens, smudge fires made in the four directions for the cattle, all his followers fed, all tasks completed, and lamps lit here and there. He himself ate rice with milk, and while lying on a grand bed, seeing his own prosperity and glory, with a joyful heart, hearing the sound of thunder from the west, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) while still lying down: "I have cooked my rice, I have milked my cows."

In that inspired utterance, the word-explanation is as follows: "Pakkodano" means one who has cooked rice. "Duddhakhīro" means one who has milked the cows and obtained the milk. The word "ahaṃ" indicates himself, and "asmi" shows his state of being. The meaning is: "I am one who has cooked rice and milked the cows." "Iti" means "thus he said." In the Niddesa, the word "iti" is explained as a word-junction, a word-combination, a word-filler, a harmony of letters, a smoothness of consonants, and a sequence of words. This explanation should be understood as referring to this very "iti." Because the word "iti" is used with the subsequent word, such as "Metteyyo iti" or "Bhagavā iti," to show the meaning "thus he said" for all words connected with the preceding word, and not otherwise.

"Dhaniya Gopa" is the combination of the merchant son's name and occupation. Among the five types of wealth such as permanent wealth, excluding the "following wealth" (anugāmika-dhana) like giving and virtue that follow to the next life, cattle-wealth is distinguished as "There is no wealth equal to cattle," being of great benefit to the world by providing the five products of the cow (pañcagorasa). Because he was endowed with such cattle-wealth, he was called "Dhaniya," and because he protected the cows, he was called "Gopa." One who protects his own cows is called "Gopa." One who is hired for wages by others to herd cows is called "Gopālaka." Since this man protected only his own cows, he is called "Gopa."
26:
"Anutīre" means near the bank. "Mahiyā" means in the river named Mahī. One who lives with attendants who behave in accordance with oneself is called "samānavāsa." This Dhaniya is such a person. Therefore, it is said "samānavāso." "Channā" means made so as not to get wet by rain with roofs of grass and leaves. "Kuṭī" is a name for a dwelling house. "Āhito" means brought or kindled. "Ginī" means fire. In various places, fire is called "ginī." "Atha ce patthayasi" means "now, if you so desire." "Pavassa" means "rain down," "pour," or "release water." "Deva" is an address to the rain. This is the word-by-word commentary (padavaṇṇanā) here.

## This is the commentary on the meaning (atthavaṇṇanā).

Thus, this Dhaniya the herdsman, lying on a great bed in his sleeping house, heard the sound of thunder and, saying "I have cooked my rice," showed that he possessed the means for the cessation of bodily suffering and the cause of bodily happiness. By saying "I have milked the cows," he showed the means for the cessation of mental suffering and the cause of mental happiness. By the words "near the Mahī river," he showed the perfection of his dwelling place. By the word "samānavāso," he showed the absence of sorrow, which has the separation from loved ones as its proximate cause at such a time. By the words "the hut is roofed," he showed the removal and prevention of bodily suffering. By the words "the fire is kindled"—herdsmen usually make three kinds of fires: a perimeter fire, a smoke fire, and a wood fire. Since all these fires had been made in his house, by saying "the fire is kindled" with reference to the perimeter fire in all directions, he showed the prevention of the coming of wild beasts. With reference to the smoke fire made with cow dung etc. in the midst of the cattle, he showed the absence of harm to the cattle from gadflies, mosquitoes, etc. With reference to the wood fire in the herdsmen's sleeping place, he showed the prevention of the harm of cold for the herdsmen. While Dhaniya was showing this, because there was no danger arising from the rain for himself, the cattle, or his attendants, he became joyful and glad and said, "O rain-god, if you desire, rain down."

While Dhaniya was reciting this verse, the Blessed One, staying in the Gandhakuṭi of the Jetavana Mahāvihāra, heard it with the divine ear (dibba-sota) which is purified and surpasses that of humans. Having heard it, while surveying the world with the Buddha-eye (buddha-cakkhu), He saw Dhaniya and his wife. He reflected, "Both of these people are endowed with special causes (pāramīs). If I go and preach the Dhamma, both will ordain and reach the fruit of Arahantship. If I do not go, they will perish tomorrow in a flood of water." At that very moment, He traveled through the air from Sāvatthī to Dhaniya's dwelling place, seven hundred leagues away, and stood above his hut. Dhaniya was [reciting] that verse again and again...
27:
Dhaniya was still reciting the verse; he had not yet finished. Even when the Blessed One arrived, he continued to recite. The Blessed One, having heard his words, in order to show, "They are not satisfied or confident with just this much, but rather they are like this," [spoke]:

"I am free from anger, my spiritual fallows are gone; I stay for but one night on the bank of the Mahī.
My hut (the body) is open (without the roof of defilements), the fire (of defilements) is extinguished. O rain-god, if you desire, rain down."
He spoke this responsive verse, which is similar in sound but not in meaning. For the words "pakkodano" and "akkodhano" etc. do not agree in meaning, like the near and far banks of the great ocean. However, because they are somewhat similar in syllables, they are verses similar in sound. Between those two verses, the meaning of the similar words in the previous verse should be understood in the same way as already stated.

The explanation of the distinct words is as follows: "Akkodhano" means having the nature of not getting angry. For that anger which arises from the previously mentioned grounds for resentment (āghātavatthu), even if it is very slight in some people, when it arises, it burns the heart and then subsides. In another, because of a stronger anger than that, he merely makes a facial grimace. In another, because of a stronger anger than that, wishing to speak harsh words, he merely moves his jaw. Another, with a stronger anger than that, speaks harshly. Another, with a stronger anger than that, looks around for a stick or a weapon. Another, with a stronger anger than that, handles a stick or a weapon. Another, with a stronger anger than that, takes a stick etc. and chases. Another, with a stronger anger than that, gives one or two blows. Another, with a stronger anger than that, even takes the life of a relative. Some, with a stronger anger than that, later feeling remorse, even take their own lives, like the minister living in Kālagāma village in the island of Sīhaḷa (Sri Lanka). By this much, anger reaches its peak of expansion. Since the Blessed One had already abandoned that anger at the very seat of enlightenment (Bodhimanda), cutting it off at the root and making it like a palm-tree stump, He said, "I am free from anger."

"Vigatakhilo" means the absence of spiritual fallows (khila). Because they bind the mind, they are called the five spiritual fallows (cetokhila). Just as in a land with fallows, even if it rains for four months, crops do not grow; likewise, for one who has spiritual fallows in the mind, even if the rain of merit, which is the Dhamma of the virtuous, falls, merit cannot flourish. Since the Blessed One had already abandoned those fallows completely at the Bodhimanda, He said, "I am one whose spiritual fallows are gone." Because He stays for only one night, He is called "ekarattivāsa." For example, while Dhaniya stays permanently in that place for the four months of the rainy season, the Blessed One does not stay permanently. Because the Blessed One arrived and stayed only on that night out of desire for Dhaniya's welfare, He said, "one who stays for one night." "Vivaṭā" means...
28:
Just as crops do not grow on land filled with stumps and thorns even if it rains for four months, likewise, even if the rain of merit, such as hearing the True Dhamma, falls, merit does not flourish or grow (for one who has defilements like stumps and thorns). Because the Blessed One has completely abandoned those five things resembling stumps and thorns at the very seat of enlightenment (Bodhimaṇḍa), the Blessed One said, "I am one whose mental obstructions are gone (vigatakhila)."

He is called "Ekarattivāsa" because he stays for only one night. For example, unlike Dhaniya who has come to reside permanently in that place for the four months of the rainy season, the Blessed One does not reside there permanently. The Blessed One came to stay in that place for that night only, out of a desire for Dhaniya's welfare. Therefore, He said, "One who stays for only one night."

"Vivaṭā" means having the covering removed. "Kuṭī" refers to the individual existence (attabhāva). Indeed, this individual existence is called "body" (kāya), "cave" (guhā), "form" (deha), "accumulation" (sandeha), "boat" (nāvā), "chariot" (ratha), "wound" (vaṇa), "banner" (dhaja), "anthill" (vammika), "hut" (kuṭī), or "little hut" (kuṭikā) depending on various reasons. In this context, however, it is called "kuṭī" because it is reckoned as such based on bones and so forth, just as a hut is named based on wood and so forth.

As it is said:
"Just as, friends, when a space is enclosed by wood, creepers, clay, and grass, it comes to be known as a 'house';
Even so, friends, when a space is enclosed by bones, sinews, flesh, and skin, it comes to be known as 'form' (rūpa)."

Alternatively, it is called "kuṭī" because it is the dwelling of the monkey-like mind. As it is said:
"This hut of a skeleton is a dwelling for monkeys;
The monkey-like mind, entering the little hut with five openings,
Goes around through the doors, knocking again and again."

Because that hut of individual existence is covered by the roof of craving, conceit, and wrong view (taṇhā, māna, diṭṭhi), the rain of defilements such as lust (rāga) falls excessively upon beings again and again. As it is said:
"The rain leaks into what is covered, it does not leak into what is open;
Therefore, open that which is covered, so the rain will not leak into it."
29:
This verse was spoken in two places: in the Vinaya Khandhaka and in the Theragāthā. In the Khandhaka, it was spoken concerning this meaning: "The monk who conceals an offense (āpatti), for him, defilements and offenses rain down excessively again and again. But for the monk who does not conceal it, the rain of defilements does not fall excessively."
