In the Theragāthā, it means: "For one who has the covering of lust and so forth, because lust and so forth arise again toward desirable objects and so forth, that hut of individual existence which is covered becomes excessively wet and leaky. Alternatively, for one who tolerates the arisen defilements, the hut of individual existence covered by the roof of tolerated defilements allows the rain of defilements to fall excessively again and again. But for one whose roof of defilements has been destroyed and opened by the wind of the knowledge of the Path of Arahatship (arahatta-magga-ñāṇa), the rain of defilements no longer leaks in." This is the meaning intended here. The Blessed One has destroyed the aforementioned roof of defilements by the aforementioned method; therefore, He said, "The hut is opened."

"Nibbuto" means peaceful or extinguished. "Gini" means fire. All this is burning with the eleven kinds of fire. As it is said in detail: "It is burning with the fire of lust (rāga)." The Blessed One extinguished that fire at the foot of the Bodhi tree by sprinkling it with the water of the Noble Path; therefore, He said, "The fire is extinguished."

Even while speaking thus, He rebukes, admonishes, and instructs Dhaniya, who was delighting in what is not delightful, by using other reasons. How? By saying "I am free from anger (akkodhana)," He shows: "Dhaniya, you are delighted thinking 'I have cooked the rice (pakkodana),' but the cooking of rice must be done throughout life by the exhaustion of wealth, and the exhaustion of wealth is a proximate cause for the suffering of guarding it and so forth; thus, you are delighted only with suffering. I, however, being delighted in being 'free from anger,' am delighted by the absence of suffering in this life and in the round of rebirths."

By saying "I am free from mental obstructions (vigatakhila)," He shows: "Though you are delighted thinking 'I have milked the milk (duddhakhīra),' you are delighted while having unfinished tasks, thinking 'I have finished my task.' I, however, being delighted in being 'free from mental obstructions,' am delighted only because my task is truly finished."

By saying "I stay for only one night on the banks of the Mahī," He shows: "Though you are delighted to live together on the banks of the Mahī, you are delighted with a permanent residence for the four months of the rainy season. Permanent residence occurs through attachment to a dwelling (āvāsasaṅga), and that is suffering; thus, you are delighted only with suffering. I, however, being delighted in 'staying for only one night,' am delighted by the absence of permanent residence. The absence of permanent residence occurs through the absence of attachment to a dwelling, and the absence of attachment is happiness; therefore, I am delighted only with happiness."
30:
By saying "The hut is open" (vivaṭā kuṭī), [the Buddha shows]: While you, saying "The hut is thatched" (channā kuṭī), are joyful because your house is covered, even though your house is covered, the rain of defilements (kilesavassa) pours heavily into the hut of your own being (attabhāva-kuṭī). Being swept away by the four floods (ogha) produced by that rain of defilements, you might reach ruin and destruction. This being so, you are joyful in what is not worthy of joy. I, however, saying "The hut is open," am joyful because there is no covering of defilements in the hut of my being. Thus, in my open hut of being, that rain of defilements cannot fall. I cannot reach the ruin of misfortune by being swept away by the four great floods produced by that rain of defilements. This being so, I am joyful in what is truly worthy of joy.

By saying "The fire is extinguished" (nibbūto gini), [the Buddha shows]: While you, saying "The fire is kindled" (āhito gini), are joyful in the fire, you are joyful thinking you have averted danger when you have not yet done so. I, however, saying "The fire is extinguished," am joyful because I have averted danger due to the absence of the eleven fires of defilement.

By saying "So rain, O sky, if you wish" (atha ce patthayasi pavassa deva), [the Buddha shows]: Such words are fitting for those like us who are free from suffering, have attained happiness, and have completed all that is to be done. If you wish, O rain-god, then rain; whether you rain or not, there is neither increase nor decrease for us. Why do you speak thus? Therefore, what was said—"Speaking thus to Dhaniya, He rebukes, admonishes, and instructs him by another means regarding his joy in what is not worthy of joy"—is very aptly stated.

Hearing this verse spoken by the Blessed One, Dhaniya the cattleman did not ask, "Who speaks this verse?" but being greatly pleased by those well-spoken words and wishing to hear more of such speech, he spoke another verse beginning with "Andhakamakasā." In that verse, "andhakā" is a name for black flies; some say they are gadflies (piṅgala). "Makasā" refers to mosquitoes. "Na vijjare" means they do not exist. "Kacche" refers to two types of banks—riverbanks and mountain slopes; here it means a riverbank. "Ruḷhatiṇe" means in the lush, grown grass. "Caranti" means they perform the act of grazing. "Vuṭṭhimpi" refers to many kinds of rain such as wind-rain, etc., but here it refers to the falling rain. "Saheyyuṃ" means they can endure. The remaining terms are clear. Here, Dhaniya wishes to show that since those gadflies and mosquitoes, which gather to suck blood and can bring cattle to ruin in a moment, are absent, the cowherds must ward them off with dust and branches just after it rains. He shows that because those mosquitoes are absent, the cattle are safe, and because they graze on the grass of the riverbank, there is no exhaustion from long travel or from hunger. He shows: "The cattle of others, unable to endure the touch of gadflies and mosquitoes, becoming exhausted and withered from long travel, cannot endure even a single downpour; but my cattle are not like that. Because my cattle are free from the aforementioned conditions, they can endure rain that falls even two or three times."
31:
The cowherds ward off gadflies and mosquitoes with dust and branches. Because those mosquitoes are absent, the cattle are safe. Wishing to show the absence of exhaustion from traveling long distances and the absence of weariness from hunger due to grazing on the grass growing on the riverbank, he shows: "The cattle of others, unable to endure the touch of gadflies and mosquitoes, becoming exhausted and withered from long travel, cannot endure even a single downpour; but my cattle are not like that. Because my cattle are free from the aforementioned conditions, they can endure rain that falls even two or three times."

Then the Blessed One, seeing that Dhaniya, while living on an island in the middle of the river, saw danger, bound a raft, crossed the Great Mahī river, and having come to that grass-grove, thought, "I have come well, I stand in a place free from fear." However, he was still standing in a place where there was danger. Therefore, wishing to praise His own arrival as being far superior and more sublime than Dhaniya's arrival, He spoke this verse, "The raft is bound" (baddhāsi bhisī), which is similar in meaning but different in wording. In that verse, "bhisī" in the world refers to a bound raft that has been spread out and made wide. In the Dhamma-Vinaya of the Noble Ones, however, this is a designation for the Noble Path (ariya-magga). The Noble Path is explained in various verses as: "The path, the light, the way, the track, the straight road, the vehicle, the boat, the bridge, the raft, the float, and the crossing. The journey and the source are revealed here and there."

By this verse also, it should be understood that the Blessed One, wishing to admonish Dhaniya in the same manner as before, said: "Dhaniya, you bound a raft, crossed the great river, and came to this place. You will have to bind a raft again, and the river must be crossed again; this place of yours is not free from danger. I, however, have bound a raft with the bond of wisdom, having combined the path-factors in a single mind. That raft is well-constructed because it is complete with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma), has reached the state of a single essence, does not conflict with itself, has no need to be bound again, and cannot be loosened by anyone among gods or humans. Having crossed over with that raft, I have reached the shore that was previously yearned for. Even in going, I did not go to just any place like the Stream-enterers and others; rather, having reached the other shore, I have reached Nibbāna, the end of all taints (āsava), the further shore of all phenomena, the supreme safety. Alternatively, 'crossed over' (tiṇṇo) means reaching Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), and 'gone to the far shore' (pāragato) means reaching the Fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala)."
32:
I have reached [the other shore]. If it is asked, 'Having abandoned what has he reached the other shore?', it means that having abandoned and crossed over the fourfold floods (ogha) such as the flood of sensuality (kāmogha), he has reached that other shore, which is Nibbāna. Now, since there is no longer any need for me to cross over again, there is no need for the raft of the Path. Therefore, it is fitting for me to say, 'So, if you desire, O sky-deity, let it rain.'

Upon hearing those words of the Buddha, Dhaniya spoke this verse in the same manner as before: 'My wife Gopi is obedient.' In this verse, 'Gopi' refers to his wife. 'Assavā' means being obedient and listening for what task needs to be done. 'Alolā' (not fickle) refers to the fact that women are often fickle in five ways: fickleness in food, fickleness in adornment, fickleness in other men, fickleness in wealth, and fickleness in wandering (feet). Indeed, a woman may be so fickle regarding food such as rice, cakes, and liquor that she would even desire to eat leftover rice from the previous night, or eat food so hot it burns her hands, or drink liquor even by paying double the price. Being fickle in adornment, if she cannot find other ornaments, she would even sprinkle her hair with water as if it were oil and rub her face. Being fickle in other men, if she is called while in a secluded place even by her own son, she first thinks of misconduct. Being fickle in wealth, it is as said, 'By seizing the Golden Goose, they were deprived of the gold.' Being fickle in wandering, she develops a habit of going to gardens and such, thereby destroying all wealth. Among these five types of fickleness, Dhaniya said 'Alolā' to show that 'My wife Gopi does not have even a single fickleness.'

'Dīgharattaṃ saṃvāsiyā' means living together for a long time, having grown up together since childhood. By this, he shows that she knows no other man. By the word 'Manāpā' (pleasing), he shows that, not knowing other men, her heart is attached only to him. 'Tassā na suṇāmi kiñci pāpaṃ' means showing that he has never heard even the slightest fault of misconduct, such as laughing or talking with a man of such-and-such a name.

Then, the Blessed One, wishing to admonish Dhaniya who was delighted with these virtues of his wife, spoke this verse in the same manner as before, with similar meaning and phrasing: 'My mind is obedient.' In that verse, the words have clear meanings. The intention is: Dhaniya, you are delighted thinking 'Gopi is my obedient wife,' but that wife may or may not follow your will. The mind of a woman is especially difficult to know. Indeed, even if one carries a woman in one's womb, one cannot guard her. Because her mind is so difficult to guard, people like you cannot truly know a woman as 'not fickle,' or 'fit for companionship,' or 'pleasing,' or 'free from evil.' My mind, however, follows my instructions and acts according to my will; I do not act according to its will. I [have tamed] the fickleness of that mind...
33:
(Gopi) may or may not follow your will. Especially, the mind of a woman is difficult to know. Even if they carry a woman in their womb, they cannot guard (her mind). Because the mind is thus difficult to guard, people like you are unable to know a woman as 'not fickle,' or 'fit for companionship,' or 'pleasing,' or 'free from evil.'

My mind, however, is obedient according to my instructions and acts according to my will; I do not follow the will of that mind. That state of the mind's obedience became manifest to all people during the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya), when the six-colored flames and streams of water were occurring. To create fire, one must attain the fire-kasiṇa (tejo-kasiṇa); to create water, the water-kasiṇa (āpo-kasiṇa); to create blue and other colors, the blue-kasiṇa (nīla-kasiṇa) and so on. Even for Buddhas, two thoughts do not arise simultaneously; yet a single mind, through its state of obedience, acted according to the will in this way. Furthermore, that mind is liberated (vimutta) because it is free from all fetters of defilements; because it is liberated, that very mind is not fickle, unlike your Gopi. And because it has been cultivated for a long time (saṃvāsiyā) through generosity, virtue, and so on since the time of Dīpaṅkara Buddha, it is well-associated, unlike your Gopi. That mind of mine is well-tamed because it has been tamed by the unsurpassed training; because it is well-tamed, it has abandoned the unwholesome states occurring in the six doors by its own will and follows only my intention, thus it is pleasing (manāpa), unlike your Gopi.

By the words 'No evil exists in me,' the Blessed One shows the absence of evil in his own mind, just as Dhaniya showed that he had not heard of Gopi's faults. That absence of evil is to be understood not only at the time he became a Buddha, but even while living as a householder for twenty-nine years during the time he had passion. Even then, no bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, or mental misconduct censured by the wise ever arose in him, as was appropriate for his status as a householder. Thereafter, Mara also followed the Tathāgata for seven years—six years before enlightenment and one year after enlightenment—with the intention, 'Perhaps I might see some evil conduct even as small as a hole pierced by the tip of a hair.' That Mara, being weary from not seeing any, spoke this verse:

'For seven years I followed the Blessed One step by step. I could not find any opening (fault) in the mindful Awakened One.'

Even after he became Buddha, the youth Uttara followed him for seven months, wishing to observe his conduct. That youth, seeing no fault at all, went away thinking, 'The Blessed One is of pure conduct.' Indeed, there are four things that need no guarding (arakkheyya) for the Tathāgata. As he said:
34:
“Bhikkhus, there are these four things of the Tathāgata that need not be guarded. What are the four? Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata is of perfectly pure bodily conduct; there is no bodily misconduct in the Tathāgata that he would need to guard, thinking, ‘May another not know this of me.’ He is of perfectly pure verbal conduct... (similarly)... he is of perfectly pure mental conduct... (similarly)... Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata is of perfectly pure livelihood; there is no wrong livelihood in the Tathāgata that he would need to guard, thinking, ‘May another not know this of me.’” (A. Ni. 7.58).

Thus, because evil did not exist in the Tathāgata’s mind not only at the time of becoming a Sammāsambuddha but also in the past, he said, “Evil does not exist in me.” The meaning of those words is: It is impossible to hear of any evil in my mind, but it is possible to hear of evil in the mind of your (Dhaniya’s) wife, Gopiyā. Therefore, if you are pleased with these qualities, you should say, “Rain, O sky-deva, if you desire”; I too have said this.

Upon hearing those words, Dhaniya, wishing to drink the elixir of the Dhamma further well-spoken and desiring to show his status as a free man, said, “I am one who is supported by my own wages.” In that verse, ‘atta-vetana-bhato’ means: I am supported only by my own food and clothing; I live by doing only my own work; I do not take another’s wages to do another’s work—this is what he wished to show. ‘Puttā’ refers to both daughters and sons, and all of them are collectively called ‘puttā’. ‘Samāniyā’ means they are nearby, not separated. ‘Arogā’ means they are free from disease; it shows that all have the strength of thighs and arms. “I hear no evil of them” means he does not hear any evil regarding those children, such as being thieves, or adulterers, or being immoral.

When this was said, the Blessed One, admonishing Dhaniya in the same manner as before, spoke this verse: “I am not a hireling.” In this verse too, the words have clear meanings. This is the intention: Although you are pleased, thinking, “I am a free man,” in the ultimate sense, even though you live by doing your own work, you are still a slave because you are a slave to craving (taṇhādāsa), and you are not free from the status of a hireling. For it is said: “The world is deficient, never sated, a slave to craving.” (M. Ni. 2.305). In the ultimate sense, I am not a hireling of anyone. I am not a hireling of another, nor am I a hireling of myself. For what reason?
35:
He considers himself and is pleased, thinking “I am.” In the ultimate sense, however, although he lives by doing his own work, he is only a slave because he is a slave to craving. He is not free from the designation of a hireling. Thus it is said: “The multitude of people, never sated and being slaves to craving, are always deficient.” In the ultimate sense, I am not a hireling; I am not a hireling of any other person, nor am I a hireling of myself. For what reason? Because I wander in the whole world having earned my wages (or having completed my task).

Indeed, from the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara until the Bodhi tree, I was a hireling for the sake of Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa). But upon reaching Omniscient Knowledge, I am one who has earned his wages, like a royal servant who has received his pay, one who is free from the stains of defilements. By that state of Omniscience which has earned its wages, and by the bliss of supramundane concentration (lokuttara-samādhi), I live. For me, because there is now no further task to be done and no habit to be practiced, there is no benefit to be obtained through wages, unlike those who have not yet abandoned rebirth. Therefore, if you are pleased with the state of not being a slave, you should say, “Rain, O sky-deva, if you desire”; I too have said this.

Even after hearing those words, Dhaniya, not yet sated by the well-spoken deathless Dhamma, wishing to show the completeness of his fivefold herd of cattle, spoke the verse beginning with “Atthi vasā.” In that verse, ‘vasā’ are the mature cows that are not yet tamed. ‘Dhenupā’ are the young suckling calves or milch cows. ‘Godharaṇiyo’ are the pregnant cows. ‘Paveṇiyo’ are the cows that have reached maturity and desire mating with the bulls. ‘Usabho gavampati’ refers to the bull, the lord of the herd, whom the cowherds bathe early in the morning, feed, mark with five-finger marks, adorn with garlands, and send off saying, “Come, dear one, lead the cows to the pasture, protect them, and bring them back.” It shows that such a bull, the lord of the herd, who avoids unsuitable places, grazes them in the pasture, protects them from dangers like lions and tigers, and brings them back, exists in my herd.

When this was said, the Blessed One, wishing to admonish Dhaniya in the same way, spoke the opposing verse beginning with “Natthi vasā.” The meaning in this verse is: In this Dispensation (Sāsana) of ours, there are no obsessions (pariyuṭṭhāna) called ‘vasā’ in the sense of being untamed and mature. There are no latent tendencies (anusaya) called ‘dhenupā’ in the sense of being a root (referring to young calves) or in the sense of flowing (referring to milch cows). There are no volitional formations of merit, demerit, or imperturbability (puññābhisaṅkhāra, apuññābhisaṅkhāra, āneñjābhisaṅkhāra) called ‘godharaṇi’ in the sense of bearing the womb of rebirth. There is no craving (taṇhā) called ‘paveṇi’ in the sense of desiring union. There is no karmic consciousness (abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa) similar to the ‘bull, lord of the herd’ in the sense of lordship, precedence, and excellence. I, such as I am, am pleased by this absence which is the security from all bondage (yogakkhema). You, however, are pleased by the presence [of cattle] which is the cause of sorrow and so forth. Therefore, only I, who am pleased in the security from all bondage, am fit to say, “Rain, O sky-deva, if you desire.”

Even after hearing those words, Dhaniya, not yet sated and wishing to take the well-spoken deathless Dhamma, desiring to show the completeness of the stakes and ropes of his cattle herd, spoke the verse beginning with “Khilā nikhātā.” In that verse, ‘khilā’ are the small and large stakes driven and dug into the ground. ‘Asampavedhī’ are the stakes that do not shake. ‘Dāmā’ are the special ropes made with knots and loops for tying the young calves. ‘Muñjamayā’ means made of muñja grass. ‘Navā’ means newly twisted. ‘Susaṇṭhānā’ means ropes of good appearance or ropes that have a beautiful appearance because they are well-twisted. He says that the young calves are unable to break those ropes. When this was said, the Blessed One [said] to that Dhaniya...
36:
You rejoice because of the existence of causes such as anxiety and so forth. I, however, rejoice in Nibbāna, which is the end of all yokes (yoga). Therefore, it is fitting for me, who rejoices thus, to say, "Rain, O sky-deva, if you so desire."

Even after hearing those words, Dhaniya was not yet satisfied. Desiring to attain the taste of the well-expounded Deathless Dhamma, and wishing to show the completeness and strength of the stakes and ropes of his herd, he spoke the verse beginning with "The stakes are driven into the ground."

In that verse, "khilā" refers to the stakes for tying the cattle. "Nikhātā" means stakes that have been driven into the ground by striking, or small and large ones that have been dug in and set. "Asampavedhī" means stakes that are unshakable. "Dāmā" refers to special ropes with knots and loops made for tying young calves. "Muñjamayā" means ropes made of muñja grass. "Navā" means newly made, recently twisted. "Susaṇṭhānā" means ropes of good appearance or those that look beautiful because they are well-twisted. "Na hi sakkhanti" means they are simply unable; even the young heifers are unable to break those ropes.

When this was said, the Blessed One, knowing that the time for the maturation of Dhaniya's faculties had arrived, and wishing to instruct him as before, spoke this verse which illustrates the Four Noble Truths:

## Usabhoriva chetvā

In that verse, "usabho" refers to the father of the cattle, the leader of the cattle, the great bull that rules the herd. Some teachers say that a bull greater than a hundred cattle is an "usabha", one greater than a thousand is a "vasabha", and one greater than a hundred thousand is a "nisabha". Other teachers say that a bull great within the territory of one village is an "usabha", one great within two villages is a "vasabha", and one who is great and unobstructed in all places is a "nisabha". All these are merely elaborations. In truth, all terms—usabha, vasabha, and nisabha—should be understood in the sense of being peerless and supreme. As it was said: "Friends, the ascetic Gotama is indeed a peerless nisabha." In the word "usabhoriva", the letter 'r' is a consonant inserted for euphonic combination (sandhi).

"Bandhanāni" refers to both the binding with ropes and the binding with defilements (kilesa). "Nāgo" refers to a noble elephant. "Pūtilataṃ" refers to a creeper vine (the gaḷocī vine) wrapped around the neck. Just as a body, though golden-colored, is called a "putrid body" (pūtikāya), and a hundred-year-old dog is called a "kukkura", and a newborn jackal is called an "old jackal," so too the fresh gaḷocī vine is called a "rotten creeper" (pūtilatā) because it lacks essence. "Dālayitvā" means having broken or severed.

"Gabbhaseyyaṃ" means both the chamber of conception and the bed; hence it is called gabbhaseyya (womb-lying). In this context, by the word "gabbha", beings born from a womb (jalābuja) are taken, and by the word "seyya", the remaining three types of birth are taken. Or it should be understood that all beings are meant, using gabbhaseyya as the primary example. The meaning of the remaining words is quite clear.

The meaning here is: Dhaniya, you rejoice in bonds. I, however, am weary of bonds. Like a powerful bull that [breaks] the ropes which are bonds...
37:
The meaning here is: Dhaniya, you rejoice and are glad in bonds. I, however, being weary of bonds, stand like a great bull endowed with strength and energy, having severed the bonds of the five higher fetters (saṃyojana) with the strength and energy of the fourth Noble Path; and like a noble elephant breaking a rotten creeper, I stand having broken the bonds of the five lower fetters with the strength and energy of the three lower Paths. Or else, like a bull standing after severing bonds, I stand having severed the latent tendencies (anusaya); and like a noble elephant standing after breaking a rotten creeper, I stand having broken the outbursts of defilements (pariyuṭṭhāna). Therefore, I shall not again enter a womb. I, being fully released from all suffering rooted in the suffering of birth, shine forth, saying, "Rain, O sky-deva, if you so desire." Therefore, if you also wish to speak like me, sever those bonds.

Herein, the bonds are the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca); lying in a womb is the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca). In the phrase "I shall not again enter," the non-entering is the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca) by way of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa). In the phrase "having severed and broken," the severing and breaking is the Truth of Cessation by way of Nibbāna with remainder (saupādisesa). That by which one severs and breaks is the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca).

Having heard this verse illustrating the Four Noble Truths, at the conclusion of the verse, the four persons—Dhaniya, his wife, and his two daughters—were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). Then Dhaniya, established in faith rooted in the Tathāgata through unwavering confidence, saw the Dhamma-body of the Blessed One with the eye of wisdom. With a heart urged by the nature of things (dhammatā), he thought: "I have severed the bonds, and for me there is no more lying in a womb." He thought, "Who else from the Avīci hell up to the peak of existence (bhavagga) could roar such a lion's roar except the Blessed One? My Teacher has indeed arrived." Then the Blessed One released the radiance of his body, which was variegated with a net of six-colored rays and like a golden liquid, into Dhaniya's house, saying, "Now, look as you please."

Then Dhaniya, seeing the house shining as if the moon and sun had entered within, or as if illuminated by a thousand lamps all around, gave rise to the thought, "The Blessed One has arrived." At that very moment, it also rained. Therefore, the reciters (saṅgītikārā) said the verse: "Filling the hollows and the high ground." Therein, "ninna" means a depression or pond. "Thala" means high ground or a bank. Thus, the great cloud rained, beginning to fill and level all the high and low ground. "Tāvadeva" means at the very moment the Blessed One released his bodily radiance, and Dhaniya [gave rise to] a mind full of faith, [thinking] "My Teacher has arrived"...
38:
(The Blessed One) emitted rays of light, and at that moment, it rained. Some teachers, however, explain that "the sun rose at that very moment as well."

31-32. Thus, hearing the sound of the rain falling at the moment of Dhaniya’s arising of faith, the spreading of the Tathāgata’s radiance, and the rising of the sun, Dhaniya, filled with joy and satisfaction, spoke these two verses: "Great indeed are our gains..."

In those verses, because Dhaniya, along with his wife and children, had seen the Dhammakāya of the Blessed One by penetrating the Ariyan Path, had seen the Rūpakāya with the supramundane eye, and had gained faith with the worldly eye, he said: "Great indeed are our gains, we who have seen the Blessed One."

In that context, "vata" is an exclamation expressing wonder. "No" means "our." "Anappakā" means "abundant" or "not small." The rest is clear.

Regarding the phrase "Saraṇaṃ taṃ upema" (We go to you as a refuge): although his taking of refuge was already accomplished through the penetration of the Path, he now performs the act of self-surrender through speech. Alternatively, having reached the state of self-surrendering refuge and unshakable refuge by the power of the Path, he makes that refuge manifest to others through speech, going to the refuge of prostration. "Cakkhumā": The Blessed One is called "The One with Vision" because he is endowed with the five eyes: the physical eye, the divine eye, the eye of wisdom, the universal eye, and the Buddha-eye. Addressing the Blessed One, he said: "We go to you as a refuge, O One with Vision." The words "Be our teacher, O Great Sage" are spoken to complete the taking of refuge by entering the state of a disciple. The words "The cowherd’s wife and I are obedient; we shall live the holy life under the Sugata" are spoken by way of undertaking (the practice).

In that context, "Brahmacariya" (the holy life) is a designation for abstinence from sexual intercourse, the Path, the practice of a recluse (samaṇadhamma), the Dispensation (sāsana), and contentment with one's own wife. In passages such as "Brahmacārī," abstinence from sexual intercourse is called "brahmacariya." In passages such as "Pañcasikha, this holy life leads to total disenchantment," the Path is called "brahmacariya." In passages such as "Sāriputta, I recall having lived the holy life endowed with four factors," the practice of a recluse is called "brahmacariya." In passages such as "This holy life is successful and prosperous," the Dispensation is called "brahmacariya."
39:
In passages such as "We do not transgress against our wives, nor do our wives transgress against us; apart from them, we live the holy life, therefore our young ones do not die," contentment with one's own wife (sadārasantosa) is called "brahmacariya." In this sutta, however, the "holy life" intended is the higher Path preceded by the practice of a recluse.

"Sugate" means "in the presence of the Sugata." The Blessed One is called "Sugata" because he has gone well by not approaching the two extremes, because he is endowed with the beautiful going of the Ariyan Path, and because he has gone to the excellent state known as Nibbāna. Here, the locative case is used in the sense of proximity (samīpa); thus, it means "in the presence of the Sugata." "Carāmashe" means "we shall practice" (carāma). What is called "carāmasi" in Sanskrit is here called "carāmashe." The teachers of the Commentaries, however, say that "she" is a particle. For that reason, they also suggest the reading "carema she" with the sense of a request. One may accept whichever is preferred.

Thus, Dhaniya, having requested ordination from the Blessed One on the pretext of practicing the holy life, spoke as follows to show the purpose of ordination: "May we be those who reach the far shore of birth and death, and who make an end of suffering." The "far shore of birth and death" is Nibbāna, and they wish to go to that Nibbāna by the Path of Arahatship. They wish to bring the suffering of the round of rebirths to non-existence. "Bhavāmashe" means "may we become," and it should be understood in the same way as explained for "carāmashe." Having spoken thus, it is said that both husband and wife prostrated before the Blessed One and requested ordination, saying, "Blessed One, please grant us ordination."

Then, Māra the Evil One, seeing both of them prostrating and requesting ordination, thought: "These people wish to transcend my domain; let me create an obstacle for them." Coming forward and wishing to show the virtues of the household life, he spoke this verse: "One with sons rejoices because of sons." In that verse, "nandati" means to be pleased and to rejoice. "Puttehi" means rejoicing together with sons and daughters, or rejoicing because of sons and daughters. "Puttimā" refers to a person who has sons. "Māra" is a certain mischievous deity in the Vasavatti realm. He is one who hinders those who wish to transcend his domain if he is able to do so. For those he cannot hinder...
40:
If he is able to kill a person, he kills them. Even if he cannot kill them, he desires their death. Because of this nature of killing, he is called 'Māra'. 'Pāpimā' refers to a base person or one of evil conduct. These are the words of the Reciters (Saṅgītikāras), and such expressions are found in all the verses. Just as one with sons rejoices with his sons, so too the cattle-owner rejoices with his cattle. Whoever possesses cattle is called a cattle-owner (gopiya). The meaning is that he rejoices likewise, either together with the cattle or because of the cattle as the cause.

Having said this, he now points out the supporting reason for that meaning with the words: 'Acquisitions (upadhi) are indeed the source of man's delight.' In that verse, 'upadhi' refers to the four types of acquisitions: the acquisition of sensual pleasures (kāmūpadhi), the acquisition of the aggregates (khandhūpadhi), the acquisition of defilements (kilesūpadhi), and the acquisition of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhārūpadhi). Sensual pleasures are called 'upadhi' because they are the basis for the pleasure and joy that arise dependent on the five cords of sensual pleasure, as it is said: 'Whatever pleasure and joy arise dependent on the five cords of sensual pleasure, this is the gratification of sensual pleasures' (M. Ni. 1.166); thus, pleasure is established therein. The five aggregates are also called 'upadhi' because they are the basis for suffering rooted in the aggregates; defilements because they are the basis for suffering in the woeful states; and volitional formations because they are the basis for suffering in existence. Here, however, the acquisition of sensual pleasures (kāmūpadhi) is intended. That kāmūpadhi is of two kinds: regarding beings and regarding formations. Among them, that which is connected with beings is primary. Desiring to show that acquisition connected with beings, he said 'with sons and with cattle' and stated the reason: 'Acquisitions are indeed the source of man's delight.' The meaning of those words is: since these acquisitions of sensual pleasure are the source of man's delight, bringing joy and happiness to man, therefore it should be understood: 'The one with sons rejoices with his sons; the cattle-owner likewise rejoices with his cattle.' (Māra says:) 'And since you are one with sons and a cattle-owner, rejoice with these; do not desire the monkhood. For one who has gone forth, these acquisitions do not exist; this being so, even if you long for the end of suffering, you will only be miserable.'

Now, he points out the supporting reason for that meaning with the words: 'He who is without acquisitions (nirūpadhi) does not rejoice.' The meaning is: since one who does not have these acquisitions is separated from beloved kinsmen and lacks possessions and requisites, he cannot rejoice. Therefore, if you abandon these acquisitions and become a monk, you will only be miserable.

Then the Blessed One, knowing that 'this evil Māra has come to create an obstacle for these people,' as if knocking down a fruit with another fruit, wishing to destroy Māra's doctrine using the very same analogy brought by Māra, reversed that verse (and spoke thus):
41:
Wishing to show that "Upadhi (acquisitions/attachments) is the cause of grief," he said, "One with sons grieves because of sons." In that verse, all the meanings of the words are clear. This is the intended meaning: "O Evil Mara, do not say, 'One with sons rejoices because of sons.'" This law of separation and parting from all that is dear and pleasing is unavoidable. Because of separation from those dear and pleasing sons, wives, cattle, horses, mules, silver, gold, and so forth, beings whose hearts are pierced by the intense dart of grief even go mad and lose their minds; they reach death or suffering equal to death. Therefore, understand it thus: "One with sons grieves because of sons." Just as one with sons grieves because of sons, so too the owner of cattle grieves because of cattle. For what reason? Because upadhis alone are the cause of grief for humans. Since upadhis alone are the cause of grief for humans, therefore he said, "Indeed, he does not grieve who is without upadhi." He who becomes free from upadhi by abandoning the attachment that clings to upadhis is easily contented with robes sufficient to cover the body and almsfood sufficient to sustain the belly; wherever he goes, he goes taking only those (requisites). Just as a winged bird flies... he knows that there is no more rebirth in this world. Thus, by being able to eradicate all grief, he said, "Indeed, he does not grieve who is without upadhi." In this way, the Blessed One concluded the teaching with Arahantship as its climax. Alternatively, he who is without upadhi, who is without defilements, does not grieve. As long as defilements exist, all upadhis result only in grief. But for one who has abandoned defilements, there is no grief. In this way too, he concluded the teaching with Arahantship as its climax. At the end of the teaching, both Dhaniya and his wife Gopĩ ordained. The Blessed One went to Jetavana through the air. Having ordained, they realized Arahantship. At the place where they resided, the cowherds built and offered a monastery. That monastery is still well-known today as the "Gopālaka Vihāra."
## The explanation of the Dhaniya Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary of the Khuddakapāṭha Commentary named Paramatthajotikā is finished.
42:
## 3. Commentary on the Khaggavisāṇa Sutta

The sutta beginning with "Sabbesu bhūtesu" is the Khaggavisāṇa Sutta. What is the origin (uppatti) of this sutta? The origins of all suttas are of four kinds: spoken by one's own inclination (attajjhāsaya), spoken by the inclination of others (parajjhāsaya), spoken because a matter has arisen (atthuppatti), and spoken on account of a question (pucchāvasita). Indeed, the Dvayatānupassanā Sutta and others originate from one's own inclination; the Metta Sutta and others originate from the inclination of others; the Uraga Sutta and others originate because a matter has arisen; and the Dhammika Sutta and others originate on account of a question.

Among these four, the origin of the Khaggavisāṇa Sutta is generally on account of a question. Specifically, however, some verses in this sutta were spoken by various Paccekabuddhas when questioned; other verses were spoken as inspired utterances (udāna) in accordance with the path they had attained, even without being questioned. Therefore, some verses originated on account of a question, while others originated from one's own inclination.

Regarding these origins, the general origin on account of a question should be understood from the beginning as follows: At one time, the Blessed One was staying in Sāvatthī. Then, while the Venerable Ānanda was in seclusion and solitary meditation, this thought arose in his mind: "The aspiration (patthanā) and the resolution (abhinīhāra) of the Buddhas are evident; likewise, the resolution of the disciples is evident. But the resolution of the Paccekabuddhas is not evident. What if I were to approach the Blessed One and ask him about this?" Then, the Venerable Ānanda, having emerged from seclusion, approached the Blessed One and asked about that matter in due order. Then the Blessed One spoke the Pubbayogāvacara Sutta to the Venerable Ānanda:

"Ānanda, there are these five benefits for a person who has practiced in the past (pubbayogāvacara) in wholesome states connected with the supramundane. He attains the fruit of Arahantship early in this very life. If he does not attain the fruit of Arahantship early in this very life, he attains the fruit of Arahantship at the time of death. If he does not attain the fruit of Arahantship at the time of death, he attains the fruit of Arahantship while being a son of the devas. If he does not attain it thus, he becomes a person of quick direct knowledge (khippābhiññā) in the presence of the Buddhas. If he does not become so, he becomes a Paccekabuddha in the final time."

Having spoken thus, he said again:

"Ānanda, those called Paccekabuddhas are persons who have practiced in the past and are endowed with resolution. Therefore, the longing (patthanā) and the resolution (abhinīhāra) of all—Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples—should be desired."
43: The Venerable Ānanda asked, "Venerable Sir, for how long does the aspiration of the Buddhas endure?" The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, the aspiration of the Buddhas is, at the minimum, four asankheyyas and a hundred thousand aeons (kappa); at the medium level, eight asankheyyas and a hundred thousand aeons; and at the maximum level, sixteen asankheyyas and a hundred thousand aeons." This distinction should be understood by way of those in whom wisdom is predominant (paññādhika), those in whom faith is predominant (saddhādhika), and those in whom energy is predominant (vīriyādhika). For the wisdom-led Bodhisattas, faith is slow and wisdom is keen. For the faith-led Bodhisattas, wisdom is medium and faith is strong. For the energy-led Bodhisattas, faith and wisdom are slow and energy is strong. Without reaching the four asankheyyas and a hundred thousand aeons, even if one gives gifts like the gifts of King Vessantara every single day, or accumulates all the perfections (pāramī) such as virtue in accordance with that, it is impossible for one to become a Buddha in the intervening period. Why is that? Because the knowledge has not yet taken hold of the embryo, has not reached expansion, and has not reached maturity. For example, a crop that is produced only after three, four, or five months cannot be produced in the intervening period of half a month or a month, even if one cherishes it a thousand times a day or waters it, before that time is reached. Why is that? Because the crop has not yet taken hold of the embryo, has not reached expansion, and has not reached maturity. In the same way, without reaching the four asankheyyas... and so on, it is impossible to become a Buddha. Therefore, one should fulfill the perfections for the duration mentioned in order to mature the knowledge. One who aspires for Buddhahood for such a long time should desire the eight conditions in making the great resolution (abhinīhāra). To explain this further: 'Human birth, the male sex, the possession of sufficient cause, the sight of the Teacher, the going forth, the possession of qualities, dedication, and strong desire—by the combination of these eight factors, the resolution succeeds' (Bv. 2.59). Abhinīhāra is a synonym for the original resolution (mūlapaṇidhāna). Among those eight, manussatta means being of the human race. For, other than the human race, even if one is in the celestial race as a deva, the resolution does not succeed. Therefore, one who aspires for Buddhahood should perform meritorious deeds such as giving and aspire only for human birth. Having stood in that human life, the resolution should be made. Only in this way does it succeed. Liṅgasampatti means being a true male. For women, eunuchs (napumsaka), and hermaphrodites (ubhatobyañjanaka), even if they are in the human race, the resolution cannot succeed. Therefore, one who aspires for Buddhahood should perform meritorious deeds such as giving and aspire only for the male sex. Having stood in that male state, the resolution should be made.
44: In this way (only when endowed with the eight factors), the aspiration is fulfilled. Hetu (cause) means the perfection of the supporting condition for the fruit of Arahantship. Only a person who, if they were to strive in that very life, would be capable of attaining Arahantship, can fulfill the aspiration; not anyone else, just like Sumedha the Wise. That Sumedha the Wise, having gone forth at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, was capable of attaining Arahantship in that very life. Satthāradassana (seeing the Teacher) means seeing the Buddhas face-to-face. Only by seeing them face-to-face is the aspiration fulfilled, not otherwise, just like Sumedha the Wise. That Sumedha the Wise made his aspiration after seeing the Buddha Dīpaṅkara face-to-face. Pabbajjā (going forth) means the state of a recluse who has renounced the world. That state of a recluse is appropriate whether it be within the Dispensation (Sāsana) or among the groups of ascetics or wanderers who are Kammavādī (believers in action) and Kiriyavādī (believers in the efficacy of action), just like Sumedha the Wise. That wise one named Sumedha made his aspiration after becoming an ascetic. Guṇasampatti (attainment of qualities) means the acquisition of virtues such as the Jhanas. Even if one is a recluse, the aspiration is fulfilled only for one endowed with qualities such as Jhanas and supernormal powers, not for others, just like Sumedha the Wise. That Sumedha the Wise made his aspiration after attaining the five supernormal powers and the eight meditative attainments. Adhikāra (dedication) means great service, which implies the sacrifice of one's body and life. Only for one who makes the aspiration by sacrificing life and so on is it fulfilled, not for others, just like Sumedha the Wise. That ascetic Sumedha: "May the Buddha, together with his disciples, tread upon me and proceed; May he not tread upon the mud; Doing this will be for my benefit and welfare." Thus, he made his aspiration by sacrificing his life. Chandatā (desire) means the will to act. For whomsoever that desire is strong, for him it is fulfilled. The strength of that desire should be understood thus: if someone were to say, "Who desires Buddhahood after being cooked in hell for four incalculable periods and a hundred thousand aeons?" and upon hearing this, one has the courage to say, "I do," then his desire is to be known as strong. Likewise, if someone were to say, "Who desires Buddhahood by treading across an entire world-system filled with glowing coals without flames? Who desires Buddhahood by treading across an entire world-system bristling with spears and spikes? Who desires Buddhahood by swimming across an entire world-system filled with water to the brim? Who desires Buddhahood by treading through an entire world-system covered with dense bamboo thickets?" and upon hearing this, one has the courage to say, "I do," then his desire is to be known as strong. Sumedha the Wise, endowed with such a will to act, made his aspiration.
45: ## Being thus endowed with these factors, the Bodhisatta who has made the aspiration for Buddhahood does not reach these eighteen unfavorable places (abhabbaṭṭhāna). From the life in which he makes that aspiration for Buddhahood, he is not born blind, he is not born deaf, he does not become insane, he is not mute, he is not crippled (with deformed limbs), he is not born among wild hill tribes, he is not born in the womb of a slave woman, he does not hold fixed wrong views, he does not undergo a change of sex, he does not commit the five heinous crimes (pañcānantariyakamma), he does not become a leper, even if born in the animal kingdom he does not have a body smaller than a quail, he is not born among the hungry ghosts (peta) who are consumed by hunger and thirst, he is not born among the Kālakañcika Asuras, he is not born in the Avīci hell, he is not born in the inter-world hells (lokantarika), he does not become a Māra in the sensual realms, he is not born in the realm of unconscious beings (asaññasatta) in the fine-material realms, he is not born in the Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa), he is not born in the immaterial realms (arūpabhava), and he does not move to another world-system. He is also endowed with the four Buddha-grounds (buddhabhūmi) called ussāha, ummagga, avatthāna, and hitacariyā. Among these four: "Ussāha means energy (viriya); ummagga means wisdom (paññā); avatthāna means determination (adhiṭṭhāna); hitacariyā means the development of loving-kindness (mettā-bhāvanā)." Thus it should be understood. He is also endowed with the six inclinations (ajjhāsaya) that serve to mature the Omniscient Knowledge: nekkhammajjhāsaya (inclination toward renunciation), pavivekajjhāsaya (inclination toward solitude), alobhajjhāsaya (inclination toward non-greed), adosajjhāsaya (inclination toward non-hatred), amohajjhāsaya (inclination toward non-delusion), and nissaraṇajjhāsaya (inclination toward liberation). Because they are endowed with these inclinations, Bodhisattas with nekkhammajjhāsaya tend to see the faults in sensual pleasures; Bodhisattas with pavivekajjhāsaya tend to see the faults in socializing; Bodhisattas with alobhajjhāsaya tend to see the faults in greed; Bodhisattas with adosajjhāsaya tend to see the faults in hatred; Bodhisattas with amohajjhāsaya tend to see the faults in delusion; and Bodhisattas with nissaraṇajjhāsaya tend to see the faults in all forms of existence. He is indeed endowed with these six inclinations. If it is asked, "How long must the aspiration be made for Paccekabuddhas?", for Paccekabuddhas it is for two incalculable periods and a hundred thousand aeons. It cannot be achieved in a shorter time than that. The reason for this should be understood in the same manner as previously mentioned. For one who aspires to Paccekabuddhahood for this length of time, five perfections (sampatti) are required in making the aspiration (abhinīhāra). For them—
46:
Humanity, being of the male sex, the sight of those free from taints—Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, or disciples—great effort [even at the cost of life], and strong desire: these five are the causes for the aspiration to Paccekabuddhahood.

Among these five, "the sight of those free from taints" means the sight of any one of the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, or disciples. The remaining terms are to be understood as previously explained.

Furthermore, if it is asked how long the aspiration of disciples should last: for the two Chief Disciples, it is one asankheyya and one hundred thousand kappas; for the eighty Great Disciples, it is one hundred thousand kappas; likewise, for the mother, father, attendant, and son of a Buddha, it is one hundred thousand kappas. It cannot be less than one hundred thousand kappas. The reason here is as previously stated. The aspiration of all these individuals is successful only when it is endowed with the two factors: great effort and strong desire.

Thus, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) for the various durations mentioned through this longing and aspiration, when Buddhas appear in the world, they are born in either a Khattiya family or a Brāhmaṇa family. Paccekabuddhas are born in any one of the Khattiya, Brāhmaṇa, or Gahapati families. Chief Disciples, like Buddhas, are born only in Khattiya or Brāhmaṇa families. All Buddhas do not appear in a samvaṭṭa-kappa (dissolving aeon) but only in a vivaṭṭa-kappa (evolving aeon). Paccekabuddhas do not meet with Omniscient Buddhas; they appear only in the intervals when Buddhas do not appear. Buddhas both realize [the truth] themselves and make others realize it. Paccekabuddhas realize it themselves but do not make others realize it. They penetrate only the essence of the meaning (attha-rasa), but they do not penetrate the essence of the doctrine (dhamma-rasa). Those Paccekabuddhas are unable to formulate the supramundane Dhamma into conventional teaching and preach it. Their realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) is like a dream seen by a mute person, or like the taste of a city dish experienced by a forest dweller.

They attain all varieties of psychic powers (iddhi), attainments (samāpatti), and analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Due to their superior qualities, they are below Omniscient Buddhas but above disciples. They ordain others and make them practice the training rules concerning minor conduct (ābhisamācarika-sikkhāpada). They perform the uposatha with this brief exhortation: "Mental purification should be practiced; one should not fall back," or by the mere words, "Today is the uposatha day." When they perform the uposatha, they assemble at the jeweled stone-platform near the Mañjūsaka tree on Mount Gandhamādana.

Thus, the Blessed One, having told the Venerable Ānanda about the aspiration and longing of Paccekabuddhas in all their aspects, now, in order to speak of those various Paccekabuddhas who succeeded through this longing and aspiration, spoke this Khaggavisāṇa Sutta, beginning with "Sabbesu bhūtesu nidhāya daṇḍaṃ—" (Putting aside the rod for all beings...). This is the general reason for the arising of the Khaggavisāṇa Sutta. Now, I shall speak specifically. In that specific account, the origin of the first verse should be known as follows: When this Paccekabuddha-to-be entered the stage of attaining Paccekabodhi-knowledge, he fulfilled the perfections for two asankheyyas and one hundred thousand kappas. Having been ordained in the Dispensation of the Blessed Kassapa Buddha, he lived in the forest and practiced the duty of going and coming (gatapaccāgata-vatta) while striving in the Dhamma of a recluse. There is no one who reaches Paccekabodhi-knowledge without fulfilling this duty of going and coming. What is this duty of going and coming? It is carrying [the meditation subject] while going and carrying it while returning. To make that duty clear, we shall speak. In that Dispensation, some monks carry the meditation subject when going but do not carry it when returning. Some monks carry it when returning but do not carry it when going.
47:
## Khaggavisāṇa Sutta

He spoke this Khaggavisāṇa Sutta in the manner beginning with "Sabbesu bhūtesu nidhāya daṇḍaṃ." This is first the general origin (uppatti) of the Khaggavisāṇa Sutta based on a question.

Now, I shall speak specifically. In that specific account, the origin of this first verse should be known as follows: When this Paccekabuddha-to-be entered the stage of attaining Paccekabodhi-knowledge, he fulfilled the perfections for two asankheyyas and one hundred thousand kappas. Having been ordained in the Dispensation of the Blessed Kassapa Buddha, he lived in the forest and practiced the duty of going and coming (gatapaccāgata-vatta) while striving in the Dhamma of a recluse. There is no one who reaches Paccekabodhi-knowledge without fulfilling this duty of going and coming. What is this duty of going and coming? It is carrying [the meditation subject] while going and carrying it while returning. To make that duty clear, we shall speak.

In this Dispensation, some monks carry [the meditation subject] when going but do not carry it when returning. Some monks carry it when returning but do not carry it when going. Some monks do not carry it when going and do not carry it when returning. Some monks carry it both when going and when returning.

Among those duties, a certain monk rises early and performs the duties of the stupa courtyard and the Bodhi tree courtyard, sprinkles water on the Bodhi tree, fills the drinking water pot and places it in the water-stand, and performs the duties toward his teacher and preceptor. He practices by undertaking the eighty-two minor duties and the fourteen major duties. That monk, having attended to his bodily needs, enters his dwelling and spends the time in a secluded seat until the time for alms-round. Knowing the time, he adjusts his inner robe, fastens his waist-band, puts on his upper robe, places his outer robe on his shoulder, takes his alms-bowl, and while attending to his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), goes to the stupa courtyard and pays homage to the stupa and the Bodhi tree. Near the village, he wraps himself in his robes, takes his bowl, and enters the village for alms.

Even when entering in this way, that monk, who easily obtains alms and possesses merit, is treated with respect and honor by the lay devotees. While staying at a devotee's house or in a rest hall, he is asked various questions by the devotees. By answering their questions and through the distraction of preaching the Dhamma, he abandons that attention to his meditation subject and departs. Even upon returning to the monastery, he is asked questions by other monks and answers them, recites the Dhamma, and engages in various tasks. Thus, having been delayed by talking with the monks during the afternoon, the first watch, and the middle watch, he is overcome by bodily fatigue and falls asleep in the last watch. He no longer attends to his meditation subject at all. This monk is called "one who carries [the meditation subject] when going but does not carry it when returning."
48:
The monk who is frequently ill and, upon rising at dawn, is unable to perform the various major and minor duties as previously mentioned or to focus on the meditation subject, but instead, desiring gruel or medicine, takes his bowl and robes and enters the village early. Having obtained gruel, medicine, or almsfood in that village and finished his meal, knowing the proper measure and being calmed (from his ailment), he sits on a prepared seat and focuses on the meditation subject. Whether he attains a distinction (path or fruit) or not, he returns to the monastery and dwells with that same focus. This monk is called "one who brings it back but did not take it (out)." Monks of this nature, having drunk gruel and undertaken insight meditation, have reached Arahantship in the Buddha's Dispensation in numbers beyond counting. Even in the island of Sri Lanka (Sīhaḷadīpa), in the rest houses of various villages, there is almost no place where a monk has not reached Arahantship after drinking gruel.

The monk who dwells negligently, having abandoned his duties and destroyed all observances, dwells with a mind bound by the five mental shackles and bonds. Without engaging in the focus on a meditation subject, he enters the village for alms, becomes entangled in worldly talk with laypeople, and comes out empty-handed. This monk is called "one who neither takes it nor brings it back."

The monk who rises early and, having fulfilled all duties according to the previous method, sits cross-legged and focuses on the meditation subject until the time for alms-round. There are two types of meditation subjects: Sabbatthaka (universal) and Pārihāriya (personal). Loving-kindness (mettā) and mindfulness of death (maraṇassati) are called sabbatthaka meditation subjects. They are called "universal" because they are desirable in all places. Loving-kindness is desirable in all places such as the residence and so forth. A monk who dwells in loving-kindness in monasteries is loved by his fellow practitioners and thus dwells happily without conflict. One who dwells in loving-kindness toward deities dwells happily, being protected and guarded by the deities. One who dwells in loving-kindness toward kings, royal ministers, and so forth, dwells happily, being cherished by them. One who dwells in loving-kindness while on alms-round in villages, market towns, and so forth, dwells happily, being respected and honored by people. Through the meditation on the mindfulness of death, one abandons the longing for life and dwells diligently.

The meditation subject which is taken up because it is suitable to one's own temperament—one of the ten foulness subjects (asubha), ten kasinas, or ten recollections (anussati), or the determination of the four elements—is called "pārihāriya" (personal) because it should be carried, guarded, and developed at all times.
49:
The root meditation subject (mūlakammaṭṭhāna) is indeed that same subject (pārihāriyakammaṭṭhāna). Among these two types of meditation subjects, I shall show the method of first attending to the universal meditation subject (sabbatthakakammaṭṭhāna) and then attending to the meditation subject to be maintained (pārihāriyakammaṭṭhāna) by way of the analysis of the four elements (catudhātuvavatthāna).

This meditator contemplates this body, just as it stands and is placed, by way of the elements. In this body, among the twenty parts, that which has the nature of hardness or roughness is the earth element (pathavīdhātu). Among the twelve parts, that which performs the function of cohesion and has the nature of fluidity is the water element (āpodhātu). Among the four parts, that which performs the function of maturing and has the nature of heat is the fire element (tejodhātu). Among the six parts, that which performs the function of supporting and has the nature of motion is the air element (vāyodhātu). The space or gap in this body that is not touched by the four great elements is the space element (ākāsadhātu). The mind that knows those elements is the consciousness element (viññāṇadhātu). Apart from these elements, there is no other being or person. (He contemplates) that this body is in reality merely a heap of pure formations (saṅkhāra).

Having thus attended to the meditation subject in terms of the beginning, middle, and end, and knowing the proper time, he rises from his seat, puts on his robes, and enters the village for alms in the same manner as previously described. When going for alms, he does not become deluded like blind worldlings who, in such acts as stepping forward, are deluded thinking, "The self steps forward, the self brings about the stepping forward," or "I step forward, I bring about the stepping forward." Instead, without delusion, he understands: "When the thought 'I will step forward' arises, together with that mind, the supporting air element born of the mind (cittasamuṭṭhāna-vāyodhātu) arises. That air element pervades the skeleton, which is designated as the 'body,' where the earth element and others are combined. Then, by the power of the diffusion of the air element produced by the mind, this skeleton designated as the 'body' moves forward."

As he thus moves forward, in each lifting of the foot, among the four elements, the fire element followed by the air element is predominant, while the others are weak. In stretching forward, moving across, and drawing back, the air element followed by the fire element is predominant, while the others are weak. In lowering the foot, the water element followed by the earth element is predominant, while the others are weak. In placing the foot on the ground and pressing down, the earth element followed by the water element is predominant, while the others are weak. Thus, these elements, together with the respective minds that produce them, break up right in those respective places. If this is so, who is the individual that steps forward, or whose stepping forward is it? Thus, in each aspect such as the lifting of each foot, the elements that arise in each aspect, the remaining material phenomena (rūpadhamma) inseparable from them, the mind that produces those material phenomena, and the mental factors (cetasika) associated with that mind...
50:
The remaining mental phenomena are likewise the phenomena of mind and matter. Beyond that, they do not reach any other state in the processes of passing over or crossing over, but perish right where they arise. Therefore, they are impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is non-self. Thus, he proceeds, contemplating the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) complete in all its aspects.

Indeed, sons of good family, desiring their own welfare, having gone forth in the Dispensation, whether they be ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, or a hundred monks living together, they dwell having made an agreement: 'Friends, you have not gone forth because of debt, nor out of fear, nor for the sake of a livelihood; rather, you have gone forth in this Dispensation desiring to be liberated from suffering. Therefore, suppress the defilements that arise while walking, even while walking; suppress the defilements that arise while standing, sitting, or lying down, even while standing, sitting, or lying down.'

Having made such an agreement, when they go for alms, they proceed contemplating their meditation subject, using stones at intervals of half an usabha, one usabha, half a gāvuta, or one gāvuta as landmarks. If a defilement arises in any monk while walking, he suppresses it right there. If he is unable to do so, he stands still. Then, the monk following behind him also stands still. That monk, admonishing himself, 'This monk knows the thought that has arisen in you; this is unbecoming of you,' develops insight (vipassanā) and attains the stage of a Noble One (ariya) right there. If he is unable to do so while standing, he sits down. Then, the monk following behind him also sits down; the method is the same. Even if he cannot yet attain the stage of a Noble One, he dispels that defilement and proceeds only while contemplating his meditation subject. He does not lift a foot with a mind devoid of the meditation subject. If he does lift it, he turns back and returns to the previous spot, like Mahāphussadeva Thera, a resident of Ālindaka in the island of Sīhaḷa.

It is said that he lived for nineteen years fulfilling the duty of going and returning (gatapaccāgatavatta). Even people plowing, sowing, and threshing along the way, seeing the Elder traveling in that manner, would say, 'This Elder turns back again and again; is he perhaps confused about the way, or has he forgotten something?' Disregarding their words and practicing the recluse's dhamma with a mind joined with the meditation subject, he attained Arahatship within twenty years. On the day he attained Arahatship, a deity residing at the end of his walkway (caṅkama) stood there lighting a lamp with her fingers. The four Great Kings, Sakka the king of gods, and Brahma Sahampati also came to attend him. Seeing that radiance, Mahātissa Thera of Vanavāsī, on the second day...
51:
Mahātissa Thera of Vanavāsī asked, 'Last night, there was a radiance in the presence of the venerable one; what was that radiance?' The Elder, attempting to deflect (so as not to reveal his attainment), said, 'Radiance can be the light of a lamp, or the radiance of a gem,' and so on. When Mahātissa Thera persistently urged, 'Please do not hide it,' he admitted, 'Yes,' and informed him.

It was the same with Mahānāga Thera, a resident of Kāḷavallimaṇဍapa. He too, while fulfilling the duty of going and returning, resolved, 'First, I shall honor the Great Exertion (mahāpadhāna) of the Blessed One,' and for seven years he undertook only standing and walking. Then, after fulfilling the duty of going and returning for sixteen years, he attained Arahatship. In this way, he would lift his foot only with a mind joined with the meditation subject; if he lifted it with a mind devoid of it, he would turn back. Upon reaching the vicinity of a village, standing in a place where one might be doubted as 'Is it a cow or a monk?', he would put on his outer robe (saṅghāṭi), take his bowl, and reaching the village gate, he would take water from under his armpit, rinse his mouth, and enter the village holding a mouthful of water. When he saw people approaching to give alms or to pay respects, he entered with the thought, 'Let there be no distraction to my meditation subject even by the mere words "May you live long."' If people asked the day, saying, 'Venerable sir, is today the seventh or the eighth?', he would swallow the water and inform them. If there were no one asking the day, he would depart, spitting out the water at the village gate at the time of leaving.

It was also like the fifty monks who entered the rains retreat at Kalambatittha Monastery in the island of Sīhaḷa. On the Uposatha day of entering the rains, they made an agreement: 'We shall not speak to one another until we have attained Arahatship.' When entering the village for alms, they entered holding a mouthful of water at the village gate. If asked the day, they swallowed the water and replied; if not asked, they spat out the water at the village gate and returned to the monastery. The people there, seeing the place where the water was spat, knew, 'Today one came, today two came.' And they thought, 'Do these venerable ones not speak only with us, or do they not speak even among themselves? If they do not speak even among themselves, they must surely be in a quarrel. Come, let us make them forgive one another.' So they all went to the monastery. Among the fifty monks who had entered the rains there, they did not see two monks together in one place. Then, a wise man among them said, 'Friends, the dwelling place of quarreling people is not like this. The courtyard of the shrine and the courtyard of the Bodhi tree are well-swept. The brooms are well-placed. The drinking water and washing water are well-provided.'
52:
They returned from there. Those monks, having practiced insight meditation (vipassanā) within the three months of the rains retreat, attained Arahatship and performed the Visuddhi Pavāraṇā on the day of the Great Pavāraṇā.

In this way, like the Elder Mahānāga who resided at Kāḷavallimandapa, and like the monks who observed the rains retreat at Kalambatittha Monastery, they walked with a mind joined only with meditation (kammaṭṭhāna). Upon reaching the vicinity of the village, they took a mouthful of water, observed the streets, and entered a street where there were no drunkards, brawlers, or wild elephants and horses. In going for alms, they did not go with excessive haste; there is no such ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) as 'fast-paced alms-gathering.' One must go steadily, like a cart filled with water traveling over uneven ground. When entering houses in order, they observed who wished to give and who did not, waited for a suitable time, and received the alms-food. Then, sitting in a proper place, they applied their minds to meditation, established the perception of the repulsiveness of food (āhāre paṭikūlasaññā), and consumed the food endowed with the eight factors while reflecting through similes such as greasing an axle, applying ointment to a wound, or eating the flesh of one's own son. It is not for fun, not for intoxication... (and so on). After eating, they attended to the water-bowl, rested for a moment to relieve the fatigue caused by the meal, and then, just as before the meal, they applied their minds to meditation during the afternoon, the first watch of the night, and the last watch of the night. Such a monk is said to be 'one who goes and also returns.' This duty of going and returning is called the 'Gatapaccāgata-vatta.'

If a person who fulfills this duty is endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya), they attain Arahatship in the first stage of life. If they do not attain it in the first stage, they attain it in the middle stage. If not in the middle stage, they attain it at the time of death. If not at the time of death, they attain it after becoming a deva. If not after becoming a deva, they attain parinibbāna as a Paccekabuddha. If they do not attain parinibbāna as a Paccekabuddha, they become either a person of swift realization (khippābhiññā) like the Elder Bāhiya, or a person of great wisdom like the Elder Sāriputta, in the presence of a Buddha.

This Paccekabodhisatta, having ordained in the dispensation of the Blessed Kassapa Buddha and having lived as a forest-dweller, fulfilled this Gatapaccāgata-vatta for twenty thousand years. Upon passing away, he was reborn in the sensual-sphere deva realm. Passing away from there, he took conception in the womb of the Chief Queen of the King of Bārāṇasī. Wise women recognize the establishment of a fetus on that very day, and she, being one of those wise women, informed the King of the establishment of the pregnancy. This is the natural order (dhammatā): when a meritorious being is conceived in the womb, the woman receives pregnancy protection (gabbhaparihāra). Therefore, King Bārāṇasī provided pregnancy protection to the Queen. From that time on, she was not allowed to consume anything that was too hot, too cold, too sour, too salty, too spicy, or too bitter. If the mother eats food that is too hot, the being in the womb feels as if they are in a hell of molten metal. If the mother eats food that is too cold...
53:
Since she was one of those wise women, she informed the King of the establishment of the pregnancy. It is the natural order that when meritorious beings are conceived in the womb, women receive pregnancy protection. Therefore, the King granted her pregnancy protection. From then on, she was not allowed to consume anything that was too hot, too cold, too sour, too salty, too spicy, or too bitter. For if the mother consumes food that is too hot, it is for the fetus like living in the Lohakumbhī hell; if too cold, it is like living in the Lokantarika hell. If food that is too sour, salty, spicy, or bitter is eaten, the limbs of the fetus experience intense pain, as if being cut with a knife and doused with vinegar and such. They also restrained her from excessive walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, saying, 'Let there not be the suffering of displacement for the one in the womb.' She was allowed to perform activities like walking only in moderation on ground covered with soft rugs, and she received pleasant and suitable food endowed with good color and scent. They assisted her by supporting her whenever she walked, sat, or stood up.

Being thus protected, when the pregnancy reached full term, she entered the maternity chamber and, at dawn, gave birth to a son who was endowed with the marks of great merit and fortune, resembling a lump of realgar (manosilā) rubbed with cooked oil. Then, on the fifth day, they presented the decorated and prepared prince to the King. The King, being delighted, had him attended by sixty-six nurses. Growing up with all forms of prosperity, he soon reached the age of discretion. When he was about sixteen years old, the King consecrated him in the kingship and provided various dancers to entertain him. The consecrated prince, named Brahmadatta, ruled in twenty thousand cities throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa. Indeed, in ancient times, there were eighty-four thousand cities in Jambudīpa. As they declined, there were sixty thousand; then declining further, forty thousand; and in the time of total decline, there were only twenty thousand. This King Brahmadatta arose during the time of total decline. Therefore, he had twenty thousand cities, twenty thousand palaces, twenty thousand elephants, twenty thousand horses, twenty thousand chariots, twenty thousand infantry, twenty thousand women—including both the harem and dancers—and twenty thousand ministers. While exercising his great sovereignty, he performed the preliminary work for the kasina meditation and produced the five higher powers (abhiññā) and the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti). However, since a consecrated king must necessarily sit in the hall of judgment, one day, having eaten his morning meal early, he sat in the place of judgment. There, the people made a loud and great noise. He thought, 'This noise is an impurity to meditative attainment.'
54:
He ascended to the upper level of the palace and sat down, thinking, "I will enter into a meditative attainment," but he was unable to do so. His attainment declined due to the distractions of kingship. Then he reflected, "Which is better: kingship or the life of a recluse?" He then realized, "The happiness of kingship is small and full of many dangers, whereas the happiness of a recluse's life is vast, brings many benefits, and is practiced by great men of virtue." Having understood this, he commanded a certain minister, "Govern this kingdom righteously and justly; do not act unrighteously." After handing over everything, he ascended the palace and dwelt in the bliss of meditative attainment. No one was allowed to approach him except for those who provided water for washing his face, tooth-sticks, and those who brought his meals.

When about half a month had passed, the queen asked, "The Great King is not seen anywhere—not going to the park, not inspecting the troops, nor watching the dancers. Where has he gone?" They informed the queen of the matter. She sent a messenger to the minister, saying, "Since you have accepted the kingdom, you must also accept me (as a wife). Come and consort with me." The minister covered both ears and rejected the proposal, saying, "This is something that should not be heard." The queen sent messengers a second and third time, and when the minister remained unwilling, she threatened him, saying, "If you do not do as I say, I will remove you from your position and take your life." Fearing this, the minister thought, "Women are firm in their resolve; she might indeed do such a thing." One day, he went to a secluded place and consorted with the queen on the royal bed. The queen, being a woman of merit, had a pleasant touch. The minister, infatuated with the sensation of her touch, went there frequently. Eventually, he began to enter and leave without hesitation, like the master of his own house.

Then the king's men reported this matter to the king. The king did not believe it. When they reported it a second and third time, he hid himself and saw it with his own eyes. He then summoned all the ministers and informed them. The ministers pointed out various punishments, saying, "This minister has offended the king and deserves to have his hands cut off, his feet cut off, or even to be impaled on a stake." The king said, "If I kill, bind, or beat this man, it would cause me distress. If I take his life, it would be the act of taking life (pāṇātipāta). If I seize his wealth, it would be the act of taking what is not given (adinnādāna). It is not right to do such things. Simply banish him from my kingdom." The ministers banished him from the country. Taking his wealth, wife, and children, the minister went to another country. The king of that country, having heard of him, asked, "Why have you come?" He replied, "Great King, I wish to serve you." The king accepted him. After a few days, having gained the king's trust, the minister said to him, "Great King..."
55:
“I see honey without flies, but there is no one to eat it,” he said. The king, thinking, “Why does this man wish to mock me?” did not listen to him. The minister, finding an opportunity, praised it even more highly and reported it again. The king asked, “What is this?” He replied, “It is the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, O King.” The king said, “Do you wish to lead me there and have me killed?” The minister replied, “O King, do not say such a thing. If you do not believe me, send men to investigate.” The king sent men. They went, dug under the gate, and appeared inside the king's bedchamber.

When the king saw them, he asked, “Why have you come?” They replied, “Great King, we are thieves.” The king ordered wealth to be given to them and admonished them, saying, “Do not do this again,” and released them. They returned and reported to their king. That king tested him in the same way two or three more times and, realizing, “He is indeed a virtuous king,” he prepared his fourfold army.
