Approaching a city on the border, he sent a message to the minister there: “Either give me the city or give me battle.” The minister had the matter reported to King Brahmadatta: “May the King give the order: shall I fight or shall I give up the city?” The king sent word, “There must be no fighting. Give up the city and come here.” The minister did so. The rival king took that city and sent messengers to the remaining cities in the same manner. Those ministers also reported to King Brahmadatta, and being told, “There must be no fighting; come here,” they all came to Vārāṇasī.

Then the ministers said to King Brahmadatta, “Great King, let us fight with him.” The king forbade them, saying, “It would be an act of taking life (pāṇātipāta) for me.” The ministers said, “Great King, we will capture him alive and bring him here,” and after making the king understand through various means, they began to prepare to go, saying, “Come, Great King.” The king said, “If you do not kill, strike, or plunder living beings, I will go.” The ministers replied, “O King, we will not do so; we will only frighten them and make them flee.” They prepared the fourfold army, placed lamps inside jars, and set out at night. The rival king had taken a city near Vārāṇasī that day and, thinking, “What will happen now?” he had his armor and weapons removed and fell into a deep sleep along with his troops. Then the ministers, taking the King of Vārāṇasī with them, went to the rival king's camp, had the lamps taken out of all the jars, and made a great noise with the army amidst the sudden light. The rival king's minister, seeing the vast army and becoming terrified, approached his king and shouted loudly, “Rise! Eat the honey without flies!” He did so a second and third time. Because of that sound, the rival king...
56:
When the enemy king woke up, he was overcome with fear and trembling. Hundreds of shouts arose. He lamented throughout the night, thinking, "By believing the words of others, I have fallen into the hands of my enemy." On the second day, he thought, "A righteous king does not oppress others; I will go and ask for his forgiveness." He approached the Great King, knelt down, and said, "Great King, please forgive my offense." The King admonished him and said, "Arise, I forgive you." As soon as the Great King said this, the other king felt great relief and obtained kingship in a province near Bārāṇasī. They became friends with each other.

Then, King Brahmadatta, seeing both armies standing together in joy, thought, "For the sake of protecting my own mind, not even a drop of blood as small as a fly's drink has been shed among this multitude of people. Oh, how good! Oh, how pure! May all beings be happy, may they be free from enmity, and may they be free from suffering." Thus, he developed the jhāna of loving-kindness (mettā-jhāna). Taking that very jhāna as a basis, he contemplated the formations (saṅkhāra) and, realizing the knowledge of Private Enlightenment (paccekabodhi-ñāṇa), he attained the state of a self-enlightened Pacceka-buddha. While he sat happily on the back of the state elephant in the bliss of the Path and Fruit, the ministers paid homage to him and said, "Great King, it is time to depart. Honor should be paid to the victorious troops, and provisions should be given to the defeated troops."

He replied, "Friends, I am no longer a king; I am called a Pacceka-buddha." When they asked, "What does Your Majesty say? Such persons cannot be Pacceka-buddhas," he asked, "Friends, what is the nature of Pacceka-buddhas?" They replied, "Pacceka-buddhas have hair and beards two inches long and are endowed with the eight requisites." He stroked his head with his right hand, and at 그 moment, his lay appearance vanished and the appearance of a monk appeared. He looked like an elder of a hundred years of seniority, complete with hair and beard two inches long and the eight requisites. He entered the fourth jhāna, rose from the back of the elephant into the air, and sat upon a lotus flower. The ministers bowed and asked, "Venerable Sir, by what meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) and how did you attain this?" Because he had attained it by practicing insight (vipassanā) based on the meditation of loving-kindness, he spoke this verse, which was both an exultant utterance (udāna) and an explanatory verse (byākaraṇa), to show that matter: "Laying aside the rod against all beings..."

In that verse, "sabbesu" means all without exception. "Bhūtesu" means among living beings. This is a summary here; I shall explain it in detail in the commentary on the Ratana Sutta. "Nidhāya" means having laid aside.
57:
"Daṇḍa" refers to the rod of misconduct of body, speech, and mind. This word "daṇḍa" is a name for bodily misconduct and so on. Indeed, bodily misconduct is called "daṇḍa" because it punishes; it means it harms and leads to ruin and destruction. Likewise, verbal misconduct and mental misconduct are also called "daṇḍa." Alternatively, a weapon or a stick is called "daṇḍa," and it also means having laid aside that weapon. "Aviheṭhayaṃ" means not harming. "Aññataraṃ" means even any single person without distinction. "Tesaṃ" means among all those beings. "Na puttam iccheyya" means one should not desire any son among the four types of sons: the biological son (atraja), the son born of the wife (khettaja), the adopted son (dinnaka), and the pupil son (antevāsika). If one does not even desire a companion, why would one desire a son?

"Eko" (alone) means being alone in the sense of monkhood (pabbajjā), being alone in the sense of having no companion, being alone by the abandoning of craving (taṇhā), being alone by being absolutely free from defilements (kilesa), and being alone by having realized the Private Enlightenment (paccekasambodhi) by oneself. Even when staying in the midst of a thousand monks, one is alone because the fetters of a layman have been cut; thus, one is alone in the sense of monkhood. One stands alone, walks alone, sits alone, lies down alone, and maintains the postures alone; thus, one is alone in the sense of having no companion.

It is said: "A man with craving as his companion, wandering for a long time in saṃsāra, does not transcend the cycle of rebirth, which consists of this state and other states. Knowing this danger—that craving is the source of suffering—a bhikkhu should wander alone, free from craving, without grasping, and mindful."

Thus, one is alone in the sense of abandoning craving. All his defilements have been abandoned, their roots cut, made like a palm-tree stump, rendered non-existent, and are of a nature not to arise again in the future; thus, one is alone as one whose defilements are absolutely gone. Having no teacher, being self-enlightened, and having realized the Private Enlightenment by oneself; thus, one is alone as one who has realized the Private Enlightenment.

"Care" (should wander/practice) refers to these eight types of conduct (cariyā). They are: the conduct of postures (iriyāpatha-cariyā) in the four postures for those endowed with aspiration; the conduct of sense bases (āyatana-cariyā) in the internal sense bases for those who guard the doors of the senses; the conduct of mindfulness (sati-cariyā) in the four foundations of mindfulness for those who dwell in heedfulness; the conduct of concentration (samādhi-cariyā) in the four jhānas for those devoted to the higher mind (adhicitta); the conduct of knowledge (ñāṇa-cariyā) in the four Noble Truths for those endowed with wisdom; the conduct of the path (magga-cariyā) in the four Noble Paths for those who have practiced rightly; and for those who have attained the fruits, the conduct of the fruits of recluseship (sāmañña-phala-cariyā) in the four...
58:
The practice of attainment (patticariyā) in the fruits; the conduct for the benefit of the world (lokatthacariyā) of the three [types of] Buddhas towards all beings; in that conduct for the benefit of the world, it exists partially for Paccekabuddhas and disciples. As it is said: 'Conduct (cariyā) refers to the eight types of conduct, beginning with the conduct of postures (iriyāpathacariya),' and so on, the details should be understood. The meaning is that one should be endowed with those types of conduct. Alternatively, another eight types of conduct are mentioned: 'One conducts oneself with faith while being resolved; one conducts oneself with energy while exerting; one conducts oneself with mindfulness while being present; one conducts oneself with concentration while being undistracted; one conducts oneself with wisdom while knowing; one conducts oneself with consciousness while perceiving; one conducts oneself with the conduct of the sense bases (āyatanacariya) because wholesome states accumulate in one who practices thus; one conducts oneself with the conduct of distinction (visesacariya) because the person practicing thus attains the distinction of the Path and Fruit.' The meaning is that one should be endowed with these other eight types of conduct as well. In the term 'khaggavisāṇakappo,' 'khaggavisāṇa' refers to the horn of a rhinoceros. I shall explain the detailed meaning of the word 'kappa' in the commentary on the Maṅgala Sutta. However, in this context, it should be understood as having the meaning of 'resembling' or 'like,' as in the words 'Indeed, sir, [they are] consulting with a disciple who is like the Teacher (satthukappena).' 'Khaggavisāṇakappo' means resembling the horn of a rhinoceros. This is the word-by-word explanation of the meaning.

Regarding the connection of the intended meaning (adhippāyānusandhi), it should be understood thus: The violence (daṇḍa) inflicted upon beings is not beneficial. By not inflicting that violence upon them, and through loving-kindness (mettā) which is the opposite of that violence, and by promoting the welfare of others, one has laid down the stick (nidhāya daṇḍaṃ) towards all beings. Because of having laid down the stick, one does not harm even a single being, unlike those beings who have not laid down the stick and who harm other beings with a stick, a weapon, the hand, or a stone. Having practiced this meditation on loving-kindness, and having practiced insight (vipassanā) into the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness present therein, as well as other formations in that same manner, one thinks, 'I have attained this Paccekabodhi-knowledge.' This is the intended meaning.

Regarding the sequence of events (anusandhi): When this was said, those ministers asked, 'Venerable sir, where will you go now?' Then, the Paccekabuddha, reflecting on 'Where do the former Paccekabuddhas dwell?' and knowing 'On Mount Gandhamādana,' replied accordingly. The ministers asked again, 'Venerable sir, are you now abandoning us and no longer desire us?' Then the Paccekabuddha spoke the entire verse beginning with 'One should not desire a son.' The intention therein is: 'I no longer desire anyone, even a son born of myself; how could I desire companions like you? Therefore, among you, he who wishes to go with me or to be like me should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.' This is the meaning for that person. Alternatively, when the ministers said, 'Venerable sir, you are now abandoning us and do not desire us,' that Paccekabuddha, saying 'One should not desire a son, how much less a companion,' saw the benefit of wandering alone as previously stated, and being filled with joy, rapture, and happiness, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna): 'One should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.' Having said this, while the great multitude was watching, he flew into the air and went to Mount Gandhamādana.
59:
'I do not even desire a son; how could I desire a companion like you? Therefore, among you, he who wishes to go with me or to be like me should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn,' he said. Or else, when those ministers said, 'Venerable sir, you have now abandoned us and no longer desire us,' that Paccekabuddha said, 'One should not desire a son, how much less a companion,' and seeing the benefit of wandering alone as stated above, he became joyful and filled with rapture and happiness, and uttered this inspired utterance: 'One should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.' Having spoken thus, while the great crowd was watching, he rose into the air and went to Mount Gandhamādana.

Mount Gandhamādana is located in the Himālaya beyond seven mountains: Cūḷakāḷa, Mahākāḷa, Nāgapaliveṭhana, Candagabbha, Suriyagabbha, Suvaṇṇapassa, and Himavanta. On that mountain, the mountain slope named Nandamūlaka is the dwelling place of Paccekabuddhas. There are three caves: the Golden Cave, the Gem Cave, and the Silver Cave. At the entrance of the Gem Cave, there is a tree named Mañjūsaka, one league in height and one league in breadth. That tree makes all flowers that exist in water or on land bloom, especially on the day a Paccekabuddha arrives. Above that tree, there is a terrace (māḷa) made of all kinds of jewels. On that terrace, the sweeping wind (sammajjanaka-vāta) discards the refuse; the leveling wind (samakaraṇa-vāta) levels the jeweled sand; the sprinkling wind (siñcanaka-vāta) brings water from Lake Anotatta and sprinkles it; the scenting wind (sugandhakaraṇa-vāta) brings the fragrance of all scented trees from the Himālaya; the plucking wind (ocinaka-vāta) plucks flowers and drops them; and the spreading wind (santharaka-vāta) spreads them everywhere. Seats are always prepared there, where all Paccekabuddhas assemble and sit on the day a Paccekabuddha is born and on Uposatha days. This is the natural custom of that place.

A Paccekabuddha who has fully realized the Four Noble Truths goes there and sits on the prepared seat. At that time, if there are other Paccekabuddhas, they also assemble at that moment and sit on the prepared seats. Having sat, they enter into some meditative attainment and then emerge. Then, the Sangha Elder (saṅghatthera), for the sake of gladdening everyone, asks the newly arrived Paccekabuddha about his meditation subject, saying, 'How was it attained?' Then, he recites his own verse of inspired utterance. Again, when the Blessed One was asked by the Venerable Ānanda, he spoke that same verse, and Ānanda recited it at the Council. Thus, each verse is spoken four times: at the place of attaining Paccekabodhi, at the Mañjūsaka terrace, when asked by the Venerable Ānanda, and at the time of the Council.

The commentary on the first verse is finished.

What is the origin of this verse 'Saṃsaggajātassa'? This future Paccekabuddha practiced the Dhamma of a recluse (samaṇadhamma) for twenty thousand years during the dispensation of the Buddha Kassapa in the same manner as before. At the end, he performed the preliminary work for a kasina, attained the first jhāna, distinguished mind and matter, contemplated the characteristics [of existence], followed the sequence of the Noble Path, and was reborn in the Brahma realm. Passing away from that Brahma realm, he was conceived in the womb of the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī and grew up in the same manner as before. From the time when he [realized], 'This person is a woman, this person is...'
60:
This verse was preached four times: at the Mañjūsaka terrace, at the time when it was asked by the Venerable Ānanda, and at the time of the Council.

## End of the Commentary on the First Verse.

What is the origin of the verse beginning with "Saṃsaggajātassa"? This future Paccekabuddha, during the dispensation of the Blessed Kassapa Buddha, practiced the ascetic Dhamma for twenty thousand years in the same manner as previously mentioned. Having performed the preliminary work for the kasina and attained the first jhāna, he defined mentality-materiality and contemplated the three marks of existence; however, without attaining the Noble Path, he was reborn in the Brahma realm. Passing away from that Brahma realm, he was conceived in the womb of the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī. Growing up in the same manner as before, from the time he could distinguish, "This is a woman, this is a man," he no longer delighted in the hands of women. He could not even endure being rubbed, bathed, or adorned by them. Only men cared for and looked after the child. When it was time for breastfeeding, the wet-nurses were made to wear jackets and were disguised as men to feed him. If the child smelled the scent of women or heard their voices, he would cry. Even when he reached the age of discretion, he had no desire to look at women; therefore, people knew and called him "Anitthigandha" (One who has no scent of women).

When Prince Anitthigandha reached the age of sixteen, the King thought, "I shall establish the lineage." He brought suitable maidens from various families and commanded a minister, "Make the prince delight in them." The minister, wishing to make the prince delight through a stratagem, had a curtain-wall erected not far from the prince and arranged for dancers to perform. When the prince heard the sound of singing and music, he asked, "Whose sound is this?" The minister replied, "O Prince, this is the sound of your dancing women. Such dancers belong to those with great merit. O Prince, you are one of great merit; please enjoy yourself." The prince had the minister beaten with a stick and driven out. The minister reported this matter to the King. The King went together with the prince's mother, asked for the prince's forgiveness, and again entrusted the minister to him. Being extremely pressured and harassed by them, the prince gave them fine gold and commanded the goldsmiths, "Fashion a beautiful image of a woman." The goldsmiths created and displayed a female image adorned with all kinds of ornaments, as if fashioned by the celestial architect Vissakamma. Upon seeing it, the prince shook his head in amazement and sent word to his parents, saying, "If I obtain a woman such as this, I shall take her as my wife."
61:
The parents thought, "Our son is one of great merit; surely some maiden who has performed merit together with him must have been born in the world." Having placed that golden statue on a chariot, they entrusted it to the ministers, saying, "Go and search for a maiden with such an appearance." Taking the golden statue, those ministers wandered through the sixteen Great Janapadas. Whenever they reached various villages and saw a gathering of people at places such as water-fetching ghats, they would set up the golden statue like a goddess, make offerings with various flowers and garments, hang a canopy, and stand in a suitable place, thinking, "If anyone has seen someone of such an appearance before, how will they start a conversation and inquire?" By this means, they wandered through all the Janapadas except for the Madda kingdom. Regarding the Madda kingdom as merely a small country, they did not go there at first but turned back.

Then it occurred to them, "Let us go to the Madda kingdom as well, lest the King send us out again even after we have entered Bārāṇasī." So they went to the city of Sāgala in the Madda kingdom. In the city of Sāgala, there was a king named Maddava. His daughter was sixteen years old and was exceedingly beautiful. Her attendants went to the water-ghat to fetch water for her bath. When they saw the golden statue placed there by the ministers from afar, they said, "The princess herself has come after sending us to fetch water!" Approaching it, they said, "This is not our mistress; our mistress is even more beautiful than this." When the ministers heard these words, they approached the King and requested the maiden in a suitable manner, and the King granted her. Then they sent word to the King of Bārāṇasī, asking, "We have found the maiden. Will the King come in person to take her, or shall we bring her ourselves?" The King replied, "If I come myself, it will cause hardship to the people of the countryside; you yourselves bring her." 

The ministers took the maiden, left the city, and sent a messenger to the prince, saying, "We have found a maiden who resembles the golden statue." As soon as the prince heard this, he was overcome by lust and fell away from the first jhāna. He sent a succession of messengers, saying, "Bring her quickly! Bring her quickly!" By staying only one night at each place, they reached Bārāṇasī and, stopping outside the city, asked the King, "Shall we enter the city today or not?" The King commanded, "Since the maiden has been brought from a noble family, we shall perform the auspicious rites and bring her into the city with great honor. For now, take her to the park." The ministers did as commanded. That princess, having an extremely delicate body, was oppressed by the jolting of the chariot and the exhaustion of the long journey, and due to the wind ailment that arose, she became like a withered flower...
62:
(The princess) became like (a withered flower) and passed away that very night. The ministers lamented, "We have fallen away from honors and rewards." The King and the citizens also lamented, "The lineage is destroyed." A great commotion arose in the city. Upon merely hearing the news, intense sorrow arose in the prince. Then the prince strove to dig up the root of sorrow. He reflected, "This thing called sorrow does not happen to one who is not born; it only happens to one who is born. Therefore, sorrow exists because of birth (jāti)." He continued, "On what does birth depend?" and then, "Birth exists because of existence (bhava)." Thus, through the power of his previous meditations, reflecting wisely (yoniso manasikāra) and seeing Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) in forward and reverse order, and contemplating formations (saṅkhāra), he realized the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha while sitting right there.

Seeing the prince sitting there, happy with the bliss of the Path and Fruit, with peaceful faculties and a peaceful mind, the ministers paid homage and said, "O Prince, do not grieve. The island of Jambudīpa is vast; we will bring another maiden more beautiful than that princess." The prince replied, "I am not one who grieves; I am a Paccekabuddha, free from sorrow." Apart from this, since the rest of the explanation is the same as the previous verse, I shall omit it and provide the commentary on the verse.

In the commentary, "saṃsaggajātassa" means for one in whom association has arisen. In that context, there are five kinds of association (saṃsagga): association through seeing (dassana), hearing (savana), physical contact (kāya), conversation (samullapana), and enjoyment (sambhoga). Among these, lust that arises through the process of eye-consciousness upon seeing each other is called association through seeing. An example of this association through seeing is a merchant's daughter in the village of Kāḷadīghavāpī on the island of Sīhaḷa (Sri Lanka), who saw a young monk, a reciter of the Dīgha Nikāya (Dīghabhāṇaka) living at Kalyāṇavihāra, while he was on alms round. Her heart became attached, and unable to obtain him by any means, she died. The young monk, upon seeing a piece of the cloth she used to wear, thought, "I did not get to live with the one who wore such a garment," and his heart broke, and he died. These two are the examples.

Lust that arises through the process of ear-consciousness, either by hearing others describe someone's beauty or by hearing their laughter, talk, or singing, is called association through hearing. In that association through hearing, the daughter of a blacksmith living in Girigāma went to a lotus pond with five maidens. While she was bathing, wearing flowers, and singing loudly, the young monk Tissa of Pañcaggala Cave, who was traveling through the air, heard the sound. Due to sensual lust, he fell away from his attained distinctions (jhānas) and met with ruin. This is the example.

Lust that arises from touching each other's limbs is called association through physical contact. A young monk who was a Dhamma-preacher is the example here. It is said that while a young monk was preaching the Dhamma at Mahāvihāra, a crowd arrived, and the King also came with the ladies of the court. Then, a princess, focusing on the appearance and voice of that young monk, felt intense lust. The young monk also felt lust upon seeing the princess. The King, realizing this, had a curtain drawn. The young monk and the princess touched each other's limbs and embraced. When the curtain was removed and people looked, they saw that both had died. This is the example. Lust arising from calling out to and talking with each other is association through conversation. Lust arising when a monk makes use of things together with bhikkhunīs is association through enjoyment.
63:
He preached the Dhamma. When the crowd gathered at that monastery, the King also came together with the ladies of the palace. At that time, strong passion (rāga) arose in the princess, focusing on the appearance and voice of that young monk; and for that young monk, upon seeing the princess, passion also arose. The King, realizing this matter, had them surrounded by a curtain wall. The two touched and embraced each other. Later, when the curtain was removed and they were looked upon, both were seen to have passed away.

Passion arising from mutual calling and conversing is called samullapana-saṃsagga (association through conversation). Passion arising when a monk makes use of things together with a nun is called sambhoga-saṃsagga (association through common use). In both these types of association, the monk and the nun who reached pārājika (defeat) are the evidence. It is heard that at the festival of the Maricivaṭṭi Mahāvihāra, the Great King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi Abhaya prepared a great alms-giving and served both sides of the Saṅgha. At that offering, when hot gruel was being donated, a junior novice nun gave an ivory bangle to a junior novice monk who had no bowl-stand and engaged in conversation. After both of them were ordained as bhikkhus and had reached sixty years of seniority (vassa), they arrived at the other shore. By conversing with each other, they regained their former perception, and at that very moment, affection arose; they transgressed the training rules and became pārājika.

Thus, among the five kinds of association, affection (sneha) arises in one who is mixed with any kind of association. Due to the cause of former lustful passion, strong passion arises. From that, this suffering which follows affection arises. Following only that affection, various kinds of suffering such as sorrow and lamentation occurring in the present and in the future arise, occur, happen, and are born. Other teachers, however, say: "The release of the mind toward an object is called association (saṃsagga)." Therefore, affection arises, and because of affection, this suffering arises.

After speaking this half-verse with such various meanings, that Paccekabuddha said: "While I was digging out the root of that suffering, such as sorrow, which follows affection, I attained the Paccekasambodhi (Solitary Enlightenment)." When he said this, those ministers asked: "Venerable Sir, what should we do now?" Then that Paccekabuddha said: "Whether it be you or others, whoever desires to be liberated from this suffering, all such persons, seeing the danger born of affection, should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn."

In this context, the statement "this suffering which follows affection arises" should be understood as being spoken in reference to that very danger, as in "seeing the danger born of affection." Alternatively, it should be understood that the fourth line was spoken in the same manner as previously mentioned, connecting it thus: affection arises in one who is mixed with the aforementioned association; this suffering follows affection; seeing this danger born of affection as it truly is, I have attained (the Dhamma).
64:
It should be understood that it was spoken by way of an inspired utterance (udāna) in the very manner previously mentioned. After that, the entire sequence of words is just the same as what was said in the previous verse.

## The Explanation of the Verse on Association is Finished.

What is the origin of the verse beginning with "Mitte suhajje"? This future Paccekabuddha, having been born in the same manner as mentioned in the previous verse, was reigning in the city of Bārāṇasī. Having attained the first jhāna, he reflected, "Is the recluse's Dhamma superior, or is kingship superior?" He then handed over the kingdom into the hands of four ministers and practiced the recluse's Dhamma. Although the ministers were told, "Govern with justice and righteousness," they took bribes and governed unrighteously. Taking bribes, they caused the rightful owners to lose their cases, and on one occasion, they caused a person who was a favorite of the King to lose. That person entered with the King's food-bearer and reported everything. On the second day, the King himself went to the place of judgment. Then the great crowd of people made a loud noise, saying, "The ministers are making the owners non-owners," and it became like a great battle.

Then the King rose from the place of judgment, ascended the palace, and sat down to enter into an attainment (samāpatti), but his mind was distracted by that noise and he was unable to enter it. That King thought, "What benefit is there for me in kingship? The recluse's Dhamma alone is superior." He abandoned the royal bliss, attained the samāpatti again, and while developing insight (vipassanā) in the manner previously mentioned, he realized the Paccekasambodhi-knowledge. When asked about his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), he spoke this verse:

"One who is compassionate toward friends and well-wishers, with a bound heart, neglects the goal.
Seeing this danger in intimacy, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn."

In that verse, they are called 'friends' (mitta) by way of loving-kindness. They are called 'well-wishers' (suhajja) by way of having a good heart. For some are friends only because they truly desire one's welfare, but are not well-wishers. Some are well-wishers only because they produce heart-felt happiness in going, coming, standing, sitting, and conversing, but are not friends. Some are both well-wishers and friends by way of both those qualities. Those friends are of two kinds: laypeople and recluses.

Among them, lay friends are of three types: the helper (upakāra), the one who is the same in happiness and sorrow (samānasukhadukkha), and the compassionate one (anukampaka). Recluse friends are specifically those who point out the benefit (atthakkhāyī). They are endowed with four factors. As the Buddha said: "Householder's son, the helper friend should be known by four grounds: he protects the one who is negligent, he protects the property of the one who is negligent, he is a refuge for the one who is afraid, and when duties arise, he provides double the required wealth. Furthermore, householder's son, the friend who is the same in happiness and sorrow..."
65:
“Young householder, a friend who is a helper (upakāra) should be known as a good-hearted friend based on four grounds: (1) he protects one who is heedless, (2) he protects the property of one who is heedless, (3) he is a refuge for one who is afraid, and (4) when duties arise, he provides double the required wealth” (DN 3.261).

Likewise: “Young householder, a friend who is the same in happiness and sorrow (samānasukhadukkha) should be known as a good-hearted friend based on four grounds: (1) he tells one his secrets, (2) he keeps one's secrets strictly, (3) he does not abandon one in times of danger, and (4) he would even sacrifice his life for that friend's sake” (DN 3.262).

Likewise: “Young householder, a friend who is compassionate (anukampaka) should be known as a good-hearted friend based on four grounds: (1) he does not rejoice in one's downfall, (2) he rejoices in one's prosperity, (3) he restrains others from speaking ill of one, and (4) he praises those who speak well of one” (DN 3.264).

Likewise: “Young householder, a friend who points out what is beneficial (atthakkhāyī) should be known as a good-hearted friend based on four grounds: (1) he restrains one from evil, (2) he establishes one in good deeds, (3) he makes one hear what one has not heard before, and (4) he points out the path to heaven” (DN 3.263).

In this context, lay friends are intended. However, in terms of meaning, all types of friends are applicable. These friends are called good-hearted. 'Anukampamāno' means one who is compassionate in due order, desiring to bring them happiness and to remove their suffering.

Regarding 'diminishes the benefit' (hāpeti atthaṃ), benefit is threefold: benefit in the present life, benefit in future lives, and the ultimate benefit. Similarly, it is threefold as: one's own benefit, the benefit of others, and the benefit of both. One diminishes or destroys the benefit in two ways: by destroying benefits already obtained and by preventing the arising of benefits not yet obtained. 'One with an attached mind' (paṭibaddhacitto) refers to someone who, even if placing themselves in a lowly position, thinks, “I cannot live without this person; this person is my destination, this person is my refuge.” Or, even if placing themselves in a high position, thinks, “These people cannot live without me; I am their destination, I am their refuge.” Here, such an attached mind is intended. 'This danger' (etaṃ bhayaṃ) refers to the danger of diminishing benefits caused by such attachment. This is spoken with reference to the falling away from one's own meditative attainments (samāpatti).
66:
Intimacy (santhava) is of three kinds: intimacy through craving (taṇhā-santhava), intimacy through views (diṭṭhi-santhava), and intimacy through friendship (mitta-santhava). Among these, craving with its 108 varieties is taṇhā-santhava; views with their 62 varieties are diṭṭhi-santhava; and compassion for a friend due to an attached mind is mitta-santhava. Here, this mitta-santhava is intended. Indeed, because of it, his meditative attainments were lost. Therefore, he said: “Seeing this danger in intimacy, I have attained [Private Enlightenment].” The rest should be understood as being similar to what has already been stated.

## The Explanation of the Verse on Good-hearted Friends is Finished.

What is the origin of the verse “Vaṃso visālo”? It is said that formerly, during the dispensation of the Blessed Kassapa Buddha, three future Paccekabuddhas went forth as monks. For twenty thousand years, they fulfilled the duty of going and returning (gatapaccāgatavatta) and were reborn in the deva realm. When they passed away from there, the eldest was reborn in the royal family of Bārāṇasī, while the other two were reborn in the royal families of the border regions. Those two also learned meditation subjects, renounced their kingdoms, and went forth. In due course, they became Paccekabuddhas and lived in the Nandamūlaka cave. One day, after emerging from meditative attainment, they reflected, “What good deed did we perform to attain this supramundane bliss?” and saw their practice during the time of Kassapa Buddha.

Then, reflecting “Where is the third person?”, they saw him reigning in the city of Bārāṇasī and remembered his virtues. “By nature, he was endowed with virtues such as fewness of wishes. He used to be our instructor and advisor, patient in speech, and a censurer of evil. Come, let us show him an object [of contemplation] and liberate him [from saṃsāra].” Seeking an opportunity, they saw him one day going to the park adorned with all ornaments. They came through the air and stood at the foot of a bamboo thicket at the park gate. The great multitude could not get enough of looking at the King. Then the King, looking around to see if there was anyone unconcerned with seeing him, saw the Paccekabuddhas. As soon as he saw them, affection for them arose in him.

The King descended from the elephant's back and approached them with a calm manner, asking, “Venerable sirs, what are your names?” They replied, “Great King, we are called 'Asajjamāna' (the unattached).” “Venerable sirs, what is the meaning of 'Asajjamāna'?” When asked, they replied, “Great King, it means non-clinging.” Then, pointing to that bamboo thicket, they said: “Great King, just as this bamboo thicket stands completely entwined with roots, trunks, branches, and twigs, so that a man with a sword in hand, having cut it at the base, would not be able to pull it out; even so, Great King, people are entwined and attached within and without by the defilements. Great King, just as a single bamboo stalk in the middle of that thicket, having no branches entwined with other bamboos, stands unattached, so that if one cuts the top and the base, it can be pulled out; even so, Great King, there are those who are unattached and unentangled. They can go wherever they please.” Having spoken thus, they immediately entered into jhāna and, while the King was watching, departed through the air to the Nandamūlaka cave. Thereafter, the King thought, “When shall I too become unattached and unentangled like those venerable ones?”
67:
...just as [one is unable] to extract [it], even so, you are entangled by the tangle of defilements both within and without, repeatedly clinging and stuck therein. Alternatively, for example, just as this bamboo shoot in the middle of the grove remains unstuck to anything because its branches have not yet grown, and can be extracted by cutting it at the tip or the root, even so, we go to all directions without being attached to anything." At that very moment, while the king was watching, having attained the fourth jhāna, they departed through the air to the Nandamūlaka cave. Then the king thought, "When shall I too become unattached like this?" Sitting right there and practicing insight (vipassanā), he realized the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha (Paccekabodhi-ñāṇa). Being asked about his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) in the same manner as before, he uttered this verse:

"Just as a wide bamboo grove is entangled, so is the longing for sons and wives; like a bamboo shoot unattached, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn."

In that verse, 'vaṃsa' means bamboo. 'Visāla' means extensive. The word 'ca' has the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa), or it is the word 'eva' where the 'e' sound was dropped due to euphonic combination (sandhi). It should be connected with the following word; we shall show the combination later. 'Yathā' is in the sense of comparison. 'Visatta' means stuck, entangled, or entwined. 'Puttesu dāresu ca' means in sons, daughters, and wives. 'Yā apekkha' means that craving, that sap of affection. 'Vaṃsakkaḷīrova asajjamāno' means not sticking like a bamboo shoot. What is meant is: Just as a wide bamboo grove is entangled, so too the longing for sons and wives is indeed an entanglement because it remains entwining and binding those objects of sensual desire. Seeing the danger in that longing and cutting it off with Path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa), I have attained Paccekabodhi, being unattached through the power of craving, conceit, and views regarding forms and so on, greed and so on, sensual existence and so on, or views and so on, just like this bamboo shoot. The rest is to be understood in the same manner as before.

## The Explanation of the Bamboo Shoot Verse is finished.

Regarding the verse beginning with 'Migo araññamhi' (A deer in the forest), the origin is as follows: A certain monk was a practitioner (yogāvacara) during the dispensation of the Blessed Kassapa Buddha. After passing away, he was reborn in Bārāṇasī in a wealthy merchant's family with great wealth and possessions, and was named Subhaga. Furthermore, because he had committed the act of adultery (paradārika-kamma), when he passed away from that life, he was reborn in hell. After suffering in that hell, due to the remaining result of the adultery, he took conception as a female in the womb of a merchant's wife. The bodies of those coming from hell are very hot; therefore, that merchant's wife carried the fetus with great difficulty and pain due to her hot womb, and in due time, gave birth to a daughter. From the day she was born...
68:
Cutting that longing with Path-knowledge, I have attained Paccekabodhi, being unattached through the power of craving, conceit, and views regarding forms and so on, greed and so on, sensual existence and so on, or doctrines and so on, just like this bamboo shoot. The rest is to be understood in the same manner as before. The explanation of the Bamboo Shoot Verse is finished.

Regarding the verse 'Migo araññamhi' (A deer in the forest), what is the origin? A certain monk was a practitioner (yogāvacara) in the dispensation of the Blessed Kassapa Buddha. After passing away, he was reborn in Bārāṇasī in a wealthy merchant's family with many possessions and great wealth, and he was named Subhaga. Furthermore, because he was one who practiced adultery (paradārika-kamma), when he passed away from that life, he was reborn in hell. After suffering in that hell, due to the residue of the result of the adultery, he took conception as a female in the womb of a merchant's wife. The bodies of those coming from hell tend to be hot. Therefore, the merchant's wife carried that fetus with great difficulty and pain due to her hot womb, and in due time, gave birth to a daughter. From the day she was born, she was only a person to be disliked (hateful) to her parents and to the rest of her relatives and attendants. When she reached age and was given in marriage to a certain family, she was also only a person to be disliked, unpleasant and disagreeable to her husband and her parents-in-law.

Then, when a festival was proclaimed, the merchant's son did not wish to play with that wife, so he brought a prostitute and played with her. That merchant's daughter heard about this from the maidservants, approached the merchant's son, and coaxing him in various ways, said: 'My lord, even if a woman were the younger sister of ten kings or the daughter of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti), she is still one who must serve her husband. If the husband remains silent, she experiences suffering as if she were placed on a stake. If I am worthy of your favor, please favor me. If you do not wish to favor me, then release me; I will return to my own relatives' house.' The merchant's son said: 'Very well, lady, do not worry. Prepare for the festival; we shall play at the festival together.' The merchant's daughter, encouraged by just that much talk, said, 'I will play at the festival tomorrow,' and prepared many kinds of hard and soft food. On the second day, the merchant's son went to the place of the festival without informing her. That merchant's daughter, waiting and looking at the road, thinking 'He will send for me now, he will send for me now,' saw that the day was late and sent people to investigate. They returned and reported, 'The merchant's son has gone.' That merchant's daughter took all the prepared food, mounted a vehicle, and set out to go to the park.

At that time, a Paccekabuddha living in the Nandamūlaka cave emerged from the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) on the seventh day. Having washed his face at Lake Anotatta and used a nāgalatā tooth-stick, he reflected, 'Where shall I wander for alms today?' He saw the merchant's daughter and knew, 'By making an offering to me, that [bad] kamma of hers will come to an end.' Standing on the Manosila plateau, which is sixty leagues in extent near the Nandamūlaka mountain range, he dressed in his lower robe, took his bowl and robes, entered the jhāna that is the basis for supernormal powers, and departed through the air. He descended on the path where the merchant's daughter was traveling and proceeded towards the city of Bārāṇasī. Seeing that Paccekabuddha, and having heard [about such beings] from the maidservants...
69:
Standing on the realgar-colored stone surface, sixty leagues in extent, near the Nandamūlaka cave, he dressed in his lower robe, took his bowl and robes, and entered the jhana which is the basis for higher knowledge. Having traveled through the air, he descended in front of the merchant's daughter and proceeded towards Bārāṇasī. Seeing the Paccekabuddha, the maidservants informed the merchant's daughter. She descended from her vehicle, paid respect with great reverence, and filled the bowl with food of all flavors. She covered it with a lotus flower and also placed a lotus flower beneath it. Holding a bunch of lotus flowers in her hand, she approached the Paccekabuddha, offered the bowl into his hands, and after paying homage, she made an aspiration while holding the bunch of lotus flowers: "Venerable Sir, just like this lotus flower, wherever I am reborn, may I be loved and liked by all people." After making this aspiration, she made a second aspiration: "Venerable Sir, dwelling in a womb is very painful; may I not have to dwell in a womb, but be reborn only within a lotus flower." She made a third aspiration: "Venerable Sir, being a woman is loathsome; even the daughter of a Universal Monarch must follow the will of others. Therefore, may I not become a woman, but only a man." She made a fourth aspiration: "Venerable Sir, having crossed over the suffering of this cycle of rebirths, may I at the end reach Nibbāna, the deathless state, which you have attained."

Having made these four aspirations, she offered the bunch of lotus flowers in worship, paid homage to the Paccekabuddha with the five points of contact, and made a fifth aspiration: "May my scent and complexion be just like a lotus flower." Then, the Paccekabuddha took the bowl and the bunch of flowers, and standing in the air, he said:

"May the wish you have desired and longed for be fulfilled quickly.
May all your intentions be fulfilled, like the moon on the fifteenth day."

Having given this blessing to the merchant's daughter with this verse, he made a determination, "May the merchant's daughter see me as I go," and departed for the Nandamūlaka valley. Seeing this, the merchant's daughter felt great joy. The unwholesome kamma she had committed in another life, having no opportunity to ripen, was exhausted, and she became pure like a copper vessel washed with tamarind juice. At that very moment, all the people in her husband's house and her relatives' house were delighted and sent pleasant words and gifts, asking, "Lady, what can we do for you?" The merchant's son also sent men, saying, "I came to the garden having forgotten her; bring the merchant's daughter quickly." From then on, he cherished and cared for her like sandalwood paste applied to the chest, like a string of pearls worn, or like a garland of flowers.
70:
The merchant's daughter, after enjoying the happiness of sovereignty and wealth for the rest of her life in that existence, passed away and was reborn as a male in a lotus flower in the celestial realm. Whether that young deva was walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, he did so only within the interior of a lotus flower. They named that deva "Mahāpaduma Deva." Thus, by the power of that psychic potency, he wandered through the six celestial realms in both direct and reverse order.

At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī had twenty thousand concubines. The King did not obtain a son from the womb of even a single woman. The ministers addressed the King, saying, "Great King, a son is needed to protect the lineage; if a biological son does not exist, even an adopted son (khettaja) can carry on the lineage." The King, excluding the Chief Queen, ordered the remaining dancing girls and concubines, "Perform a Dhamma-play (religious drama) for seven days," and allowed them to wander outside as they pleased. Even though they did so, he did not obtain a son.

Again, the ministers said, "Great King, the Chief Queen is superior to all women in merit and wisdom; perhaps the King might obtain a son from her womb." The King informed the Chief Queen of this matter. The Queen said, "Great King, only a woman who speaks the truth and possesses virtue can obtain a son; how can one who lacks moral shame and moral dread (hiri-ottappa) obtain a son?" She then ascended the palace, undertook the Five Precepts, and repeatedly reflected upon them. While the virtuous princess (the Queen) was reflecting on the Five Precepts, as soon as the thought of aspiring for a son arose, the throne of Sakka, King of Devas, became hot and trembled.

Then, Sakka, reflecting on the cause of the throne's heat and knowing the reason, thought, "I will grant a son to the virtuous princess." He came through the air, stood before the Queen, and asked, "Queen, what boon do you ask for?" "Great King, I desire a son," she replied. "Queen, I shall give you a son; do not worry," he said. He returned to the celestial realm and reflected, "Is there any deva here whose lifespan is exhausted?" Knowing that "This Mahāpaduma Deva is about to pass away from this realm to be reborn in a higher celestial realm," he went to that deva's mansion and pleaded, "Dear Mahāpaduma, please go to the human world." The deva replied, "Great King, do not say so; the human world is loathsome." Sakka said, "Dear son, you came to be here because you performed merit in the human world; you must fulfill the perfections (pāramīs) while staying in that very human world. Go, dear son." "Great King, dwelling in a womb is very painful; I cannot live there," he said. Sakka replied, "Dear son, what will happen to you by dwelling in a womb? Did you not perform such kamma in the past..."
71:
“Dear son, what benefit is there for you to stay in a mother's womb? For that reason alone, you have performed a deed. In such a way that you will be born only in the interior of a lotus, go, dear son, in that manner.” When spoken to repeatedly, he consented.

Then, the deity Mahāpaduma, passing away from the deva world, was reborn in the interior of a lotus in a stone-slab pond in the garden of the King of Bārāṇasī. On that night, at dawn, the Chief Queen, surrounded by twenty thousand women, went to the garden and had a dream as if she had obtained a son in the interior of a lotus in the stone-slab pond. When the night had brightened, she, observing the precepts, went to that garden just as she had dreamed and saw a single lotus flower. That lotus was neither on the shore nor in deep water. As soon as she saw it, motherly love for the child arose in her. She herself entered the water and took the flower. As soon as the flower was taken, the petals bloomed. In the center of that flower, she saw a child like a cast golden statue. Upon seeing him, she cried out, “I have obtained a son!” The multitude of people uttered thousands of cheers (Sādhukāra) and sent word to the King.

When the King heard this, he asked, “Where was he found?” and upon hearing the location, he said, “The garden, the pond, and the lotus are all our domain. Therefore, because he was born in our domain, this son shall be named Khettaja.” He had him brought into the city and appointed twenty thousand women to perform the duties of nurses. Whichever woman, knowing the prince's desire, fed him whatever food he craved, she received a thousand pieces of money. The whole city of Bārāṇasī was stirred, and all the people sent thousands of gifts to the prince. The prince, being brought various foods and repeatedly told, “Eat this, consume that,” felt oppressed by the food and became weary. He went to the city gate and played with lacquered balls.

At that time, a certain Paccekabuddha was residing in Isipatana, depending on Bārāṇasī. That Paccekabuddha, having risen early and performed all duties such as cleaning the monastery, bodily hygiene, and reflection, emerged from seclusion and reflected, “Where shall I go for alms today?” Seeing the prince's prosperity, he investigated, “What deed did this youth perform in the past?” He realized, “He offered alms-food to a Paccekabuddha like me and made four aspirations. Among those four, three have been fulfilled, but one is not yet fulfilled. I will show him an object of contemplation by some means.” Thinking thus, he went to the prince's presence on his alms round. Seeing him, the prince said, “O monk, do not come here; these people will say to you too, ‘Eat this, consume that.’” With just that one word, the Paccekabuddha turned back from there.
72:
(The Paccekabuddha) turned back and entered his own dwelling. The prince said to his attendants, “This monk turned back as soon as I spoke; is he perhaps angry with me?” Then, although they said, “O Lord, those who have gone forth are not prone to anger; they subsist on whatever is given by others with a clear mind,” the prince thought, “This monk must surely be angry with me; I will ask for his forgiveness.” Having informed his parents, he mounted an elephant and went to Isipatana with great royal majesty.

Seeing a herd of deer, he asked, “What are these called?” They replied, “Lord, these are called deer.” He asked, “Are there people who look after them, saying, ‘Eat this snack, eat this food, taste this lickable food’?” They replied, “Lord, there is no one who feeds them. They live wherever grass and water are easy to find.”

The prince took this as an object of reflection: “Just as these deer live wherever they wish without guardians, when shall I also live like this?” The Paccekabuddha, knowing his coming, swept the dwelling area, the path, and the walkway (caṅkama) to make them smooth. He walked on the walkway once or twice to show his footprints, swept the day-quarters and the leaf-hut to make them smooth, showed the footprints entering but did not show the footprints exiting, and went elsewhere. 

The prince arrived there, and seeing the area swept and smooth, heard his attendants say, “I think the Paccekabuddha lives here.” He said, “In the morning, that monk seemed angry; now, seeing his place trampled by elephants and horses, he might become even more angry. You all stay right here.” Descending from the elephant's back, he entered the dwelling alone. Seeing the footprints in the well-swept place, starting with the duties, he thought, “This monk, while walking here, did not think of trade or agriculture; surely, I think he thought only of his own benefit.” With a clear mind, he ascended the walkway, discarded many worldly thoughts, sat on a stone slab, and with a concentrated mind, entered the leaf-hut. While practicing insight (vipassanā), he attained the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha (Paccekabodhi-ñāṇa). As before, when the chaplain (purohita) asked about his meditation subject, he sat in the air and spoke this verse:

“Like a deer in the forest that goes unfettered to its desired grazing ground,
So the wise person, seeing that lack of fetters,
Should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.”

In that verse, ‘migo’ refers to two types: the eṇī-deer and the pasada-deer. Alternatively, although the name ‘migo’ refers to all four-footed animals living in the forest, in this verse, the pasada-deer is intended. ‘Araññamhi’ refers to the area excluding the village and its precincts, but in this verse, the garden is intended. Therefore, it means ‘in the garden’. ‘Yathā’ means ‘similarly’. ‘Abaddho’ shows grazing freely without being tied by ropes and so on. ‘Yenicchakaṃ’ means going to various directions as one wishes.
73:
“Just as a deer in the forest, being unbound, goes wherever it desires for its pasture, so a wise person, looking for independence, should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.”

In that verse, ‘migo’ (deer) refers to two types: the eṇī-deer and the pasada-deer. Alternatively, it is a general term for all four-footed creatures living in the forest. In this context, however, the pasada-deer is intended. ‘Araññamhi’ (in the forest) refers to the area remaining after excluding the village and its surroundings; here, however, a garden is intended, thus it means ‘in the garden’. ‘Yathā’ is used in the sense of comparison. ‘Abaddho’ (unbound) means being free from bonds such as ropes, thereby illustrating free movement. ‘Yenicchakaṃ gacchati gocarāya’ means that to whichever direction it wishes to go, it goes to that direction for its pasture.

This matter was also taught in detail by the Blessed One as follows: “Monks, for example, a forest deer wandering in the woods and groves goes freely, stands freely, sits freely, and lies down freely. Why is that? Monks, it is because it has not come within the range of the hunter. In the same way, monks, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures... enters and dwells in the first jhāna. Monks, this monk is said to have blinded Māra, destroyed the eye of Māra, and gone to a place where the Evil One cannot see.” This should be understood in detail.

‘Viññū naro’ means a wise person. ‘Seritaṃ’ refers to independence from others in connection with living according to one's own will. Just as a deer in the forest, being unbound, goes for pasture by whatever path it desires, so too, the wise person, aspiring for what they desire—thinking, ‘How good it would be if I could live like this, having cut the bond of craving’—should wander alone.
74:
‘Viññū naro’ means a wise man. ‘Seritaṃ’ means acting according to one's own will, independence from others. ‘Pekkhamāno’ means contemplating with the eye of wisdom. Alternatively, there are ‘dhamma-serita’ and ‘puggala-serita’. Indeed, supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma) are called ‘serino’ (free) because they do not follow the power of defilements; the persons possessed of those states are also free, and the description of their state is ‘serita’ (freedom). Contemplating that freedom is what is meant. What is being said? “Just as a deer in the forest, unbound, goes wherever it desires for its pasture, when shall I too go in such a way?” Thus, I, who was bound by all of you standing around me here and there and unable to go where I desired, saw the disadvantage in not being able to go where I desired and the advantage in going where I desired, and gradually brought Samatha and Vipassanā to fulfillment. From that, I attained Paccekabodhi. Therefore, another wise and clever man, looking for independence, should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn. The rest should be understood in the same manner as already stated.

## The Commentary on the Verse of the Forest Deer is Finished.

What is the origin of the verse beginning with ‘Āmantanā hoti’? In the past, there was a king named Ekavajjika Brahmadatta who was of a gentle nature. Whenever the ministers wished to consult with him on matters, whether appropriate or inappropriate, they would take him aside individually to a secluded place. One day, when he had gone to take a nap during the day, a certain minister requested to go to a secluded place, saying, “Sire, I have a matter that should be heard.” The king arose and went. Again, one minister made a request while the king was sitting in the great assembly, another while on the back of an elephant, another on the back of a horse, another in a golden chariot, and another while he was going to the garden sitting in a palanquin. The king would descend from those places and go to a secluded spot. Another made a request while the king was traveling through the countryside; having heard that minister's words, the king descended from the elephant and went to a secluded spot. In this way, becoming weary of those ministers, he went forth as a monk. The ministers grew in power through their authority. One of them went and said to the king, “Great King, give me such-and-such a district.” The king said, “A minister named so-and-so is enjoying that district.” Disregarding the king's words, that minister thought, “I will go and take that district and enjoy it,” and having gone there and quarreled, both ministers came back to the king and reported each other's faults. The king thought, “It is no longer possible to satisfy these people.”
75:
"Please give me the district of this name," he said. Although the King of Bārāṇasī said, "That district is being enjoyed by a minister of this name," that minister did not heed the King's words. Thinking, "I will go and take that district for myself," he went to that district and a conflict broke out. Then, both ministers came to the King and accused each other of faults. The King thought, "I am unable to satisfy these ministers," and seeing the danger in their greed, he developed insight (vipassanā) and realized Paccekasambodhi. That Paccekabuddha then uttered this inspired verse in the same manner as before:

"In the midst of companions, there is calling; in staying, in standing, in going, and in wandering. Looking for the freedom that is not coveted by others, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn."

The meaning of that verse is: For one living in the midst of companions, there is calling or requesting in various ways such as, "Listen to this word of mine," or "Give me this object," whether during daytime sleep (staying), in a place where many people gather (standing), when going to a garden (going), or when wandering through the countryside (wandering). Therefore, becoming weary of such requests, and seeing the state of a monk—which is frequented by the noble ones, brings many benefits, is purely blissful, yet is not desired by the base who are overcome by greed—and seeing the freedom of living according to one's own will through the power of a person of Dhamma without being under the control of others, he began insight and gradually attained Paccekasambodhi. The rest is as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Āmantanā Verse is finished.

How did the verse "Khiḍḍā rati" arise? In the city of Bārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta who had an only son. That son was dear to him, pleasing, and as precious as his own life. The king used to hold his son in all four postures. One day, when going to the garden, he left the son behind. On that very day, the young prince died of a sudden illness. The ministers, thinking, "The King's heart might break due to his love for his son," cremated the prince without informing the King. The King, intoxicated with liquor in the garden, did not remember his son; likewise on the second day during bathing and meal times. Then, while sitting after a meal, he remembered and said, "Bring my son to me." The ministers informed him of the event in a suitable manner. Then, overcome by grief, the King sat and reflected wisely: "When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises." Thus, contemplating Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) in forward and reverse order, he realized Paccekabodhi. The rest is similar to what was said in the verse on association (saṃsagga), so only the explanation of the verse's meaning will be presented.

"In the midst of companions, there is play and delight in the five cords of sensual pleasure. There is great affection for sons and daughters. Loathing the separation from the beloved, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn," he declared. In that verse, it should be understood: "Khiḍḍā" means play. This play is of two kinds: physical and vocal. Physical play includes playing with elephants, horses, chariots, etc. Vocal play includes singing, reciting verses, making a drum-sound with the mouth, etc. "Rati" means delight in the five cords of sensual pleasure. "Vipula" (great) refers to affection that reaches the bone marrow and pervades the entire body. The rest is clear. The connection (anusandhi) in this verse should be understood in the same way as stated in the Saṃsagga verse. In the remaining verses, everything should be understood in the same way.

## The Commentary on the Khiḍḍā-rati Verse is finished.
76:
In explaining the meaning, "Khiḍḍā" means play. This play is of two kinds: physical (kāyika) and vocal (vācasika). Among these, physical play means playing with elephants, horses, chariots, bows, swords, and so on. Vocal play means singing, composing and reciting verses, making a drum-sound with the mouth, and so on. "Rati" means delight in the five cords of sensual pleasure. "Vipula" means pervasiveness throughout the whole body, reaching even to the bone marrow. The rest is quite clear. The connection in this verse should be understood in the same way as stated in the "Saṃsagga Verse." Hereafter, everything should be understood in the same way.

## The Commentary on the Khiḍḍā-rati Verse is finished.

How did the verse "Cātuddiso" arise? Long ago, during the dispensation of the Blessed Kassapa Buddha, five future Paccekabuddhas went forth as monks and, having fulfilled the practice of going and returning (gatapaccāgatavatta) for twenty thousand years, were reborn in the celestial realm. When they passed away from there, the eldest among them became the King of Bārāṇasī, and the others became ordinary kings. Those four kings also learned meditation subjects, renounced their kingdoms, went forth, and gradually became Paccekabuddhas. While residing in the Nandamūlaka Cave, they emerged from meditative attainment one day. Just as described in the "Vaṃsakaḷīra Verse," they reflected on their own past deeds and their companions, and sought an opportunity to present an object of contemplation to the King of Bārāṇasī by means of a stratagem.

That King used to be terrified three times a night, crying out in fear and running about on the palace terrace. Although the chaplain priest (purohita) rose early and asked if he had slept well, the King replied, "Teacher, where could there be peaceful sleep for me?" and told him the whole story. The chaplain thought, "This illness cannot be cured by any medical treatment such as emetics or purgatives; however, an opportunity for my own gain has arisen." Thinking thus, he frightened the King even more, saying, "Great King, this terror is a premonitory sign of the loss of your kingdom or a danger to your life." To appease that danger, he urged the King to perform a sacrifice, saying, "A sacrifice must be performed by giving so many elephants, horses, chariots, etc., and gold and silver as a religious gift."

Then, the Paccekabuddhas, seeing the many thousands of living beings being gathered for the sacrifice, thought, "If this deed is done, it will be difficult for the King to understand the Dhamma. Let us go and see him beforehand." Thinking thus, they arrived as described in the "Vaṃsakaḷīra Verse" and, while wandering for alms, walked in order through the palace courtyard. The King, standing at the window and looking at the courtyard, saw them. As soon as he saw them, loving-kindness (mettā) arose within the King.
77:
The King of Bārāṇasī saw the Paccekabuddhas. As soon as he saw them, affection arose in him. Then, he had them invited and seated on the seats prepared in the open air, and respectfully served them food. When the meal was finished, he asked, "Venerable sirs, who are you?" "Great King, we are called Cātuddisā," they replied. "Venerable sirs, what is the meaning of the name Cātuddisā?" he asked. "Great King, in any of the four directions, there is no danger or mental terror for us," they said. "Venerable sirs, why does that danger not occur to you?" he asked again. "Great King, we develop loving-kindness (mettā), we develop compassion (karuṇā), we develop sympathetic joy (muditā), and we develop equanimity (upekkhā). Therefore, that danger does not occur to us," they said, and rising from their seats, they went to their own dwelling.

Then the King thought, "These ascetics say that by developing mettā and so on, danger does not occur. The Brahmins, however, praise the killing of many thousands of living beings. Whose word is true?" Then it occurred to him: "The ascetics wash away impurity with purity. The Brahmins wash away impurity with impurity. It is not possible to wash away impurity with impurity. Only the word of the ascetics is true." The King, by way of "May all beings be happy" and so on, developed the four Brahma-vihāras. With a mind pervading with welfare, he ordered his ministers, "Release all living beings. Let them drink cool water, let them eat green grass, and let a cool breeze blow upon them." The ministers did as commanded.

Then the King, thinking, "I have been freed from evil kamma through the words of good friends (kalyāṇamitta)," practiced insight (vipassanā) while sitting right there and realized the knowledge of Paccekabodhi. When the ministers said at mealtime, "Great King, it is time to eat; please have your meal," he replied, "I am no longer a king," and after saying everything as before, he uttered this verse of inspired utterance (udāna):

"He is one of the four directions and is without resentment,
Being content with whatever comes his way,
Enduring dangers and being undaunted,
One should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn."

In that verse, "cātuddiso" means one who dwells happily as he wishes in the four directions. Alternatively, by way of "pervading one direction and dwelling" and so forth, he is "cātuddiso" because he possesses the four directions pervaded by the development of the Brahma-vihāras. In any of those directions...
78:
Because he is not struck by fear toward living beings or formations (saṅkhāra), he is "appaṭigho" (without resentment). "Santuassamāno" means one who is content by virtue of the twelvefold contentment. "Itarītarena" means with whatever requisites, whether high or low. In the phrase "parissayānaṃ sahitā achambhī," "parissaya" (danger/peril) is so called because it causes the body and mind to decline, or because it causes prosperity (sampatti) to diminish, or because it arises depending on that body and mind. It is a designation for external dangers such as lions and tigers, and internal dangers such as sensual desire (kāmacchanda) and other afflictions of body and mind. Because he endures those dangers through patient endurance (adhivāsana-khanti) and through qualities such as energy (vīriya), he is "parissayānaṃ sahitā." Because he is without the fear that causes the body to tremble, he is "achambhī."

What is meant is this: Just like those four ascetics, being content with even a small amount of requisites, established in contentment which is the proximate cause of practice, he becomes "cātuddisa" (one who can live as he wishes in the four directions) by developing meditations such as mettā in the four directions. He is also "appaṭigho" because he is free from the fear that strikes at beings and formations. Because he is cātuddisa, he is one who can endure the aforementioned dangers, and because he is appaṭigho, he is also one who does not tremble (achambhī). Thus, seeing the benefits of the practice and practicing properly, he attained Paccekabodhi knowledge. Or else, knowing that by being content with few requisites like those ascetics, one becomes cātuddisa as described, and aspiring to such a state of cātuddisa, he practiced properly and attained [Paccekabodhi]. Therefore, if another person also aspires to such a position, they should become an endurer of dangers through being cātuddisa, and be undaunted through being appaṭigho, and wander alone like a rhinoceros horn. The rest is as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Cātuddisa Verse is Finished.

What is the origin (uppatti) of the verse "Dussangaha"? It is said that the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī passed away. Then, after the days of mourning had passed, one day the ministers requested, "Great King, for kings, a chief queen is certainly needed for various duties. It would be good, Your Majesty, if you brought another queen." The King said, "If that is so, friends, find one." While searching, they found that in a neighboring kingdom, the king had died and the queen was ruling the country. She was pregnant. The ministers, thinking "This queen is suitable for our king," made a request. She said, "A pregnant woman is not pleasing to people. If you can wait until I give birth, let it be so; if not, look for someone else." The ministers reported this to the King. The King said, "Even if she is pregnant, bring her." They brought her. The King consecrated her, gave her all the enjoyments of a queen, and honored her attendants with gifts. In due time, the queen gave birth to a son. The King treated the boy like his own heart's blood, carrying him on his shoulder and holding him in his lap at all times. The queen's attendants thought, "The King is excessively favoring the prince. The minds of kings are of a nature to be very affectionate. Now we shall destroy [the bond] to separate the prince [from the King]." Then, to the prince, [they said], "Prince, you are the son of our King..."
79:
(The King) supported (the queen's attendants) with various kinds of gifts. In due time, the queen gave birth to a son. The King treated the child as if he were his own son, keeping him on his shoulder and in his lap during all activities. Then, the queen's attendants and servants thought: "The King supports the prince excessively. The hearts of kings are very trusting. Let us now cause a rift (between the King and the prince)."

Thereafter, they said to the prince: "Dear child, you are the son of our king, not the son of this king. Do not place your trust in this king."

Then the prince, even when called by the King saying "Come, dear son," or even when pulled by the hand, did not approach the King as before. When the King investigated, "What is the meaning of this behavior?" and learned the reason, he thought: "Friends, even though I have supported these people in this way, they are of a repulsive nature." Feeling weary, he renounced the kingship and became a monk. Hearing that "The King has become a monk," many ministers and attendants also became monks. Knowing that "The King has become a monk along with his retinue," people offered excellent requisites.

The King (now a monk) had the excellent requisites distributed according to seniority. In doing so, the monks who received good items were pleased. The other monks grumbled: "While we perform all duties such as sweeping the monastery grounds and so forth, we receive only coarse food and worn-out robes." The King-monk, knowing of this grumbling, thought: "Friends, even when distributed according to seniority, they still grumble. How amazing! This assembly is difficult to support." Taking his bowl and robes, he entered the forest alone, began practicing insight (vipassanā), and realized the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha. When those who arrived asked about his meditation subject, he spoke this verse:

"Some who have gone forth are difficult to support, as are some householders living in homes.
Being free from concern for the children of others, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn."

The meaning of that verse is clear. This is the word-connection (yojanā): Some who have gone forth, overcome by discontent, are difficult to support; likewise are householders living in homes. Loathing this state of being difficult to support, I began practicing insight and attained the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha. The rest should be understood in the same manner as before.

## The Explanation of the Verse on Difficulty of Support is finished.
80:
What is the origin (uppatti) of the verse beginning with "Oropayitvā"? It is said that in the city of Vārāṇasī, a king named Cātumāsika Brahmadatta went to the garden in the first month of the summer (Tagu). Seeing a Koviḷāra tree densely covered with dark green leaves in a pleasant spot, he said, "Prepare my bed at the foot of this Koviḷāra tree," and after enjoying himself in the garden, he slept there in the evening.

Again, in the middle month of summer (Kason, Nayon), he went to the garden. At that time, the Koviḷāra tree was in bloom. He did the same as before. Again, in the last month of summer (Waso), he went again. At that time, the Koviḷāra tree had shed its leaves and was like a dry tree. Even then, without looking at the condition of the tree, he ordered his bed to be prepared in the same place as per his previous habit. Although the ministers knew, they prepared the bed at the foot of that Koviḷāra tree out of fear of the King's command.

After enjoying himself in the garden, while resting there in the evening, the King saw the tree and thought: "Friends, previously this Koviḷāra tree, covered with leaves, was as beautiful to behold as if made of gems. Then, with flowers like coral sprouts placed among branches the color of dark gems, it was glorious and lovely to see. The ground beneath it, strewn with sand like pearls and covered with Koviḷāra flowers fallen from their stalks, was like a red woolen carpet spread out. Now, such a tree stands with only branches remaining, like a dry tree. Alas, old age (jarā) has destroyed and oppressed the Koviḷāra tree."

He reflected: "If even non-sentient things (anupādinnaka) are thus oppressed by old age, what need is there to mention sentient things (upādinnaka)?" and he gained the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā). Based on that perception of impermanence, while contemplating all conditioned things (saṅkhāra) as suffering (dukkha) and non-self (anatta), he aspired: "Alas, if only I could be like the Koviḷāra tree that has shed its leaves, free from the marks of a householder." Gradually, while lying on his right side on that very bed, he realized the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha. Then, at the time of returning, when the ministers said, "Great King, it is time to go," he said, "I am no longer a king," and so on, and spoke this verse in the same manner as before:

"Having cast off the marks of a householder, like a Koviḷāra tree that has shed its leaves;
Having cut the bonds of a householder, the hero should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn."

In that verse, "Oropayitvā" means having removed. "Gihi-byañjanāni" refers to hair, beard, white clothes, ornaments, flowers, scents, ointments, wife, children, female slaves, male slaves, and so on. For these things... (End of page)
81:
They manifest the state of a layman; therefore, they are called "layman's signs" (gihibyañjanāni). "Sañchinnapatto" means having fallen leaves. "Chetvāna" means having cut with the knowledge of the Path (magga-ñāṇa). "Vīro" means one endowed with Path-energy (magga-vīriya). "Gihibandhanāni" means the bonds of sensual desire (kāma-bandhanāni). Indeed, the cords of sensual pleasure are the bonds of laypeople. This is the meaning of the words. "Ayaṃ pana adhippāyo"—this is the intended meaning: "Oh, would that I too, having discarded the signs of a layman, might be like a koviḷāra tree with fallen leaves!" Thinking thus, he began insight meditation (vipassanā) and attained the knowledge of a Private Buddha (paccekabodhi-ñāṇa). The rest of the meaning should be understood in the same way as the previous method.

## The Explanation of the Koviḷāra Verse is finished. The First Group is concluded.

45-46. What is the origin (uppatti) of the verse beginning with "Sace labhetha"? It is said that formerly, during the dispensation of the Blessed Kassapa Buddha, two future Private Buddhas (paccekabodhisattas) went forth as monks and, having fulfilled the duty of going and returning (gatapaccāgatavatta) for twenty thousand years, were reborn in the celestial world. When they passed away from that celestial world, the elder of them became the son of the King of Bārāṇasī, and the younger became the son of the chaplain (purohita). Having taken conception on the very same day and having emerged from their mothers' wombs on the very same day, they became childhood friends playing together in the dust. The chaplain's son was wise. He said to the prince, "Friend, you will obtain the kingship upon the passing of your father, and I shall obtain the position of chaplain.
