"Appāṇake" means in water that is without life, or in a great body of water where there are no living beings that would die by being covered by the milk-rice. This was said for the sake of protecting the grass and the living beings, along with the creatures that depend on the grass.
139:
The milk-rice makes a sound like 'cicciṭa'. 'Saṃdhūpāyati' means smoking all around. 'Sampadhūpāyati' means smoking excessively in the same manner. Why did this happen? It was due to the majesty of the Blessed One, not the majesty of the water, nor the milk-rice, nor the Brahmin, nor other devas, yakkhas, and so forth. Indeed, the Blessed One performed this determination (adhiṭṭhāna) to cause spiritual urgency (saṃvega) in the Brahmin Kasi Bhāradvāja. The phrase 'Seyyathāpi nāma' is merely for illustrating a simile. 'Yathā phālo' means just like a heated plowshare; this is all that is meant. He was agitated in mind and his body was covered in horripilation. It is said that the ninety-nine thousand pores on his body stood on end like ruby nails and ivory pegs driven into a golden wall. The rest is clear.

Prostrating at the feet of the Blessed One and greatly rejoicing in the Dhamma teaching, he said to the Blessed One: 'Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama!' Here, the word 'Abhikkanta' is used in the sense of great rejoicing. Its detailed explanation will appear in the commentary on the Maṅgala Sutta. Since it is in the sense of rejoicing, it should be understood as meaning 'Sadhu, Sadhu, Master Gotama'.

'In fear, anger, praise, haste, wonder, joy, grief, and devotion, the wise should use repetition (āmeḍita).'

According to this rule, it should be understood that the word 'Abhikkanta' is spoken twice here due to the power of devotion and praise. Alternatively, 'Abhikkanta' means extremely desirable, extremely pleasing, extremely beautiful, and extremely excellent.

Of these two 'Abhikkanta' words, with one he praises the teaching, and with the other he praises his own devotion. The meaning here is: 'Master Gotama, this Dhamma teaching of Master Gotama is excellent; my devotion that has arisen based on Master Gotama's Dhamma teaching is also excellent.' Or, he praises the words of the Blessed One with reference to two meanings: Master Gotama's words are excellent because they destroy faults and because they lead to the attainment of virtues. Similarly, they are excellent because they generate faith, generate wisdom, are full of meaning, are full of phrasing, have clear words, have deep meaning, are pleasant to the ear, reach the heart, do not exalt oneself, do not disparage others, are cool with compassion, are pure with wisdom, are delightful upon contact, can withstand scrutiny, are pleasant to hear, and have benefits that can be investigated, and so forth.
140:
Furthermore, he praises the teaching itself with four similes. Among those similes, 'Nikkujjita' refers to a pot or similar object placed face down. 'Ukkujjeyya' means to set it face up. 'Paṭicchanna' refers to an object covered with grass, leaves, and so forth. 'Vivareyya' means to uncover it. 'Mūḷha' refers to one who is lost. 'Maggaṃ ācikkheyya' means to take one by the hand and say, 'This is the path.' 'Andhakāre' refers to the darkness endowed with four factors caused by the forest and thick clouds at midnight on the fourteenth day of the waning moon. This is the initial meaning of the words.

This is the application of the meaning: Just as someone might set upright what was overturned, so too, by raising me up from the false Dhamma (asaddhamma) in which I had fallen, having turned my back on the true Dhamma (saddhamma); just as one might reveal what was concealed, so too, by revealing the Dispensation (Sāsana) which had been covered by the thicket of wrong views since the disappearance of the Dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa; just as one might point out the path to one who is lost, so too, by pointing out the right path to heaven and Nibbāna to me who had reached the wrong path (kummagga); just as one might hold up an oil lamp in the darkness, so too, for me who was submerged in the darkness of delusion (moha) and could not see the nature of the Jewels such as the Buddha, by holding up the lamp of the teaching which destroys the darkness of delusion that concealed those Jewels—Master Gotama has revealed the Dhamma in many ways, as it has been taught by Master Gotama through these various methods.

In another way, this Dhamma is like setting upright what was overturned because, by showing the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca), it abandons the perversion (vipallāsa) of perceiving the foul (asubha) as 'beautiful' (subha). It is like revealing what was concealed because, by showing the truth of the origin (samudaya-sacca), it abandons the perversion of perceiving suffering (dukkha) as 'happiness' (sukha). It is like pointing out the path to one who is lost because, by showing the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca), it abandons the perversion of perceiving the impermanent (anicca) as 'permanent' (nicca). It is like lighting a lamp in the darkness because, by showing the truth of the path (magga-sacca), it abandons the perversion of perceiving non-self (anatta) as 'self' (atta). Therefore, it is revealed as: 'Just as if one were to set upright what was overturned... so that those with eyes might see forms'.

In this context, the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) is revealed through faith and bodily restraint, and so forth. The aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha) is revealed through wisdom. The aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha) is revealed through shame (hiri) and fear (ottappa), and so forth. Cessation (nirodha) is revealed through Nibbāna, the end of yokes. Thus, the two Noble Truths—the Noble Path consisting of the three aggregates and Cessation—are revealed in their essence. Among them, since the Path is the opposite of the Origin, and Cessation is the opposite of Suffering, the other two Truths are also revealed by way of opposition. Thus, in this way, the Four Noble Truths are revealed. Therefore, it should be understood that the Dhamma has been revealed in many ways.
141: In the phrases beginning with 'Esāhaṃ', 'Eso ahaṃ' is expressed as 'Esāhaṃ'. Regarding 'Saraṇaṃ gacchāmi' (I go for refuge), although he had already taken refuge by prostrating at the feet, he now speaks to formally undertake it by word of mouth. Alternatively, having taken refuge in the Buddha alone through prostration, he now speaks to approach the remaining Dhamma and Saṅgha as well, starting with the Buddha. 'Ajjatagge' means 'starting from today'. There is also a reading 'Ajjadagge'; the letter 'da' is a euphonic sandhi-consonant. It means 'starting from today'. 'Pāṇupetaṃ' means 'endowed with life' (as long as life lasts). It means, 'May the Blessed Gotama recognize me as one who has gone for refuge through the three refuges, having no other teacher, for as long as my life lasts.' By this much, this brahmin shows the practice that is in accordance with what he has heard. Alternatively, by the words 'Nikkujjita' and so on, the perfection of the Teacher, the Blessed One, is shown; and by these words 'Esāhaṃ' and so on, the perfection of the disciple is shown. Or, by those words, the acquisition of wisdom is shown, and by these words, the acquisition of faith is shown. Now, the wise person who has thus acquired faith, desiring to do what should be done, requests the Blessed One, saying 'Labheyyāhaṃ' (May I obtain). In that context, with a mind greatly inspired by the Blessed One’s psychic powers and so forth, he reflects, 'Even the Blessed One renounced the sovereignty of a Universal Monarch to go forth; what need is there to speak of me?' and requests the state of a monk out of faith. In making that request, desiring to fulfill the practice completely, he aspires for the higher ordination (upasampadā) through wisdom. The remaining words are clear. In the phrases beginning with 'Eko vūpakaṭṭho', 'Eko' (alone) means being alone through physical seclusion (kāya-viveka). 'Vūpakaṭṭho' (secluded) means resorting to seclusion through mental seclusion (citta-viveka). 'Appamatto' (heedful) means being diligent by not abandoning mindfulness in the meditation subject. 'Ātāpī' (ardent) means having effort that burns away the defilements, known as bodily and mental energy. 'Pahitatto' (resolute) means dwelling in one of the postures with a mind directed towards Nibbāna, without regard for body or life. 'Na cirasseva' (before long) is said starting from the time of his going forth. 'Kulaputtā' (sons of good family) are of two kinds: sons of good family by birth (jāti-kulaputta) and sons of good family by conduct (ācāra-kulaputta). This brahmin is a son of good family in both ways. 'Agārasmā' means 'from home'. The work of supporting a household, such as farming and cattle-breeding, which is for the benefit of those living in a house, is called 'āgāriya'. Because such work does not exist there, it is called 'anagāriya' (homelessness); this is a designation for the state of a monk. 'Pabbajanti' means they approach or draw near. 'Tadanuttaraṃ' means that supreme state of a monk. 'Brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ' means the fruit of Arahantship, which is the culmination of the noble holy life of the Path. For the sake of that fruit of Arahantship, sons of good family go forth. 'Diṭṭေva dhamme' means in this very existence (this life). 'Sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā' means having realized for oneself through wisdom and knowing without any other cause. 'Upasampajja vihāsီ' means having attained or fulfilled it, he dwelled. While dwelling thus, 'Birth is exhausted... etc... he understood.' By this word 'abbhaññāsi', his stage of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā) is shown.
142:
When asked, "What kind of birth is ceased for him, and how did he know its cessation?"—the answer is: His past birth cannot be ceased because it has already ceased in the past; his future birth cannot be ceased because there is no effort in the future; and his present birth cannot be ceased because it is currently existing. However, that birth which would have arisen in the realms of one, four, or five constituents, categorized by one, four, or five aggregates, due to the non-development of the Path—that birth has ceased by reaching the state of non-arising because the Path has been developed. He knows this by reviewing the defilements abandoned through the development of the Path, understanding that even though karma exists when defilements are absent, it will not lead to rebirth in the future.

"Vusitaṃ" means lived, well-lived, performed, practiced, or completed. "Brahmacariyaṃ" refers to the noble practice of the Path. "Kataṃ karaṇီyaṃ" means that the sixteen-fold task—by way of full understanding, abandoning, realizing, and developing the four truths through the four paths—has been completed. "Nāparaṃ itthattāya" means that now there is no further development of the Path for such a state, for these sixteen tasks, or for the destruction of defilements. Alternatively, "itthattāya" means from this state; that is, there is no further continuum of aggregates beyond this present continuum of aggregates of such a kind. He understood that these five aggregates remain fully understood, like a tree with its roots cut.

"Aññataro" means one person. The Venerable Bhāradvāja became one among the Arahants. The meaning here is that the Venerable Bhāradvāja became one included among the Great Disciples.

## In the Khuddaka Commentary named Paramatthajotikā,
## the Explanation of the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is finished.

## 5. Cunda Sutta Vaṇṇanā

"Pucchāmi muniṃ pahūtapaññaṃ" and so forth is the Cunda Sutta. What is its origin? Briefly, among the four types of origins—one's own inclination (attajjhāsaya), another's inclination (parajjhāsaya), a specific event (aṭṭhuppatti), and based on a question (pucchāvasika)—the origin of this sutta is "pucchāvasika," arising because of a question. In detail, once the Blessed One, while wandering among the Mallas with a large community of monks, arrived at Pāvā. There, the Blessed One stayed in the mango grove of Cunda, the smith's son. From here onwards, "Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, together with the community of monks, where..."
143:
“He approached the house of Cunda the smith's son and sat on the prepared seat.” This statement should be understood in detail according to the method mentioned in the Sutta.

While the Blessed One was seated with the Saṅgha of monks, Cunda the smith's son, while serving the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, offered golden bowls to the monks for taking curries and so on. Before the training rule was prescribed, some monks accepted the golden bowls, while others did not. As for the Blessed One, he had only his own stone bowl; Buddhas do not accept a second bowl. Among those monks, a certain wicked monk, with a mind of theft, tucked a golden bowl worth a thousand into the fold of his robe, which had come to him for his meal. After serving and washing his hands and feet, Cunda, while paying homage to the Blessed One and looking at the Saṅgha of monks, saw that monk. Even though he saw him, out of respect for the Blessed One and the elders, and thinking, “Let there be no grounds for reproach by those of wrong view,” he acted as if he did not see and did not say anything to that monk. Desiring to know, “Are only those endowed with restraint true recluses (samaṇas), or are those with broken restraint also recluses?” he approached the Blessed One in the evening and said, “Pucchāmi muniṃ” (I ask the Sage).

In that verse, the word “Pucchāmi” is according to the method stated in the Niddesa, such as “There are three kinds of questions: the question for clarifying what is not seen,” and so on. The word “Muni” is also according to the method stated in that same Niddesa: “Knowledge is called mona. That wisdom, act of understanding... right view; one endowed with that knowledge is a Sage, one who has attained mona; there are three types of sageliness (moneyya): bodily sageliness,” and so on. The summary here is: requesting permission by saying “Pucchāmi,” he addresses the Blessed One as “Muni.” Words such as “Pahūtapanna” (of great wisdom) are words of praise; with them, he praises the Sage. Among them, “Pahūtapanna” means having extensive wisdom. His wisdom should be known as extensive because it reaches the limit of what is to be known. The two words “Iti Cundo Kammāraputto” are according to the method stated in the Dhaniya Sutta. From this point onwards, without repeating such words and leaving aside all previously mentioned methods, I shall comment only on the methods not yet mentioned.

“Buddha” refers to the third type of Buddha among the three kinds of Buddhas. “Dhammassāmi” (Lord of Dhamma) means the Lord of Dhamma, the Master of Dhamma, the King of Dhamma, the one who has mastery over Dhamma, because he originates the Path-Dhamma, like a father to a son or like a teacher to a student regarding the arts and sciences he has taught. This has also been said—
144:
“For he, Brahmin, is the Blessed One, the originator of the path that had not arisen, the producer of the path that had not been produced, the declarer of the path that had not been declared, the knower of the path, the cognizer of the path, the one skilled in the path. And now the disciples dwell following the path, becoming endowed with it afterwards” (M. Ni. 3.79).

“Vītatanhaṃ” means one whose craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence have departed. “Dvipaduttamaṃ” means the best among bipeds. In this regard, although the Blessed One is not only the best among bipeds, but is indeed the best among all beings—whether footless, bipeds, many-footed... or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient—he is called “best of bipeds” by way of the highest category. For bipeds are the highest among all beings because Wheel-turning Kings, Great Disciples, and Paccekabuddhas arise among them; and when it is said he is the best of them, it is already said that he is the best of all beings.

“Sārathīnaṃ pavaraṃ” (Excellent among charioteers): one who guides is called a “sārathi” (charioteer/tamer); this is a designation for elephant tamers and so on. The Blessed One is excellent among them because he is capable of taming men fit to be tamed with unsurpassed taming.

As the Blessed One said: “Monks, an elephant fit to be tamed, when guided by an elephant tamer, runs in only one direction: east, west, north, or south. Monks, a horse fit to be tamed... a bull fit to be tamed... runs in only one direction. But, monks, a man fit to be tamed, when guided by the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, runs in eight directions: A possessor of forms sees forms; this is the first direction... having attained the cessation of perception and feeling, he dwells; this is the eighth direction” (M. Ni. 3.312).

“Katī” is a word asking about the distinction of meanings. “Loke” means in the world of beings. “Samaṇā” is the indication of the subject being asked. “Ingha” is an indeclinable in the sense of requesting. “Tadingha” means “Therefore, I urge you.” “Brūhi” means “Tell, speak.”

When this was said, the Blessed One, seeing that Cunda the smith's son was not asking a layman's question such as “Venerable Sir, what is wholesome? What is unwholesome?” but was asking a question about recluses, reflected and understood, “He is asking with reference to that wicked monk.” Desiring to show that such a person is not a true recluse but only one by common designation, he said, “There are four recluses.” There, “caturo” is the delimitation of number. “Samaṇā” means:

The Blessed One sometimes teaches the doctrine of recluses to wanderers of other sects, saying, “Many recluses and brahmins have noisy auspicious signs.” Sometimes he teaches worldlings, “Monks, the people know well: ‘Recluse, recluse’.” Sometimes he teaches those in training (sekha), “Monks, in this dispensation, this recluse is the second recluse.” Sometimes he calls an Arahant a recluse, “Because of the destruction of taints, he is called a recluse.” Sometimes he teaches regarding himself, “Monks, this word ‘recluse’ is a name for the Tathāgata.” In this context, however, by the word “katī” and the other three terms found in the Majjhima Nikāya, all noble persons (ariya) and virtuous worldling monks are included; and by the fourth type, the path-polluter monk, he refers to one who is not a recluse and is distinct from the other three types...
145:
The Blessed One sometimes speaks of sectarians (titthiyas) using the term 'samaṇa'. For instance, the Blessed One said: "There are those many samaṇas and brahmins who have various practices, curiosities, and auspicious signs." (M. Ni. 1.407). Sometimes he uses the term for worldlings (puthujjanas), as he said: "Monks, the people recognize them as 'samaṇas, samaṇas'." (M. Ni. 1.435). Sometimes he uses it for learners (sekkhas), as he said: "Monks, only here is a samaṇa, here is a second samaṇa." (M. Ni. 1.139, Dī. Ni. 2.214, A. Ni. 4.241). Sometimes he uses it for those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsavas), as he said: "One is a samaṇa because of the destruction of the taints (āsavas)." (M. Ni. 1.438). Sometimes he uses it for himself, as he said: "Monks, 'samaṇa' is a designation for the Tathāgata." (A. Ni. 8.85).

In this verse, however, all noble ones (ariyas) and virtuous worldling monks are included within the first three terms. With the fourth term, the 'Path-corrupter' (maggadūsī), he includes even those who are not true samaṇas but merely have shaven heads and wear the dyed robe, being called 'samaṇa' only by convention; thus he said, "the four samaṇas". "There is no fifth samaṇa" means that in this Dhamma-Vinaya, there is no fifth kind of samaṇa even by convention or by mere claim.

"I shall make them clear to you" means "I shall make those four samaṇas manifest to you". "Sakkhipuṭṭho" means being questioned face-to-face. "Maggajina" (Path-conqueror) means one who has conquered all defilements by means of the Path. "Maggadesaka" (Path-teacher) means one who points out the Path to others. "Magge jīvati" (One who lives in the Path) means that among the seven types of learners (sekkhas), any learner who has not yet completed the dwelling in the Path is said to live in the supramundane Path; also, a virtuous worldling is said to live in the mundane Path. Alternatively, a virtuous worldling should be understood as "living in the Path" because he lives for the sake of the supramundane Path. "Yo ca maggadūsī" (And he who is a Path-corrupter) means an immoral monk who, through a practice that is contrary to the Path—namely, wrong view—is a destroyer of the Path.

When the Blessed One thus pointed out the four samaṇas in brief, Cunda Kammāraputta, being unable to penetrate and understand, "This one is the Maggajina, this one is the Maggadesaka, this one is the Maggejīvī, this one is the Maggadūsī," asked again: "Who is the Maggajina?" In that verse, "Magge jīvati me" means "Tell me of the one who lives in the Path when I have asked". The remaining terms are clear.

Now, the Blessed One, wishing to describe all four samaṇas with four verses, said: "Yo tiṇṇakathaṅkatho visallo" (He who has crossed over doubt, free from the dart). Therein, the phrase "tiṇṇakathaṅkatho visallo" follows the same method as explained in the Uraga Sutta. However, there is this distinction: since in this verse the 'Buddha-samaṇa' is intended by the term 'Maggajina',
146:
he should be understood as "tiṇṇakathaṅkatho" (one who has crossed over doubt) because he has crossed over the ignorance (aññāṇa) that resembles doubt regarding all things through his omniscience.

Indeed, by the method previously mentioned, those who have crossed over doubt such as Stream-enterers up to Paccekabuddhas are, in a figurative sense, "not crossed over doubt" because their power of knowledge is obstructed in matters ranging from the scope of a Once-returner up to the scope of a Buddha. The Blessed One, however, has crossed over doubt in every possible way. "Nibbānābhirato" means one who greatly delights in Nibbāna; it means his mind is always inclined toward Nibbāna by virtue of fruition attainment (phala-samāpatti). The Blessed One is of such a nature. As he said: "Indeed, Aggivessana, at the conclusion of that talk, I settle, steady, unify, and concentrate my mind internally on that same former sign of concentration (Nibbāna)." (M. Ni. 1.387).

"Anānugiddho" means one who does not crave any phenomenon with the greed of craving. "Lokassa sadevakassa netā" (Leader of the world with its devas) means that by teaching the Dhamma in accordance with the inclinations and underlying tendencies of those to be led, and by bringing about the penetration of the Truths for countless devas and humans in many discourses such as the Pārāyana and Mahāsamaya, he is the leader, the guide, the one who delivers, and the one who brings them to the further shore of Nibbāna. "Tādiṃ" means one who is unshakable (tādisa) by the worldly conditions (lokadhamma) of the aforementioned kinds. The rest here is clear.

Thus, the Blessed One, having described the Buddha-samaṇa as "Maggajina" with this verse, now said the verse beginning with "Paramaṃ paramaṃ" to describe the samaṇa whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava). In that verse, "Paramaṃ" refers to Nibbāna, meaning the highest and supreme of all phenomena. "Paraman-ti yodha ñatvā" means having known that Nibbāna as "the supreme" in this Dispensation through the knowledge of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa). "Akkhāti vibhajate idheva dhammaṃ" means he declares the Dhamma of Nibbāna; having penetrated it himself, he makes it manifest to others, saying, "This is Nibbāna". He analyzes the Path Dhamma, saying, "These are the four foundations of mindfulness... the Noble Eightfold Path". Or, with both terms, he declares it with a brief teaching for those of quick intuition (ugghaṭitaññū) and analyzes it with a detailed teaching for those who understand through expansion (vipanñcitaññū). While thus declaring and analyzing, he proclaims with a lion's roar: "Only in this Dispensation is this Dhamma (the path to Nibbāna) found, not outside of here." Therefore, it is said: "Akkhāti vibhajate idheva dhammaṃ". "Taṃ kaṅkhachidaṃ muniṃ anejaṃ" means that sage who, by penetrating the Four Noble Truths, has cut off his own doubts and, through his teaching, cuts off the doubts of others...
147: The Blessed One, who is able to cut off doubts and is called a Muni because he is endowed with the wisdom to be practiced by monks, and is called Aneja because he is free from the agitation of craving, is said to be the second type of monk, the 'Way-shower' (Magga-desī). ## Thus, although he himself produced the unsurpassed path and is the unsurpassed Way-shower in teaching, like a king's messenger or a scribe who reads the writing, he points to the Arahant—who carries out and illuminates his Dispensation—as a 'Way-shower' (Magga-desī). Now, wishing to point out the trainee monk (sekha) and the virtuous worldling monk (sīlavanta-puthujjana), he spoke the verse beginning with 'Who in the path of Dhamma' (Yo dhammapade). In that verse, the word-commentary is clear. As for the meaning-commentary: In the well-expounded Dhamma, which is called Dhamma-pada because it is the foundation for the Dhamma of Nibbāna, taught without approaching the two extremes, or taught in various ways such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) according to the inclinations [of beings]—the monk who lives by the path because his task of the path is not yet finished though he is endowed with the path, who is restrained by the restraint of virtue, who is mindful with well-established mindfulness in the body etc., who is faultless because of the absence of even the slightest flaw, and who cultivates the faultless practices leading to Nibbāna known as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) starting from the knowledge of dissolution (bhaṅga-ñāṇa)—that monk is called the third type of monk, the 'Way-liver' (Magga-jīvī). ## Thus, having pointed out the trainee monk and the virtuous worldling monk as 'Way-liver' (Magga-jīvī) with this verse, the Blessed One now, wishing to point out the one who is a monk in name only, with a shaven head and merely carrying the dyed robe around the neck, spoke the verse beginning with 'Having made a cover' (Chadanaṃ katvāna). There, 'having made a cover' (chadanaṃ katvāna) means having taken a suitable appearance, having assumed the guise, or wearing the marks [of a monk]. 'Of the well-vowed' (suvattānaṃ) means of the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and their disciples. Because those noble ones have excellent vows, they are called 'well-vowed' (suvatta). 'Intruder' (pakkhandī) means one who jumps in or enters within. Just as one might use a cover of grass or leaves to hide excrement, a monk of bad conduct (dussīla) makes a cover of the 'well-vowed' (the monastic guise) to hide his own bad conduct, and intrudes into the midst of monks saying, 'I too am a monk.' When gains are given with the words, 'This should be taken by a monk of such-and-such seniority,' he intrudes to take the gain, saying, 'I have such-and-such seniority.' Therefore, it is said, 'Having made a cover, he intrudes among the well-vowed.' He is called a 'corrupter of families' (kula-dūsaka) because he destroys the faith of the four classes [of people] such as kings through unsuitable conduct. 'Impudent' (pagabbha) means endowed with eight kinds of bodily impudence, four kinds of verbal impudence, and many kinds of mental impudence. This is the summary here; the detail will be explained in the commentary on the Metta Sutta. He is also called 'deceitful' (māyāvī) because he is endowed with deceit (māyā), which has the characteristic of hiding what has been done. He is called 'unrestrained' (asaññata) because of the absence of restraint in virtue. He is called 'chaff' (palāpa) because he is like empty rice husks. For example, just as chaff appears like a grain of rice from the outside due to the husk, even though it is empty of rice inside, so too some in this Dispensation appear like a good monk from the outside by assuming the guise of the virtuous, even though they are empty of virtues such as morality inside. Because he is thus like chaff, he is called 'chaff' (palāpa).
148: He is called 'deceitful' (māyāvī) because he is endowed with deceit (māyā), which has the characteristic of hiding what has been done. He is called 'unrestrained' (asaññata) because of the absence of restraint in virtue. He is called 'chaff' (palāpa) because he is like empty rice husks. For example, just as chaff appears like a grain of rice from the outside due to the husk, even though it is empty of rice inside, so too in this Dispensation some appear like a good monk from the outside by the guise of a monk—the cover of the well-vowed—even though they are empty of the essence of virtues such as morality inside. Because he is thus like chaff, he is called 'chaff' (palāpa). In the Ānāpānassati Sutta, however, it is taught: 'Monks, this assembly is without chaff, this assembly is free of chaff; it is pure and established in the essence.' In that context, even a virtuous worldling (puthujjana-kalyāṇa) is referred to as 'chaff'. But in this sutta and the Kapila Sutta, it is said: 'Therefore, blow away the chaff, those who are not monks but think themselves monks.' Thus, a monk who has been defeated by a parājika offense is called 'chaff' (palāpa). 'Corrupting the harmonious while wandering in disguise' (patirūpena caraṃ samaggadūsī) means that when a monk wanders making a cover of the well-vowed, people know him as: 'This monk is a forest-dweller, a tree-root-dweller, a rag-robe-wearer, an alms-food-eater, one of few desires, one who is contented.' Such a person, wandering with a suitable, outwardly polished conduct, should be known as a 'Way-corrupter' (Magga-dūsī) because he destroys his own supramundane path and the path to happy destinations for others. ## Thus, having pointed out the person who is a monk in name only and without virtue as a 'Way-corrupter' (Magga-dūsī) with this verse, the Blessed One now, wishing to show their mutual distinctness, spoke the words beginning with 'And these he pierced' (Ete ca paṭivijjhi). The meaning of that verse is: Whatever householder—whether a king, a brahmin, or anyone else—pierces, knows, and realizes these four types of monks through the characteristics mentioned. By merely hearing the characteristics of these four types of monks, he becomes 'one who has heard' (sutavā). Because he has heard those characteristics from the Noble Ones, he is called a 'noble disciple' (ariyasāvaka). By merely knowing those monks as 'this one and that one have such characteristics,' he is called 'wise' (sappañño). Knowing that 'the Way-corrupter taught last is of such a nature, and all the others are not like him,' and seeing thus, even when he sees this evil monk committing such evil [his faith is not destroyed]. The grammatical connection in that verse is: Whatever householder, who is learned, a noble disciple, and wise, pierces these [four types]. While he lives knowing through his wisdom that 'not all monks are of such a nature,' even when he sees an evil monk committing evil deeds, his faith (saddhā) does not diminish and is not destroyed.
149:
Thus, having shown the unmixed nature of those monks by this verse, [the Buddha] now spoke the words "Kathañhi duṭṭhena" and so forth, wishing to praise the Noble Disciple who knows "Not all are like this" even upon seeing [evil]. The connection of these words is as follows: Even upon seeing someone committing evil, knowing that "Not all are like this" is indeed appropriate for a learned Noble Disciple. Why is that? For how could a corrupt person be made equal to one who is not corrupt, or a pure person to one who is impure? The meaning of that verse is: How could a learned and wise Noble Disciple know that the other three types of recluses, who are not corrupt and are pure, are the same as the last type of recluse—the one who is corrupt by the failure of virtue, a destroyer of the Path, impure in bodily conduct and so forth, and a recluse merely by name? At the end of the Sutta, it is not mentioned that the lay follower (Cunda) attained the Path or Fruit. This is because only his doubts were dispelled.

## In the Khuddaka Commentary named Paramatthajotikā,
## the explanation of the Cunda Sutta of the Suttanipāta Commentary is finished.
## 6. Explanation of the Parābhava Sutta

"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Parābhava Sutta. What is the occasion for its arising (uppatti)? It is said that after hearing the Maṅgala Sutta, the deities had this thought: "In the Maṅgala Sutta, while the Blessed One was teaching the progress and safety of beings, He spoke only of prosperity (bhava), not of decline (parābhava). Now, let us ask Him about the decline by which beings deteriorate and perish." Then, on the second day after the Maṅgala Sutta was taught, deities from the ten thousand world systems, wishing to hear the Parābhava Sutta, assembled in this single world system. They created subtle forms so that ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, or even eighty deities could fit into a space the size of the tip of a single hair. Surrounding the Blessed One, who sat on the prepared noble Buddha-seat, outshining all deities, Māras, and Brahmās with His glory and power, they stood there. Then, a certain son of the gods (devaputta), commissioned by Sakka, the king of gods, questioned the Blessed One regarding the problem of decline. Thereupon, the Blessed One spoke this Sutta in response to the question.
150:
In that Sutta, the words "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth were spoken by the Venerable Ānanda. The alternating verses beginning with "Parābhavaṃ purisaṃ" were spoken by the deity. The alternating verses beginning with "Suvijāno bhavaṃ" and the final verse were spoken by the Blessed One. All these together are called the "Parābhava Sutta." Regarding the words "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth in this Sutta, whatever needs to be said will be stated in the explanation of the Maṅgala Sutta.

In the verses beginning with "Parābhavaṃ purisaṃ," the word "parābhavaṃ" means declining or perishing. "Purisaṃ" refers to any being or person. "Mayaṃ pucchāma Gotama" means that the deity, identifying himself along with the other deities and seeking permission, addresses the Blessed One by His clan name. "Bhavaṃ puṭṭhumāgamma" means "We have come from various world systems to question the Blessed One." By these words, he shows respect. "Kiṃ parābhavato mukhaṃ" means "Tell us, who have thus arrived, what is the cause (mukha), what is the door, what is the source, what is the reason for a declining man, by which we may know the man who is in decline?" By this, he asks for the cause of decline of the declining man mentioned in the phrase "parābhavaṃ purisaṃ." For if the cause of decline is known, any declining person can be recognized by that common cause.

Then, in order to make it very clear to the deity, the Blessed One, showing the opposite and using a discourse based on persons (puggalādhiṭṭhāna) to explain the cause of decline, said "Suvijāno bhavaṃ" and so forth. The meaning of that verse is: This man who is prospering and not declining is easy to know (suvijāno); he can be known easily without difficulty or hardship. The man who declines (parābhavati) is also easy to know. How? This man, being a lover of Dhamma (dhamma-kāmo), prospers; he desires, cherishes, longs for, listens to, and practices the Dhamma of the ten wholesome courses of action (dasa-kusalakamma-patha). He is easy to know because he can be recognized by seeing or hearing of that practice. The other one, being a hater of Dhamma (dhamma-dessī), declines; he hates that very Dhamma, does not desire it, does not cherish it, does not long for it, does not listen to it, and does not practice it. He is easy to know because he can be recognized by seeing or hearing of that wrong practice. Thus, it should be understood that the Blessed One, by showing the opposite, showed that in essence, loving the Dhamma is the cause of prosperity, while hating the Dhamma is the cause of decline.
151:
Then that deity, greatly rejoicing in the words of the Blessed One, said: "So it is, indeed." The meaning of that statement is: Just as the Blessed One has spoken, so do we understand it, accept it, and bear it in mind. That cause of ruin, characterized by hatred for the Dhamma, is the first downfall (parābhava). Among the causes of ruin that we have come to know, this aforementioned one is the first cause of ruin.

In the word "parābhava," the grammatical derivation (vigraha) is: by this cause, beings decline and are ruined; therefore, it is called "parābhava." By what cause are they ruined? By that very cause which is the source or reason for ruin. Here, in calling it "parābhava" or "the source of ruin (parābhavato mukhaṃ)," there is a difference only in the phrasing, but in terms of meaning, there is no distinction. Having rejoiced thus, knowing one cause of ruin, and wishing to know further, the deity asked again: "Blessed One, please tell us the second; what is the cause of ruin?" In the subsequent third, fourth, and other verses, the meaning should be understood in this same manner.

In the section of the explanation as well, since various beings are possessed of various causes of ruin—not one person with all, nor all with just one—it should be understood that the Blessed One explained the various causes of ruin through a discourse based on individuals (puggalādhiṭṭhāna), starting with the method "Asantassa piyā honti" (They love the wicked), in order to show those respective causes of ruin to those respective people.

In that verse, the brief explanation of the meaning is: "Asanta" (the wicked) refers to the six [heretical] teachers, or others who are possessed of unpeaceful actions of body, speech, and mind; they are the ones loved by the wicked, just as the naked ascetic Korakhattiya and others were loved by Sunakkhatta and his like. "Santa" (the virtuous) refers to the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and their disciples (sāvakas). Or, others who are possessed of peaceful actions of body, speech, and mind are also called the virtuous. "He does not love the virtuous" means he does not hold them as dear, desired, pleasant, or agreeable. It should be understood that here, the grammatical variation (vacanabheda) is made according to the disposition of those to be taught (veneyya). Alternatively, "sante na kurute" means he does not associate with the virtuous; just as grammarians say "he makes the king dear" in the sense of "he serves the king." "Piyaṃ" means loving, being pleased with, or rejoicing in.
152:
The "doctrine of the untrue" (asataṃ dhammo) refers to the sixty-two wrong views or the ten unwholesome courses of action. He delights in, yearns for, desires, and practices that doctrine of the untrue. Thus, by this verse, the three-fold cause of ruin is stated: loving the wicked, not loving the virtuous, and delighting in the false doctrine. A person possessed of these qualities is ruined and declines; he attains no growth either in this world or the next. Therefore, it is called a "cause of ruin." The detail of this matter will be explained in the commentary on the verse: "Not associating with fools, and associating with the wise."

"Niddāsīlī" (habitually sleepy) refers to one who is drowsy even while walking, sitting, standing, or lying down. "Sabhāsīlī" (fond of company) refers to one who constantly delights in the pleasure of company and the pleasure of idle chatter. "Anuṭṭhātā" (one who lacks initiative) means one who is devoid of the power of energy and lacks the habit of exertion. Even when urged by others, if he is a layman, he does not undertake the work of a layman; if he is a monk, he does not undertake the work of a monk. "Alaso" (the lazy one) means one who is naturally lazy and is constantly overcome by sloth; he remains just as he is when standing, and just as he is when sitting, not changing to another posture through his own effort. The lazy man in the past who did not flee even when a forest fire broke out is an example here. This is the extreme limit of laziness; however, one with less laziness than that is also to be understood simply as lazy. Just as a banner is the mark of a chariot, and smoke is the mark of fire, one whose anger is prominent as a mark is called "kodhapannāṇo" (marked by anger). A person of angry temperament, who is easily provoked and has a mind like an old sore, is of such a nature. By this verse, the five-fold cause of ruin is stated: being habitually sleepy, delighting in company, lacking initiative, laziness, and having prominent anger. A person possessed of these qualities, if a layman, cannot reach the prosperity of laymen; if a monk, he cannot reach the prosperity of monks, but indeed declines and is ruined. Therefore, it is called a "cause of ruin."

"Mātā" should be understood as the biological mother. "Pitā" is the biological father. "Jiṇṇakaṃ" is due to the frailty and aging of the body. "Gatayobbanaṃ" means being past youth, aged eighty or ninety, and unable to perform tasks by oneself. "Pahu santo" means being capable and able to live comfortably while being able to provide support. "Na bharati" means he does not support or nourish them. By this verse, the single cause of ruin—not supporting, not nourishing, and not attending to one's parents—is stated. One who is possessed of this quality, who...
153:
"Because of such service and care, the wise praise that person in this very life, and in the afterlife, they rejoice in heaven" (as stated in the Itivuttaka and Anguttara Nikāya), describing the benefits of supporting one's mother and father. That person [who does not support them] does not obtain those benefits; instead, they meet with ruin, receiving blame such as "If they do not support even their own mother and father, whom else will they support?", being marked as a wrongdoer, and reaching a bad destination. Therefore, it is called "a cause of ruin."

One is called a Brāhmaṇa because of having warded off evil; one is called a Samaṇa because of having calmed evil. Alternatively, one born in a Brahmin family is a Brāhmaṇa, and one who has entered the monkhood is a Samaṇa; or any other unspecified mendicant. One deceives them with false speech. Deceiving with false speech means inviting them by saying, "Venerable sir, please speak [your needs] regarding the four requisites," and then, when they ask or after having promised, failing to give later, thereby disappointing the mendicant's hope. By this verse, deceiving Brahmins and others with false speech is stated as a single cause of ruin. Indeed, one endowed with such deception meets with blame in this life, a bad destination in the next life, and even if they reach a good destination, they face the failure of their desired prosperity. It has been stated:

"For the immoral one whose virtue has failed, a bad reputation spreads far and wide" (as stated in the Dīgha Nikāya, Anguttara Nikāya, and Vinaya Mahāvagga).

Likewise:

"Monks, a person endowed with four things is cast into hell as if carried there. What four? Being a liar..." and so forth.

Likewise:

"Sāriputta, here in this world, a certain person approaches a recluse or a Brahmin and invites them, saying, 'Venerable sir, please speak [your needs] regarding the four requisites.' That person does not give the requisites they offered. If that person passes away from that life and comes to this human state, whatever trading business they engage in results only in loss. But Sāriputta, in this Dispensation... if that person does not give the offered requisites as intended, when they return to the human state, the trading business they engage in will not yield the intended [profits]."

Thus, a person who receives blame and so forth meets only with ruin, and therefore it is called "a cause of ruin." "Pahūtavitto" means possessing much gold, silver, and precious gems. "Sahiraṇṇo" means being endowed with coins/money. "Sabhojano" means being endowed with many kinds of curries and food. Despite being so endowed, they do not give even to their own children and eat alone in a secluded place. In this verse, stinginess regarding food (bhojanamacchariya) is stated as a single (cause of ruin).
154:
A person who meets with such blame and so forth is indeed one who declines and meets with ruin; therefore, it is called "a cause of ruin."

"Pahūtavitta" means possessing much gold, silver, and precious gems. "Sahiraṇṇa" means being endowed with coins/money. "Sabhojana" means being endowed with many kinds of curries and food. "Eko bhuñjati sādūni" means eating delicious food alone in a hidden place without giving even to one's own children. By this verse, stinginess regarding food caused by greed for food is stated as a single cause of ruin. In truth, one endowed with this stinginess suffers blame, fault, and rebirth in a bad destination, and thus meets with ruin; therefore, it is called "a cause of ruin." In the same manner as previously stated, the entire Sutta should be applied accordingly. However, fearing it would be too long, I will not show the method of application now but will only state the meaning.

One who is "stiff with pride of birth" (jātitthaddho) is one who generates conceit, thinking "I am well-born," and because of that birth, becomes puffed up like a leather bag filled with air, not bowing to anyone. The same should be understood for those stiff with pride of wealth (dhana) or clan (gotta). "Despising one's own relatives" means despising one's own kin based on birth, just as the Sakyans did to Prince Viṭaṭūbha. Also, based on wealth, one despises them, saying "This person is destitute, this person is poor," and does not even perform the proper duties of respect. Then, those relatives desire only that person's ruin. By this verse, four types by way of object and one type by way of characteristic are stated as causes of ruin.

"Itthidhutto" (a womanizer) is one who is infatuated with women, giving away whatever wealth they have and taking one woman after another. Similarly, "surādhutto" (a drunkard) is one who pawns all their possessions and is addicted to drinking liquor. "Akkhadhutto" (a gambler) is one who pawns even the clothes they are wearing and is constantly engaged in gambling. Because these three causes destroy whatever wealth has been obtained, such a person is known as a destroyer of all wealth they acquire. Such a person meets only with ruin; therefore, by this verse, three causes of ruin are stated.

"Sehi dārehi" means with one's own wives. A person who is not satisfied with their own wives and commits misconduct with prostitutes or, likewise, with the wives of others.
155:
Because that person meets with ruin through royal punishment and so forth, by giving wealth to prostitutes and by committing adultery with others' wives, these two causes of ruin were spoken of in this verse.

'Atītayobbano' means one who, having passed his youth and being eighty or ninety years old, takes or maintains a wife. 'Timbarutthanim' refers to a young girl whose breasts are like the timbaru fruit. 'Tassā issā na supati' means that a young girl cannot find delight or companionship with an elderly man and will only long for a young man; thus, out of jealousy, he cannot sleep while guarding her. Because that person, burning with sensual lust and jealousy, meets with ruin by being unable to apply himself to external tasks, this one cause of ruin—sleeplessness due to jealousy—was spoken of in this verse.

'Soṇḍim' refers to one who is frivolous and greedy for fish, meat, and so forth. 'Vikiraṇim' refers to one who has the habit of squandering wealth like dust for the sake of those things (fish, meat, etc.). 'Purisaṃ vāpi tādisaṃ' refers to placing such a man or woman in a position of authority, or appointing them to manage household affairs or trade and commerce by giving them signet rings and so forth. Because that person reaches the exhaustion of wealth and meets with ruin due to the faults of the appointee, this one cause of ruin—appointing such a person to authority—was spoken of in this verse.

'Appabhogo' means having little wealth due to the absence of accumulated riches and sources of income. 'Mahātaṇho' means being possessed of great craving for wealth and not being content with what is obtained. 'Khattiye jāyate kule' means being born in a Khattiya (warrior-noble) family. Such a person born in a Khattiya family, due to great craving, desires kingship that is not his rightful inheritance or belongs to another, through improper means and out of order. Because such a person, while desiring thus, gives away even the little wealth he has to soldiers and so forth but fails to attain kingship and meets with ruin, this one cause of ruin—desiring kingship—was spoken of in this verse.
156:
Beyond this verse, if that deity had asked, "Venerable Sir, please speak the thirteenth... Venerable Sir, please speak the hundred-thousandth," the Blessed One would have spoken it. However, that deity, thinking, "What is the use of these verses already asked? There is not a single thing among these causes of ruin that leads to growth," and having no further desire to hear those causes of ruin, remained silent after asking only this much, feeling regret. Therefore, the Blessed One, knowing the deity's inclination and wishing to conclude the teaching, spoke this verse: "Ete parābhave loke..."

In that verse, "paṇḍito" refers to a person endowed with wisdom capable of comprehensive investigation. "Samavekkhiya" means having investigated with the eye of wisdom. "Ariyo" does not mean noble because of the Path or the Fruit; rather, he is called noble because he does not move towards (fall into) those ignoble states known as causes of ruin (parābhava). Because he is endowed with the vision and wisdom by which he sees the causes of ruin and avoids them, he is called "dassanasampanno." "Sa lokaṃ bhajate sivaṃ" means that such a person reaches the peaceful, secure, supreme, and harmless deva world. At the conclusion of the teaching, the deities who attained the fruits of Stream-entry, Once-returning, and Non-returning through proper effort in accordance with the sense of urgency (saṃvega) that arose from hearing the causes of ruin were beyond counting. As it is said:

"In the Mahāsamaya Sutta and the Maṅgala Sutta,
In the Samacitta, Rāhulovāda, Dhammacakka, and Parābhava Suttas.
The assembly of deities there was immeasurable and innumerable,
And the realization of the Dhamma therein was also beyond counting."

## In the Khuddaka Nikāya Commentary named Paramatthajotikā,
## the Explanation of the Parābhava Sutta in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is finished.

## 7. Aggikabhāradvāja Sutta Vaṇṇanā

The Aggikabhāradvāja Sutta, beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ," is also called the "Vasala Sutta." How did it originate? The Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jetavana monastery, the park of Anāthapiṇḍika. As described in the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta, at the end of his duties after the meal, with the Buddha-eye...
157:
When the Blessed One surveyed the world, he saw the Brahmin Aggikabhāradvāja, who possessed the potential (upanissaya) for the refuges and the precepts. Knowing, "If I go there, a conversation will arise, and at the end of that conversation, having heard the Dhamma, this Brahmin will go for refuge and undertake the precepts," he went to that place. In the ensuing conversation, being requested by the Brahmin to teach the Dhamma, he spoke this Sutta. In this Sutta, the words "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth will be explained in the commentary on the Maṅgala Sutta; "Atha kho bhagavā pubbaṇhasamayaṃ" and so forth should be understood in the same way as stated in the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta.

Among the words "Te nakhopana samayena aggikabhāradvājassa" and so forth, I shall only explain those points that have not been mentioned before. In detail—that Brahmin was well-known by the name "Aggika" because he tended and served the sacrificial fire, and "Bhāradvāja" was his clan (gotta). Therefore, it is said "Aggikabhāradvājassa." "Nivesane" means in the house. It is said that there was a sacrificial fire hall (aggihutasālā) in the middle of the street at the entrance of that Brahmin's house. Since that area was included within the precincts of the house, it is said "in the house." Alternatively, the locative case is used in the sense of proximity, meaning "near the house."

"Aggi pajjalito hoti" means that the fire in the hearth, having had the ashes removed, wood added, and being fanned, was blazing with flames rising upwards. "Āhuti paggahitā" means that after bathing from the head down, milk-rice, ghee, honey, molasses, and so forth were prepared with great ceremony. Anything that is to be offered into the fire is called "āhuti." "Sapadānaṃ" means house by house. The Blessed One, for the sake of favoring all people and because of his contentment with food, wandered for alms house by house without skipping any family, whether of high or low lineage. Therefore, it is said "sapadānaṃ piṇḍāya caramāno."

Then, why did the Brahmin's mind not gain faith even upon seeing the Blessed One, who was endowed with all excellent attributes and was altogether inspiring? Why did he address the Blessed One with such harsh words? The answer is—this Brahmin held the view that "seeing an ascetic during auspicious rites is inauspicious." Therefore, thinking, "While it is time for the offering and eating for the Great Brahmā, this wretched shaveling ascetic is approaching my house," he not only felt displeasure but even became angry. Then, being angry and displeased, he uttered displeasing words such as "Stay right there, shaveling!"
158:
In that context, because of the Brahmins' view that "a shaveling is impure," he said "shaveling" (muṇḍaka) out of loathing, thinking, "This person is impure; therefore, he is not worthy of what is offered to the gods and Brahmā." Or, because he is a shaveling, he is a disgusting person who does not deserve to come to this place; and even though he is an ascetic, he does not praise such bodily impurity—thus loathing the state of an ascetic, he said "monkling" (samaṇaka). He did not say "wretch" (vasala) merely out of anger; he said "wretch" out of loathing, thinking that this person, who ordains wretches and eats and uses things together with them, is even more degraded than a wretch. He also spoke thus thinking, "Even just seeing or hearing about the fire-offering of the wretch-born brings demerit."

Although the Blessed One was addressed in such a manner, with a clear facial expression and a sweet voice, and with a heart cooled by compassion for the Brahmin, he spoke, wishing to manifest his state of being unique among all beings: "Do you know, Brahmin?" Then the Brahmin, perceiving that state indicated by the clarity of the Blessed One's face, and hearing the sweet voice uttered with a heart cooled by compassion, felt as if his heart were sprinkled with nectar. Being delighted, with clear faculties and his pride humbled, he abandoned those habitual words of address based on birth and caste which were like spitting out snake venom, and thought: "Surely, the one whom I believed to be of low birth and a wretch is not a wretch in the ultimate sense, and low birth is likely not the quality that makes one a wretch." Thus he said, "I do not know, Master Gotama."

It is indeed a natural law (dhammatā) that even a person endowed with the right causes, who is harsh due to not receiving support, becomes gentle as soon as they receive support.

In that context, the word "Sādhu" is seen in the senses of requesting, accepting, rejoicing, goodness, and strengthening. In passages such as "Sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā saṅkhittena dhammaṃ desetu" (Please, Bhante, let the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief), it is used in the sense of requesting. In passages such as "'Sādhu, bhante' ti kho so bhikkhu bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā" (Saying 'Excellent, Bhante,' that monk, having rejoiced and approved of the Blessed One's words), it is used in the sense of accepting. In passages such as "Sādhu, sādhu, Sāriputta" (Well said, well said, Sāriputta), it is used in the sense of rejoicing.

Good is the king who delights in the Dhamma,
Good is the person who possesses wisdom,
Good is non-treachery toward friends,
Not doing evil is happiness.
159:
The word "Sādhu" is well-known in the sense of entreaty (requesting) in such passages as: "Sādhu, I entreat You; may the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief." It is known in the sense of acknowledgment (acceptance) in such passages as: "Venerable Sir, I acknowledge the words spoken by the Blessed One." It is known in the sense of rejoicing (appreciation) in such passages as: "Excellent, Sāriputta! Excellent!" It is known in the sense of excellence (goodness) in such passages as: "A king who delights in the Dhamma is good; a wise person is good." In passages such as "Listen to that Dhamma well, and pay attention," it is known in the sense of strengthening (firming). In this present context, however, it is known in the sense of entreaty.

"Tena hi" is a phrase indicating the intended meaning of the person; it means, "If you wish to know." Or, it is a statement of cause: "Brahmin, because you wish to know the cause, listen and pay attention well; I shall speak in such a way that you will understand." Thus, its connection with the other words should be understood. In that statement, "Suṇāhi" (Listen) is the prevention of the distraction of the ear faculty (sotindriya), and "Sādhukaṃ manasi karohi" (Pay attention well) is the prevention of the distraction of the mind faculty (manindriya) by applying firm attention. Here, the former phrase prevents the wrong grasp of the phrasing (byañjana), while the latter prevents the wrong grasp of the meaning (attha).

By the former phrase, one is enjoined to listen to the Dhamma; by the latter, one is enjoined to investigate and examine the meaning of the Dhamma that has been heard. By the former, it is shown that "This Dhamma is perfect in phrasing, therefore it should be heard"; by the latter, "It is perfect in meaning, therefore it should be attended to." Alternatively, by connecting the word "Sādhukaṃ" (well) with both verbs, it means: "Because this Dhamma is profound in words and profound in teaching, therefore listen well. Because it is profound in meaning and profound in penetration, therefore pay attention well." To show this meaning, He said: "Suṇāhi sādhukaṃ manasi karohi."

Then, to encourage the Brahmin who seemed to be despondent, thinking, "How can I find a footing in such a profound matter?", He said: "Bhāsiဿāmi" (I shall speak). In that regard, the intention should be understood as: "I shall speak in a clear manner with perfectly rounded words and phrases so that you may understand." Thereupon, the Brahmin Aggikabhāradvāja, having become encouraged, replied to the Blessed One, "Evaṃ bho" (Yes, sir); this means he accepted and received the words, or he listened attentively by practicing according to the instruction. Then, referring to the words now to be spoken to that Brahmin, the Blessed One uttered the verse beginning with "Kodhano upanāhī."

In that verse, "Kodhano" means one who has the habit of being angry. "Upanāhī" means one who is possessed of a grudge by making that very anger firm. One is called "Makkhī" because one smears or wipes out the virtues of others; and because that person is both evil and a denigrator, he is called "Pāpamakkhī" (an evil denigrator). "Vipannadiṭṭhi" means one whose right view is destroyed, or one who is possessed of wrong view consisting of ten bases that has reached a state of corruption. "Māyāvī" means one who has the characteristic of concealing the faults existing in oneself...
160:
...is possessed of deceit (māyā). One should know such a person as an "outcast" (vasala) because he is the locus, the pouring-place, and the constant flow of these low qualities. Thus, all these qualities of an outcast have arisen in one who is a Brahmin in name only. In the ultimate sense (paramattha), this person alone is an outcast; this is merely for the satisfaction of one's own heart, and another (by birth) is not an outcast. Thus, in this context, the Blessed One, having subdued the Brahmin's anger with the very first word, taught the qualities such as anger by way of a teaching in terms of persons (puggalādhiṭṭhāna), saying, "One who has qualities such as anger is a lowly person." Thus, by one method, He taught both the outcast and the qualities that make one an outcast.

While teaching in this way, without disparaging others or exalting Himself by saying "you" or "I," He established that Brahmin in the state of an outcast and Himself in the state of a Brahmin through the Dhamma, in a just and proper manner.

Now, there is a view among Brahmins that "Even if a Brahmin occasionally commits taking life, taking what is not given, and so on, he is still a Brahmin." To refute that view, and to show the danger to those who, being possessed of unwholesome states such as harming living beings, produce those states without seeing the danger, saying, "These states are low; they are the states that make one an outcast," He spoke the verses beginning with "Ekajaṃ vā dvijaṃ vā" to teach the outcast and the qualities that make one an outcast by other methods.

In that verse, "Ekaja" (once-born) refers to beings born from other modes of birth, excluding the egg-born (aṇḍaja). Such a being is born only once. "Dvija" (twice-born) refers to the egg-born. Such a being is born twice: once from the mother's womb (as an egg) and once from the eggshell. Whether it be that once-born or twice-born being, "yodha pāṇaṃ" means whichever living being in this world. "Vihimsati" means taking life (killing) through effort originating from bodily volition or verbal volition. There is also a reading "pāṇāni hiṃsati." In that reading, the connection should be understood as: "Whosoever harms living beings of such varieties as the once-born or twice-born." By the words "yassa pāṇေ dayā natthi" (in whom there is no compassion for living beings), He speaks of the absence of compassion in the mind. The rest of the words here are just as previously explained. In the verses following this, without saying even this much, we shall omit the words whose meanings are clear and only provide the commentary for the words not yet explained.
161:
## 
*Hanti* means killing or destroying. *Parirundhati* means staying by surrounding and blocking with an army. In the phrase *gāmāni nigamāni ca*, the word *ca* (and) also includes cities (*nagarāni*). *Niggāhako samaññāto* means being well-known in the world as a destroyer of villages, market towns, and cities due to such killing and surrounding.

*Gāme vā yadi vāraññe*: In this context, villages, market towns, and cities, along with their outskirts, are all called "village" (*gāma*). Excluding the outskirts of that village, the remaining area is called "forest" (*arañña*). Whether in that village or in the forest, regarding any living being or formation (*saṅkhāra*) possessed by others and not relinquished, *theyyā adinnamādeti* means taking with a thieving mind that which is not given or permitted by the owners. One accomplishes the act of taking by whatever effort or whatever means of theft.

*Iṇamādāya* means taking a debt, whether by pledging some of one's own property, or by taking interest with the promise, "I will give this much interest within this much time," without pledging anything, or by arrangements such as, "The profit from this will be my principal and yours alone," or "We shall both share the profit." *Cujjamāno palāyati na hi te iṇamatthi* means when the creditor demands, "Give me the debt," one denies it even while living in the house, saying, "There is no debt to be paid to you; who is the witness that I took it?"

*Kiñcikkhakamyatā* means because of desiring even a small thing. *Panthasmiṃ vajantaṃ janaṃ* refers to any woman or man traveling on a path. *Hantvā kiñcikkhamādeti* means taking that person's belongings by killing or beating them.

*Attahetu* means for the sake of one's own life. Similarly, *parahetu* is for the sake of others. *Dhanahetu* means for the sake of one's own wealth or the wealth of others. The word *ca* indicates an alternative (*vikalpa*) in all instances. *Sakkhipuṭṭho* means being asked, "Tell what you know." *Musā brūti* means saying "I know" when one does not know, or "I do not know" when one knows. It is making the owner a non-owner and the non-owner an owner.
162:
## 
*Ñātīnaṃ* means relatives. *Sakhīnaṃ* means friends of the same age. *Dāresu* means among the wives possessed by others. *Paṭidissati* means appearing in a loathsome manner, or it means appearing as one who transgresses. *Sāhasā* means by force, against her will. *Sampiyena* means it is also by the power of mutual affection, as those wives of friends are desired by him and he himself is desiring them.

*Mātaraṃ pitaraṃ vā* refers to the mother and father who are the basis for loving-kindness (*mettā*). *Jiṇṇakaṃ gatayobbanaṃ* refers to those who are aged and past their youth, who are the basis for compassion (*karuṇā*). *Pahu santo na bharati* means not supporting or nourishing one's parents despite being endowed with wealth and resources.

*Sasuṃ* means mother-in-law. *Hantī* means striking with the hand, a stone, or anything else. *Rosetī* means provoking anger with harsh words.

*Atthaṃ* refers to any benefit among the benefits of the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal (*paramattha*). *Pucchito santo* means when being questioned. *Anatthanumanusāsati* means advising only what is harmful to that person. *Paṭicchannena mantetī* means consulting with words concealed by obscure terms and syllables so that the person cannot understand, even when speaking of a benefit; or it means acting with a "teacher's fist" (*ācariya-muṭṭhi*), making them stay for a long time, and then consulting only with the remainder.

*Yo katvā*: In this context, I have previously spoken of evil desire (*pāpicchatā*). It appears as: "Here, someone, having committed misconduct by body, speech, and mind, harbors an evil desire for the sake of concealing that misconduct, wishing, 'May others not know me.'" One whose actions are concealed by acting so that others cannot know, or by not revealing the deeds done, is called *paṭicchannakammanto* (one of concealed actions).

*Parakulaṃ* means the house of relatives or the house of friends. *Āgataṃ* means when a person, at whose house one has previously eaten, comes to one's own house, one does not honor them in return with drinks and food, or does not give, or gives only leftovers.

The term *yo brāhmaṇaṃ vā* is in the same manner as stated in the *Parābhava Sutta*.
163:
“Bhattakāle upaṭṭhite” means when the time for a meal has arrived. There is also a variant reading “upaṭṭhitaṃ,” which means a person who has arrived at mealtime. “Roseti vācā na ca deti” means abusing with harsh and improper words without reflecting, “This person desires my welfare and has come to make me perform merit by force,” or at the very least, not even facing that person, let alone giving food.

“Asataṃ yodha pabrūti” means in this world, a person speaks the words of the untruthful according to the appearance of signs, saying, “On such and such a day, this and that will happen to you.” There is also a variant reading “asantaṃ,” meaning false speech. “Pabrūti” means speaking like a rogue who deceives another’s wife or another’s slave girl, saying, “In such and such a village, I have such wealth; come, let us go there, you shall be my housewife, and I will give you this and that.” “Nijigīsāno” means desiring and seeking, with the intention of deceiving that person, taking something, and running away.

“Yo cattānaṃ” means a person who exalts himself. “Samukkaṃse” means exalting through birth and so on, placing oneself in a high position. “Pare ca mavajānāti” means despising or belittling others through those same factors of birth and so on. The letter “ma” is inserted for euphonic conjunction (padasandhi). “Nihīno” means one who has declined from virtue or one who has reached a low state. “Sena mānena” means through one’s own conceit, which is described as exalting oneself and despising others.

“Rosako” means one who causes anger in others through body and speech. “Kadariyo” means a harsh miser; this is a term for one who prevents others while they are giving or performing other meritorious deeds. “Pāpiccho” means one possessed of evil desires, wanting to be esteemed for virtues one does not possess. “Maccharī” means one associated with stinginess, such as stinginess regarding dwellings (āvāsa-macchariya) and so on. “Saṭho” means one possessed of fraudulence, characterized by displaying non-existent virtues, or one who speaks untruthfully, saying “I will do it” and so on, even when not wishing to do so. Such a person lacks “hiri,” characterized by the loathing of evil, and lacks “ottappa,” characterized by the dread of consequences; therefore, he is called “ahirika” (shameless) and “anottappī” (fearless of wrongdoing).

“Buddhaṃ” means the Sammāsambuddha (the Fully Enlightened Buddha). “Paribhāsati” means reviling with words such as “He is not omniscient” and so on, and also reviling a disciple (sāvaka) with words such as “He is of bad conduct” and so on. “Paribbājaṃ gahaṭṭhaṃ vā” is merely an attribute of the word “sāvaka.” It refers to a monk disciple or a lay disciple who is a donor of requisites. Ancient teachers, however, say it refers to reviling an external wanderer or any layperson with false blame.
164:
This term “paribbājakaṃ vā gahaṭṭhaṃ vā” is merely an attribute (visesana) of the word “sāvaka.” It means a disciple of that Buddha, whether a monk or a layperson who is a donor of requisites. Alternatively, ancient teachers intend the meaning here as reviling an external wanderer or any layperson with false blame.

“Anarahaṃ santo” means while being one whose defilements are not yet exhausted. “Arahaṃ paṭijānāti” means claiming “I am an Arahant.” To make others know him as “This person is an Arahant,” he utters words in that manner, exerts himself bodily, and desires and accepts it with his mind. “Coro” means a thief. “Sabrahmake loke” is said by way of eminence, referring to the world together with the Brahmās, which means in the entire world. Indeed, in the world, those who plunder the wealth of others by breaking through walls, highway robbery, looting, surrounding a single house to rob it, or waiting in ambush on the road, etc., are called thieves. In the Sāsana (Dispensation), however, there are those who plunder requisites and so on by means of having a wealth of followers and so on. With reference to this meaning, the Blessed One said:

“Monks, there are these five great thieves found existing in the world. Which five? Here, monks, a certain great thief has this thought: ‘When shall I, surrounded by a hundred or a thousand followers, wander through villages, towns, and royal capitals, killing and causing to kill, cutting and causing to cut, cooking and causing to cook?’ At a later time, that great thief, surrounded by a hundred or a thousand followers, wanders through villages, towns, and royal capitals, killing... causing to cook. Even so, monks, here a certain evil monk has this thought: ‘When shall I, surrounded by a hundred or a thousand disciples, wander through villages, towns, and royal capitals, being honored, respected, revered, worshipped, and esteemed, and receiving robes, alms-food... and medicinal requisites from both laypeople and monks?’ At a later time, that monk, surrounded by a hundred or a thousand disciples, wanders through villages, towns, and royal capitals, being honored... receiving requisites. Monks, this monk is the first great thief found existing in the world.

Furthermore, monks, here a certain evil monk, having learned the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, claims it as his own. Monks, this monk is the second [great thief found existing] in the world.”
165:
Monks, furthermore, in this Dispensation, a certain evil monk accuses a monk who is pure and of perfectly pure holy life with a groundless charge of unchastity (sexual intercourse). Monks, this monk is the third great thief in the world.

Monks, furthermore, in this Dispensation, a certain evil monk uses the Saṅgha’s heavy property and heavy equipment—namely, a park, a park-site, a monastery, a monastery-site, a bed, a chair, a mattress, a pillow, a copper pot, a copper jar, a copper water-pot, a copper basin, a knife, a hatchet, an axe, a hoe, a chisel, creepers, bamboo, muñja grass, pabbaja grass, common grass, clay, wooden articles, and clay articles—to win over and entice laypeople. Monks, this monk is the fourth great thief in the world.

Monks, in the world with its devas... in the world with its devas and humans, the monk who speaks of a superhuman state (jhāna, path, and fruit) that is non-existent and untrue in himself is the supreme great thief. (Pārājika 195)

Among those thieves, worldly thieves steal only worldly wealth such as money and grain. Among the thieves mentioned in the Dispensation, the first thief steals only such requisites as robes and so forth. The second thief steals the Dhamma of learning (pariyatti). The third thief steals another's holy life. The fourth thief steals the Saṅghika heavy property. The fifth thief steals the wealth of mundane and supramundane qualities consisting of the distinctions of jhāna, concentration, attainment, path, and fruit, as well as the collection of mundane requisites such as robes and so forth. It is as the Blessed One said: "Monks, the country’s alms-food has been eaten by you by way of theft." Among those five great thieves, the Blessed One said "a thief in the world with its Brahmās" with reference to this fifth great thief. Because he steals mundane and supramundane wealth, he is called the supreme great thief in the world with its devas... in the world with its devas and humans, who speaks of a superhuman state that is non-existent and untrue in himself. Therefore, he is revealed here also by this supreme distinction: "in the world with its Brahmās."

"Eso kho vasalādhamo"—In this phrase, the word "kho" has the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa); therefore, only he is the lowest of outcasts. He is determined as the lowest and the very last among outcasts. Why? Because he is base due to his desire to steal in relation to a distinguished object, and because as long as he does not give up that claim (of attaining jhāna, path, and fruit), he is not free from the behavior of an outcast.
166:
## Ete kho vasalāti

Now, in the first verse, by way of corruption of intention (āsaya), five persons such as the angry one and so forth are mentioned; or by dividing the words pāpa (evil) and makkha (hypocrisy), six persons are mentioned. In the second verse, by way of corruption of effort (payoga), one who harms living beings. In the third verse, also by way of corruption of effort, one who oppresses villages and market towns. In the fourth verse, by way of theft, one person. In the fifth verse, by way of deceiving regarding debt, one person. In the sixth verse, by way of plundering by force, one who destroys travelers. In the seventh verse, by way of false witness, one person. In the eighth verse, by way of betraying a friend, one person. In the ninth verse, by way of ingratitude, one person. In the tenth verse, by way of destroying and harassing one who has performed a service, one person. In the eleventh verse, by way of deceiving the heart, one person. In the twelfth verse, by way of having concealed actions, two persons. In the thirteenth verse, by way of ingratitude, one person. In the fourteenth verse, by way of deception, one person. In the fifteenth verse, by way of harassment, one person. In the sixteenth verse, by way of deception, one person. In the seventeenth verse, by way of self-exaltation and disparaging others, two persons. In the eighteenth verse, by way of corruption of effort and intention, seven persons such as the reviler and so forth. In the nineteenth verse, by way of reviling, two persons. In the twentieth verse, by way of being the supreme great thief, one person. Thus, thirty-three or thirty-four outcasts are mentioned.

Pointing out those outcasts, He said: "These indeed are the outcasts mentioned, who have been revealed by Me." The meaning is: those outcasts who were previously mentioned in brief as "Do you know, O Brahmin, the outcast?", are here revealed in detail. Or, those outcasts who were mentioned by way of person are here also revealed by way of Dhamma. Or else, those whom I have revealed by the method beginning with "He is angry and holds a grudge," the Noble Ones call outcasts only by way of their actions (kamma), not by way of their birth (jāti).

Thus, the Blessed One, having shown the state of being an outcast, now, because the Brahmin was excessively attached to his own view, wishing to prohibit that view, spoke the verse beginning with "One is not an outcast by birth." The meaning is: in the ultimate sense, one is not an outcast by birth, nor is one a Brahmin by birth. But rather, by action one becomes an outcast, and by action one becomes a Brahmin. By having impure actions, one is an outcast; by having pure actions and being able to remove impurity, one is a Brahmin. Or, because you regard a low birth as an outcast and a high birth as a Brahmin...
167:
You consider only those of noble birth to be Brahmins. Therefore, wishing to make known this meaning—that one becomes an outcast through low, unwholesome deeds and a Brahmin through noble, wholesome deeds—he spoke thus.

137–139. Now, to demonstrate this very meaning with an example, he spoke the three verses beginning with "Tadamināpi jānātha." Among these, two verses have four lines (pādas) and one has six lines. The meaning of these verses is: "By this reason which I shall state, know also that one does not become an outcast by birth," and so on. "Know this example by this method, by this characteristic," is what is meant. What is the example? It is "The son of a Caṇḍāla, Sopāka... reaching the Brahma world."

The son of a Caṇḍāla is called Caṇḍālaputta. He is called Sopāka because he obtains and cooks dead dogs for his own food. He was famous by the name Mātaṅga. Thus, he was well-known by his low birth, his livelihood, and his name.

That Mātaṅga reached supreme fame, an extraordinary and excellent reputation. "Which is very difficult to obtain" means it is difficult even for those born in noble families to attain, and much more so for those born in low families. To that Mātaṅga, who was thus endowed with fame, many Khattiyas, Brahmins, and others such as Vessas and Suddas, mostly inhabitants of Jambudīpa, came to attend upon and serve him.

Endowed with such service, that Mātaṅga, being free from the dust of defilements (viraja), having traveled the great path (mahāpatha) trodden by the Great Ones like the Buddhas, and having mounted the vehicle of the eight attainments (samāpatti) known as the "vehicle to the deva world" (devalokayāna) because it is capable of leading to the deva world known as the Brahma world, he dispelled sensual lust through that practice.
