Upon the breaking up of the body, he was one who reached the Brahma world. Although his birth was low, that birth could not prevent him from reaching the Brahma world.

This meaning should be understood as follows: In the past, the Great Being (Bodhisatta), performing the welfare of beings through various means, was born into a Caṇḍāla family that lived by cooking dogs. His name was Mātaṅga. Being very ugly in appearance, he lived in a leather-covered hut outside the city and made his living by begging for alms inside the city. Then one day, when a grand festival was proclaimed in the city of Vārāṇasī, drunkards were playing with their followers. Others also...
168:
Then one day, when a liquor festival was proclaimed in that city of Vārāṇasī, drunkards were playing with their respective followers. A certain daughter of a wealthy Brahmin (Mahāsāla), about fifteen or sixteen years old, beautiful and pleasing to behold like a celestial maiden, thought, "I shall play in a manner suitable to my family lineage." She had many snacks, food, and playthings loaded onto carts and, mounting a carriage drawn by pure white mares, went to the park with a large retinue. That merchant's daughter was known by the name Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā. It is said that she did not wish to see any sight of poor form, considering it an ill omen (amaṅgala). Therefore, she came to be known only as Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā ("One who sees omens").

At that time, the Bodhisatta Mātaṅga, having risen early, dressed in worn-out clothes, tied a brass gong to his hand, and holding a bowl, entered the city. Upon seeing people, he would strike the brass gong even from a distance. Then, Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, being escorted by men who were clearing away low-class people from the front, shouting "Move aside! Move aside!", saw Mātaṅga in the middle of the city gate and asked, "Who is this?" "I am Mātaṅga Caṇḍāla," he replied. Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā said, "Where can there be prosperity for those who travel after seeing such a person?" and had her carriage turned back.

The people, angry, said, "We would have gone to the park and received snacks and food, but Mātaṅga has caused an obstacle to that." Saying "Seize the Caṇḍāla!", they beat him with clods of earth. Saying "He is dead," they grabbed him by the feet, discarded him in a certain place, covered him with rubbish, and left. Mātaṅga, regaining consciousness, stood up and asked the people, "Sirs, how is it? Is the gate common to all, or is it made only for Brahmins?" The people said, "It is common to all." He said, "The people of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā have brought me to such ruin and destruction even though I entered through a gate common to all and was sustaining myself with alms-food." Thus, wandering from street to street and informing the people, he lay down at the Brahmin's door, saying, "I will not rise until I get Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā."

The Brahmin, hearing that Mātaṅga was lying at the door, said, "Give him a kākaṇika coin; let him smear his limbs with oil and go." Mātaṅga did not want that money and said only, "I will not rise until I get Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā." Then the Brahmin said, "Give him two kākaṇika coins; let him eat a cake with one and buy oil with the other to smear his limbs and go." Mātaṅga did not want that money and said the same. The Brahmin had him offered a māsaka, an aḍḍhamāsaka, a kahāpaṇa, two, three, up to a hundred coins. Mātaṅga did not want them and said the same. While this pleading was going on, the sun set. Then the Brahmin woman descended from the palace, had a curtain-wall set up around him, approached Mātaṅga, and said, "Dear Mātaṅga, please forgive Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā's fault. Take a thousand coins, take two thousand, three thousand, take up to a hundred thousand coins."
169:
"Let him go after anointing his limbs with oil bought for a kākaṇika (a small coin)," he said. He did not desire that and spoke in the same way (that he would not rise). Hearing this, the Brahmin ordered, "Give him a māsaka, a pāda (a quarter), half a kahāpaṇa, one, two, three kahāpaṇas," up to a hundred kahāpaṇas. He did not desire it and spoke in the same way. While they were thus pleading, the sun set. Then the Brahmin's wife descended from the palace, had a curtain-wall surrounded, approached Matanga, and pleaded, "Dear Matanga, forgive the offense of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā. Take a thousand kahāpaṇas, two thousand, three thousand..." up to a hundred thousand. He remained silent and just lay there as before.

When four or five days had passed in this way, although they gave many gifts, they could not get Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā. Princes and others whispered in Matanga's ear, "Men, having made effort for many years, reach their desired goal. Do not be discouraged; surely after two or three days, you will get Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā." He remained silent and just lay there as before. Then on the seventh day, the neighbors rose up and said, "Either make Matanga get up or give him the girl; do not let us all be destroyed." For this was their belief: "If a Caṇḍāla dies lying thus at someone's door, the residents of seven houses in every direction, including that house, become Caṇḍālas."

Then, they made Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā wear old, dark clothes, gave her a ladle and a rice pot, and led her, weeping, to Matanga, saying, "Take the girl and get up and go." Standing by his side, she said, "Get up." He said, "Take me by the hand and make me get up." She made him get up. Having sat up, he said, "We are not allowed to live inside the city. Come, lead me to the leather-covered hut outside the city." She took him by the hand and led him there. "Having placed him on her back," say the Jātaka reciters. After leading him there, she anointed his body with oil, bathed him with hot water, and cooked and gave him gruel.

He thought, "Let this Brahmin girl not be ruined," and without performing any sexual union, he regained his strength for about half a month. Then he said, "I am going to the forest; do not be weary thinking I am taking too long," and he commanded the household members, "Do not neglect this woman," and left the house. Having left the house, he went forth as an ascetic, practiced the kasiṇa preliminaries, and within a few days, attained the eight meditative attainments and the five superknowledges. Then, thinking, "Now I will cause Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā to have a clear mind," he came through the air, descended at the city gate, and to Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā...
170:
Thinking, "I will cause Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā to have a clear mind," he came through the air, descended at the city gate, and sent a message to Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā. Hearing this, she thought, "Perhaps some relative of mine has gone forth and, knowing I am in distress, has come to see me." She went and, recognizing him, prostrated at his feet and said, "Venerable sir, why did you leave me helpless?"

The Great Being said, "Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, do not be distressed. I will arrange for the inhabitants of the whole of Jambudīpa to pay you honor." He then said, "Go and make a proclamation: 'My husband is not a Caṇḍāla; he is the Great Brahmā. That Great Brahmā will break through the moon's mansion and come to me on the seventh day.'" Then Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā said, "Venerable sir, although I am the daughter of a wealthy Brahmin (Brāhmaṇamahāsāla), I have reached this state of a Caṇḍāla due to my own bad kamma. I do not dare to say such a thing."

The Great Being said, "You do not yet know the power of Matanga." To make her believe, he showed many miracles and, having commanded her to do exactly as he said, he returned to his dwelling. Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā did as she was told. People mocked and laughed, saying, "How can this woman, who has reached the state of a Caṇḍāla due to her own bad kamma, again make him the Great Brahmā?"

Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, becoming very bold in mind, wandered through the city every day, proclaiming, "On the sixth day from today, the fifth, the fourth, the third, tomorrow, today, the Great Brahmā will come." When the people heard her confident words, they thought, "Sometimes such a thing might happen." They built pavilions in front of their houses, prepared curtain-walls, adorned their grown-up daughters, and sat looking up at the sky, waiting, saying, "When the Great Brahmā comes, we will offer our daughters to him."

Then, on the full moon day, when the moon had risen into the sky, the Great Being broke through the moon's mansion and emerged in the form of the Great Brahmā before the eyes of the multitude. The people thought, "Two moons have appeared!" Seeing him descend gradually from there, they became convinced, saying, "What Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā said is true. This is indeed the Great Brahmā; he previously came in the guise of Matanga to tame Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā."

Thus, while being seen by the multitude, the Great Brahmā descended to the place where Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā lived. At that time, Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā was in her menses. The Great Being touched her navel with his thumb, and through that touch, she conceived. Then, to her, "You are pregnant..."
171:
(The pregnancy) was well-established. Saying, "When the son is born, live depending on him," he entered the Moon Mansion again while the multitude watched.

The Brahmins said, "Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā is the wife of Mahābrahmā; she has become our mother," and they came from various places. Because of the crowding of people who wished to pay homage to Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, there was no space at the city gates. They placed Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā on a heap of gold, bathed her, adorned her, placed her on a chariot, and had her circumambulate the city with great honor. They had a pavilion built in the center of the city and kept her there in a place visible to the public, saying, "She is the wife of Mahābrahmā." They said, "Let her stay here in this pavilion until we can make a suitable dwelling for her." Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā gave birth to her son in that very pavilion.

On the day of the naming ceremony, they performed the head-washing ceremony for the child and the mother. Because he was born in a pavilion (maṇḍapa), they named the boy "Maṇḍavya Kumāra." From then on, the Brahmins surrounded the boy, saying, "He is the son of Mahābrahmā." At that time, countless hundreds of thousands of gifts arrived. The Brahmins placed guards for the prince, so those who arrived could not easily see him.

As the prince gradually grew up, he began to give alms. Maṇḍavya Kumāra gave only to Brahmins and not to the poor and beggars who came to the alms-hall. The Great Being reflected, "What kind of alms does my son give?" Seeing that he gave only to Brahmins, he thought, "I will act so that he gives to everyone." He donned his robes, took his bowl, came through the air, and stood at his son's door. Seeing him, the prince became angry, thinking, "From where has this outcaste of such ugly appearance come?" and spoke this verse:

"From where do you come, you wearer of foul clothes, looking like a frightening dust-goblin?
You who wear rags from a dust-heap around your neck, you who are unworthy of offerings, who are you?"

The Brahmins said, "Seize him, seize him!" and they caught and beat him, causing him great harm. He went through the air to the outskirts of the city...
172:
(The ascetic Mātaṅga) stood (outside the city). The deities, being angry, seized Maṇḍavya Kumāra by the neck and held him upside down with his feet up and head down. The young Maṇḍavya suffered painful sensations, with blood flowing from his eyes and saliva dripping from his mouth, making a 'gharu-gharu' sound as he breathed. Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā heard of this and asked, "Has anyone come?" They replied, "Yes, lady, an ascetic came." "Where did he go?" she asked. "He went this way," they said. Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā went to where the ascetic was and, begging, "Venerable sir, forgive your servant's son," she prostrated herself on the ground at the ascetic's feet.

At that time, the Great Being, having wandered for alms and obtained gruel, was sitting there drinking it. The Great Being gave the small amount of remaining gruel to Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā. He said, "Go, put this gruel in a water pot, stir it, and pour it into the eyes, faces, ears, and nostrils of those who are possessed by spirits. Sprinkle it on their bodies as well. In this way, they will be free from affliction and be healed." Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā did as instructed. Afterwards, when the prince's body returned to normal, she said, "Come, dear Maṇḍavya, let us ask the ascetic for forgiveness." She made her son and all the Brahmins lie prostrate at the ascetic's feet to ask for forgiveness.

The ascetic exhorted them, saying, "Alms should be given to all people," and after preaching the Dhamma, he went to his own dwelling. He reflected, "I have disciplined Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, who is famous among women, and I have disciplined Maṇḍavya Kumāra, who is famous among men. Now, who else should be disciplined?" Then he saw the ascetic Jātimanta, who lived on the banks of the Kumbhavatī River near the city of Bandhumatī. That ascetic thought, "I am noble by birth; I will not use water used by others," and lived upstream. The Great Being took up residence upstream from that ascetic and, at the time the ascetic was using the water, chewed a tooth-stick and threw it into the river.

The ascetic, seeing the tooth-stick floating in the water, went upstream to see who had thrown it. Seeing the Great Being, he asked, "Who is here?" "Teachers, it is Mātaṅga the outcaste," he replied. "Begone, outcaste! Do not live upstream," the ascetic said. The Great Being said, "Very well, teacher," and lived downstream. However, the tooth-stick floated upstream and reached the ascetic. The ascetic went again and said, "Begone, outcaste! Do not live downstream; live only upstream." The Great Being said, "Very well, teacher," and did so. Again, the same thing happened. The ascetic, displeased that he did so again, cursed the Great Being: "When the sun rises, may your head split into seven pieces!" The Great Being replied, "Very well, teacher, but I will not allow the sun to rise," and he prevented the sun from rising.

From the time he prevented it, the night did not brighten, and there was darkness. The people of Bandhumatī, being afraid, went to the ascetic Jātimanta and asked, "Teacher, will there be well-being for us?" The townspeople regarded that ascetic as an Arahant. The ascetic told them the whole story. The townspeople approached the Great Being and pleaded, "Venerable sir, please release the sun." The Great Being said, "If your teacher, who is an Arahant, comes and asks for my forgiveness..."
173:
He prevented the rising of the sun. From that time on, the night did not brighten and darkness prevailed. The frightened residents of Bandhumatī went to the ascetic and asked, "Teacher, will there still be safety and well-being for us?" They regarded that ascetic as an "Arahant." The ascetic told them the whole story. They then approached the Great Being and pleaded, "Venerable sir, please release the sun."

The Great Being said, "If your Arahant comes and asks for my forgiveness, I will release it."

The people went and said to the ascetic, "Venerable sir, come and ask for the forgiveness of the wise Matanga. Let us not be destroyed because of your quarrel." The ascetic replied, "I will not ask for forgiveness from an outcast (Caṇḍāla)." The people said, "You are destroying us!" and they seized the ascetic by his hands and feet and carried him to the Great Being. The Great Being said, "If he lies prostrate on his belly at my feet and asks for forgiveness, I will forgive him." The people said, "Do so." When the ascetic said, "I will not pay homage to an outcast," the people said, "You shall not pay homage according to your own will," and they seized him by his hands, feet, beard, and neck, and made him lie down at the feet of the Great Being.

The Great Being said, "I forgive this man. However, it is only out of compassion for him that I have not yet released the sun. As soon as the sun rises, this man's head will split into seven pieces." The people asked, "Venerable sir, what should be done now?" The Great Being said, "In that case, place this ascetic in water up to his neck and cover his head with a lump of clay. When touched by the sun's rays, the lump of clay will split into seven pieces. When that lump of clay splits, let this man go elsewhere." They seized the ascetic by his hands and feet and did exactly as instructed. As soon as the sun was released, the lump of clay split into seven pieces and fell, and the ascetic fled in terror.

Seeing this, the people said, "Friends, behold the power of the recluse!" They spoke in detail about everything, starting from the incident of throwing the tooth-stick, and saying, "There is no other recluse like this," they gained great faith in the wise Matanga. From then on, kings, Brahmins, householders, and monastics from all over Jambudīpa came to serve and attend to the wise Matanga. He remained for the full span of his life and, upon the dissolution of the body, was reborn in the Brahma realm. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke the verse beginning with: "By this also you may know... rebirth in the Brahma realm."

140-141. Having thus proven that "One does not become an outcast by birth, but by action one becomes an outcast," he now spoke the words beginning with "Ajjhāyakakule" to prove the point that "One does not become a Brahmin by birth, but by action one becomes a Brahmin."
174:
In the verse "Jātā ...pe... duggatyā garahāya vā," the phrase "ajjhāyakakule jātā" refers to those born into a Brahmin family accustomed to reciting the Vedic mantras. There is also a variant reading "ajjhāyakākuḷe jātā," which means one born into a blameless Brahmin family that recites the Vedas. Because the Vedic mantras they have composed are like friends to them, they are called "Mantabandhavā." It means those who have the Vedas as their refuge. Even though they are born into such a family and have the mantras as their kinsmen, if they repeatedly commit evil deeds such as killing living beings (pāṇātipāta), they become blameworthy in this very life and reach a miserable destination (duggati) in the life hereafter.

Even in this life, the parents of those who are notorious for such evil deeds will reproach them, saying, "These are not our sons; they are like embers that destroy the lineage; drive them out!" The Brahmins will also say, "These are merely householders; they are not Brahmins. Do not let them enter the sacrificial festivals such as the Srāddha and Thālipāka; do not speak with them." Other people will also criticize them, saying, "These are people of evil deeds; they are not Brahmins." In the life hereafter, there are only miserable destinations such as hell for them. Reaching suffering in the world beyond is what is called "duggati." Even if you believe in birth as having essence, such birth cannot prevent Brahmins who are notorious for evil deeds from reaching a miserable destination in the life hereafter, nor from being blamed in the present life.

In this way, the Blessed One showed how even Brahmins born into families of Vedic scholars fall into a low state in the present life due to blameworthy actions, and how the status of being a Brahmin by birth does not exist in the life hereafter because of their descent into miserable destinations. Thus, having established the meaning that "One does not become a Brahmin by birth, but by action one becomes a Brahmin," he now spoke as follows to conclude both meanings: "O Brahmin, thus—
Not by birth is one an outcast, not by birth is one a Brahmin.
By action is one an outcast, by action is one a Brahmin."

The remaining meanings are the same as those explained in the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta. Specifically, the application of the words beginning with "nikkujjitaṃ vā" (as if what was overturned) should be understood thus: Just as someone might turn upright what was overturned, even so, the Venerable Gotama has lifted me up from the doctrine of birth (jātivāda) in which I was immersed, ignoring the law of kamma. Just as one might reveal what was hidden, he has revealed the doctrine of action (kammavāda) which was hidden by the doctrine of birth. Just as one might point out the right path to one who is lost, he has shown the straight path of the Brahmin and the outcast. Just as one might bring a lamp into the darkness, he has brought the lamp of the example of the wise Matanga. Thus, the Venerable Gotama has revealed the Dhamma to me through various means.
175:
Just as one might set upright what had been overturned, so too has the Dhamma been revealed in many ways by the Venerable Gotama. He has raised me from the wrong view of birth-based status—where I had turned my back on kamma and fallen into the doctrine of birth, believing that 'one becomes a brahmin or an outcast by birth'—and has opened up the doctrine of kamma which was covered by the doctrine of birth, just as one might open what was covered. He has shown the straight path of the status of brahmin and outcast, just as one might point out the way to one who is lost. He has held up the lamp of the example of Mātaṅga and others, just as one might hold up an oil lamp in the darkness.

## In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha
## The Explanation of the Aggikabhāradvāja Sutta in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is finished.

## 8. Explanation of the Metta Sutta

This sutta beginning with "Karaṇīyamatthakusala" is the Metta Sutta. What is its origin (uppatti)? It is said that monks who were harassed by deities on the slopes of the Himalayas came to the Buddha in the city of Sāvatthī. The Blessed One taught them this sutta for the purpose of protection (paritta) and as a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). This is the summary.

The following is the detailed account: At one time, the Blessed One was staying in Sāvatthī as the time for the rains retreat (vassa) approached. At that time, many monks from various countries, having taken meditation subjects from the Blessed One, approached Him with the desire to enter the rains retreat in various places. Then, the Blessed One taught meditation subjects suitable for the eighty-four thousand types of temperaments in this manner: for those of lustful temperament (rāgacarita), eleven types of foulness (asubha) meditation subjects based on animate and inanimate objects; for those of hateful temperament (dosacarita), the four meditation subjects beginning with loving-kindness (metta); for those of deluded temperament (mohacarita), meditation subjects such as mindfulness of death (maraṇassati); for those of speculative temperament (vitakkacarita), mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati) and the earth kasina (pathavīkasiṇa); for those of faithful temperament (saddhācarita), meditation subjects such as mindfulness of the Buddha (buddhānussati); and for those of intellectual temperament (buddhicarita), meditation subjects such as the definition of the four elements (catudhātuvavatthāna).

Then, about five hundred monks, having learned meditation subjects from the Blessed One and searching for suitable lodgings and alms villages, gradually saw a mountain...
176:
...at the edge of the Himalayas, which was connected to the range, having a stone surface like blue crystal, adorned with a dense cool shade and green forest, with ground covered with sand like pearl nets or silver plates, and surrounded by pure, pleasant, and cool waters. Then, those monks stayed there for one night, and when the night had turned to dawn, they performed their bodily ablutions and entered a certain village not far from that forest for alms. That village was populated by a thousand families living in close proximity. The people there were faithful and devoted. Because it was rare to see a monk in that remote region, as soon as they saw the monks, they were filled with joy and served them food. They requested, "Venerable sirs, please stay here for the three months of the rains retreat," and having built five hundred small meditation huts, they provided all requisites such as couches, stools, and pots for drinking and washing water.

On the second day, the monks entered another village for alms. There too, the people served them in the same way and requested them to stay for the rains retreat. The monks accepted, saying, "If there are no obstacles," and entered that forest grove. Being possessed of effort exerted day and night, they struck the wooden gong to mark the time and dwelt with much wise attention (yoniso manasikāra), approaching the roots of trees to stay. Due to the spiritual power (teja) of the virtuous monks, the tree deities, whose own power was eclipsed, descended from their respective mansions (vimāna) and wandered here and there carrying their children. It was just as when kings or great ministers of the king arrive at a village and occupy the villagers' houses, the householders must leave their homes and live elsewhere, looking from afar and wondering, "When will they go?" In the same way, the deities abandoned their mansions and wandered here and there, looking from afar and wondering, "When will the venerable ones depart?"

Later, they collectively thought: "These monks who have entered the first rains retreat will surely stay for the full three months. We cannot stay away for so long carrying our children. Let us show the monks terrifying objects." That night, at the time when the monks were performing their recluse-dharma, the deities manifested frightening ogre-forms (yakkha) and stood before them, making terrifying noises. Seeing those forms and hearing those sounds, the monks' hearts trembled; they became pale and haggard, and were unable to concentrate their minds. Because their minds were not concentrated and they were repeatedly terrified by fear, their mindfulness was lost. Then, to those who had lost mindfulness, the deities presented foul-smelling objects. Because of those foul odors, the monks' brains felt as if they were being oppressed, and severe headaches arose. They did not inform one another of this. Then one day, at the time of the assembly of the Saṅgha, the Elder of the Saṅgha asked: "Friends, when you first entered this forest grove, your appearance was very pure and your faculties were clear. Why is it that now you are emaciated, pale, and haggard? Do you have some unsuitable (asappāya) condition?" Then, a certain monk spoke:
177:
Their brains felt as if they were being crushed by that foul stench. Severe headaches arose. They did not inform one another of this occurrence.

Then one day, at the time of attending upon the Elder of the Saṅgha, when all the bhikkhus had assembled, the Elder asked: "Friends, when you first entered this forest grove, for a few days your complexion was very pure and bright, and your faculties were serene. But now, why are you emaciated, of poor complexion, and pale like withered leaves? What is unsuitable for you here?" Then a certain bhikkhu said: "Venerable sir, at night I see such terrifying sights and hear such sounds, and I smell such foul odors. Because of that, my mind cannot attain concentration." In this manner, all the bhikkhus reported the matter. The Elder of the Saṅgha said: "Friends, the Blessed One has prescribed two periods for entering the rains-retreat. This lodging is unsuitable for us. Come, friends, let us go to the Blessed One and ask for another suitable lodging." "Very well, venerable sir," the bhikkhus replied, consenting to the Elder's words. They all packed up their lodgings, took their bowls and robes, and without being attached to the lay families and without informing anyone, they set out on a journey toward Sāvatthī. In due course, they reached Sāvatthī and approached the Blessed One.

When the Blessed One saw those bhikkhus, he said: "Bhikkhus, I have prescribed a training rule that one should not wander on a journey during the rains-retreat. Why are you wandering on a journey?" They reported the whole matter to the Blessed One. As the Blessed One reflected, he did not see any suitable lodging for those bhikkhus in the whole of Jambudīpa, not even a space the size of a four-legged stool. Then the Blessed One said to those bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus, there is no other suitable lodging for you. Only by living in that very place will you attain the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya). Go, bhikkhus, and live depending on that same lodging. If you desire safety from the deities, learn this protection (paritta). This sutta will be both a protection and a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) for you." Thus he spoke this Metta Sutta.

Other teachers, however, say: After saying, "Go, bhikkhus, and live depending on that same lodging," the Blessed One said: "Indeed, a bhikkhu living in a forest should know the practices to be maintained. That is to say—by way of practice in the evening and morning: twice developing loving-kindness, twice reciting the protection, twice developing the perception of foulness (asubha), twice developing the mindfulness of death (maraṇassati), and reflecting on the eight great grounds for sense of urgency (saṃvega)." The eight great grounds for sense of urgency are: birth, aging, sickness, and death—these four—and the four sufferings of the woeful planes. Alternatively: birth, aging, sickness, and death—these four; fifth, the suffering of the woeful planes; the suffering rooted in the round of rebirth in the past; the suffering rooted in the round of rebirth in the future; and the suffering rooted in the search for nutriment in the present. Having thus shown the practices to be maintained repeatedly, the Blessed One taught this Metta Sutta to those bhikkhus for the sake of loving-kindness, for the sake of protection, and for the sake of insight (vipassanā).
178:
The sufferings of the woeful planes are, in another way: birth, aging, sickness, and death—these four; and the suffering of the woeful planes as the fifth; the suffering rooted in the round of rebirth in the past; the suffering rooted in the round of rebirth in the future; and the suffering rooted in the search for nutriment in the present. In this way, the Blessed One made known the practices to be maintained and taught this Metta Sutta to those bhikkhus for the purpose of developing loving-kindness, for the purpose of protection, and for the purpose of jhāna as a basis for insight.

In the first verse of that Metta Sutta beginning with "Karaṇīyamatthakusalena," first, the word-by-word commentary is as follows: "Karaṇīyaṃ" means what should be done, having the sense of what is worthy of being done. "Attha" means the practice (paṭipadā); or, because it is approached for one's own benefit, it is called "attha." "Approached" means "to be reached." One who is skilled in benefit is called "atthakusala" (a bhikkhu skilled in what is beneficial). The word "yaṃ" is an indefinite nominative case, and "taṃ santaṃ padaṃ" is a phrase associated with the accusative case. In that phrase, it is called "santa" (peaceful) by way of its characteristic; it is called "pada" (state/path) because it is to be reached; this is a designation for Nibbāna. "Abhisamecca" means having fully realized or approached. "Sakka" means one who is able, capable, and endowed with strength. "Ujū" means having an upright nature. Being well-upright is called "suhuju." One who is easy to speak to is called "suvaca." "Assa" means "should be." "Mudū" means having a gentle nature. "Anatimānī" means not being overly conceited.

Here, the explanation of the meaning is: In the verse "Karaṇīyamatthakusalena yaṃ taṃ santaṃ padaṃ abhisamecca," first, there is "what should be done" (karaṇīya) and "what should not be done" (akaraṇīya). Among those two, briefly, the group of the three trainings is called "karaṇīya," what should be done. Failure in virtue (sīla-vipatti), failure in view (diṭṭhi-vipatti), failure in conduct (ācāra-vipatti), failure in livelihood (ājīva-vipatti), and so forth, are called "akaraṇīya," what should not be done. Similarly, there is the bhikkhu skilled in what is beneficial (atthakusala) and the bhikkhu skilled in what is not beneficial (anatthakusala).

Among those two, a certain bhikkhu, though having gone forth in this Dispensation, does not apply himself properly, is deficient in virtue, and makes a living depending on the twenty-one kinds of improper search (anesana). Those improper searches are: giving bamboo, giving leaves, giving flowers, giving fruits, giving tooth-sticks, giving water for washing the face, giving water for bathing, giving bath powder, giving clay, flattering lay followers (cāṭukamyata), speaking "bean-soup-like" speech (muggasūpyata), acting as a nursemaid, acting as a messenger (jaṅghapesaniya), practicing medicine, acting as an envoy, going on errands for laypeople, giving alms in exchange for alms, the art of building sites, the art of astrology, and the art of physiognomy. Furthermore, in the six kinds of improper resorts (agocara)...
179:
...wanders. What are these resorts? They are the unsuitable resorts such as courtesans, widows, old maids, eunuchs, bhikkhunīs, and taverns. He lives associating with kings, royal ministers, sectarians, and disciples of sectarians in an improper social mingling with laypeople. Or else, he frequents, associates with, and attends upon families who have no faith or devotion toward monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen; who are abusive and reviling; who do not desire their welfare; who desire their harm, ill-being, and lack of security. Such a person is called 'unskilled in what is beneficial' (anatthakusala).

In this Dispensation, one who, having gone forth, applies himself rightly, abandons improper search (anesanā), and, desiring to be established in the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla), fulfills the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha led by faith; the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties led by mindfulness; the virtue of purification of livelihood led by energy; and the virtue concerning the use of requisites led by wisdom—this person is called 'one skilled in what is beneficial' (atthakusala).

Or else, one who purifies the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha by means of cleansing the seven categories of offenses; the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties by preventing the arising of covetousness and so forth when sense objects strike the six doors; the virtue of purification of livelihood by avoiding improper search and by using requisites praised by the wise, the Buddha, and the Buddha's disciples; the virtue concerning the use of requisites by reflection as previously stated; and clear comprehension (sampajañña) by reflecting on the purposefulness and so forth while moving through the four postures—this person is also called 'one skilled in what is beneficial.'

Just as one cleanses a soiled cloth by means of alkaline water, or a mirror by means of ashes, or gold by means of a furnace; even so, knowing that virtue is purified by means of wisdom, one who cleanses and purifies his virtue with the water of wisdom [is skilled]. And just as a jungle hen guards her egg, or a yak its tail, or a mother her only beloved son, or a one-eyed man his single eye; even so, one who guards his virtue with extreme heedfulness and, when reflecting evening and morning, does not see even a flaw as small as a speck of dust—this person is also called 'one skilled in what is beneficial.'

Or else, one who, being established in virtue that leads to non-remorse, exerts the practice of suppressing the defilements, and having exerted that, performs the preliminary work for kasiṇas and produces the meditative attainments—this person is also called 'one skilled in what is beneficial.' Or else...
180:
...having emerged from the meditative attainment and contemplated the conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra), reaches the fruit of Arahatship—this monk is the foremost among those skilled in what is beneficial.

Among them, those who are praised as 'skilled in what is beneficial' by virtue of being established in virtue that leads to non-remorse, by exerting the practice of suppressing the defilements, or by the Path and Fruit, are intended as 'atthakusala' (one skilled in what is beneficial) in this context. And those monks were of such a nature. Therefore, the Blessed One, referring to those monks, said 'Karaṇīyamatthakusalena' (What should be done by one who is skilled in the good) in a discourse based on a single individual.

After saying this, to those monks in whom doubt had arisen as to 'What should be done?', He said again: 'Yantaṃ santaṃ padaṃ abhisamecca' (Having understood that state of peace). The meaning here is: what should be done by one skilled in what is beneficial who wishes to dwell having realized, through the power of penetration, that peaceful state of Nibbāna praised by the Buddhas, the Paccekabuddhas, and the Noble Disciples. In this verse, the word 'yaṃ' follows by way of authority (adhikāra) the word 'karaṇīyaṃ' mentioned at the beginning of the verse. It also follows the phrase 'taṃ santaṃ padaṃ abhisamecca'. Since this meaning is an elliptical statement in the Pali, it should be understood that the phrase 'viharitukāmena' (by one who wishes to dwell) is added.

Alternatively, 'santaṃ padaṃ abhisamecca' means: having known through mundane wisdom by way of hearsay and so forth that the state of Nibbāna is peaceful, what should be done by one who wishes to attain it follows by way of authority. Thus, the meaning should be understood here as: 'That which should be done, should be done by one skilled in what is beneficial.' Alternatively, when 'Karaṇīyamatthakusalena' was said, to the monks who were wondering 'What is it?', He said 'Yantaṃ santaṃ padaṃ abhisamecca'. Its meaning should be understood thus: having understood the peaceful state of Nibbāna through mundane wisdom, that which should be done, that is what is meant. 'That which should be done' means it is a task to be performed, it is truly worthy of being done.

But what is that task? What else could it be other than the means for attaining that Nibbāna? Indeed, this is already stated by the very first word 'karaṇīyaṃ', which has the sense of 'worthy of being done' and indicates the three trainings (sikkhā). Accordingly, in the explanation of that word, we have said: 'There is that which should be done and there is that which should not be done. Therein, in brief, the three trainings are what should be done.' However, because it was taught in extreme brevity, some of those monks understood it, while others did not. Therefore, to make it known to those who did not understand, that practice which should be done especially by a forest-dwelling monk...
181:
Wishing to show in detail, he first spoke this half-verse: "Able, upright, and very upright, easy to speak to, gentle, and not arrogant."

What does this mean? A forest-dwelling monk who wishes to dwell having penetrated the peaceful state of Nibbāna, or who practices for its attainment having penetrated it with mundane wisdom, being endowed with the second and fourth factors of striving (padhāniyaṅga), should be able to practice for the penetration of the Truths without regard for body or life. Likewise, in the preliminary work of the kasina, in undertaking duties, etc., in repairing one's own bowl and robes, etc., and in the various major and minor duties to be performed for fellow practitioners according to seniority, and in other such matters, he should be one who is able, skillful, diligent, and capable without being lazy.

Though being able, he should also be upright (uju) by being endowed with the third factor of striving. Though being upright, he should not be satisfied with being upright just once, but should be very upright (su-uju) by being firm again and again throughout life without slackening. Alternatively, he is upright (uju) due to lack of deceit, and very upright (su-uju) due to lack of guile. He is upright (uju) by abandoning crookedness of body and speech, and very upright (su-uju) by abandoning crookedness of mind. Alternatively, he is upright (uju) by not making manifest qualities he does not possess, and very upright (su-uju) by not accepting gains that arise through non-existent qualities. Thus, through meditation on the object and characteristics (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna and lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna), through the first two words and the third training, and through purity of effort and intention (payogāsaya-suddhi), he should be upright and very upright in body, speech, and mind.

Not only upright and very upright, but he should also be easy to speak to (suvaca). For a person who, when told "This should not be done," says "What did you see? What did you hear? Who are you to tell me? Are you my preceptor, teacher, friend, or companion?" or who harasses by remaining silent, or who accepts but does not act accordingly—such a person is far from the attainment of distinction. But a person who, when admonished, says "It is well, Bhante, you have spoken well; one's own faults are indeed hard to see; please tell me again if you see such a fault in the future out of compassion; I have received admonition from you after a long time," and practices according to the instruction—such a person is near to the attainment of distinction. Therefore, accepting and following the words of others, he should be easy to speak to (suvaca).

Just as he is easy to speak to, so should he be gentle (mudu). "Gentle" means that when employed by householders for errands or as a messenger, etc., he does not show gentleness there but remains firm; however, in the duties and the entire holy life (brahmacariya), he should be gentle, capable of being applied to various wholesome deeds like well-refined gold. Alternatively, "gentle" means he should be one with an open countenance, without frowning.
182:
He should be one with a habit of courtesy, easy to converse with, like a good landing place at a river that is easy to descend into. Not only gentle, but he should also be not arrogant (anatimānī). He should not despise others because of birth, lineage, or other grounds for conceit; he should dwell with a mind like that of a young outcaste boy, like the Elder Sāriputta.

Thus, the Blessed One, having spoken of some duties for the forest-dwelling monk who wishes to dwell having reached the peaceful Nibbāna or who is practicing to attain it, and wishing to speak of further qualities, spoke the second verse beginning with "Santussako ca" (And contented).

In that verse, "santussako" means one who is contented with the twelvefold contentment as previously described. Alternatively, he is "tussako" because he is contented; "santussako" because he is contented with what is his own (saka), with what is present (santa), and with equanimity (sama). Therein, "what is his own" (saka) refers to the group of the four requisites pointed out at the time of ordination as "depending on alms-food..." and accepted by himself. Whether that requisite is good or bad, given respectfully or disrespectfully, if he sustains himself without showing any change of mind at the time of receiving or using it, he is called "contented with what is his own." "What is present" (santa) means the requisites he has already obtained and are in his possession. Being contented with only those existing requisites, not desiring more, and abandoning greed, he is called "contented with what is present." "Equanimity" (sama) means the abandoning of attraction and repulsion towards the desirable and undesirable. Being contented with all objects through such equanimity, he is called "contented with equanimity."

He is "subhara" because he is easily supported; it means he is easy to maintain. For a monk who, even when given a bowl full of rice and meat, etc., shows a sour face or dissatisfaction, or who, in the presence of the donors, disparages that alms-food saying "What is this you have given?" and gives it away to novices or householders—this monk is difficult to support (dubbhara). Seeing him, people avoid him from afar, saying "This monk is difficult to support; it is not possible to maintain him." But a monk who, having received whatever is coarse or fine, little or much, is satisfied and sustains himself with a clear countenance—this monk is easy to support (subhara). Seeing him, people become very confident and undertake to support him, saying "Our noble lord is easy to support; he is contented with little; we will support him." Such a monk is intended here as "subhara".
183:
"They are satisfied even with a little, and we will support this venerable one," having made such a promise, they support him. One of such a nature is here meant by "easy to support" (subhara).

One who has few duties is called appakicca. This refers to one who is not preoccupied with many activities such as delighting in new work, delighting in talk, or delighting in company. Alternatively, it means one who is free from tasks such as construction work in the entire monastery, Sangha affairs, or supervising novices and monastery attendants, and instead, performs only personal tasks like shaving hair, cutting nails, and repairing the bowl and robes, while being devoted to the duties of a recluse (samaṇadhamma).

One who has a light livelihood is called sallahukavutti. Unlike some monks with many possessions who, when departing for another region, have many people carry bowls, robes, mats, oil, molasses, etc., on their heads or waists, this monk has few requisites. He carries only the eight requisites of a monk, such as the bowl and robes. When departing for another region, he goes like a winged bird, taking only its wings as it flies. Such a person is here meant by sallahukavutti. One who has peaceful faculties is called santindriya. This means one whose faculties are not agitated by lust, etc., regarding pleasant objects and so forth. Nipaka means one who is prudent, discerning, and wise. It refers to being endowed with the wisdom that guards virtue, the wisdom that reflects on requisites like robes, and the wisdom that distinguishes the seven kinds of suitable things (sappāya) such as dwellings.

One who is not impudent is called appagabbha. This means being free from the eight types of bodily impudence (kāyapāgabbhiya), the four types of verbal impudence (vacīpāgabbhiya), and the many types of mental impudence (manopāgabbhiya).

Bodily impudence (kāyapāgabbhiya) in eight places refers to behaving inappropriately with the body in the midst of the Sangha, in the midst of a group, in the presence of an individual, in the dining hall, in the sauna (jantāghara), at the bathing place, on the alms-round path, and when entering a house. For instance, in this Dispensation, someone might sit in the midst of the Sangha with knees clasped or with feet crossed, and so on. Likewise, they behave thus in the midst of a group (an assembly of the fourfold community) or in the presence of senior persons. In the dining hall, they do not give up seats to seniors or they block the seats of juniors. Similarly, in the sauna, they light a fire, etc., without asking permission from the seniors. At the bathing place, disregarding the rule that "one should bathe in the order of arrival without making a distinction between junior and senior"...
184:
Disregarding such words, even if arriving later, they enter the water and disturb both seniors and juniors. On the alms-round path, desiring the best seat, the best water, or the best food, they walk in front of the seniors, brushing shoulders with them. When entering a village, they enter before the seniors. They engage in physical play with juniors. Such things are called bodily impudence (kāyapāgabbhiya).

Verbal impudence (vacīpāgabbhiya) in four places refers to uttering inappropriate words in the midst of the Sangha, a group, an individual, or in a village. For instance, in this Dispensation, someone might preach the Dhamma in the midst of the Sangha without asking permission from a senior. Likewise, they preach without permission in a group or in the presence of senior persons as mentioned before. When questioned by people there, they answer first without asking the senior. In a village, they say things like: "Is such-and-such a woman there? Is there gruel, or snacks, or food? What will you give me? What shall I chew today? What shall I eat? What shall I drink?" and so on.

Mental impudence (manopāgabbhiya) in many instances refers to various kinds of inappropriate thoughts, such as sensual thoughts, occurring only in the mind without resulting in physical or verbal transgression in those various places.

"Kulesu ananugiddho" means not being greedy towards the families one visits, either through craving for requisites or through improper socializing with laypeople. It means not grieving with them, not rejoicing with them, not being happy when they are happy, not being sad when they are sad, and not involving oneself in their affairs that arise. In this verse, the word "assa" in "suvaco cassa" should be understood as connected to all terms, such as "santuṭṭhako ca assa" (he should be easily contented) and "subhara ca assa" (he should be easy to support).

Thus, the Blessed One, having explained the further duties for a forest-dwelling monk who wishes to dwell having realized the state of peace (Nibbāna) or who wishes to practice for its attainment, now wishing to explain what should not be done, spoke this half-verse: "Na ca khuddamañcare kiñci, yena viññū pare upavadeyyuṃ." Its meaning is: A monk performing these duties should not practice any mean conduct, which is called misconduct of body, speech, and mind. In not practicing it, it means he should not practice even a little, not even a minute fault, let alone gross misconduct.
185:
Then, he shows the fault in that monk's conduct that is visible even in the present life with the words: "for which other wise people might censure him." Here, other unwise people are not the standard. They might treat what is faultless as faulty, or a minor fault as a major one. Only the wise are the standard. For they, having investigated and scrutinized, speak blame of those deserving blame and praise of those deserving praise; therefore, it is said "other wise people" (viññū pare).

Thus, the Buddha, having explained the preliminary practice of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna-upacāra) by distinguishing what should and should not be done for all monks who wish to dwell having penetrated the peaceful state of Nibbāna with these two and a half verses, or who wish to practice for its attainment—especially for forest-dwelling monks, taking the forest-dwelling as the primary example—now begins to speak the discourse on loving-kindness (metta-kathā) by way of "May they be happy and safe," etc., both as a protection (paritta) to ward off the danger of harassment by deities for those monks, and as a subject of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) by way of jhāna which is the basis for insight (vipassanā).

In that verse, "sukhin" means those endowed with happiness. "Khemin" means those who are safe, meaning free from fear and calamities. "Sabbē" means without exception. "Sattā" means living beings. "Sukhitattā" means those with happy minds. Here, they should be understood as "sukhin" through bodily happiness, "sukhitattā" through mental happiness, and "khemin" through both or through the cessation of all fears and calamities. Why is it spoken thus? To show the method of developing loving-kindness. For loving-kindness should be developed thus: "May all beings be happy," or "May they be safe," or "May they be happy-hearted."

Having thus shown the development of loving-kindness in brief from the access (upacāra) to the peak of absorption (appanā), he now speaks the two verses beginning with "Ye keci" to show it in detail. Alternatively, because a mind accustomed to many objects cannot settle on a single object at the very beginning, but can settle gradually by following the various types of objects, he speaks the two verses beginning with "Ye keci" so that the mind may settle by following the objects consisting of dyads and triads such as "the trembling" (tasa) and "the firm" (thāvara). Or, whatever object is clear to a particular monk, his mind settles easily on that object. Therefore, wishing to establish the mind of those monks on whichever object is clear to them, he speaks these two verses beginning with "Ye keci" which illustrate the various objects in dyads and triads such as "the trembling" and "the firm."
186:
In this Metta Sutta, there are four dyads (duka): the trembling and the firm (tasa-thāvara), the seen and the unseen (diṭṭha-adiṭṭha), the distant and the near (dūra-santika), and those who have come to be and those seeking birth (bhūta-sambhavesī). Among the six terms beginning with "long" (dīgha), because the term "medium" (majjhima) can be applied in three places and the term "tiny" (aṇuka) in two places, he shows three triads (tika): the long-short-medium triad, the large-tiny-medium triad, and the gross-tiny-medium triad. In that verse, the words "Ye keci" mean all without exception. Only living beings are called "bhūta," hence "pāṇabhūtā." Alternatively, those beings of the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra) connected with inhalation and exhalation should be taken as "pāṇa." Because they have come into being, they are called "bhūta." By this word "bhūta," beings of one-constituent and four-constituent existence are to be taken. "Atthi" means they exist, they are found to be present.

Thus, having shown all beings encompassed by the dyads and triads collectively with the words "Ye keci pāṇabhūtatthi," he now shows them again by encompassing all those beings with this dyad: "whether trembling or firm, without exception" (tasā vā thāvarā vā anavasesā).

In that verse, they are called "tasā" because they tremble; this is a designation for those with craving and fear. They are called "thāvarā" because they stand firm without trembling; this is a designation for Arahants who have abandoned craving and fear. "Anavasesā" means there is no remainder among those beings; it means all beings. The phrase "sabbē sattā bhavantu sukhitattā" (may all beings be happy-hearted) found at the end of the second verse should be connected to all the dyads and triads. Thus: "Whatever living beings there are, whether trembling or firm, all without exception, may these beings also be happy-hearted." This should be connected to all, up to "whether they have come to be or are seeking birth" (bhūtā vā sambhavesī vā).

Now, in illustrating the three triads of long, short, medium, etc., among the six terms beginning with "dīghā vā," "dīghā" refers to beings with long bodies such as nagas, fish, and monitor lizards. Indeed, in the great ocean, the bodies of nagas are many fathoms long. The bodies of fish, monitor lizards, etc., are also many yojanas long. "Mahantā" refers to beings with large bodies, such as fish and turtles in the water, elephants and nagas on land, and Danava asuras among non-humans. It is also said: "Among those with bodies, Rāhu is the foremost." The body of that Rāhu Asurinda is 4,800 yojanas in height. The arms are 1,200 yojanas in extent. The space between the eyebrows is 50 yojanas. Likewise, the spaces between the fingers and the palms of the hands are 200 yojanas each. "Majjhimā" refers to beings with medium-sized bodies such as horses, cattle, buffaloes, and pigs. "Rassakā" refers to beings such as dwarfs who are of a smaller size than the long and medium beings in those respective species. "Aṇukā" means...
187:
Beings who are not within the range of the physical eye but are within the scope of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), such as those born in water etc., having subtle bodies, or beings such as lice, are called 'aṇuka' (small). Alternatively, beings who are smaller in size than the large, medium, stout, or average types in various species should be known as 'aṇuka'. Beings with rounded bodies such as fish, turtles, shells, and snails (sambuka) etc., are called 'thūla' (large/stout).

Having thus shown all beings without exception through these three triads, He now shows them comprehensively through three dyads starting with 'diṭṭhā vā yeva adiṭṭhā'.

In that verse, 'diṭṭhā' (seen) refers to beings previously seen by way of coming into the range of one's own vision. 'Adiṭṭhā' (unseen) refers to beings residing in other oceans, other mountains, other world-systems (cakkavāḷa), and so on. By the dyad 'ye vā dūre vasanti avidūre', He shows beings living far from or near to one's own person (attabhāva). These should be understood by way of comparison. Beings living in one's own body are called 'avidūre' (near); those living outside the body are called 'dūre' (far). Similarly, those living within the vicinity (upacāra) are 'near', and those outside the vicinity are 'far'. Those living in one's own monastery, village, district, island, or world-system are called 'near', while those in another world-system are said to be living 'far'.

'Bhūta' means those who have been born or have come into existence. This term refers to the Arahants, who are counted as those who have already become and will not be born again. 'Sambhavesī' means those seeking birth because they seek to come into existence in the future as they have not yet abandoned the fetters of existence (bhava-saṃyojana). This is a term for trainees (sekkha) and worldlings (puthujjana). Alternatively, among the four types of birth, egg-born (aṇḍaja) and womb-born (jalābuja) beings are called 'sambhavesī' as long as they have not yet broken the eggshell or the membrane (vatthikosa). Once they break the shell or membrane and come out, they are called 'bhūta'. Moisture-born (saṃsedaja) and spontaneously-born (opapātika) beings are called 'sambhavesī' at the first moment of consciousness. From the second moment of consciousness onwards, they are called 'bhūta'. Or, they are called 'sambhavesī' as long as they remain in the posture (iriyāpatha) in which they were born and have not yet reached another posture. After that, they are called 'bhūta'.

Thus, the Blessed One, through these two and a half verses starting with 'sukhi-no vā', in various ways, by way of wishing for the welfare and happiness of those monks, towards beings...
188:
Having shown the development of loving-kindness (mettā-bhāvanā), the Blessed One now speaks the words starting with 'na paro paraṃ nikubbetha', wishing to show it also by way of the desire that others do not encounter harm or suffering. This is the ancient reading (porāṇa-pāṭha); however, nowadays some read it as 'paraṃ hī', but that reading is not good.

In that verse, 'paro' means another person. 'Paraṃ' means another person (as object). 'Na nikubbetha' means one should not deceive. 'Nātimaññetha' means one should not look down upon or despise. 'Katthaci' means in any place—whether in a village, a town, a field, among relatives, or among a group, etc. 'Naṃ' means that person. 'Kañci' means anyone—whether a king, a brahmin, a householder, a monk, a wealthy person, or a poor person, etc. 'Byārosanā paṭighasaññā' refers to harming through physical or vocal distortion (byārosanā) and harboring ill-will through mental distortion (paṭighasaññā). In fact, although it should be said as 'byārosanāya paṭighasaññāya', it is stated as 'byārosanā paṭighasaññā', just as 'sammadaññāya vimuttā' is stated as 'sammadaññā vimuttā', and 'anupubbasikkhāya anupubbakiriyāya anupubbapaṭipadāya' is stated as 'anupubbasikkhā anupubbakiriyā anupubbapaṭipadā'. 'Nāññamaññassa dukkhamiccheyya' means one should not desire suffering for one another. What is meant? Loving-kindness should be developed not only through the reflection 'may they be happy or safe', etc. But also, one should develop it by reflecting: 'May no person whatsoever deceive any other person through trickery or fraud; may no one despise any other person in any place through the nine grounds of conceit (mānavatthu) such as birth, etc.; and may they not desire suffering for one another through either harming or resentment.'

Thus, having shown the development of loving-kindness in terms of its meaning through the desire that others do not encounter harm or suffering, He now speaks the words starting with 'mātā yathā niyaṃ puttaṃ' to show that same development of loving-kindness with a simile.

The meaning of that verse is: Just as a mother would protect her own son, born from her own breast, and if he were an only son, she would protect him even at the cost of her own life; just as she would protect him by sacrificing her own life to prevent him from encountering suffering, even so, one should develop this heart of loving-kindness towards all beings, generating it again and again, and increasing it. One should develop it immeasurably, either by taking immeasurable beings as the object or by pervading a single being without exception.
189:
Having shown the development of loving-kindness in every way, he now says "Mettāñca sabbalokasmiṃ" (And loving-kindness towards the whole world) to show its expansion.

In that verse, one is called a 'friend' (mitta) because they love and protect. The meaning is that they are sticky [attached in a good way] due to a disposition for welfare and protect against the arrival of harm. The state of a friend is 'loving-kindness' (mettā). 'Sabbalokasmiṃ' means in the entire world without exception. 'Lokasmiṃ' means in the world of beings (sattaloka). It is called 'mānasa' (mental state) because it arises in the mind. It is so called because that loving-kindness is associated with consciousness. 'Bhāvaye' means one should develop. It is called 'aparimāṇa' (immeasurable) because there is no limit to that mind of loving-kindness. It is so called because it takes immeasurable beings as its object. 'Uddhaṃ' (above) refers to the upper direction; by this word, the formless realm (arūpabhava) is taken. 'Adho' (below) refers to the lower direction; by this word, the sense realm (kāmabhava) is taken. 'Tiriyaṃ' (across) refers to the middle (horizontal) direction; by this word, the fine-material realm (rūpabhava) is taken. 'Asambādhaṃ' (unobstructed) means being free from confinement, meaning the boundaries have been broken. 'Boundary' refers to an enemy; the meaning is that loving-kindness occurs even towards that enemy. 'Averaṃ' (without enmity) means being free from enmity, meaning free from the arising of intentions of ill-will even at intervals. 'Asapattaṃ' means the absence of rivals. For a person who dwells in loving-kindness is dear to humans and dear to non-humans (amanussa), and has no enemies; therefore, because their mind is free from rivals, it is called 'asapattaṃ'. 'Paccatthika' and 'sapatta' are synonyms meaning enemy. This is the word-by-word commentary (anupada-vaṇṇanā).

The intended meaning here (adhippetattha-vaṇṇanā) is: regarding the statement "Thus should one develop an immeasurable mind of loving-kindness towards all beings," one should develop that immeasurable mind of loving-kindness towards the whole world, making it reach growth, increase, and abundance. How should it be developed? One should develop it above, below, and across. Above as far as the peak of existence (bhavagga), below as far as the Avīci hell, and across to the remaining directions without exception. Alternatively, one should develop it by pervading the formless realm above, the sense realm below, and the fine-material realm across without exception. While developing it thus, one should develop it making it free from confinement, enmity, and rivals, so that there is no confinement or harboring of enmity. Alternatively, when one reaches the perfection of development, it is 'unobstructed' (asambādha) due to gaining opportunity everywhere. It is 'without enmity' (avera) by removing one's own ill-will towards others, and 'without rivals' (asapatta) by removing the ill-will of others towards oneself. One should develop and increase that immeasurable mind of loving-kindness—unobstructed, without enmity, and without rivals—in the whole world through the three-fold division of above, below, and across.
190:
Having shown the expansion of the development of loving-kindness, he now says "Standing, walking... [pe]... one should resolve" to show the absence of restriction in postures for one who dwells devoted to that development.

The meaning of that verse is: a monk developing this mind associated with loving-kindness does not restrict his posture as in passages like "sitting down, having crossed his legs and set his body erect," but rather, while dispelling the discomfort of any particular posture as he pleases, whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down, as long as he is free from drowsiness, he should resolve upon this mindfulness associated with the mettā-jhāna.

Alternatively, having shown the expansion of the development of loving-kindness, he now says "Standing, walking," etc., to show the state of mastery (vasībhāva). For one who has attained mastery, in whatever posture—standing, walking, sitting, or lying down—he wishes to resolve upon this mindfulness of mettā-jhāna, [he can do so]. Alternatively, standing, walking, etc., do not cause obstacles for him; rather, for as long as he wishes to resolve upon this mindfulness of mettā-jhāna, he resolves upon it being free from drowsiness, and there is no sluggishness in him. Therefore, he said: "Standing, walking, sitting, or lying down, as long as he is free from drowsiness, he should resolve upon this mindfulness."

The meaning of that verse is: regarding the development of loving-kindness mentioned as "one should develop a mind associated with loving-kindness towards the whole world," one should develop that loving-kindness such that in postures like standing, etc., or regardless of standing, etc., for as long as one wishes to resolve upon this mindfulness of mettā-jhāna, one should resolve upon this mindfulness being free from drowsiness.

Thus, showing the mastery of the development of loving-kindness and urging one towards that dwelling in loving-kindness by saying "one should resolve upon this mindfulness," he now says "This dwelling they call divine here" to praise that dwelling.

The meaning of that verse is: the dwelling in loving-kindness described from "May beings be happy and secure" until the end "one should resolve upon this mindfulness"—this dwelling is called a 'Brahma-dwelling' (brahmavihāra) or the 'supreme dwelling' here in the Dhamma-Vinaya of the Noble One, because it is faultless among the four dwellings (divine, Brahma, noble, and postural) and because it brings benefit to oneself and others. Therefore, constantly, continuously, and without interruption, whether standing or walking...
191:
Whether sitting or lying down, as long as one is free from drowsiness, one should resolve on this mindfulness associated with loving-kindness. Thus, the Blessed One, having shown the development of loving-kindness (mettā-bhāvanā) to those monks in various ways, now, because loving-kindness has beings as its object and is therefore close to the view of self (attadiṭṭhi), he wished to show the monks the attainment of the stage of an Ariya by making that very mettā-jhāna the basis through the means of prohibiting and abandoning the adherence to views. Thus, he concluded the teaching with the verse beginning with "Diṭṭhiñca anupaggamma".

The meaning of that verse is: This dwelling in mettā-jhāna, which is praised as "this is called the divine abiding (brahmavihāra) in this Dispensation"—having emerged from that, one should grasp the mental factors such as initial thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra) present therein, and following their physical bases and so on, grasp the material phenomena (rūpa-dhamma). By thus distinguishing mind and matter (nāmarūpa), one realizes, "This is merely a heap of formations (saṅkhāra); no being is to be found here." In this way, without falling into wrong views, one becomes virtuous through successive supramundane virtue (lokuttara-sīla) and becomes endowed with vision (dassana), which is the right view of the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga-sammādiṭṭhi) associated with supramundane virtue. Thereafter, whatever greed for sensual pleasures (kāmagadha) remains unabandoned, one should subdue and calm it by making it thin through the path of Once-returner (sakadāgāmi-magga) and by abandoning it without remainder through the path of Non-returner (anāgāmi-magga). Then, "he surely does not come to a womb again"; he is reborn in the Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa), attains Arahatship there, and attains Parinibbāna.

Having thus concluded the teaching, the Blessed One said to those monks: "Go, monks, and dwell in that same forest grove. Recite this sutta after striking the wooden gong on the eight days of Dhamma hearing each month. Hold Dhamma discussions, converse, and express appreciation (anumodanā). Devote yourselves to, develop, and practice this very meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) frequently. If you do so, those non-humans (amanussa) will not show you those fearful objects; on the contrary, they will become those who desire your welfare and benefit." Having replied "Very well" to the Blessed One, those monks rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him, went to that forest, and did exactly as instructed. The deities, thinking "The venerable ones desire our welfare and benefit," became filled with joy and happiness. They themselves swept the dwellings, prepared hot water, massaged the monks' backs and feet, and provided protection. Those monks, likewise developing loving-kindness...
192:
Making that very mettā the basis and undertaking insight (vipassanā), all those monks attained the highest fruit, Arahatship, within that very rainy season and performed the pure Pavāraṇā on the Great Pavāraṇā day.

Thus, having practiced the duty to be performed,
Taught by the Tathāgata, the Lord of Dhamma,
Who is skilled in what is beneficial,
And having experienced the supreme peace of heart,
Those of complete wisdom reach the state of peace.

Therefore, desiring to dwell having reached that state of peace,
Which is deathless, wonderful, and dear to the Ariyas,
A wise person, endowed with stainless virtue, concentration, and wisdom,
Should constantly fulfill the duty to be performed.

## The commentary on the Mettā Sutta in the Paramatthajotikā, the Khuddaka Commentary,
## and the Suttanipāta Commentary, is finished.
## 9. Hemavata Sutta Commentary

The sutta beginning with "Ajja pannaraso" is the Hemavata Sutta. What is its origin? Its origin is based on questions. Indeed, being asked by the yakkha Hemavata, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with "Chasu loko samuppanno". Therein, the part beginning with "Ajja pannaraso" was spoken by the yakkha Sātāgiri; the part beginning with "Iti sātāgiro" was spoken by the reciters (saṅgītikāra); the part beginning with "Kacci mano" was spoken by Hemavata; and the part beginning with "Chasu loko" was spoken by the Blessed One. All these words combined are called the "Hemavata Sutta". Some teachers also call it the "Sātāgiri Sutta".

In that sutta, there is the verse beginning with "Ajja pannaraso". Its origin should be known thus: In this very Bhadda Kappa, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, the Kassapa Sammāsambuddha arose. After remaining for sixteen thousand years, he attained Parinibbāna. A great ceremony of worship and funeral rites was performed for him. The relics of that Blessed One...
193:
The relics of the Buddha Kassapa remained as a single solid mass like a block of gold, without being scattered. This is the nature of long-lived Buddhas. Short-lived Buddhas, however, pass away before many people have had the chance to see them; therefore, out of compassion, thinking, "Let people in various places gain merit by worshipping the relics," they resolve, "May my relics be scattered." Consequently, their relics disperse like gold dust, just like the relics of our Blessed One.

People built a single relic chamber for that Blessed One and established a stupa one league (yojana) in height and circumference. There were four gates at intervals of one gāvuta each. King Kikī took charge of one gate; his son, the prince named Pathavindhara, took one; the ministers led by the general took one; and the country folk led by the treasurer took one. There were bricks made of solid red gold, appearing like liquid gold, and bricks made of various jewels, each worth a hundred thousand [pieces of money]. They used orpiment and realgar for the mortar and fragrant oil instead of water to establish that stupa.

When the stupa was thus established, two young men of good family who were friends went forth from the world and were ordained in the presence of the elders who were direct disciples of the Buddha. In the dispensation of long-lived Buddhas, only direct disciples grant the going forth (pabbajjā), the full ordination (upasampadā), and the dependence (nissaya); others do not have the opportunity to do so. Then those young men asked, "Venerable sirs, how many duties (dhura) are there in the Sasana?" The elders replied, "There are two duties: vāsadhura and pariyattidhura."

"Among them, a young man of good family who has gone forth should stay for five years in the presence of his teachers and preceptors, fulfilling the major and minor duties. Having mastered the Pātimokkha and two or three recitation sections (bhāṇavāra) of the Suttantas, and having taken a meditation subject, he should enter the forest, free from attachment to family or group, and strive and exert himself to realize Arahatship. This is called vāsadhura. On the other hand, according to one's own capacity, one should master one Nikaya, or two, or all five Nikayas, and apply oneself to the Sasana so that it is well-purified in both text (pariyatti) and meaning (attha). This is called pariyattidhura."

Then those young men said, "Between the two duties, vāsadhura is indeed the most excellent. However, we are still young; we will fulfill vāsadhura when we are old. For now, let us fulfill pariyattidhura." They then began their study (pariyatti). Being naturally wise, they soon became knowledgeable in the entire Word of the Buddha (Buddhavacana) as it is, and became extremely skilled in the analysis of the Vinaya. Because of their study, a following arose for them...
194:
Based on that scriptural study (pariyatti), gains and honors arose; each elder monk had a retinue of five hundred monks. Those elders lived illuminating the Dispensation (Sāsana) of the Blessed One, and it became once again as if it were the time of the Buddha.

At that time, two monks lived in a small village: a speaker of Dhamma (Dhammavādī) and a speaker of non-Dhamma (Adhammavādī). The Adhammavādī monk was harsh, coarse, and talkative; his improper conduct was evident to the other (Dhammavādī) monk. Therefore, that Dhammavādī monk admonished him, saying, "Friend, this action of yours is not suitable for the Dispensation."

That Adhammavādī monk rejected the accusation, saying, "What did you see? What did you hear?" The other monk replied, "The experts in the Discipline (Vinayadhara) will know."

Then the Adhammavādī monk, realizing, "If the Vinaya experts decide this matter, I will certainly have no standing in the Dispensation," and wishing to win them over to his side, immediately took his requisites and approached those two elder monks. He offered them monastic requisites and began to live under their tutelage (nissaya). He served those elders in all duties, great and small, acting as if he were one who respectfully wished to fulfill all obligations.

Then one day, having gone to serve them and paid his respects, he remained standing even though the elders gave him leave to depart. The elders asked him, "Is there something you wish to say?" He replied, "Venerable sirs, yes. There is a dispute between me and another monk regarding improper conduct. If that monk comes here and reports this matter, please do not decide it according to the rule."

The elders said, "It is not proper to refrain from deciding a case that has been brought forward according to the rule." He pleaded, "Venerable sirs, if you do so, I will have no standing in the Dispensation. Let that evil fall upon me alone; please do not decide it." Being pressured by him, those elders consented.

Having obtained their promise, he returned to that monastery and, saying, "I have settled everything with the Vinaya experts," he treated the Dhammavādī monk with even greater contempt and spoke to him with harsh words. The Dhammavādī monk, realizing, "This man has become free from doubt (fearless)," immediately departed and approached the thousand monks who were the retinue of the elders, saying, "Friends, should not a case that has been brought forward be decided according to the Dhamma? Or, without bringing it to a formal hearing, should not harmony be established by making each party confess their faults? Now, these elders have neither decided the case nor established harmony. What is the meaning of this?"

Upon hearing this, those monks remained silent, thinking, "Surely the teachers must know something." 

Then the Adhammavādī monk, taking the opportunity, came and said, "Formerly you said, 'The Vinaya experts will know.' Now, go and report it to those Vinaya experts!" He then oppressed the Dhammavādī monk, saying, "From this day forth, you are the loser; do not come to this monastery," and went away. Then the Dhammavādī monk approached the elders and cried out with a loud voice, "You have disregarded the Dispensation and favored only the person, thinking, 'He serves us and pleases us.' You have protected the person instead of the Dispensation. From this day forth, you are no longer fit to give decisions. Today, the Blessed One Kassapa has attained Parinibbāna!" Lamenting, "The Dispensation of the Teacher is destroyed!" he departed.

Then those monks, their minds filled with agitation, felt remorse, thinking, "By protecting a person, we have thrown the jewel of the Dispensation into a pit (or slough)." Oppressed by that remorse, those monks were unable to be reborn in the celestial realm. One teacher was reborn as a Yakkha named Hemavata on Mount Hemavata in the Himalayas. The second teacher was reborn in the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa)...
195:
...oppressing that Dhammavādī monk, saying, "From this day forth, you are the loser; do not come to this monastery," he departed. Furthermore, the Dhammavādī monk approached the elder monks and cried out with a loud voice, "Venerable sirs, you have disregarded the Dispensation and favored only the person, thinking, 'He serves us and pleases us.' You have protected the person instead of the Dispensation. From this day forth, you are no longer fit to give a decision. Today, the Blessed One Kassapa has attained Parinibbāna!" Lamenting, "The Dispensation of the Teacher is destroyed!" he departed.

Then those monks, their minds filled with agitation, felt remorse, thinking, "By protecting a person, we have thrown the jewel of the Dispensation into a pit (or a chasm)." Those monks, their minds being oppressed by that remorse, were unable to be reborn in the celestial realm when they passed away. One teacher was reborn as a Yakkha named Hemavata on Mount Hemavata in the Himalayas. The second teacher was reborn as a Yakkha named Sātāgira on Mount Sāta in the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa). The student monks who were the retinue of those teachers, having followed the will of those teachers, were also unable to be reborn in the celestial realm and were reborn only as Yakkhas in the retinue of those teachers. However, the lay people who were the donors of requisites to those monks were reborn in the celestial realm. Hemavata and Sātāgira became powerful Yakkha kings among the twenty-eight Yakkha generals.
