The custom of the Yakkha generals is as follows: Every month, for eight days, there is a gathering of deities at the Nāgavatī Pavilion on the Manosilātala (Red Arsenic Plain) in the Himalayas for the purpose of deciding matters of Dhamma; it is the custom that they must assemble in that pavilion. At that time, Sātāgira and Hemavata saw and recognized each other at that assembly. "Friend, where were you reborn? Where are you?" Having asked each other about their places of rebirth, they became displeased. "Friend, although we practiced the recluse's Dhamma for twenty thousand years in the past, we have been reborn in the womb of Yakkhas because we relied on a bad friend; we are ruined. Our donors of requisites, however, have been reborn in the celestial realms of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara)," they said.

Then the Yakkha Sātāgira said, "Friend, the Himalayan region is known for its wonders and marvels. If you see or hear of any wonder, please inform me as well." The Yakkha Hemavata also said, "Friend, the Middle Country is known for its wonders and marvels. If you see or hear of any wonder, please inform me as well." Thus, while those two friends lived without being able to abandon their existence as Yakkhas, having made this pact with each other, one Buddha-interval (buddhantara) passed. The great earth rose up by one yojana and three gāvutas.
196:
At that time, our Bodhisatta, having fulfilled the perfections from the time he made the aspiration at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara up until the Vessantara Jātaka, was reborn in the Tusita heaven and remained there for the full lifespan. As stated in the Dhammapada-nidāna, being requested by the deities, he made the five great investigations. After informing the deities and while the thirty-two omens were appearing, he took conception in this human world, causing the ten thousand world systems to tremble. Even upon seeing those signs, these yakkhas did not know, thinking, 'They have arisen due to this cause.' Some teachers say, 'They did not see them because they were engrossed in play.' This same principle applies to his birth, the great renunciation, and his attainment of Enlightenment. However, when the Blessed One was turning the noble Wheel of Dhamma, characterized by three rounds and twelve aspects, while addressing the group of five monks (pañcavaggiya), among those deities, Sātāgira alone was the first to see the great earthquake omen and the miracles. Knowing the cause of the arising of those signs, he approached the Blessed One with his retinue and listened to the Dhamma, yet he did not attain any special distinction. Why? Because while listening to the Dhamma, he remembered the yakkha Hemavata and looked around the assembly, wondering, 'Has my friend arrived or not?' When he did not see him, his mind became distracted, thinking, 'My friend is truly at a loss, for he does not hear the Blessed One's Dhamma taught with such wonderful brilliance.' Even though the sun had set, the Blessed One did not conclude the discourse.

Then Sātāgira thought, 'I will fetch my friend and listen to the Dhamma together with him.' He created elephant-carriages, horse-carriages, garuḍa-carriages, and so on, and surrounded by five hundred yakkhas, he set out towards the Himavanta. At that time, Hemavata was also coming. Because the thirty-two omens appear and then vanish only at the moments of conception, birth, renunciation, Enlightenment, and Parinibbāna—they do not last long—but at the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, those signs appear specially and remain for a longer time before vanishing. Therefore, seeing that wonderful manifestation in the Himavanta, Hemavata thought, 'Since I was born, I have never seen this mountain so delightful; now, I will fetch my friend Sātāgira and enjoy this glory of flowers together with him.' Thus, he set out towards the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa). The two met in the sky above Rājagaha and questioned each other about the reason for their coming. Hemavata said, 'Friend, since I was born, I have never seen this Himavanta mountain so delightful with trees blooming out of season; therefore, I have come to enjoy this glory of flowers with you.'
197:
"I have come," said Hemavata. Sātāgira asked, "Friend Hemavata, do you know the reason why this miracle of unseasonal flowers has occurred?" "Friend Sātāgira, I do not know," Hemavata replied. "Friend Hemavata, this miracle has occurred not only in the Himavanta, but indeed throughout the ten thousand world systems. The Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) has arisen in the world; today He has turned the Wheel of Dhamma. It is for that reason that this miracle has occurred," said Sātāgira. Thus, after informing Hemavata of the arising of the Buddha, Sātāgira, wishing to lead him to the presence of the Blessed One, spoke this verse. Some teachers, however, say that the Blessed One spoke this verse beginning with "Ajja pannaraso" while residing at the Gotamaka Cetiya.

In that verse, "Ajja" (today) means this night is the fifteenth day by the reckoning of the fortnight (pakkha), and because it is to be observed, it is called the Uposatha day. Or, among the three kinds of Uposatha, today is the fifteenth-day Uposatha; it is not the fourteenth-day Uposatha, nor the Sāmaggi-uposatha (Uposatha of Unity). Furthermore, the word "Uposatha" is used in many senses, such as the recitation of the Pātimokkha, the eightfold virtue, fasting (upavāsa), designation, and the day itself. In sentences such as "Come, friend Kappina, we shall go to the Uposatha," the word Uposatha refers to the recitation of the Pātimokkha. In sentences such as "Visākhā, the Uposatha endowed with eight factors is thus observed," it refers to the eight factors (precepts) beginning with abstinence from taking life. In sentences such as "For the pure, it is always Phaggu (the month of Phagguna); for the pure, it is always Uposatha," it refers to fasting or observance. In sentences such as "The Nāga king named Uposatha," it refers to a designation (name). In sentences such as "On that Uposatha day, the fifteenth, for one who has washed his head," it refers to the day. Therefore, excluding other meanings and specifying only the full-moon day of Āsāḷha, it is said, "Today is the fifteenth-day Uposatha." When counting as the first day of the fortnight, the second day, and so on, it means today is the fifteenth day.

They are called "dibba" because they occur in the celestial realm (deva-loka). Or, they are called "dibba" because there are shining lights in this night. What are those lights? They are the visual forms (the radiance of the deities). On that full-moon night of Āsāḷha, the entire Jambudīpa was as if decorated by the radiance of the bodies, garments, ornaments, and mansions of the deities who had assembled from the ten thousand world systems, and by the light of the moon which was free from defilements such as clouds. It was especially decorated by the bodily radiance of the Blessed One, who is the supreme deity by purity (visuddhi-deva). Therefore, it is said, "The divine (or radiant) night has arrived."
198:
It is called 'divine' (divba) because it occurs in the celestial realm and because there are lights shining in the night. What lights shine? They are the radiance of the devas' bodies and the radiance of their garments and ornaments. Indeed, on that night of the full moon of Āsāḷha, the entire island of Jambudīpa was as if specially adorned by the radiance of the bodies, garments, and mansions of the devas who had gathered from the ten thousand world systems, as well as by the radiance of the moon in a cloudless sky. It was also particularly beautiful due to the physical radiance of the Blessed One, who is the supreme Suddhideva (God by Purity). Therefore, it is said, 'divbā ratti upaṭṭhitā' (the divine night has arrived).

Thus, by praising the qualities of the night, Sātāgira generated clarity of mind in his friend. Wishing to announce the arising of the Buddha, he said: 'Anomanāmaṃ satthāraṃ, handa passāma gotamaṃ' (Come, let us see the Teacher of high name, the Gotama). In that verse, 'anomanāmaṃ' means one who has a name due to qualities that are not inferior but complete in every aspect. For this reason, he is named 'Buddha' because he has realized the Four Noble Truths and because he awakens other beings, and so on, thus possessing a name through noble qualities. He is named 'Bhagavā' because he has broken lust (rāga), broken hatred (dosa), and so on, thus possessing a name through noble qualities. This same method should be understood for terms such as 'Arahaṃ, Sammāsambuddho, Vijjācaraṇasampanno'. He is called 'Satthā' (Teacher) because he constantly admonishes devas and humans regarding their present and future welfare, saying, 'Abandon this unwholesome deed, undertake and practice this wholesome deed.' Alternatively, the Blessed One is called 'Satthā' because, like a caravan leader (satthavāha), he enables beings who are ready to be liberated to cross over the difficult wilderness of saṃsāra. This refers to that Teacher of noble name. The particle 'handa' is used in the sense of determination. 'Passāma' (let us see) is a present tense verb that includes oneself in the action. 'Gotamaṃ' refers to the Buddha who is of the Gotama lineage. What is meant is: 'Do not have doubt as to whether he is the Teacher or not; being fully determined, come, let us see the Gotama Buddha.'

When this was said, Hemavata thought: 'This Sātāgira, by saying "the Teacher of high name," is proclaiming his omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). Omniscient Buddhas are very rare in the world. The world is only oppressed by those like Pūraṇa Kassapa who falsely claim to be omniscient. If this Gotama is indeed omniscient, he will surely be endowed with the characteristic of "tādi" (steadfastness/equanimity). Therefore, I will examine him in this way.' Thinking thus, and wishing to ask about the characteristic of tādi, he spoke the verse beginning with 'Kacci mano'.

In that verse, 'kacci' is an interrogative. 'Mano' is the mind. 'Supatiṭṭhito' means well-established, unshakable, and steady. 'Sabbabhūtesu' means towards all living beings. 'Tādino' refers to one who has reached the characteristic of tādi. Alternatively, this is a question: 'Does your Teacher possess the quality of tādi towards all beings, or not?' 'Iṭṭhe aniṭṭhe ca' refers to such objects (pleasant and unpleasant). 'Saṅkappā' are thoughts or initial applications of mind (vitakka). 'Vasīkatā' means brought under control (mastered). The meaning is: 'Is the mind of that Teacher you speak of, who has reached the characteristic of tādi, well-established towards all beings? Or does it only appear well-established as long as it does not encounter a cause for agitation? Does your Teacher possess the quality of tādi with an even mind towards all beings, or not? Do the thoughts that arise through the power of lust or hatred towards pleasant or unpleasant objects follow the will of that Teacher, or does he sometimes follow the will of those thoughts?'
199:
Do thoughts arise through the power of lust and hatred towards pleasant and unpleasant objects? Are those thoughts mastered by that Teacher, or does he occasionally act under their influence?

Then Sātāgira, because of his firm conviction in the Blessed One's omniscience, acknowledged all the qualities of an Omniscient One and said, 'Mano cassa supatiṭṭhito' and so on. In that verse, 'supatiṭṭhito' means having a well-established heart. He is like the earth in the sense of not being resentful. He is like Mount Sineru in the sense of being well-established and unshakable. He is like a city pillar (indakhīla) in the sense of being immovable by the four Maras and the groups of opponents. This is not surprising; it is natural that the mind of the Blessed One, who is now endowed with all excellent attributes and stands in omniscience, should be well-established and unshakable.

Even in the past, when he still had lust and other defilements, while born in the Chaddanta elephant lineage as an animal, he remained unshakable even when struck by a poisoned arrow. He did not feel malice toward the hunter who killed him; instead, he even cut off his own tusks and gave them to that hunter. Likewise, when he was the Monkey King and was struck on the head with a large stone, he still showed the way to that person. Similarly, when he was Vidhura the Wise and was seized by the feet and thrown into the sixty-league-deep chasm of the Kāla mountain, he instead preached the Dhamma for the benefit of that yakkha. Therefore, Sātāgira rightly said, 'Mano cassa supatiṭṭhito'.

'Sabbabhūtesu tādino' means that the mind of the Blessed One, who has reached the characteristic of tādi towards all beings, is always well-established and firm, not just as long as he does not encounter a cause. In this context, the Blessed One's characteristic of tādi should be understood in five ways. As it is said: 'The Blessed One is tādi in five ways: he is tādi in the pleasant and unpleasant; he is tādi because he has abandoned (catta); he is tādi because he is liberated (mutta); he is tādi because he has crossed over (tiṇṇa); and he is tādi because he points out those truths (niddesaka). How is the Blessed One tādi in the pleasant and unpleasant? The Blessed One is tādi even in gain...' and so on.

All such details should be taken according to the method stated in the Niddesa. The details regarding the Buddha's gain and so forth should be understood according to the method expanded in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā. Alternatively, if this is taken as a question: 'Is that Teacher of yours tādi towards all beings, or not?'—the meaning is that our Teacher is called tādi because of his even-mindedness towards all beings. This Blessed One has an even mind towards all beings through his desire to bring them happiness and his desire to remove their suffering. Just as he feels toward himself, so he feels toward others.
200:
Just as he has such a state of mind towards his mother Mahāmāyā, so he has towards Ciñcamāṇavikā. Just as he has such a state of mind towards his father, King Suddhodana, so he has towards King Suppabuddha. Just as he has such a state of mind towards his son Rāhula, so he has towards those who would kill or harm him, such as Devadatta, the elephant Dhanapāla, and Aṅgulimāla. He is likewise 'tādi' (steadfast) in the world including the devas. Therefore, the deity Sātāgira said well: "He is tādi towards all beings."

Furthermore, in the phrase "iṭṭhe aniṭṭhe ca" (in the pleasant and the unpleasant), the meaning should be understood thus: In any object, whether pleasant (iṭṭha) or unpleasant (aniṭṭha), whatever thoughts (saṅkappa) might arise by the power of lust (rāga) or hatred (dosa) in every way—those thoughts are brought under control by the Blessed One because lust and so on have been abandoned by the unsurpassed Path of Arahantship; he never follows the power of those defilements. For that Blessed One has thoughts that are not turbid, a mind well-freed, and wisdom well-freed. Here, by being of a well-established mind, it means the absence of inappropriate attention (ayonisomanasikāra). In whatever object the Blessed One might be among all beings, through pleasant or unpleasant objects, that object is said to be twofold according to the distinction of beings and formations (saṅkhāra). By the mastery over thoughts, because there is no [defiled] attention to that object, it means the abandonment of defilements. By being of a well-established mind, the purity of mental conduct (manosamācārasuddhi) is stated; by being tādi towards all beings, the purity of bodily conduct (kāyasamācārasuddhi) is stated; and by the mastery over thoughts, because it is rooted in thought (vitakka), the purity of verbal conduct (vacīsamācārasuddhi) is stated. Likewise, due to being of a well-established mind, there is the absence of all faults such as greed; due to being tādi towards all beings, there is the presence of virtues such as loving-kindness (mettā); and due to the mastery over thoughts, the noble power (ariya-iddhi) such as perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive is stated. By that noble power, it should be understood that the Blessed One's state of omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa) is also stated.

Thus, the deity Hemavata, having previously asked about the state of being tādi through the mind-door alone and hearing this confirmation, now asks through the three doors to make it firmer; or, having previously asked about the purity of the body, speech, and mind-doors in brief and hearing this confirmation, he now asks in detail to make it firmer, saying "Kacci adinnaṃ" and so on. In that verse, for the sake of ease in versification, he first asks about the abstinence from taking what is not given (adinnādāna). With the phrase "ārā pamādamhā," he asks about the abstinence from unchastity (abrahmacariya), which is the distance from the release of the mind into the five cords of sensual pleasure. They also read "ārā pamadamhā," which means he should be far from women (mātugāma). With the phrase "jhānaṃ na riñcati," he asks about the strength of the abstinence from those three types of bodily misconduct. For the abstinence (virati) of one endowed with jhāna is powerful.
201:
Then the deity Sātāgira, because the Blessed One has abstained from taking what is not given (adinnādāna) and so on for a long time in the past, not only now; and because of the power of those various abstinences, he obtained the various marks of a Great Man (mahāpurisalakkhaṇa); and the world including the devas speaks his praise in such ways as "The recluse Gotama abstains from taking what is not given." Therefore, uttering a lion's roar with a confident voice, he said, "He does not take what is not given." That is clear in meaning. In the third line (pāda) of this verse, there are two readings: "pamādamhā" and "pamadamhā." In the fourth line, "jhānaṃ na riñcati" means he does not make jhāna empty or void, he does not abandon it—thus the meaning should be understood.

Having thus heard of the purity in the body-door, he now asks about the purity in the speech-door, saying: "Does he not tell lies?" Here, "khīṇa" has the meaning of harmful or harsh. The path of speech is called "byappatha"; one who has a harsh path of speech is called "khīṇabyappatha." Negating that with the word "na," he asks "na khīṇabyappatho," which means he has no harsh speech. There is also a reading "nākhīṇabyappatho," which means one whose words do not remain unconsumed (unpleasant) in the hearts of others. Harsh speech tends to remain unexhausted in the hearts of others. It means, "Does he have such speech?" "Vibhūti" means destruction; because it causes destruction, it is "vibhūtika"; that same "vibhūtika" is called "vebhūtika"; it is also called "vebhūtiyaṃ." This is a designation for slander (pesuñña). For it causes destruction by dividing beings from one another. The rest of the words are clear in meaning.

Then the deity Sātāgira, because the Blessed One has abstained from lying (musāvāda) and so on for a long time in the past, not only now; and because of the power of those various abstinences, he obtained the various marks of a Great Man; and the world including the devas speaks his praise, saying "The recluse Gotama abstains from lying." Therefore, uttering a lion's roar with a confident voice, he said, "And he does not tell lies." There, "musā" (lying) refers to deceptive speech intended to mislead others, such as saying one has not seen when one has seen. The Blessed One does not speak such words. In the second line, according to the first meaning, the reading is "na khīṇabyappatho," and according to the second meaning, it is "nākhīṇabyappatho." In the fourth line, "mantā" refers to wisdom. Because the Blessed One, having discerned with that wisdom, speaks only what is beneficial, his speech is not divorced from meaning, not...
202:
He does not speak frivolous words. Indeed, for the Buddhas, there is no useless speech preceded by a lack of wisdom. Therefore, it is said: "That Buddha speaks only what is beneficial through wisdom." The rest of the words here are clear.

Having heard thus about the purity of the door of speech, [Hemavata], now wishing to ask about the purity of the door of mind, said: "Does He not lust after sensual pleasures?" In that statement, 'sensual pleasures' (kāma) refers to objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma). By asking whether He lusts after those sensual objects with subjective sensuality (kilesa-kāma), he is asking about the state of being free from covetousness (anabhijjhālu). By asking "Is He not agitated?", he refers to the state of being agitated by ill-will, thus asking about the state of being free from ill-will (abyāpāda). By asking "Has He overcome delusion?", he asks about the state of possessing Right View (sammā-diṭṭhi) through the overcoming of that delusion by which one becomes muddled and holds Wrong View (micchā-diṭṭhi). By asking "Does He have vision in all things?", he considers that "one cannot be omniscient merely by the purity of the three doors," and thus asks about the state of possessing omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), either by the power of the eye of knowledge (ñāṇa-cakkhu) which is unobstructed in all things, or by the power of the five eyes (pañca-cakkhu) regarding the things that are the objects of those five eyes.

Then, the yakkha Sātāgiri, knowing that the Blessed One does not lust after sensual pleasures because He had already abandoned sensual lust and ill-will through the path of Non-returning (anāgāmi-magga) even before reaching the fruit of Arahantship; that He is not agitated in mind by ill-will; that He has overcome delusion because He had abandoned, even by the path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga), the delusion that conceals the Four Noble Truths and causes Wrong View; and that He has attained the name 'Buddha' which is a name ending in liberation (vimokkhantika-nāma) by personally penetrating the Truths, as well as the aforementioned eyes—wishing to proclaim the Blessed One's purity of the door of mind and His omniscience, Sātāgiri said: "He does not lust after sensual pleasures."

In this way, the yakkha Hemavata, having heard of the Blessed One's purity of the three doors and His omniscience, was joyful and elated. Being one whose path of speech was unhindered due to the clarity of wisdom from his great learning in past lives, and wishing to hear the attributes of omniscience which are of an amazing and wonderful nature, he asked: "Is He endowed with knowledge (vijjā)?" In that statement, by asking about being endowed with knowledge, he asks about the attainment of vision (dassana-sampatti). By asking about being of pure conduct (saṃsuddha-caraṇa), he asks about the attainment of progress (gamana-sampatti). Here, according to the meter, the letter 'ca' is lengthened to 'cā', meaning 'saṃsuddha-caraṇa'. By the words "Are His taints (āsavas) exhausted?", he asks about the attainment of the first Nibbāna element (nibbāna-dhātu), known as the destruction of taints, which is to be reached through that attainment of vision and progress. By the words "Is there no further existence?", he asks about the capacity to reach the second Nibbāna element, or the state of remaining after knowing the attainment of the supreme relief through reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa).
203:
Furthermore, the threefold knowledge (vijjā) is taught in the Bhayabherava Sutta and others in the manner beginning with: "He (recollects) his manifold past lives..." The eightfold knowledge is taught in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta and others in the manner beginning with: "When his mind is thus concentrated... he directs his mind toward knowledge and vision." The Blessed One is endowed with all those knowledges in every aspect.

"Mahānāma, here the noble disciple is endowed with virtue, guards the doors of his senses, is moderate in eating, is devoted to wakefulness, is possessed of the seven good qualities (saddhamma), and obtains at will the four jhānas which belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life." Having thus pointed this out, the fifteenfold conduct (caraṇa) is explained in the Sekha Sutta in the manner beginning with: "And how, Mahānāma, is a noble disciple endowed with virtue?" Because of the abandonment of all defilements, the Blessed One's conduct is exceedingly pure.

The four taints, such as the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava), have also been completely exhausted by the Blessed One, along with their surroundings and latent tendencies (vāsana). Since the Blessed One, having become one whose taints are exhausted through this endowment of knowledge and conduct, then remained after reviewing that "Now there is no further existence," Sātāgiri, with a heart encouraged by his certain realization of the Blessed One's omniscience, spoke in approval of all the attributes: "He is indeed endowed with knowledge."

Thereafter, the yakkha Hemavata, becoming free from doubt regarding the Blessed One, thinking "The Blessed One is the Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha)," while still standing in the air, spoke to praise the Blessed One and to please Sātāgiri: "The Sage's mind is perfect." The meaning of that is: The Sage's mind is perfect, being full and complete through the state of 'suchness' (tādibhāva) mentioned in the verse "His mind is well-directed." It means it is full and complete through the bodily action mentioned in "He does not take what is not given," through the mental action mentioned in "He does not lust after sensual pleasures," and through the verbal action mentioned in "He does not speak falsehood."

Being thus of a perfect mind and being endowed with knowledge and conduct because of His endowment with the unsurpassed knowledge and conduct, He is called 'Vijjācaraṇasampanna'. By the manner beginning with "His mind is well-directed," he praises Him through these attributes according to the Dhamma, praising Him according to His nature, according to the truth, and according to what is real; he shows that he does not praise Him merely through faith alone.
204:
165-166. After that, Sātāgira the deva, with the intention of pleasing Hemavata, said: "Friend Hemavata, you have understood and rejoiced in these qualities well," and spoke the verse: "Sampannaṃ munino...pe... dhammato anumodasī." Having said this, wishing to praise the Blessed One again for the sake of seeing Him, he spoke the verse: "Sampannaṃ...pe... handa passāma gotamaṃ."

Then, Hemavata, wishing to praise the Blessed One through the qualities he greatly admired and by the power of the knowledge he had heard in previous lives, spoke the verse to Sātāgira: "Eṇijaṅghaṃ...pe... ehi passāma gotamaṃ." The meaning of that verse is: He is called 'Eṇijaṅgha' because his legs are like those of an antelope (eṇī). For the Buddhas, the legs are gradually rounded like those of an antelope. It is not that there is no flesh on the front, nor is it bulging at the back like the belly of a crocodile. The Buddhas are slender because they are endowed with the perfection of limbs and minor parts in places that should be long, short, even, or rounded; they are not stout like other men. Alternatively, they are slender (lean) because they have scraped away the defilements with wisdom. They are called "Vīra" (Heroic) because they have destroyed internal and external enemies (defilements). They eat little because they eat only at one sitting and consume a limited amount of food. They do not eat two or three times, nor do they eat greedily.

Regarding this, He said: "Udāyī, sometimes I eat from this bowl until it is level with the rim, or even more. If my disciples were to respect, revere, honor, and worship me, and live depending on me, thinking, 'The ascetic Gotama eats little and speaks in praise of eating little.' Udāyī, among my disciples, there are those who eat only a cupful (kosa), half a cupful, a beluva-fruit's measure, or half a beluva-fruit's measure. These disciples would not respect me...pe... or live depending on me because of this practice of eating little."

Because they have no desire or lust for food, they eat food endowed with eight factors without greed, being sages (munis) endowed with the perfection of sagehood. Because of their state of being homeless and having minds inclined toward seclusion, they meditate in the forest. Therefore, Hemavata the Yakkha spoke the verse: "Eṇijaṅghaṃ...pe... ehi passāma gotamaṃ."

Having said this, wishing to hear the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One again, he spoke this verse: "Sīhaṃveka-caraṃ." The meaning of that verse is: "Sīhaṃva" means...
205:
Having spoken that verse and said these words, wishing once more to listen to the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One, he spoke the verse beginning with "Sīhaṃveka-caraṃ." The meaning of that verse should be understood as follows: He is like a lion (kesara-sīha) in the sense of being unconquerable by others, in the sense of being patient, and in the sense of being fearless. Because of the absence of that craving (taṇhā) of which it is said, "A man with craving as his companion," He wanders alone (ekacara). Alternatively, He wanders alone because two Buddhas do not arise simultaneously in a single world system. The meaning of various terms should also be understood according to the method stated in the Khaggavisāṇa Sutta.

"Nāga" means one who does not go to rebirth again, one who does not come back. Alternatively, He is called "Nāga" because He does not commit low, unwholesome deeds, or because He possesses great strength. (One sees) that Buddha called Nāga. "Being without longing for sensual pleasures" means having no longing because of the absence of desire and lust for both types of sensual pleasures: objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma) and subjective sensuality (kilesa-kāma). Let us approach such a Great Seer (Mahesi) and ask about Nibbāna, the liberation from the snare of Death, which is the round of existence in the three planes. Or, let us ask about the means of liberation from the snares of Death, known as suffering and its origin. Hemavata spoke this verse referring to Sātāgira, Sātāgira’s retinue, and his own retinue.

At that time, the festival of the full moon of Āsāḷha was being proclaimed. Then, in the city of Rājagaha, a female lay follower named Kāḷī from Kuraraghara, as if enjoying the glory in a decorated city of the devas, ascended her palace and opened the lion-window (siha-pañjara). While standing in a place with fresh air to take in the season and dispel the weariness of her pregnancy, she heard the conversation of those Yakkha generals concerning the qualities of the Buddha from the beginning, middle, and end. Having heard it, she thought, "The Buddhas are indeed endowed with such various qualities," and she aroused joy with the Buddha as the object. By that joy, she suppressed the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and, standing right there, she was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). For that reason, the Blessed One placed her in the foremost position (etadagga), saying: "Monks, among my female lay followers who are confident through hearsay, the foremost is Kāḷī, the lay follower from Kuraraghara."

Those Yakkha generals, along with their retinue of a thousand Yakkhas, reached Isipatana at the time of the middle watch of the night. They approached the Blessed One, who was seated in the same cross-legged posture as when He set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion. After paying homage, they praised the Blessed One with this verse and asked for an opportunity, saying: "Akkhātāraṃ pavattāraṃ." The meaning of that verse is: Setting aside craving, He is the "Akkhātāra" (Proclaimer) because He taught the Four Truths by defining them in the three planes of existence, in such a way as: "Now this, monks, is the Noble Truth of Suffering." He is the "Pavattāra" (Setter-in-motion) because He set in motion the knowledge of what is to be done (kicca-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of what has been done (kata-ñāṇa) regarding those Truths, in such a way as: "Monks, this Noble Truth of Suffering is to be fully understood." Or, He is the "Akkhātāra" because He taught the designations of things as they should be expressed. Of those things...
206:
He is the Teacher who, by teaching through conventional usage, declares [the Dhamma], and who causes those very dhammas to proceed according to the nature of beings. Or, He is the Teacher who declares the teaching to those of quick understanding (ugghaṭitaññū) and those who understand through elaboration (vipañcitaññū), and who causes it to proceed by leading those who require guidance (neyya) through gradual practice. Or, He is the Teacher who declares by way of summary (uddesa), and who causes it to proceed by teaching through various modes of analysis (vibhaṅga). Or, He is the Teacher who declares the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya dhammas) along with their individual characteristics, and who causes them to proceed within the mental continuities of beings. Or, He is the Teacher who declares the Truths in brief through the three rounds (parivaṭṭa), and who causes them to proceed in detail. He is the Teacher who causes [the Dhamma] to proceed because He sets in motion the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka), which is elaborated in the method of the Paṭisambhidāmagga, starting with: 'Faith-faculty is a dhamma; because it causes that dhamma to proceed, it is called the Wheel of Dhamma.'

'Sabbadhammānaṃ' means of the dhammas belonging to the four planes [of existence]. 'Pāragū' means one who has reached the further shore (the end) through six modes. These six are: higher knowledge (abhiññā), full understanding (pariññā), abandoning (pahāna), development (bhāvanā), realization (sacchikiriyā), and attainment (samāpatti). Because the Blessed One reached [the shore] while knowing all dhammas through higher knowledge, He is called 'Abhiññā-pāragū'. Because He reached it while fully understanding the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha), He is called 'Pariññā-pāragū'. Because He reached it while abandoning all defilements, He is called 'Pahāna-pāragū'. Because He reached it while developing the four paths, He is called 'Bhāvana-pāragū'. Because He reached it while realizing Nibbāna, the cessation, He is called 'Sacchikiriyā-pāragū'. Because He reached it while entering into all attainments, He is called 'Samāpatti-pāragū'. Thus, He is the one who has reached the end of all dhammas. 'Buddhaṃ verabhayātītaṃ' means He is called 'Buddha' because He has awakened from the sleep of ignorance (avijjā). Or, He is called 'Buddha' by all the meanings stated in the explanation of the Refuges. He is called 'Verabhayātīta' because He has transcended the five enmities and fears (verabhaya). Thus, praising the Blessed One, they asked for permission, saying, 'O Blessed Gautama, let us ask a question.'

Then, among those Yakkhas, Hemavata, who was supreme in power and wisdom, wishing to ask the problem he desired to inquire about, spoke this verse beginning with 'Kismiṃ loko'. In the first foot of that verse, the word 'Kismiṃ' is in the locative case (sattamī) in the sense of characterizing an action by another action (bhāvena bhāvalakkhaṇa). The meaning here is: 'When what dhamma exists does the world arise?' He asks with reference to the world of beings (sattaloka) and the world of formations (saṅkhāraloka). 'Kismiṃ kubbati santhavaṃ' means: In what does one form an association—the association of craving and views (taṇhā-diṭṭhi)—as 'I' or 'mine'? Here, 'Kismiṃ' is in the locative case in the sense of a locus (adhikaraṇa). In the phrase 'Kissa loko', the genitive case (chaṭṭhī) is used in the sense of the accusative (dutiyā). The meaning here is: 'Depending on what dhamma does it come to be designated as "the world"?' In this text 'Kismiṃ loko', 'Kismiṃ' is in the locative case in the senses of bhāvalakkhaṇa and cause (kāraṇa). The meaning here is: 'When what exists, and due to what cause, is the world afflicted, weary, and oppressed?'
207:
Then the Blessed One [answered thus] because when the six internal and external sense bases (āyatana) arise, the world of beings arises, and the world of formations also arises by way of wealth, grain, and so forth; and because in this matter, the world of beings forms a twofold association (craving and views) only in those six sense bases. For one grasps the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) or any of the remaining bases as 'I' or 'mine'.

For this reason, it was said: 'If anyone should say the eye is the self, that does not hold; the eye cannot be the self,' and so forth. Because the twofold world comes to be designated as 'the world' only by depending on these six sense bases, and because when those six sense bases exist, the world of beings is afflicted by the manifestation of suffering [the Blessed One answered thus].

For this reason, it was said: 'Bhikkhus, when hands exist, there is taking and putting down; when feet exist, there is coming and going; when joints exist, there is bending and stretching; when the stomach exists, there is hunger and thirst. Even so, bhikkhus, when the eye exists, pleasant and painful feelings arise within oneself with eye-contact (cakkhusamphassa) as condition,' and so forth.

Likewise, when those sense bases serve as a support, the world of formations that is struck is afflicted. For this reason, it was said: 'In the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda), which is invisible and offering resistance, [the form] strikes,' and 'Bhikkhus, the eye-sensitivity is struck by agreeable and disagreeable forms,' and so forth.

Furthermore, the twofold world is afflicted precisely because of those things which are the causes. For this reason, it was said: 'The eye-sensitivity is afflicted by agreeable and disagreeable forms,' and 'Bhikkhus, the eye is burning, forms are burning. Burning with what? Burning with the fire of lust (rāga),' and so forth.

Therefore, wishing to answer that question by way of the six internal and external sense bases, He said: 'In the six the world is born.'

Then that Yakkha, not being able to properly grasp the meaning of the answer given by the Blessed One—who had summarized the question asked by him by way of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) into the twelve sense bases—and [not grasping] that meaning and that dhamma...
208: Desiring to know the meaning of the round of existence (vaṭṭa) and its opposite, the supramundane (lokuttara), and wishing to ask briefly about the round and the escape from the round, he asked: "Katamaṃ taṃ" (What is that clinging?). In that verse, it is called 'clinging' (upādāna) because of the sense of being constantly attached. This word 'clinging' is a designation for the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca). In the phrase "wherein the world is oppressed," the Blessed One said, "The world is oppressed in the six [bases]," thus meaning the world is oppressed in the sixfold clinging. Therefore, with half a verse, he asked about the Truth of Suffering by its specific nature (sarūpa), saying "What is that clinging?" The Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca) is already included as its cause. With the half-verse "Niyyānaṃ pucchito" (Asked about the departure), he asked about the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca). Indeed, by the Truth of the Path, the noble disciple (ariya-sāvaka) fully understands the Truth of Suffering, abandons the Truth of the Origin, realizes the Truth of Cessation, and develops the Truth of the Path, thereby departing from the world; thus it is called "niyyāna" (the way out). "Kathaṃ" means in what manner. "Dukkhā pamuccati" means how one reaches liberation from the suffering of the round called 'clinging'. Thus, in this verse, he asked about the Truth of the Path by its specific nature, while the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca) is already included as its object.## Thus, when the yakkha Hemavata asked the question by way of the Four Noble Truths, both explicitly and implicitly, the Blessed One, wishing to answer in the same manner, spoke the verse beginning with "Pañca kāmaguṇā." In that verse, by taking the objects known as the five strands of sensual pleasure (kāmaguṇa), the five sense bases (āyatana) that have those objects are already included. Since the mind (mano) is the sixth among them, it is said "manosaṭṭhā" (having the mind as the sixth). "Paveditā" means they are made known. Here, among the internal sense bases (ajjhattikāyatana), by taking the sixth, the mind-base (manāyatana), its object, the mental-object base (dhammāyatana), is already included. Thus, having answered the question "Katamaṃ taṃ upādānaṃ," he again revealed the Truth of Suffering solely by way of the twelve sense bases (āyatana). Alternatively, by taking the word 'mind' (mano), the seven consciousness elements (viññāṇadhātu) are included; among those consciousness elements, by taking the first five consciousness elements, their bases, the five sense bases such as the eye (cakkhu), etc., are already included. By taking the mind-element (manodhātu) and the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu), the mental-object base (dhammāyatana), which is distinguished by their bases and objects, is already included. In this way also, he revealed the Truth of Suffering by way of the twelve sense bases. Here, the supramundane mind-base and a portion of the mental-object base are not included because they were intended in the question "Wherein the world is oppressed."## In the phrase "chandam virājetvā" (having faded away desire) in this verse, regarding the Truth of Suffering which is divided into twelve sense bases: by defining those very bases as aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), and mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa) in various ways, and applying the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa), while practicing insight (vipassanā), one completely fades away, removes, and destroys the desire (chanda) known as craving (taṇhā) through insight culminating in the Path of Arahantship. Thus, in this manner, "dukkhā pamuccati" (is liberated from suffering)...
209: ...is liberated from this suffering of the round. Thus, with this half-verse, the question "Tell me the way out; how is one liberated from suffering?" is answered. The Truth of the Path was also revealed. As for the Truth of the Origin and the Truth of Cessation, they should be understood as already revealed because they are included here according to the previous method.## Alternatively, with the half-verse, he revealed the Truth of Suffering; with the word "chanda" (desire), the Truth of the Origin; with "virāga" (fading away) in the word "virājetvā," the Truth of Cessation; and because of the statement "virāgā vimuccati" (is liberated through fading away), the Truth of the Path. By the explanation "evaṃ" (thus), he revealed the Truth of the Path; or by the statement "dukkha-nirodhaṃ" (cessation of suffering) or "liberation from suffering," he revealed the Truth of Cessation. Thus, it should be understood that the Four Noble Truths are revealed here.## Having thus revealed the way out from the round by way of the characteristics through the verse containing the Four Noble Truths, and wishing to conclude that very Truth of the Path with his own phrasing, he said: "Etaṃ lokassa niyyānaṃ" (This is the way out for the world). There, "etaṃ" (this) refers to the meaning previously stated. "Lokassa" (for the world) means for the world existing in the three planes (tebhūmaka). "Yathātathaṃ" means truly and without distortion. "I shall tell this to you" means: "Even if you were to ask me a thousand times, I would tell you only this true Dhamma of the Truths, and no other." Why? Because only by practicing thus can one be liberated from suffering, and not by any other way. Alternatively, it means: "I tell this to those who have already departed once, twice, or thrice by this way out from the round, and I tell this very same thing for the attainment of higher distinction." Why? Because only by this Truth of the Path can one be liberated from the suffering of the round without any remainder. Thus, he concluded the teaching by placing the Fruit of Arahantship at the summit. At the end of the teaching, both yakkha generals, along with a thousand follower yakkhas, were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala).## Then, the yakkha Hemavata, who was naturally respectful of the Dhamma, being now established in the stage of a Noble One (ariya), was even more insatiable. Because of the Blessed One's teaching characterized by diverse brilliance of wisdom, he wished to ask the Blessed One about the stages of the Trainee (sekha) and the Adept (asekha), and spoke the verse beginning with "Ko sūdha tarati" (Who here crosses over?). In that verse, with the words "Who here in this world crosses the flood (ogha)?", he asked about the stage of the Trainee without distinction, as in "Who crosses the four floods?". "Aṇṇavaṃ" (the ocean) does not mean merely wide or merely deep, but refers to the round of rebirths (saṃsāra-vaṭṭa) which is exceedingly wide and exceedingly deep. Indeed, this ocean of saṃsāra is wide because it has no boundaries all around, and it is deep because it has no standing ground below and no object to grasp above. Therefore, he asked about the stage of the Adept: "Who here crosses this ocean of saṃsāra? In that ocean which has no standing ground, no support, and is exceedingly deep, who does not sink?"
210:
In this verse, with the Pali phrase "Ko sudha tarati oghaṃ," the question is asked regarding the level of a trainee (sekha) without making a specific distinction: "Which person can cross the fourfold flood?" The word "aṇṇavaṃ" (ocean) does not refer merely to the extent of length and width, nor just to the extent of depth. Rather, it refers to the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), which is exceedingly wide and exceedingly deep. Indeed, this ocean of saṃsāra is called wide because it has no boundaries in any direction. It is called deep because it has no standing ground below and no object to grasp above. Therefore, the question is asked regarding the level of one beyond training (asekha): "Who can cross the ocean of saṃsāra? In that very deep ocean of saṃsāra, where there is no standing ground and nothing to grasp, who does not sink?"

Then the Blessed One, considering the monk who, even for the sake of his life, does not commit a transgression such as false speech, is always endowed with virtue (sīla), is wise with both mundane and supramundane wisdom, is well-concentrated through access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and fixed concentration (appanā-samādhi) as well as through the postures, has the habit of reflecting on his own internal nature through insight (vipassanā) by applying the three characteristics, and is endowed with constant practice and the mindfulness of diligence (appamāda-sati). Because that monk can completely cross this flood that is so difficult to cross by means of the fourth path, the Buddha, setting aside the level of a trainee, spoke this verse which is the womb of the three trainings, beginning with "Sabbadā sīlasampanno" (Always endowed with virtue).

In this verse, the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) is stated through the perfection of virtue; the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā) through mindfulness and concentration; and the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā) through wisdom reflecting on the internal nature. Thus, the three trainings are stated along with their supports and their benefits. The supports of the trainings are mundane wisdom and mindfulness, and the benefits are the fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala). Having thus shown the level of a trainee with the first verse, he now spoke the second verse beginning with "Virato kāmasaññāya" (Detached from sensual perceptions) to show the level of one beyond training (asekha).

The meaning of that verse is: one who avoids any sensual perception through the detachment of total eradication (samuccheda-virati) associated with the fourth path. There is also a reading "viratto." In that case, the word "kāmasaññāya" is in the locative case (bhumma-vacana). In the Sagāthā-vagga, there is also a reading "kāmasaññāsu." Because of having transcended the ten fetters through the four paths, he is called "one who has transcended all fetters" (sabba-saṃyojanātiga). Alternatively, he is called "one who has transcended all higher fetters" (uddhambhāgiya-sabba-saṃyojanātiga) through the fourth path alone. Because of the exhaustion of craving, known as delight in this or that existence, and because of the exhaustion of the three types of existence, he is called "one whose delight and existence are exhausted" (nandībhavaparikkhīṇa). Such an Arahant monk, whose taints are destroyed, no longer sinks in the deep ocean of saṃsāra. This is because he has attained the supreme relief by entering the element of Nibbāna with residue (sa-upādisesa-nibbāna) through the exhaustion of delight, and the element of Nibbāna without residue (anupādisesa-nibbāna) through the exhaustion of existence.

Then the yakkha Hemavata, looking at his friend Sātāgiri and the assembly of yakkhas, became filled with joy and happiness. After praising the Blessed One with verses beginning with "Gambhīrapañña" (One of deep wisdom), he paid homage together with the entire assembly and his friend, performed a circumambulation, and returned to his own dwelling place.

The following is the commentary on the meaning of those verses: "Gambhīrapañña" means being endowed with deep wisdom. Here, deep wisdom should be understood according to the method stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga. For it is stated in that text:

Because his knowledge functions by way of taking the deep aggregates (khandhas) as objects, he is called "Gambhīrapañña."

"Nipuṇatthadassī" means one who sees the meaning of subtle problems prepared by wise kings and others, or one who sees subtle causes that are difficult for others to penetrate.

Because of the absence of impediments (kiñcana) such as lust (rāga), he is called "Akiñcana."

Because of not being attached to the objects of sense-desire or the defilements of sense-desire, he is called "Asatta" (unattached).

Because of having no bond of desire and lust in all objects such as the aggregates, he is called "one freed from all acquisitions" (sabbupadhivimutta).

"Dibbe pathe caṅkamanaṃ" means walking by way of entering the noble path of the eight attainments. At the time of preaching to those Hemavata yakkhas...
211:
In that context, "Because his knowledge functions in the deep aggregates, he is called Gambhīrapañña," and so forth (Paṭi. Mag. 3.4). "Nipuṇatthadassī" means one who sees the meaning of problems specially prepared by subtle-minded wise kshatriyas and others, or one who sees subtle causes that are difficult for others to penetrate by seeing them as they are.

Because of the absence of impediments such as lust (rāga), he is called "Akiñcana." Because of not clinging to the two types of sense-desire or the three types of existence, he is called "Asatta" (unattached) in sense-desire and existence. Because of the absence of the bond of desire and lust in all objects divided into aggregates and so forth, he is called "one released in every way" (sabbadhi vippamutta).

"Dibbe pathe kamamānaṃ" means walking by way of entering the divine path consisting of the eight attainments. In this regard, although the Blessed One was not literally walking on a divine path at that time, it is said so either by referring to his previous walking, or because he possesses the power to walk there, or because he has attained mastery (vasībhāva) in those attainments. Alternatively, it is said so because of his walking in the peaceful dwelling (vihāra) which is the path of the Arahants, who are the gods of purity (visuddhideva). Because of seeking great virtues, he is called "Mahesi."

In the second verse, considering that praise has been initiated in another way, the term "Nipuṇatthadassī" is shown again. Alternatively, it means "one who shows subtle meanings." "Paññādada" means the giver of wisdom by teaching the practice that leads to the attainment of wisdom. "Kāmālaye asattaṃ" means not clinging to the two types of abodes (ālaya)—craving and views—that occur in sense-pleasures. "Sabbavidū" means the knower of all things; it means he is the Omniscient One (Sabbaññū). "Sumedha" means being endowed with "medhā," which is the wisdom of the perfections that is the path to that omniscience. "Ariye pathe" refers to the Eightfold Path or the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti). "Kamamānaṃ" means entering with wisdom and teaching after knowing the characteristics of the path, or entering the attainment of fruition moment by moment, or having previously walked with the power of walking known as the development of the fourfold path.

"Today we have seen well" means today we have seen something beautiful, or today a beautiful seeing (seeing the truth of Nibbāna) has occurred for us. "A beautiful dawn, a beautiful awakening" means today there was a good dawn or a beautiful radiance for us. And today there was a beautiful arising for us, like rising from sleep without any disturbance, meaning we have become well-established in the supramundane Dhamma. For what reason? "Because we have seen the Sambuddha." Thus, he expresses his joy by referring to his own attainment of gain.
212:
*Iddhimanto* means those (yakkhas) who are endowed with psychic power born of the fruition of kamma. *Yasassino* means those who are endowed with the highest gain and the highest retinue. "They go for refuge" (*saraṇaṃ yanti*) means that although they have reached the refuge through the Path itself, they utter these words to manifest their state of being Stream-enterers and to demonstrate their devotion.

"From village to village" (*gāmā gāmaṃ*) means from one celestial village to another celestial village. "From mountain to mountain" (*nagā nagaṃ*) means from one celestial mountain to another celestial mountain. "Paying homage to the Fully Enlightened One and the excellence of the Dhamma" means they wander about as proclaimers of the Dhamma, repeatedly praising and paying homage to the Buddha’s perfect enlightenment, the Dhamma’s excellence, and the Sangha’s good conduct, in such ways as: "The Blessed One is indeed the Perfectly Enlightened One; the Dhamma of the Blessed One is well-expounded," and "The Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples has practiced well." The meaning of the remaining words in this Hemavata Sutta is clear.

## In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya,
## the Explanation of the Hemavata Sutta in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is finished.

## 10. Explanation of the Āḷavaka Sutta

"Thus have I heard" (*Evaṃ me sutaṃ*) and so forth is the Āḷavaka Sutta. What is its origin? Its origin will become clear through the method of explaining the meaning. In the explanation of the meaning, the words "Thus have I heard, at one time the Blessed One..." have the same meaning as previously stated. Regarding "staying in Āḷavī, in the abode of the yakkha Āḷavaka," what is Āḷavī, and why did the Blessed One stay in that yakkha's abode? It is said—Āḷavī refers to both a country and a city; both are appropriate here. Even when staying near the city of Āḷavī, it is said, "He is staying in Āḷavī." That abode is near the city, not far, about a *gāvuta* away. Even when staying within the country of Āḷavī, it is said, "He is staying in Āḷavī," and that abode is indeed within the country of Āḷavī.

Now, King Āḷavaka, having abandoned various theatrical enjoyments, used to go hunting every seven days to ward off thieves, to deter rival kings, and for the sake of exercise. One day, he made an agreement with his troops: "To whomsoever..."
213:
"If a deer escapes from someone's side, that deer is that person's responsibility alone" (they made this agreement). Then, a deer escaped from the King's side itself. The King, endowed with great speed, took his bow and followed that deer on foot for three leagues. Eṇī deer also have the speed to run for three leagues. Then, having killed that deer which had exhausted its speed and stood in the water, he cut it in two. Although he had no need for the meat, in order to escape the reproach that "he could not catch the deer," he carried it on a shoulder-pole. As he was coming along, he saw a great banyan tree with thick leaves and bark not far from the city, and approached the foot of that banyan tree to relieve his fatigue.

In that great banyan tree, the yakkha Āḷavaka lived, having received a boon (a dwelling place) from the Great Kings (Cātumahārājika), and he lived there eating any living beings who entered the shaded area of that tree at midday. Seeing the King, he approached to eat him. Then the King made a pact with the yakkha: "Release me, and I will send you one human and a pot of rice every single day." The yakkha thought, "You, being negligent with royal pleasures, will forget (the promise). I am not allowed to eat those who do not approach my dwelling or those for whom I have no permission. Therefore, I should just conquer (eat) you now," and he did not release him. The King granted permission (guaranteed) himself, saying, "On whatever day I cannot send them, on that day you may seize and eat me." Then the yakkha released him, and he proceeded toward the city.

The army, having set up camp on the road, saw the King and went out to welcome him, saying, "Great King, are you thus exhausted for fear of losing your reputation?" The King did not yet tell them the matter, but returned to the city. After having his breakfast, he called the city-warden and told him the matter. The city-warden asked, "Sire, did you set a time limit?" The King said, "My friend, I did not." "Sire, you have done poorly. For non-humans only receive what is within a set limit; if there is no limit, there will be affliction for the country-folk. Let it be, Sire; even though this has been done, you enjoy the royal pleasures without anxiety. I will do what should be done in this matter." That city-warden rose early, went to the prison, and referring to those who were to be executed, said, "Whoever wishes to live..."
214:
"Let that person go out," he says. He takes the first person who comes out to his house, has him bathed and fed, and then sends him off, saying, "Give this pot of rice to the yakkha." As soon as that person reaches the foot of the tree, the yakkha creates a terrifying form and devours him like a lotus root. It is said that by the power of the yakkha, the entire body of a human, starting from the hair, becomes like a lump of butter. The men who went to take the rice for the yakkha saw this and, terrified, told their friends. From then on, the news spread that "The king catches thieves and gives them to the yakkha," and so people abstained from theft. Later, as there were no new thieves and the old ones were exhausted, the prisons became empty.

Then the city guardian informed the king. The king had his wealth discarded on the city streets, thinking, "Perhaps someone will take it out of greed." But no one touched that wealth even with their feet. Not finding any thieves, the king consulted his ministers. The ministers said, "Let us send the elderly one by one according to their lineage; they are naturally near the mouth of death anyway." The king forbade this, saying, "People will be agitated, saying, 'He is sending our father, our grandfather.' I do not like this plan." Then the ministers suggested, "Great King, then let us send infants who sleep on their backs; such children do not yet have the attachment of 'my mother, my father'." The king granted permission. The ministers did accordingly. Mothers of infants and pregnant women in the city fled to other districts with their children, raised them there, and then returned. In this way, twelve years passed.

Then one day, after searching the entire city and not finding a single infant, they reported to the king, "Great King, there are no infants in the city except for your son, Prince Āḷavaka, in the palace." The king said, "Just as my son is dear to me, so he must be to all the world; yet there is no one dearer than oneself. Go, give even him and protect my life." At that time, the mother of Prince Āḷavaka had just bathed and adorned her son, placed him on a silk cushion, and was holding him in her lap. By the king's command, the royal messengers went there and, while the mother and sixteen thousand court ladies wailed, took the son along with his nurse, saying, "Tomorrow he will be food for the yakkha." On that day, the Blessed One...
215:
The Blessed One, having arisen at dawn and entered the Attainment of Great Compassion in the Gandhakuṭi of the Jetavana Monastery, surveyed the world with his Buddha-eye. He saw the potential for Prince Āḷavaka to attain the fruit of Non-returning, for the yakkha Āḷavaka to attain the fruit of Stream-entry, and for eighty-four thousand beings to obtain the Eye of Dhamma at the end of the discourse. Having seen this, when the night had brightened, he performed his morning duties. Before his afternoon duties were finished, on the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight, as the sun set, he took his bowl and robes and, traveling alone on foot, went thirty yojanas from Sāvatthī and entered the abode of that yakkha. It is in reference to this entry that it was said, "In the abode of the yakkha Āḷavaka."

Now, did the Blessed One stay at the foot of the banyan tree where the abode of the yakkha Āḷavaka was, or did he stay inside the abode itself? To this, it is answered: He stayed inside the abode itself. For just as the yakkhas see their own abode, so too did the Blessed One see it. The Blessed One went there and stood at the entrance of the abode. At that time, the yakkha Āḷavaka had gone to a gathering of yakkhas in the Himavanta region. Then the yakkha named Gadrabha, the gatekeeper of Āḷavaka, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and asked, "Venerable Sir, why has the Blessed One come at this improper time?" "Yes, Gadrabha, I have come. If it is no trouble to you, I would like to stay for one night in the abode of Āḷavaka." "Venerable Sir, it is no trouble to me, but that yakkha is extremely fierce and harsh; he does not even show respect to his parents. May it not please the Blessed One to stay here." "Gadrabha, I know of that yakkha's harshness; no harm will come to me. If it is no trouble to you, I would like to stay for one night."

A second time, the yakkha Gadrabha said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, Āḷavaka is like a potsherd heated by fire. He knows not 'parents', nor 'recluses and brahmins', nor 'Dhamma'. He causes those who come here to go mad, he splits their hearts, and seizing them by their feet, he throws them to the other shore of the ocean or beyond the world-system." A second time, the Blessed One said: "Gadrabha, I know. If it is no trouble to you, I would like to stay for one night." A third time, the yakkha Gadrabha said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, Āḷavaka is like a potsherd heated by fire. He knows not 'parents', nor 'recluses and brahmins', nor 'Dhamma'. He causes those who come here to go mad, he splits their hearts, and seizing them by their feet..."
216: “He can throw you to the other side of the ocean or to the other side of the universe,” Gadrabha the yakkha submitted. For the third time, the Blessed One said, “Gadrabha, I know. If it is no burden to you, let us stay for one night.” “Venerable Sir, it is not a burden to me. However, if that yakkha finds out I allowed it without informing him, he might deprive me of life. Venerable Sir, let me inform Āḷavaka.” “Gadrabha, inform him as you wish,” the Blessed One said. “In that case, Venerable Sir, you yourself know best,” he said, and after paying homage to the Blessed One, he departed toward the Himavanta. The door of the mansion opened of its own accord for the Blessed One. The Blessed One entered the mansion and sat upon the divine jeweled throne where the yakkha Āḷavaka used to enjoy his glory on auspicious days, and he emitted a golden radiance. Seeing that radiance, the yakkha’s wives came, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down surrounding him. The Blessed One taught them various points of Dhamma, saying, “In the past, you attained this prosperity because you gave gifts, undertook the precepts, and honored those worthy of honor. Now, do the same; do not live overcome by mutual envy and stinginess.” Having heard the Blessed One’s sweet voice, those yakkha women uttered ‘Sādhu’ many times and remained seated surrounding him. Meanwhile, Gadrabha went to the Himavanta and informed Āḷavaka, “O friend, you should know that the Blessed One is seated in your mansion.” Āḷavaka signaled to Gadrabha, “Be quiet! I will go and do what needs to be done.” He was ashamed because of his manly pride, and thus he forbade him, thinking, “Let no one hear this in the midst of the assembly.” At that time, Sātāgira and Hemavata, having paid homage to the Blessed One at the Jetavana Monastery, were traveling through the sky with their retinues in various vehicles, saying, “Let us go to the yakkha assembly.” In the sky, there is no path everywhere for yakkhas; they must travel along the existing paths, avoiding the mansions situated in the sky. Āḷavaka’s mansion, however, was situated on the ground and was very secure, surrounded by walls and well-provided with gates, watchtowers, and battlements. It was covered above with a bronze net, resembling a box, and was three yojanas in height. There was a path above that mansion. When they reached that spot, they were unable to proceed. Indeed, from the place where Buddhas are seated upwards to the highest point of existence (Bhavagga), no one is able to pass over. Reflecting, “What is this?” they saw the Blessed One and descended like a clod of earth thrown into the sky. They paid homage, listened to the Dhamma, circumambulated him, and saying, “Venerable Sir, we shall proceed to the yakkha assembly,” they departed for the assembly while praising the Three Jewels. When Āḷavaka saw them, he stepped aside and provided them with a place, saying, “Sit here.”
217:
Those devas informed Āḷavaka, “Āḷavaka, it is a gain for you that the Blessed One is staying in your mansion. Friend, go and attend upon the Blessed One.” In this way, the Blessed One stayed in the mansion itself, not at the foot of the banyan tree where Āḷavaka’s mansion was located. Therefore, it was said, “At one time, the Blessed One was staying in Āḷavī, in the mansion of the yakkha Āḷavaka.”

Then Āḷavaka... (pe) ... said to the Blessed One, “Get out, ascetic!” If it is asked, “Why did he say this?” it is said that it was because he wished to provoke him.

In this matter, the connection from the beginning should be understood as follows: To one without faith, talk of faith is as unpleasant as talk of virtue is to the immoral. Therefore, upon hearing the praise of the Blessed One from those yakkhas, his heart sizzled with internal anger like a grain of salt thrown into a fire, and he said, “Who is this so-called ‘Blessed One’ who has entered my mansion?”

Those devas said, “Friend, do you not know the Blessed One, our Teacher, who, while staying in the Tusita heaven, made the Five Great Observations...” and so on, recounting the thirty-two omens starting from the conception up to the preaching of the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta. They challenged him, “Friend, have you not seen these wonders?”

Even though he had seen them, he said, “I have not seen them,” due to the power of his anger.

“Friend Āḷavaka, whether you see them or not, what benefit is there in your seeing or not seeing? What can you do to our Teacher? Compared to him, you appear like a newborn calf beside a great, powerful bull; like a small elephant calf beside a rutting tusker in its threefold prime; like an old fox beside a lion king adorned with a brilliant, flowing mane; like a wingless crow chick beside a king of Garudas whose body has grown to a hundred and fifty yojanas. Go and do what you have to do!”

When they spoke thus, the enraged Āḷavaka stood up, and standing with his left foot on the Manosilā stone plateau, he said, “Now see whether your Teacher is more powerful or I am!” He then stepped on the peak of Mount Kelāsa, which was sixty yojanas in size, with his right foot. That mountain peak broke into pieces and flew off like sparks from a lump of iron struck by an iron sledgehammer. Standing there, he shouted, “I am Āḷavaka!” and the sound spread throughout the whole of Jambudīpa.
218:
It is said that four great sounds were heard throughout the whole of Jambudīpa. These four are: the sound of the yakkha general Puṇṇaka, who, after defeating King Dhanañjaya Korabya at dice, slapped his arms and proclaimed, "I have won!"; the sound of Sakka, King of Gods, who, when the Dispensation of the Blessed Kassapa Buddha was declining, caused the celestial son Vissakamma to take the form of a dog and proclaim, "I shall devour all the wicked monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen, and all those who profess false doctrines!"; the sound of the Great Being in the Kusa Jātaka, who, while surrounded by the kings of seven kingdoms because of Princess Pabhāvatī, placed Pabhāvatī with him on the back of an elephant, left the city, and proclaimed, "I am the Great King Kusa, who has the voice of a lion!"; and the sound of the yakkha Āḷavaka, who stood on the peak of Mount Kelāsa and proclaimed, "I am Āḷavaka!" At that time, it was as if he stood and proclaimed at every door throughout the whole of Jambudīpa. Even the great Himavanta mountains, three thousand yojanas in width and length, trembled due to the power of the yakkha.

That yakkha Āḷavaka thought, "I will make the ascetic Gotama flee with this very windstorm," and he created a whirlwind. Those winds, blowing from the east and other directions, shattered mountain peaks half a yojana, one, two, and three yojanas in size, uprooted forest thickets and trees, and rushed into the city of Āḷavī, crushing old elephant stables and causing roof tiles to fly in the sky. The Blessed One made a resolve: "Let no harm come to anyone." When those windstorms reached the Ten-Powered One, they could not move even the corner of his robe.

Then, thinking, "I will kill the ascetic Gotama by overwhelming him with water," he created a great rain. By his power, clouds rose in layers of hundreds and thousands and poured down rain; the earth itself was rent by the force of the torrents. Although a great flood flowed over the forest trees, it could not wet even a dewdrop's worth of the Ten-Powered One's robe.

Then he created a rain of rocks; great mountain peaks, smoking and flaming, came through the sky, but upon reaching the Ten-Powered One, they turned into celestial garlands and bouquets. Then he created a rain of weapons; sharp swords, spears, and razors, single-edged and double-edged, came through the sky smoking and flaming, but upon reaching the Ten-Powered One, they became celestial flowers. Then he created a rain of live coals; coals the color of flame-of-the-forest flowers came through the sky and fell scattered at the Ten-Powered One's feet as celestial flowers. Then he created a rain of hot ashes; extremely hot ashes came through the sky and fell at the Ten-Powered One's feet as sandalwood powder. Then...
219:
He created a rain of sand; extremely fine sand, smoking and flaming, came through the sky and fell at the Ten-Powered One's feet as celestial flowers. Then he created a rain of mud; that rain of mud, smoking and flaming, came through the sky and fell at the Ten-Powered One's feet as celestial perfume. Then, thinking, "I will frighten the ascetic Gotama and make him flee," he created a mass of darkness. It was like the darkness consisting of four factors, but upon reaching the Ten-Powered One, it vanished like darkness dispelled by the light of the sun.

In this way, the yakkha, unable to make the Blessed One flee with these nine rains of wind, rain, rocks, weapons, coals, hot ashes, sand, mud, and darkness, approached the Blessed One himself with a four-fold army consisting of hosts of yakkhas of various forms, carrying various kinds of weapons. Those hosts of yakkhas, making various terrifying gestures, seemed to descend upon the Blessed One, crying, "Seize him! Kill him!" However, they were unable to approach the Blessed One, just as flies cannot settle on a glowing iron ball. Even so, unlike Māra who retreated the moment he arrived at the Bodhi-mandala, they did not retreat but caused a disturbance for half the night. Thus, unable to move the Blessed One even by showing many kinds of terrifying sights for half the night, the yakkha Āḷavaka thought, "What if I release the Dussāvudha weapon, which no one can defeat?"

It is said that there are four supreme weapons in the world: Sakka's Vajirāvudha, Vessavaṇa's Gadāvudha, Yama's Nayanāvudha, and Āḷavaka's Dussāvudha. If Sakka, being angry, were to strike the top of Mount Sineru with the Vajirāvudha, it would pierce through Sineru, which is one hundred and sixty-eight thousand yojanas high, and go out the bottom. The Gadāvudha released by Vessavaṇa when he was a worldling would strike off the heads of many thousands of yakkhas and then return to his hand. When Yama is angry, by merely looking with the Nayanāvudha, many thousands of Kumbhaṇḍas perish, scattering like sesame seeds on a hot frying pan. If the angry Āḷavaka were to release the Dussāvudha in the sky, no rain would fall for twelve years. If he were to release it on the earth, all trees, grass, and other plants would dry up and not grow again for twelve years. If he were to release it in the ocean, all the water would dry up like a drop of water on a hot frying pan. If he were to release it even on a mountain like Sineru, it would be shattered into pieces and scattered. That yakkha, releasing the Dussāvudha weapon of such great power, which he wore as an upper garment...
220:
(Āḷavaka the yakkha) took up the white cloth weapon. Generally, the devas of the ten thousand world systems gathered quickly, thinking, "Today the Blessed One will tame Āḷavaka; we shall hear the Dhamma there." Devas who wished to see the battle also gathered. Thus, the entire sky was filled with devas in every direction.

Then, Āḷavaka the yakkha circled above the Blessed One and released the white cloth weapon. That white cloth weapon, making a terrifying sound in the sky like a thunderbolt, smoking and flaming, reached the Blessed One and, in order to subdue the yakkha's pride, became a foot-wiping cloth and fell at his feet. When Āḷavaka saw this, like a bull with broken horns, like a snake with its fangs extracted, he became powerless and devoid of intoxication, his banner of pride having fallen, and he thought: "Even my white cloth weapon cannot oppress this ascetic; what could be the reason?" Then he thought, "This ascetic dwells in loving-kindness; now I will provoke him and separate him from his loving-kindness." In this connection, it is said: "Then Āḷavaka the yakkha went to where the Blessed One was... (pe)... 'Get out, ascetic!'"

In this passage, this is the meaning: "Ascetic, why have you entered my abode without my permission and sat in the midst of my harem like the master of the house? Is it not improper for an ascetic to enjoy what is not given and to associate with women? Therefore, if you stand in the Dhamma of an ascetic, get out, ascetic!" This is the intended meaning. Some teachers, however, say: "He said this only after saying these and other harsh words."

Then the Blessed One, knowing, "This yakkha is stubborn and cannot be tamed by stubbornness. If one acts with stubbornness, just as if one were to burst the gall bladder in the nose of a fierce dog, that dog would become even more fierce, so too this yakkha would become even more stubborn. He can only be tamed with gentleness," accepted his words with the pleasant address, "Very well, friend," and went out. Therefore, it is said: "The Blessed One, saying 'Very well, friend,' went out."

Then Āḷavaka thought, "This ascetic is indeed easy to speak to; he went out with just a single word. While it is so easy to make such an ascetic leave, I have oppressed him all night long with battle for no reason." Having a softened mind, he thought again: "Even now it cannot be known; did he leave because he is easy to speak to, or because of anger? Now I will test him." Then he said, "Enter, ascetic." Then the Blessed One, speaking pleasant words again to determine if the yakkha's mind had become soft and "easy to speak to," said, "Very well, friend," and entered. Āḷavaka, testing that very quality of being easy to speak to again and again...
221:
Āḷavaka the yakkha, wishing to test him, said for a second and third time, "Get out, enter." The Blessed One did likewise. If he had not done so, the naturally stubborn yakkha's mind would have become even more stubborn and would not have been a fit vessel for a Dhamma discourse. Therefore, just as a mother soothes her crying young son by giving him what he wants or doing what he desires, so too the Blessed One, to make the yakkha—who was crying with the crying of defilements—understand, did as the yakkha said. Just as a nurse coaxes a child who does not want to drink milk by giving him something and then makes him drink, so too the Blessed One, to make the yakkha drink the milk of the supramundane Dhamma, coaxed him by doing what he requested and acted in this way. Just as a man wishing to fill a gourd with the four sweet foods first cleans the inside of that gourd, so too the Blessed One, wishing to fill the yakkha's mind with the supramundane four sweet foods, went out and entered up to the third time to clean the impurity of anger from his internal being.

Then Āḷavaka thought, "This ascetic is easy to speak to; when told 'Get out,' he goes out; when told 'Enter,' he enters. What if I were to weary this ascetic in this way all night, then seize him by the feet and throw him to the other side of the Ganges?" Having given rise to such an evil thought, he said for the fourth time, "Get out, ascetic." Knowing that intention, the Blessed One said, "I will not go out, friend." Knowing that "If I say this, he will seek what further should be done and think of asking a question, which will be the opening for a Dhamma discourse," the Blessed One said, "I will not go out, friend." In that phrase, 'na' is for negation, 'khō' is for emphasis, 'ahaṃ' refers to oneself, and 'taṃ' is a causal word. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: "Friend, because you think thus, I will not go out; do what you must do."

Furthermore, in the past, when Āḷavaka came through the air, he would think, "Is this a golden mansion, or one of silver or gems? Let us see it now." He would then ask questions of the powerful hermits and wanderers who came to his mansion, and if they were unable to answer, he would harass them by causing mental derangement and so forth. How did he harass them? Non-humans cause mental derangement in two ways: by showing a terrifying form or by crushing the heart-base. But this yakkha, knowing that "Powerful ones are not frightened by the sight of terrifying forms," would use his own psychic power to create a subtle form, enter inside them, and crush their heart-base. Because of that crushing, the continuity of mind could not remain steady, and because it could not remain steady, they would fall into madness...
222:
They become deranged. He would split the hearts of those who were thus deranged, and grabbing them by their feet, he would throw them to the other side of the Ganges, thinking, "Let such people never come to my abode again."
