Therefore, recalling those questions and thinking, "It would be good if I could harass this recluse now in this way," he said, "I will ask you a question, recluse," and so on.

Where did he get those questions? It is said that his parents had attended upon the Blessed One Kassapa and learned eight questions along with their answers. They taught them to Āḷavaka when he was young. Over time, he forgot the answers. Then, thinking, "May these questions not be lost," he had them written on a gold plate with cinnabar (jātihingulaka) and kept them in his celestial abode. Thus, these questions are "Buddha-questions," belonging only to the domain of a Buddha (Buddha-visaya). The Blessed One, having heard those words, knew that no one can obstruct the loss of gains, the danger to life, or the Omniscient Knowledge (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) and the fathom-wide radiance (Byāmappabhā) of the Buddhas. Therefore, wishing to demonstrate the incomparable power of the Buddhas in the world, he said, "Friend, I do not see anyone in the world with its devas..."

In that passage, by the word "sadevaka" (with the devas), the five types of devas of the sense sphere are included, and the meaning of those terms is shown in brief, not in an expanded way according to the sequence of connection. To explain it in detail: although all devas are included by the word "sadevaka" according to the highest definition, among the host of devas assembled there, a doubt might arise: "Māra has great power; he rules over the six heavens of the sense sphere and can make others follow his will; he delights in opposition, hates the Dhamma, and performs cruel deeds. Could even that Māra not cause derangement of the mind and so on to this recluse?" To dispel their doubt, he said, "samārake" (with Māra). Then, for those who thought, "Brahmā has great power; with one finger he can provide light to a thousand world-systems, and with two... up to ten fingers to ten thousand world-systems, and he experiences the incomparable bliss of meditative attainments (jhāna-samāpatti). Could even that Brahmā not do it?"—to dispel their doubt, he said, "sabrahmake" (with Brahmā). Furthermore, for those who thought, "Could the many recluses and brahmins who are enemies of the Dispensation and possessed of powers such as mantras not do it?"—to dispel their doubt, he said, "sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā pajāya" (with the generation of recluses and brahmins). Having thus shown that there is no one in these high positions, now with "sadevamanussāya" (with devas and humans)...
223:
By the words "sadevamanussāya" (with devas and humans), referring to conventional gods (kings) and the remaining humans, he showed that even in the rest of the world of beings, there is no one (who can harass the Buddha) according to the highest definition. Thus, the sequence of connection in this context should be understood.

In this way, the Blessed One, having thwarted Āḷavaka's intention to harass him and wishing to encourage him to ask questions, said, "Friend, ask whatever you wish." The meaning of those words is: "Ask if you wish; there is no burden for me in answering questions." Or else, he issued the "Omniscient Invitation" (Sabbaññu-pavāraṇa)—"Ask whatever you wish, I will answer it all"—which is not shared by Paccekabuddhas, Chief Disciples (Aggasāvaka), or Great Disciples (Mahāsāvaka). For those disciples say, "Friend, ask; having heard it, we shall know." But the Buddhas say, "Friend, ask whatever you wish," or,
"Vāsava, ask me any question that you desire in your mind," or,
"Whether for Bāvarī or for yourselves, if there is any doubt for all of you, the opportunity is given; ask whatever you desire in your mind."
In this manner, they issue the Omniscient Invitation to devas and humans. And it is not surprising that the Blessed One, having reached the stage of a Buddha, should issue such an invitation. For even while he was in the stage of a Bodhisatta, existing with partial knowledge (padesa-ñāṇa)—
"Koṇḍañña, explain the questions; these virtuous sages are requesting you. Koṇḍañña, this is the way among men: when one approaches an elder, this burden falls upon the elder." Thus requested by the sages—
"Sirs, ask any question desired by the mind; the opportunity is given. For I shall explain each of them to you, having myself known this world and the world beyond"—(he had said so in the past).
224:
In this way, both when he was the hermit Sarabhaṅga and in the Sambhava Jātaka, having traveled throughout the entire Jambudīpa three times without finding anyone capable of resolving these questions, the Bodhisatta, while only seven years old and playing in the dust on the road, was asked by a Brahmin named Sucirata. He replied: "Indeed, I shall tell you; just as a skilled person knows, so shall I explain. The King also knows this; whether he will act upon it or not, he knows." Thus, he made an invitation in the manner of the Omniscient Buddhas (Sabbaññupavāraṇā).

In this manner, after the Blessed One had extended the invitation of the Omniscient Buddhas to the yakkha Āḷavaka, the yakkha Āḷavaka addressed the Blessed One with a verse beginning with "Kiṃ sūdha vittaṃ."

In that verse, the word "kiṃ" is an interrogative. The word "su" is a mere particle used to complete the verse (pādapūraṇa). "Idha" means in this world. "Vittaṃ" is called so because it produces delight; it is a synonym for wealth. "Suciṇṇā" refers to a well-performed practice. "Sukhaṃ" refers to bodily and mental happiness. "Āvahāti" means it brings, conveys, gives, or causes to reach. The word "have" is a particle used in the sense of certainty. "Sādutaraṃ" means the most excellent taste because it is exceedingly pleasant; there is also a variant reading "sādhutaraṃ." "Rasānaṃ" means among those things recognized as tastes (dhamma). "Kathaṃ" means in what manner. "Kathaṃjīvino" means the life of what kind of person is supreme; for the sake of the verse's meter, it is expressed with a niggahīta as "kathaṃjīvi." There is also a variant reading "kathaṃjīviṃ jīvataṃ," which means: among those who live, what kind of living is supreme? The remaining words are clear. Thus, with this verse, he asked these four questions: "What is a man's best wealth in this world? What, when well-practiced, brings happiness? What is the sweetest of tastes? Whose life do the wise say is best?"

Then the Blessed One, wishing to answer him in the same manner as the Buddha Kassapa (Kassapa Dasabala) had answered, spoke this verse beginning with "Saddhīdha vittaṃ." The meaning of that verse should be understood as follows: Just as wealth such as gold and silver brings the happiness of use and consumption, prevents the suffering of hunger and thirst, alleviates poverty, is the cause for obtaining jewels like pearls, and brings the praise of the world; so too, mundane and supramundane faith (saddhā) brings mundane and supramundane happiness according to circumstances. For those who practice with faith as their precursor, it prevents the suffering of birth, aging, and so on, alleviates the poverty of virtues, and is the cause for obtaining jewels such as the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (satisambojjhaṅga).
226:
Among all the tastes that exist on the surface of the earth, the taste of truth is indeed the sweetest. Monks and Brahmins who are established in truth cross over to Nibbāna, which is the other shore of birth and death.

'Sādutaraṃ' means especially sweet or especially sublime. 'Rasānaṃ' refers to the natures that are experienced by the tongue, such as root-taste, trunk-taste, and so forth. Furthermore, in such passages as: "Monks, I allow all fruit juices," "The Venerable Gotama is one without taste (attachment)," "Brahmin, such are the tastes of forms and the tastes of sounds," "There is no offense in [consuming] taste by taste," "This Dhamma-Vinaya has only one taste, the taste of liberation (vimutti-rasa)," and "The Blessed One is the possessor of the essence of meaning (attha-rasa) and the essence of Dhamma (dhamma-rasa)," excluding the taste of speech (vācā-rasa), other things such as syllables and so on are called 'rasa' (tastes/essences). Among those tastes, truth is indeed the sweetest. Truth alone is the best, or the most noble, or the most excellent. For tastes such as root-tastes nourish the physical body and bring about defiled happiness. The tastes of truth, namely the truth of abstinence (virati-sacca) and the truth of speech (vācā-sacca), nourish the mind through tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) and bring about undefiled happiness. The taste of liberation (vimutti-rasa) is sweet because it is permeated with the taste of ultimate truth (paramattha-sacca). The essence of meaning (attha-rasa) and the essence of Dhamma (dhamma-rasa) also arise depending on the meaning and the nature that lead to the attainment of that ultimate truth.

In the term 'paññājīviṃ' (one who lives by wisdom), among those who are one-eyed and those who are two-eyed, a layperson who is called 'two-eyed' accomplishes the lay practice such as farming, trading, taking refuge, giving, undertaking virtue, and observing the Sabbath (uposatha) through wisdom and thus makes a living. Or, a monk accomplishes the monastic practice such as virtue characterized by lack of remorse, and the higher purification of mind (cittavisuddhi) and so forth through wisdom and thus lives. The life of such a person who lives by wisdom is said to be supreme by the wise.

185-186. Having heard these four questions answered by the Blessed One, the Yakkha Āḷavaka was delighted and asked the remaining four questions with the verse beginning: "How does one cross the flood (ogha)?" Then the Blessed One, answering him in the same manner as before, spoke the verse beginning: "By faith (saddhā) one crosses the flood."

In that verse, although one who crosses the fourfold flood also crosses the ocean of Saṃsāra, transcends the suffering of the round of rebirths, and is purified from the stains of defilements,
227:
Even though this is so, because a person without faith does not believe in crossing the flood and thus does not enter into faith; and because a person who is heedless by letting the mind loose in the five cords of sensual pleasure is particularly attached only to those sensual pleasures and thus cannot cross the ocean of Saṃsāra; and because a lazy person lives miserably, being mixed with unwholesome states; and because an unwise person, not knowing the path to purity, cannot be purified; therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to show the opposite meaning, spoke this verse.

In this verse thus spoken, because the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) is the proximate cause for the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga), by the phrase "By faith one crosses the flood" (Saddhāya tarati oghaṃ), the Blessed One reveals the Path of Stream-entry and the Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) who crosses the flood of views (diṭṭhi-ogha). Because a Stream-enterer is endowed with heedfulness (appamāda), which is the constant practice in developing wholesome states, and having attained the second path, the Path of Once-returning (Sakadāgāmi-magga), crosses the ocean of Saṃsāra—the basis of the flood of existence (bhavo-ogha)—leaving only the remainder of coming back to this world once more, which was not yet crossed by the Path of Stream-entry; therefore, by the phrase "By heedfulness, the ocean" (Appamādena aṇṇavaṃ), He reveals the Path of Once-returning and the Once-returner (Sakadāgāmi). Because a Once-returner, through energy (vīriya), attains the third path, the Path of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-magga), and transcends the basis of the flood of sensuality (kāmo-ogha) and the suffering in sensuality called the flood of sensuality, which was not yet transcended by the Path of Once-returning; therefore, by the phrase "By energy one overcomes suffering" (Vīriyena dukkhamacceti), He reveals the Path of Non-returning and the Non-returner (Anāgāmi). Because a Non-returner, through pure wisdom due to being free from the mire of sensuality, attains the absolutely pure wisdom of the fourth path and abandons the supreme stain called ignorance (avijjā), which was not yet abandoned by the Path of Non-returning; therefore, by the phrase "By wisdom one is purified" (Paññāya parisujjhati), He reveals the Path of Arahatship (Arahatta-magga) and the Arahat (Arahant) who crosses the flood of ignorance (avijjā-ogha). At the conclusion of this verse, which was spoken with Arahatship as its climax, the Yakkha Āḷavaka was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).

Now, taking the word 'wisdom' (paññā) mentioned in the phrase "By wisdom one is purified," and wishing to ask a question mixed with mundane and supramundane aspects according to his own intuition, he spoke this six-line verse beginning: "How does one obtain wisdom?" (Kathaṃ su labhate paññaṃ). In that verse, "Kathaṃ su" is a question regarding the logical reason (yutti) of the meaning in all instances. This Yakkha, having known the meaning of wisdom and so forth, asks for its logical reason: "By what logic, by what cause does one obtain wisdom?" This method is the same for wealth and so forth.
228:
Then, the Blessed One, wishing to show Āḷavaka the four causes for obtaining wisdom, spoke the verse beginning with "Saddahāno." The meaning of that verse is: Through that Dhamma by which the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Arahant disciples have attained Nibbāna—characterized by bodily good conduct and so forth in the preliminary stage, and by the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma) and so forth in the later stage—one who has faith in that Dhamma of the Arahants, which leads to the attainment of Nibbāna, obtains mundane and supramundane wisdom. Furthermore, obtaining such wisdom is not achieved through faith alone; because one who has faith approaches (a teacher), by approaching he attends (to the teacher), by attending he lends an ear, and by lending an ear he hears the Dhamma. Therefore, from the moment of approaching until the hearing of the Dhamma, he gains the state of listening well. What is meant is this: having faith in that Dhamma, he approaches his teachers and preceptors at the appropriate time, attends to them by performing major and minor duties, and when the teachers' minds are satisfied by such attendance, they desire to speak something. At that time, the one who listens by lending an ear with a desire to hear, obtains wisdom. Even with such good listening, only the one who is heedful, not lacking in mindfulness, and wise, being able to distinguish between well-spoken and ill-spoken words, obtains wisdom; others do not. Therefore, it was said: "Appamatto vicakkhaṇo" (Heedful and discerning).

In this way, because of faith, he practices the path that leads to the attainment of wisdom; through good listening, he respectfully hears the means of acquiring wisdom; through heedfulness, he does not forget the meaning he has grasped; and through discernment, he grasps it without deficiency or excess and without distortion, and is able to expand upon it. Alternatively, through good listening, he lends an ear and hears the Dhamma which is the cause for obtaining wisdom; having heard it with heedfulness, he retains the Dhamma; through discernment, he investigates the meaning of the Dhamma he has retained; thereafter, he progressively realizes the ultimate truth (paramatthasacca). Therefore, when asked by the yakkha Āḷavaka, "How does one obtain wisdom?", the Blessed One, wishing to show these four causes, spoke this verse: "Saddahāno... vicakkhaṇo."

Now, wishing to answer the next three questions, He spoke the verse beginning with "Patirūpakārī." Therein, one is called "Patirūpakārī" (one who acts appropriately) because he performs the appropriate means of acquiring mundane or supramundane wealth without neglecting the proper place and time. "Dhuravā" (persistent) means one who does not lay down the burden by virtue of mental energy. "Uṭṭhātā" (active/energetic) means one who is endowed with initiative by virtue of physical energy, having unremitting effort, according to the method: "He who does not consider cold or heat more than a blade of grass," and so forth.
229:
"He gains wealth" means that just as Cūḷantevāsī soon obtained mundane wealth amounting to two hundred thousand coins starting with a single dead mouse, or as the Elder Mahallaka Mahātissa obtained supramundane wealth. That Elder made a vow, "I will dwell only in three postures (excluding lying down)," and when sloth and torpor (thīnamiddha) approached, he soaked a ring of straw in water, placed it on his head, and entered water up to his neck to dispel the sloth and torpor; practicing thus for twelve years, he attained Arahantship. "By truth" means that through verbal truth (vacīsacca), one attains fame as "one who speaks the truth, one who speaks what is real," and through ultimate truth (paramatthasacca), one attains fame as "a Buddha, a Paccekabuddha, or a Noble Disciple." "By giving" means that by giving whatever is desired or requested, one binds friends, fulfills their needs, and makes them friends. Alternatively, it means binding friends by giving what is difficult to give. Or, it should be understood that through the act of giving (dāna), all four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu) are included. It means that through these acts of giving, one makes friends.

Having thus answered the four questions by a method that mixes mundane and supramundane aspects applicable to both householders and monastics, He now spoke the verse beginning with "Yassete," wishing to answer the fifth question, "How does one not grieve after passing away?" from the perspective of a householder. The meaning of that verse is: For the faithful householder (ghara-mesino) who seeks and enjoys the five strands of sensual pleasure, and who is endowed with faith that gives rise to all wholesome qualities as mentioned in "Saddahāno arahatam," if there exist these four qualities: Truth (sacca) as described in "By truth one attains fame"; Dhamma, mentioned here by the names of listening and wisdom in "One who desires to listen obtains wisdom"; Fortitude (dhīti), mentioned here by the names of bearing the burden and initiative in "Dhuravā uṭṭhātā"; and Generosity (cāga) as described in "The giver binds friends." Such a person, indeed, does not grieve after passing from this world to the next.

Thus, the Blessed One, having answered the fifth question, spoke the words beginning with "Ingha aññepi," wishing to exhort the yakkha. Therein, "Ingha" is a particle in the sense of exhortation. "Others also" means: go and ask many other recluses and brahmins, or ask many other recluses and brahmins like Pūraṇa Kassapa and others who claim to be omniscient. If there is any cause for attaining fame greater than the Truth (sacca) described in our teaching "By truth one attains fame," or any self-control (dama) mentioned here under the terms of listening and wisdom in "One who desires to listen obtains wisdom"...
230:
Or, it is because it is the cause for the excessive attainment of mundane and supramundane wisdom. In the passage, "The giver binds friends," the various types of generosity (cāga) mentioned are the cause for excessively binding friends. In the passage, "The bearer of the burden, the one who is energetic," the patience (khanti) known as energy (viriya), which has reached the state of intense effort (ussoḷhī) by virtue of enduring great burdens for the sake of various benefits, is the cause for the excessive acquisition of mundane and supramundane wealth. In the passage, "Truth, Dhamma, fortitude, and generosity," through these four qualities, the cause for not grieving after passing from this world to the next exists excessively in this person. This is the concise explanation and commentary on the meaning here. In detail, however, each word should be understood by distinguishing them through the methods of extracting the meaning and explaining the terms.

When this was spoken, the Yakkha Āḷavaka, because the doubt with which he might have questioned others had been abandoned (through the Path), said, "How should I now question many ascetics and brahmins?" and wishing to make those who did not yet know the reason for his not questioning understand, he said: "Today I understand the benefit that pertains to the future life." In that verse, "today" (ajja) means starting from today. "I understand" (pajānāmi) means I understand in the manner already described. By the words "the benefit" (yo attho), he shows the benefit pertaining to the present life (diṭṭhadhammika) taught in the manner of "The one who desires to hear gains wisdom," and so forth. By the word "pertaining to the future life" (samparāyiko), he shows the benefit pertaining to the future life (samparāyika) which causes the absence of grief after passing away, as taught in "To whom these four qualities belong."

The word "attha" is a synonym for cause (kāraṇa). Indeed, this word "attha" occurs in the sense of the meaning of the text (pāṭhattha) in such passages as "with the meaning and the phrasing" (sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ). It occurs in the sense of purpose or need (kiccattha) in such passages as "Householder, I have need (attho) of gold and silver." It occurs in the sense of growth (vuḍḍhi) in such passages as "There is benefit (attho) for the virtuous." It occurs in the sense of wealth (dhana) in such passages as "Many people associate for the sake of wealth (attha-hetu)." It occurs in the sense of welfare (hita) in such passages as "He practices for the welfare (atthaṃ) of both." It occurs in the sense of cause (kāraṇa) in such passages as "When a cause (atthe) arises, the wise man is known." Here, it is used in the sense of cause (kāraṇa). Therefore, the concise meaning should be understood thus: "The cause of the benefit in the present life such as the attainment of wisdom, and the cause of the benefit in the future life such as the absence of grief after passing away—these I myself now understand today through the method taught by the Blessed One; how then should I now question many ascetics and brahmins?"
231:
Thus, the Yakkha, having said, "I understand the benefit pertaining to the future life," and wishing to show that this knowledge is rooted in the Blessed One, said: "Indeed, for my benefit, the Buddha (has come)." In that verse, "for benefit" (atthāya) means for welfare or for growth. "Where a gift given yields great fruit" means that I know the Buddha, the supreme recipient of offerings (aggadakkhiṇeyya), in whom a gift given with the generosity (cāga) taught in the Jātaka passage, "To whom these four qualities belong," yields great fruit. Some teachers, however, say, "This was said in reference to the Saṅgha."

Having thus shown the attainment of his own welfare with this verse, now, wishing to illustrate his practice for the welfare of others, he said: "I shall wander from village to village," and so forth. The meaning of that verse should be understood in the same way as taught in the Hemavata Sutta.

Thus, at the conclusion of this verse, at the break of dawn, at the arising of the sounds of "Sādhu," and at the time of bringing Prince Āḷavaka to the Yakkha's abode—all these events occurred at the same moment. When the king's men heard the sound of "Sādhu," they reflected, "Such a sound of 'Sādhu' does not arise for anyone except the Buddha; has the Blessed One indeed arrived?" Seeing the bodily radiance of the Blessed One, they did not stand outside as before, but entered inside without hesitation and saw the Blessed One seated in the Yakkha's abode, and the Yakkha standing with palms joined in reverence. Seeing the Yakkha, they said: "Great Yakkha, this prince has been brought for the sacrificial offering; now, eat him or consume him, or do with him as you please."

Because he was a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna), and especially because he was addressed in this way in the presence of the Blessed One, the Yakkha felt greatly ashamed. He received the prince with both hands and offered him to the Blessed One, saying: "Venerable Sir, this child was sent to me; I give him to the Blessed One. Buddhas are compassionate toward the welfare of beings; Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept this child for his welfare and happiness." And he spoke this verse:

"This prince, possessed of the marks of a hundred merits,
Endowed with all limbs and perfect in appearance,
With an uplifted and happy mind, I give him to You;
O One with Vision, who works for the welfare of the world, please accept him."

The Blessed One accepted the prince. While accepting him, for the sake of performing a blessing for the Yakkha and the prince, He spoke the Pādūna verse. The Yakkha, establishing the prince in the Refuges, completed the verse three times with the fourth line. It is as follows:
232:
"May this boy live long! O Āḷavaka Yakkha, may you also be happy. May you remain free from disease for the welfare of the world. This boy goes for refuge to the Buddha... to the Dhamma... to the Saṅgha."

The Blessed One gave the boy to the king's men and said, "Raise this child, and when he is grown, give him back to me once more." Thus, because this boy passed from the hands of the king's men to the hands of the Yakkha, from the hands of the Yakkha to the hands of the Blessed One, and from the hands of the Blessed One back to the hands of the king's men, he became known by the name "Hatthaka Āḷavaka."

Seeing the king's men returning with the boy, farmers, woodcutters, and others asked fearfully, "Does the Yakkha not want to eat the boy because he is too young?" The king's men told them everything, saying, "Do not be afraid; the Blessed One has made things safe." Then, with the sound of "Sādhu! Sādhu!" the whole city was in an uproar, and they went towards the Āḷavaka Yakkha. When it was time for the Blessed One to go for alms, the Yakkha took the bowl and robes, accompanied him halfway, and then returned.

Then the Blessed One, having wandered for alms in the city and finished his meal, sat down on the noble Buddha-seat prepared at the foot of a secluded tree near the city gate. Then a great multitude, including the king and the citizens, gathered together, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat around him, asking, "Venerable Sir, how did you tame such a fierce Yakkha?"

The Blessed One, starting from the battle, preached that very Āḷavaka Sutta, saying, "In this way he caused the nine kinds of rain to fall; in this way he created terrifying sights; in this way he asked questions; and in this way I answered him." At the end of the discourse, eighty-four thousand beings attained the realization of the Dhamma. Then the king and the citizens built a residence for the Yakkha near the residence of the Great King Vessavaṇa and established regular offerings complete with flowers, scents, and other honors.

When the boy reached the age of discretion, they sent him away, saying, "You obtained your life by depending on the Blessed One; go, attend only upon the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks." While attending upon the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks, Hatthaka Āḷavaka soon established himself in the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmiphala), mastered all the Buddha's words, and became a leader surrounded by five hundred lay followers. And the Blessed One appointed him to the foremost position (etadagga), saying, "Monks, among my lay disciples..."
233:
"...among my lay disciples who win over a following by the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu), Hatthaka Āḷavaka is the foremost," as preached in the Aṅguttara Nikāya.

## In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha,
## the explanation of the Āḷavaka Sutta in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is finished.

## 11. Explanation of the Vijaya Sutta

The discourse beginning with "Caraṃ vā yadi vā tiṭṭhaṃ" is the Nanda Sutta. It is also called the Vijaya Sutta or the Kāyavicchaṇdanika Sutta. What is the origin? Since this discourse was preached in two places, there are two types of origins. Among those two, the Blessed One gradually arrived at Kapilavatthu, and after disciplining the Sakyans, he had Prince Nanda and others ordained. When the ordination of women was permitted, three Nandās were ordained: Nandā, the sister of the Elder Ānanda; Abhirūpanandā, the daughter of King Khemaka the Sakyan; and Janapadakalyāṇī Nandā. At that time, the Blessed One was staying in Sāvatthī. Abhirūpanandā was extremely beautiful, lovely to behold, and inspiring; therefore, they named her "Abhirūpanandā." Janapadakalyāṇī Nandā was also so beautiful that she saw no one equal to herself in appearance. Both of these princesses, intoxicated with the pride of their own beauty, thought, "The Blessed One criticizes beauty, censures it, and shows the danger in beauty in many ways," and thus they did not go to the Blessed One, nor did they wish to see him.

If it is asked why they were ordained despite such lack of faith, it was because they were led by circumstances (not by choice). For Abhirūpanandā, on her very wedding day, her husband, a Sakyan prince, passed away; therefore, her parents had her ordained against her will. Janapadakalyāṇī Nandā also, when the Venerable Nanda attained Arahantship, became hopeless and thought, "My husband, my mother Mahāpajāpatī, and other relatives have all been ordained; household life without relatives is very miserable." Thus, finding no pleasure in household life, she was ordained, but not out of faith.

Then the Blessed One, knowing the maturity of their wisdom, told Mahāpajāpatī, "Let all the bhikkhunīs come in order to receive instruction." When their turn arrived, those princesses sent someone else. Then the Blessed One [said], "When their turn arrives..."
234:
“One must come oneself; another should not be sent,” he said. Then, one day, Abhirūpanandā came. The Blessed One, having caused her to be dismayed by means of a created form, spoke this Dhammapada verse: “A city is made of bones...”

“Behold, Nandā, this physical body (samussaya), which is diseased, impure, putrid, greatly desired by fools, oozing from above and trickling from below.

Develop the signless (animitta) insight, and abandon the latent tendency of conceit (mānānusaya). Then, by fully understanding and abandoning conceit, you shall live in peace, with defilements stilled,” through these Therīgāthā verses, he established her in the fruit of Arahantship in due order.

Then, one day, the residents of Sāvatthī, having given alms in the morning and observing the Uposatha, dressed and robed themselves well, took perfumes, flowers, and so on, and went to the Jetavana Monastery to listen to the Dhamma. When the Dhamma talk was over, they paid homage to the Blessed One and re-entered the city. The Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs also, after listening to the Dhamma talk, went to the bhikkhunī quarters. At that time, both the people and the bhikkhunīs spoke in praise of the Blessed One. In this world, which consists of four types of measurement, there is no one who does not feel devotion upon seeing the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha.

Those who measure by form (rūpappamāṇika) feel devotion upon seeing the physical form of the Blessed One, which has appeared in the world as if adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor marks, and is resplendent with the surrounding circle of rays (ketumālā).

Those who measure by sound (ghosappamāṇika) feel devotion upon hearing the fame of the Blessed One, which has been established through hundreds of Jātaka stories, and his Brahma-voice (brahmassara), which is endowed with eight qualities and is as sweet as the song of the karavīka bird.

Those who measure by austerity (lūkhappamāṇika) feel devotion upon seeing the austerity of his bowl and robes, or the austerity of his past practice of difficult deeds (dukkharacariya).

Those who measure by Dhamma (dhammappamāṇika) feel devotion by investigating and reflecting upon any of the aggregates of Dhamma, such as the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha). Therefore, in all places, they spoke in praise of the Blessed One.

When Janapadakalyāṇī Nandā reached the bhikkhunī quarters, she heard those people speaking in praise of the Blessed One in various ways. Having a desire to approach the Blessed One, she informed the bhikkhunīs. The bhikkhunīs took her and approached the Blessed One.

The Blessed One, knowing in advance of her coming, and wishing to remove her intoxication with beauty by means of beauty itself—just as a man might extract a thorn with a thorn, or a peg (āṇi) with a peg—created by his psychic power the image of an extremely beautiful woman about fifteen or sixteen years of age, standing by his side and fanning him. Nandā approached with the bhikkhunīs, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs. From the soles of the feet to the tips of the hair...
235:
Seeing the perfection of the Blessed One’s form, and then seeing the created woman standing by the Blessed One’s side, she thought, “Oh, how beautiful this woman is!” Abandoning her own intoxication with beauty (rūpamada), she became deeply infatuated with that woman’s beauty. Then the Blessed One showed that woman as being twenty years of age. Indeed, a woman is beautiful only at the age of sixteen; beyond that age, she is no longer so beautiful. Then, seeing the decline of that woman’s beauty, Nandā’s intense lust for that form faded away.

From there, the Blessed One showed her in the form of a woman who had not yet given birth, a woman who had given birth once, a middle-aged woman, and an old woman, until she was a hundred years old, with a bent body leaning on a staff and a body covered in freckles. While Nandā was still watching, he showed that woman dying and becoming a bloated corpse, surrounded and being eaten by creatures such as crows, emitting a foul odor, and becoming loathsome and repulsive. When Nandā saw that sequence of events, the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā) became established in her, thinking, “In this very way, for me and for others, this process is common to all.” Following that perception of impermanence, the perceptions of suffering (dukkha-saññā) and non-self (anatta-saññā) also arose, and the three realms of existence appeared to her like a house in flames, without any refuge. Then the Blessed One, knowing that Nandā’s mind had entered into the meditation subject, spoke these verses suitable for her:

“Behold, Nandā, this physical body, which is diseased, impure, putrid,
oozing from above and trickling from below,
greatly desired by fools.

As this corpse is, so shall this body of mine be;
as this body of mine is, so is this corpse.
Look at it in terms of elements (dhātu) and in terms of emptiness (suññata) of self;
do not come back to the world again.
Having dispelled desire for existence, you shall live in peace.”

At the end of the verses, Nandā was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala). Then, wishing to teach her the insight meditation subject accompanied by emptiness (suññata) for the sake of attaining the higher paths, he spoke this sutta. This is the first account of the origin of this sutta.

While the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha, there was a woman named Sirimā, the daughter of the courtesan named Sālavatī and the younger sister of Jīvaka, whose story is told in detail in the Cīvarakkhandhaka. After her mother’s death, she received that position of courtesan. In the story of the verse “Conquer anger with non-anger,” having looked down upon the daughter of the merchant Puṇṇaka, she apologized to the Blessed One, heard the Dhamma teaching, became a Stream-enterer, and for eight...
236:
Sirimā established eight regular food offerings. On account of these regular offerings, a certain monk who lived depending on them became consumed by lust. It is stated in the Dhammapada Commentary (Dhammapada-gāthā-vatthu) that he was unable even to perform his meal duties and lay down without food. While that monk was lying there in such a state, Sirimā passed away and became the queen of Suyama in the Yāma heaven. Then, the King prevented the cremation of her body and had it placed in a charnel ground. The Blessed One, surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, went to view the body, taking that monk along with Him; the citizens and the King also came. There, the people said, "In the past, even for a thousand and eight pieces of money, a sight of Sirimā was difficult to obtain; but now, there is no one who wishes to look at her even for a small coin (kākaṇika)." Sirimā, now a celestial maiden, also came to that charnel ground surrounded by five hundred chariots. On that occasion, the Blessed One preached this Vijaya Sutta for the benefit of the assembled crowd, and for the sake of instructing that monk, He spoke this Dhammapada verse: "Look at this beautified image..." (Dhp. 147). This is the second origin of this Vijaya Sutta.

In that verse, "caraṃ vā" (or walking) means when the entire physical body is moving by being carried forward toward a desired direction. "Yadi vā tiṭṭhanti" (or if standing) means when that same body is standing by way of being held upright. "Nisinno uda vā sayanti" (sitting or lying down) means when it is sitting by way of bending the lower part and holding the upper part upright, or when it is lying down by way of stretching out horizontally. "Samiñjeti pasāreti" (bending and stretching) refers to the bending and stretching of various joints.

"Esā kāyassa iñjanā" (this is the movement of the body) means that all this is merely the vibrating, moving, and struggling of this conscious body; there is no other person here who walks or stretches. Rather, when the thought "I will walk" arises, the mind-produced wind element (vāyodhātu) spreads throughout the body. Because of that wind element, the carrying forward toward the desired direction occurs, which means the manifestation of successive material groups (rūpa) from one place to another. Therefore, it is said, "he walks." Similarly, when the thought "I will stand" arises, the mind-produced wind element spreads throughout the body. Because of that wind element, the holding upright occurs, which means the manifestation of material groups in an upward position. Therefore, it is said, "he stands." Similarly, when the thought "I will sit" arises, the mind-produced wind element spreads throughout the body. Because of that wind element, the bending of the lower part and the holding upright of the upper part occur, which means the manifestation of material groups in that manner. Therefore, it is said, "he sits." Similarly, when the thought "I will lie down" arises...
237:
...the mind-produced wind element (vāyodhātu) spreads throughout the body. Because of that wind element, horizontal stretching occurs; because of the manifestation of material groups in that manner, it is said, "he lies down."

In this way, whatever venerable one with such a name is walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he is said to bend or stretch by the power of bending and stretching various joints in those respective postures. Since that bending and stretching also occur according to the aforementioned method when the mind intending to bend or stretch arises, this is merely the movement of the body. There is no other person here; it is empty of any being or person who walks or stretches. In the ultimate sense:

"Due to the diversity of mind, there is diversity of the wind;
Due to the diversity of the wind, the movements of the body occur respectively."

This is the ultimate meaning in this context.

Thus, with this verse, the Blessed One shows the characteristic of suffering (dukkha-lakkhaṇa) which is hidden by the postures (iriyāpatha), because when the body is oppressed by staying long in a single posture, the change of posture is performed to remove that oppression, as indicated by "caraṃ vā" and so on. Likewise, by saying "this is the movement of the body" regarding all these various modes like walking—since standing etc. do not exist at the time of walking—He shows the characteristic of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa) which is hidden by continuity (santati). By saying "this is the movement of the body" regarding this movement which occurs through the harmony of various causes, and thus rejecting a self (attā), He shows the characteristic of non-self (anatta-lakkhaṇa) which is hidden by the perception of compactness (ghana-saññā).

Having thus taught the meditation on emptiness (suññata-kammaṭṭhāna) by demonstrating the three characteristics, He began the verse "bound by bones and sinews" (aṭṭhinhārusamyutto) to show the foulness of both the conscious and unconscious body. The meaning of that verse is: this body which has such movements is "bound by bones and sinews" because it is joined with three hundred and sixty bones and nine hundred sinews, as explained in the description of the thirty-two parts (dvattiṃsākāra) in the Visuddhimagga by way of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation, and by the method of lack of volition. Because it is smeared with skin, such as the skin of the toes and feet, and with flesh consisting of nine hundred pieces of flesh as explained therein, it is "smeared with skin and flesh," being extremely foul-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive...
238:
The meaning of that verse should be understood as follows: In determining this body, what should be known is this—if the skin gathered from the entire body of a man of average stature were to be the size of a jujube seed, it would not be like a house wall covered with blue paint and such, because it is as delicate as a fly's wing. However, because this body is covered by such delicate skin, foolish worldlings (puthujjana) who are devoid of the eye of wisdom do not see it as it truly is.

Indeed, being stained by lust for the skin, they do not see even the skin itself as it truly is—which is called an extremely loathsome and foul thing. Regarding the body wrapped in skin:
'Nine hundred pieces of flesh are smeared upon the carcass;
It is crowded with various kinds of worms, and is foul like a cesspool.'
Thus it is said. They do not see these nine hundred pieces of flesh as they truly are. Also, those smeared with flesh:
'There are nine hundred tendons in a fathom-long carcass;
They bind the collection of bones together, like creepers binding a house.'
They do not see those tendons, nor the three hundred and sixty bones that are bound by the tendons and arranged in order, which are putrid and ill-smelling, because they cannot disregard that skin which is as delicate as a fly's wing. Because they are wrapped in skin and stained by lust for it, the various internal impurities—which are not apparent to the world, and are extremely impure, ill-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive—should be seen by penetrating them with the eye of wisdom thus: 'This body is full of intestines, full of undigested food... full of bile and grease.'

In that context, 'full of intestines' is antapūro. 'Full of undigested food' is udarapūro. Udara is a name for undigested food (udariya). It is called udara by way of the name of its location. Yakanapeḷassa means of the liver-mass. Vatthino means of urine. By way of metonymy for its location, it is called vatthi (bladder). Since the word pūro (full) is the subject under discussion, it should be connected as 'full of the liver-mass, full of urine.' This same method applies to the heart and so on. All these, such as the intestines, should be understood by way of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation, as well as by the method of lack of volition, according to the method stated in the Visuddhimagga.

199-200. Thus, the Blessed One, showing the internal corpse, said: 'In this body, there is not even a single thing to be grasped that is like a pearl or a gem; on the contrary, this body is full of impurities'...
239:
...Having shown the internal corpse, and now wishing to make it clear by showing the same internal corpse as it comes out to the exterior, and by summarizing what was said previously, He spoke the two verses beginning with 'Atha'ssa navahi sotehi.'

Therein, the word 'atha' indicates another method; it means 'see the impurity by another method as well.' 'Assa' means of this body. 'Navahi sotehi' means by the two eye-openings, two ear-openings, two nostrils, the mouth, the anus, and the urethra. 'Asuci savati' means that only impurity—which is well-known to all the world, of various kinds, extremely ill-smelling, and loathsome—flows, runs, and trickles out. No other kind of scent such as aloe or sandalwood, nor any kind of treasure such as gems or pearls, flows out. 'Sabbadā' means that such flowing occurs at all times—at night, during the day, in the morning, in the evening, while standing, and while walking. If one asks what that impurity is, it is said: 'Akkhiṃhā akkhigūthako' (from the eye, eye-wax), and so on. From the two eye-openings of this body, eye-wax, which resembles skin and flesh that has been removed, flows out. From the ear-holes, ear-wax, which is like dust and grime, flows out. From the nostrils, mucus, which is like pus, flows out. And from the mouth, it vomits. If one asks what it vomits, at times it vomits bile. The meaning is that when the unattached bile (abaddha-pitta) is disturbed, it vomits that bile. By the word 'semhañca' (and phlegm), it is not only bile; there is also phlegm about the size of a bowlful in the stomach cavity, and it sometimes vomits that phlegm as well. The color and so on of that phlegm should be understood according to the method stated in the Visuddhimagga. By the word 'ca' in 'semhañca,' it is shown that it vomits not only phlegm but also other such impurities like undigested food, blood, and so on. Thus, after showing the vomiting of impurities through the seven openings, the Blessed One—who knows the time, the person, and the assembly—without specifically mentioning the two further openings, spoke the words 'kāyamhā sedajallikā' to show the flowing of impurities from the entire body by another method. In that phrase, 'sedajallikā' refers to sweat (seda) and the dirt (jallikā) consisting of layers of salt and filth. This is connected with the phrase 'savati sabbadā' (flows at all times).

Thus, the Blessed One gave an analogy: just as when rice is being cooked, the impurities of the rice and the impurities of the water rise up with the foam, smear the rim of the pot, and overflow; even so, when the food that has been eaten and drunk is being digested by the kamma-born fire element (kammaja-tejo), the impurities that arise come out in various ways such as 'from the eye, eye-wax,' smearing the eyes and so on, and flowing out. By the power of that flowing...
240:
Having shown the impurity of the body, the Blessed One now spoke this verse beginning with "Atha'ssa susiraṃ sīsaṃ" to show the lack of essence and the impurity of the head—which is considered the highest limb in the world and is of such superior status that people do not even pay homage to those worthy of homage [without it].

In that verse, "susiraṃ" means a cavity or hole. "Matthaluṅgassa pūritaṃ" means filled with brain, like a gourd filled with curd. That brain should be understood in the manner already stated in the Visuddhimagga. "Subhato naṃ maññati bālo" means that although the body is filled with various kinds of impurities, the fool, who is prone to unwholesome thoughts, perceives it as beautiful, pure, desirable, pleasing, and lovely, through the three types of misconceptions: craving (taṇhā), views (diṭṭhi), and pride (māna). Why is this? It is because ignorance (avijjā) is the precursor, and delusion (moha), which veils the Four Noble Truths, surrounds, urges, and impels it, saying, "Take it thus, attend to it thus, perceive it thus." See how much harm this ignorance causes!

Thus, the Blessed One, having shown foulness (asubha) by way of a living corpse, now speaks the verse "Yadā ca so mato seti" to show it by way of a lifeless corpse. Alternatively, since even the body of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) is filled with the aforementioned impurities, having shown foulness in a state of success (sampatti), He now shows it in a state of ruin (vipatti).

The meaning of that verse is: When this body of such a nature dies, being devoid of life-span (āyu), heat (usmā), and consciousness (viññāṇa), it lies bloated like a wind-filled bellows, discolored and bluish-black, discarded in the cemetery like a useless log. At that time, relatives lose all regard for it, thinking, "This person will never rise again." In that verse, the word "mato" (dead) shows impermanence (aniccatā). The word "seti" (lies) shows the state of being without effort or activity. Through these two words, one is urged to abandon the intoxication of vitality. The word "uddhumāto" (bloated) shows the ruin of form. The word "vinīlako" (bluish-black) shows the ruin of complexion. Through these two words, one is urged to abandon pride in physical form and pride based on beauty of complexion. The word "apaviddho" (discarded) shows the lack of any essence to be grasped. The word "susānasmiṃ" (in the cemetery) shows the loathsome nature of the body, which is unfit to be kept indoors. Through these two words, one is urged to abandon the grasping of "my body" and the perception of beauty. The phrase "anapekkhā honti ñātayo" (relatives become regardless) shows the cessation of any remedial action, thereby urging the abandonment of pride in one's following or retinue.
241:
Thus, having shown foulness by way of an intact lifeless corpse through this verse, He now speaks the verse beginning with "Khādanti naṃ" to show it by way of its disintegration. In that verse, "ye caññe" means that other creatures such as crows, hawks, and vultures, which feed on carrion, also bite and devour that corpse. The rest of the words are clear.

Thus, having shown the body by way of the meditation on emptiness (suññata-kammaṭṭhāna) through the method beginning with "Caraṃ vā," by way of the foulness of the living body through "Aṭṭhinahārusamyutto," and by way of the foulness of the lifeless body through "Yadā ca so mato seti," He showed the conduct of the fool with the verse: "The fool, surrounded by ignorance, perceives this body as beautiful," even though the body is devoid of permanence, happiness, and self, and is absolutely foul. Having shown the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) based on ignorance, He now begins the verse "Sutvāna buddhavacanaṃ" to show the conduct of the wise person regarding that foulness, and the cessation of the cycle (vivaṭṭa) based on full understanding (pariññā).

In that verse, "sutvāna" means having properly attended to or listened. "Buddhavacanaṃ" refers to the words of the Buddha that cause the removal of desire for the body. "Bhikkhu" refers to either a trainee (sekha) or an ordinary person (puthujjana). "Paññāṇavā" means one endowed with insight (vipassanā), which is called "paññāṇa" because it proceeds by way of aspects such as impermanence. "Idha" means in this Dispensation (Sāsana). "So kho naṃ parijānāti" means that person fully understands this body through the three types of full understanding (pariññā). How does he understand it? Just as a clever merchant examines various goods, weighing them by thinking, "If I buy this for this much, there will be such a profit," and acts accordingly, eventually taking the capital along with the profit and discarding the goods; in the same way, looking with the eye of wisdom and seeing, "These are bones, tendons, etc.; these are hair, body hair, etc.," he understands it through full understanding of the known (ñāta-pariññā). Weighing them as "These phenomena are impermanent, suffering, and non-self," he understands through full understanding by investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā). Having thus investigated, when he reaches the Noble Path (ariya-magga), he understands through full understanding by abandoning (pahāna-pariññā) by way of discarding desire and lust (chanda-rāga) for that body. Alternatively, one who views by way of the foulness of the living and the lifeless understands through ñāta-pariññā. One who views by way of impermanence, etc., understands through tīraṇa-pariññā. One who removes and abandons desire for that body through the Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga) understands through pahāna-pariññā.

Why does he understand it thus? Because he sees it as it really is (yathābhūtaṃ). This is the meaning. With the words "paññāṇavā," etc., in this...
242:
Even though the meaning is already established, it is because of hearing the Buddha's words that the state of being wise arises in that person. Since this body, which is a manifest means for all people, cannot be fully understood without hearing the Buddha's words, He said, "Having heard the Buddha's words," to show the cause of knowledge for that person and to show the inability of those outside this Dispensation to see in this way. He said, "Monks," because the teaching was prompted by the bhikkhunī Nandā and that monk with a distorted mind, and also to show the monkhood of those among the noble assembly who have attained that practice.

Now, in this context of "seeing as it really is," He said, "As this is, so is that; as that is, so is this," to show how one who sees in such a way sees according to reality. The meaning of those words is: Just as this foul body, possessed of consciousness, can move, stand, sit, and lie down because life, heat, and consciousness have not yet departed; so too, that body now lying in the cemetery without consciousness was formerly the same when those states had not yet departed. And just as that body, now dead, cannot move, stand, sit, or lie down because those states have departed; so too, this body, though possessed of consciousness, will be the same when those states depart. And just as this body, possessed of consciousness, does not yet lie dead in the cemetery and has not yet reached the state of being bloated and so forth; so too, that body, now dead, was formerly the same. And just as this foul body, now without consciousness, lies dead in the cemetery and has reached the state of being bloated and so forth; so too, this body, though possessed of consciousness, will be the same.

In that regard, by the phrase "As this is, so is that," one makes one's own body equal to the dead body and thereby abandons the fault (aversion) regarding external objects. By the phrase "As that is, so is this," one makes the dead body equal to oneself and thereby abandons lust (rāga) within one's own continuity. One who knows the manner in which both are made equal abandons delusion (moha) regarding both. Thus, by seeing according to reality, one accomplishes the abandonment of the unwholesome roots even in the preliminary stage. Because a monk who practices in this way is able to reach the Path of Arahantship in due course and cause all desire and lust to fade away, He said, "Inwardly and outwardly, one should fade away desire for the body." The phrase "a monk who practices in this way in due course" is a textual supplement.

Having thus shown the plane of the trainee (sekkhabhūmi), He now said, "He is faded away from desire and lust," wishing to show the plane of one beyond training (asekkhabhūmi). The meaning is: That monk, being wise through the knowledge of the Path of Arahantship, reaches the Fruit immediately after the Path; then, entirely...
243:
Because desire and lust have been entirely abandoned, he is called "faded away from desire and lust" (chandarāgavicatto). He is said to have reached the state of Nibbāna, which is well-described as "Deathless" (amata) because there is no death or because of its sublime meaning; as "Peace" (santi) because of the stilling of all formations; as "Nibbāna" because of the absence of the binding called craving; and as "Immovable" (accuta) because there is no falling away (death). Alternatively, it should be understood that the monk, being wise through the knowledge of the Path of Arahantship and standing in the Fruit immediately following the Path, is called one who is faded away from desire and lust, and has reached the state of Nibbāna of the aforementioned nature. By the term "faded away from desire and lust," He shows that "this desire and lust has been abandoned by this monk, and this Fruit of Arahantship has been attained by him."

207-208. Having thus taught the meditation on foulness (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna) together with its completion by way of the conscious and the unconscious, He spoke the two verses beginning with "Dvipādako yaṃ" (This two-footed one), wishing to censure heedlessness (pamāda) which causes obstacles to such great benefits, through a brief teaching. In those verses, although the bodies of footless creatures and others are also impure, He said "This two-footed one" by way of the context of this teaching, or by way of defining the superior human being. Or, because other impure bodies can be processed with salt, sourness, and so forth and brought as food for humans, whereas the human body cannot be so brought; therefore, even to show its state of being more impure, He said "Two-footed one."

By the word "ayaṃ" (this), He shows the human body. "Dugganḍho parihīrati" means that although it has a foul smell, it is carried about after being specially prepared with the scent of flowers and the like. "Nānākuṇapaparipūro" means it is full of various kinds of impurities such as hair and so forth. "Vissavanto tato tato" means that although they strive to cover it with the scent of flowers and the like, making that effort fruitless, saliva, snot, and so forth constantly flow from the nine openings, and sweat and grime constantly exude from the pores of the skin. Now, behold in that foulness! With such a body, some foolish man or woman might think to be conceited. Through craving, wrong view, and pride, one might think to be conceited in such ways as "I," "Mine," or "Permanent." Placing oneself in a high position, one might despise others based on birth and so forth. Apart from the lack of seeing the Noble Truths through the Noble Path, what other cause could there be for such conceit and contempt in that person?

At the conclusion of the teaching, the bhikkhunī named Nandā, the Beauty of the Country (Janapadakalyāṇī), attained spiritual urgency (saṃvega). She thought, "O, alas! I have been foolish indeed, that I did not come to attend upon the Blessed One who has promoted such various Dhamma teachings prompted by me alone." Having thus gained spiritual urgency, she [listened] to that very Dhamma teaching...
244:
Having reflected well on that Dhamma teaching, he realized the fruit of Arahantship within a few days through that very meditation on foulness (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna). On the second occasion, at the end of the Dhamma teaching, eighty-four thousand beings attained the realization of the Dhamma; the celestial maiden Sirimā attained the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmiphala), and that monk was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala).

## The explanation of the Vijaya Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary of the Khuddaka Commentary named Paramatthajotikā is finished.

## 12. Munisuttavaṇṇanā
"Santhavāto bhayaṃ jātaṃ" (From intimacy, fear is born) and so on is the Muni Sutta. How did it arise? Not all suttas have only one origin; however, the origin of the first four verses of this Muni Sutta is as follows: While the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī, a certain poor woman living in a village, whose husband had died, had her son ordained among the monks and she herself ordained among the bhikkhunīs. Both of them, having entered the vassa (rains retreat) in Sāvatthī, constantly desired to see each other. When the mother received even a small gain, she would bring it to her son; the son also did the same for his mother. Thus, meeting each other in the evening and the morning, sharing whatever gains they received, rejoicing together, and asking about each other's well-being and suffering, they lived without suspicion.

Due to such frequent meetings, intimacy arose; from intimacy came familiarity; from familiarity came an opening (for lust). For those whose minds were overcome by lust, the perception of being ordained and the perception of being mother and son disappeared. Therefore, having transgressed the boundaries (of discipline), they engaged in misconduct (asaddhamma). Having fallen into disgrace, they disrobed and lived in the household life. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One rebuked them, saying, "Monks, does that foolish man think that a mother does not feel lust for her son, or a son for his mother?" Then, having stirred the monks with the rest of the sutta beginning with "Monks, I do not see any other single form..." (A. Ni. 5.55), He said: "Therefore, monks—

'Like the deadly Halāhala poison, like boiling oil, like molten copper, one should avoid women.'"
245:
Having said this, the Blessed One, for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to the monks once again, spoke these four verses compared to himself, beginning with "Santhavāto bhayaṃ jātaṃ" (Fear arises from intimacy). Therein, "Santhava" (intimacy) was previously mentioned as being of three kinds: craving, views, and friends. Here, however, intimacy of craving and intimacy of views are intended. Referring to that intimacy, the Blessed One said: "Monks, look at how this fear has arisen for that worthless man because of intimacy." Indeed, for him, because of the craving such as the desire to constantly see his mother, a powerful fear of defilements arose, by which, being unable to restrain himself, he acted wrongly towards his mother. Or, it refers to the great fear such as self-reproach, by which he abandoned the Dispensation and disrobed. "Niketa" (abode/attachment) refers to the various types of sense objects, as taught in the manner: "Householder, one who is attached to and bound by the signs of forms is called 'one who dwells in an abode'" (S.N. 3.3). "Jāyate rajo" means the dust of lust, hatred, and delusion is born. What is meant? Not only did fear arise for him from intimacy, but also, from that which is called "Niketa"—the objects of the taints (āsava) because they are the dwelling place of defilements—now, because of his broken restraint and his transgression of boundaries, dust arises even more from that Niketa. Because of that dust, with a defiled mind, he will reach ruin and destruction. Alternatively, "Monks, look at how this fear arose for that worthless man because of intimacy, and how dust is born from the abode (niketa) for all worldlings"—thus these two phrases should be connected.

In every way, by the first half of this verse, the Blessed One, having censured the view of worldlings and wishing to praise his own view, spoke the latter half beginning with "Aniketaṃ" (homeless/unattached). Therein, "Aniketa" is known by the rejection of the aforementioned Niketa, and "Asanthava" by the rejection of Santhava. Both of these are synonyms for Nibbāna. "Etaṃ ve munidassanaṃ" means that this Nibbāna, which is without the abode of craving and without intimacy, has been seen by the Sage (Muni), the Buddha. Therein, the word "ve" is to be understood as a particle in the sense of wonder. Therefore, the meaning is established: "While even mother and son act wrongly through the power of abode and intimacy, this state of being without abode and without intimacy has been seen by the Sage—oh, how wonderful!" Alternatively, "Muni-dassana" means the view of the Sage; "Dassana" means patience (khanti) and preference (ruci), meaning the Sage likes and desires that Nibbāna. In the second verse, "Yo jātamucchijjā" means as one abandons the defilement that has arisen, been produced, or generated in any object, just as one abandons an arisen unwholesome state...
246: A person making such an effort cuts off the defilements (kilesas) at the root so they do not arise again in that object. Because future defilements are imminent and ready to arise if such supporting conditions meet, they are called 'arising' (jāyanta) by way of the present characteristic close to the present; one should not plant them. This means that just as one strives so that unarisen unwholesome states do not arise, one should not let those defilements be produced. How should one not let them be produced? One should not let them enter continuously. One should not let the cause by which those defilements might arise enter or combine. Thus, by making the supporting factors deficient, one should not plant that which is arising. Alternatively, because of the development of the Path (magga-bhāvanā), past defilements are cut off as they no longer produce results in the future. Present defilements are not planted as they no longer enter. Future defilements cannot enter the mental continuum because the capacity for their arising has been destroyed. Therefore, one who cuts off what has arisen through the development of the Noble Path and does not plant what is arising, and does not let future arising defilements enter—such a person wandering alone is called a 'Muni.' That Mahesī (the Great Sage who seeks virtues) has seen the state of peace, Nibbāna. This is how the connection of meaning should be understood here. He is called 'Eka' (One/Alone) because of being absolutely free from defilements, or 'Eka' in the sense of being noble. 'Muninaṃ' means the Muni, or the noble one among Munis. 'Carantaṃ' means one who wanders with the practice for the benefit of the world, which is complete in every aspect, and with other practices. 'Addakkhi' means he saw. 'So' (He) refers to the Buddha-Muni who was spoken of as 'one should not plant what is arising, one should not let it enter' because of his ability to cut off what has arisen, not plant it, and not let it enter. 'Santipadaṃ' means the portion of peace. Among the three types of peace—conventional peace (sammuti-santi), temporary peace (tadaṅga-santi), and ultimate peace (accanta-santi) found in the divisions of the sixty-two views, insight, and Nibbāna—the Mahesī saw the ultimate peace, which is the most noble, in this unpeaceful world. This is how the meaning should be understood. In the third verse, 'saṅkhāya' means having calculated and delimited, having investigated and reflected, having known according to reality, and having fully understood through the full understanding of suffering (dukkha-pariññā). 'Vatthūni' refers to the bases of defilements consisting of the aggregates (khandha), sense bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) to which the people of this world are attached. 'Pamāya bījaṃ' means having oppressed and harassed the seed of those bases, which is the karmic consciousness (abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa), and having abandoned it through the abandonment by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna). 'Sinehamassa nānuppavecche' means that the seed, which is moistened by the moisture of craving (taṇhā) and views (diṭṭhi), could produce the aforementioned crop of bases through rebirth in the future; one should not let that moisture enter. This means one should not let that moisture enter through the development of the Path, which is the opposite of that moisture. 'Sa ve muni jātikhayantadassī' means that such a Buddha-Muni has seen Nibbāna, which is the end of birth and death, through the realization of Nibbāna.
247:
That Buddha, the seer of Nibbāna which is the end of the destruction of birth, having abandoned speculative thought (takka), no longer falls into the reckoning of a worldling (puthujjana). By developing these Four Truths, he abandons the ninefold unwholesome thoughts, reaches the Nibbāna element with residue (sa-upādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu), and while performing the practice for the benefit of the world, upon reaching the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu) through the gradual cessation of the final consciousness, he no longer falls into the reckoning of 'being a deva' or 'being a human.' Alternatively, just as one who has not yet attained final Nibbāna falls into the reckoning of 'this person is lustful' or 'this person is hateful' because of not having abandoned thoughts such as sensual thoughts, so too, having abandoned speculative thought, he no longer falls into reckoning. This is how the meaning should be understood here.

In the fourth verse, 'aññāya' means having known through methods such as impermanence (anicca). 'Sabbāni' means all without exception. 'Nivesanāni' refers to existences such as the sensual existence (kāma-bhava). Because beings dwell in those existences, they are called 'nivesanāni' (dwellings). Not longing for even a single one of those existences, such a Buddha-Muni, who sees the danger in views and so forth, is called 'vītagadha' (free from greed) because greed, which is craving, has vanished through the power of developing the Path. Because he is free from greed, he is 'agiddha' (not greedy). It is not like some who, while not yet free from greed, claim 'we are not greedy.' 'Nāyūhati' means he no longer performs wholesome or unwholesome deeds that produce those respective dwellings (existences). Why? Because he has reached the other shore, Nibbāna. This means such a person has reached Nibbāna, which is the end of all dwellings of existence.

Thus, with the first verse, he censures the views of worldlings and praises his own view. With the second verse, he praises his own attainment of the state of peace because of the absence of those defilements by which a worldling is unpeaceful. With the third verse, he praises his own non-entry into reckoning by abandoning speculative thought through the development of the Four Truths regarding those bases where a worldling, without abandoning speculative thought, falls into various reckonings. With the fourth verse, he praises his own non-striving because of the absence of craving for those dwellings (existences) for which a worldling, longing for them in the future, strives through craving for existence. With these four verses, placing Arahantship at the summit, he concluded the teaching which has a single theme.

## How did the topic 'Sabbābhibhū' arise?
The Great Man (Mahāpurisa), having made the Great Renunciation (Mahābhinikkhamana), gradually attained Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) and went to Vārāṇasī to preach the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta...
248:
A person of such a nature reaches Nibbāna, which is the further shore of the houses of all existences. This is the meaning. Thus, having censured the view of the worldling with the first verse, He spoke the second verse wishing to praise His own view. Wishing to praise Nibbāna, the means of reaching His own peace due to the absence of those defilements by which a worldling is made restless, He spoke the third verse. Wishing to praise the state of not falling into the category of a worldling by abandoning sensual thoughts and the like through the cultivation of the Four Noble Truths—in those objects where a worldling, without abandoning sensual thoughts and the like, falls into the category of a worldling in various ways—He spoke the fourth verse. Wishing to praise His own lack of striving, as a worldling who longs for the houses of future existences strives with the craving for existence, He concluded the teaching, which has a single origin, by placing the Fruit of Arahantship at the pinnacle with these four verses.

What is the origin of this verse beginning with 'Sabbābhibhū'? The Buddha, the Great Man, having made the Great Renunciation and gradually attained Omniscience, was traveling to Bārāṇasī to preach the Dhammacakka sermon when He met an Ājīvaka named Upaka between the Bodhi-maṇḍa and Gayā. That Upaka questioned Him in this manner: 'Friend, your faculties are very serene,' and so on. The Blessed One replied with the words, 'I am the All-Conqueror,' and so forth. Upaka said, 'It may be so, friend,' shook his head, took a side path, and departed. Traveling by stages, he reached a certain hunter's village in the Vaṅgahāra country. When the hunter chief saw Upaka, he thought, 'How wonderful! This ascetic has few desires; he does not even wear clothes. This man must be an Arahant in the world.' He took him home, served him with meat broth, and after he had eaten, the hunter, along with his wife and children, paid homage and invited him, saying, 'Venerable sir, please reside right here; I will support you with the four requisites.' He then prepared a dwelling place for him. Upaka resided there.

In the summer, when the deer departed for a cool place abundant with water, the hunter, as he was preparing to go there, commanded his daughter named Chāpā, 'Attend to our venerable Arahant with respect,' and then departed with his sons and brothers. That daughter was beautiful and possessed perfect limbs. On the second day, when Upaka came to the house and saw the young woman approaching to perform her duties and serve him, he was overcome by lust. Unable even to eat, he took the rice in a bowl, went to his dwelling, set the food aside in a place, and lay down without eating, thinking, 'If I get Chāpā, I shall live; if not, I shall die.' On the seventh day, the hunter returned and asked his daughter about Upaka. She said, 'He came only on the first day and has not returned since.' The hunter thought, 'I will approach and question him just as I have arrived,' and went immediately. Massaging Upaka's feet, he asked, 'Venerable sir, what is your ailment?' Upaka just rolled from side to side, groaning. The hunter said, 'Speak, venerable sir; whatever I can do, I will do it all.' Upaka said, 'If I get Chāpā, I shall live; if not, death right here is better.' The hunter asked, 'But do you know any craft, venerable sir?' 'I do not,' he replied. 'Venerable sir, one who knows no craft cannot maintain a household,' the hunter said. Upaka replied, 'I know no craft, but I will be a meat-carrier for you and I will sell the meat.' The hunter agreed, saying, 'This work is suitable for us,' gave him an upper garment, took him home, and gave him his daughter in marriage. As they lived together...
249:
A son was born. They named the boy Subhadda. Cāpā teased Upaka with a song to soothe the child. Unable to endure that teasing, Upaka said, "Lady, I am going to the presence of the Anantajina (Infinite Victor)," and set out towards the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa).

At that time, the Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana Great Monastery in Sāvatthī. Then the Blessed One pre-emptively instructed the monks: "Monks, if anyone comes asking for the Anantajina, show me to him."

Upaka eventually arrived at Sāvatthī, stood in the middle of the monastery, and asked, "In this monastery, there is my friend named Anantajina; where does he live?" The monks led Upaka to the Blessed One. The Blessed One taught him a suitable Dhamma. At the end of the teaching, he was established in the Fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmiphala). The monks, having heard of Upaka's past events, started a discussion: "The Blessed One first taught the Dhamma to a luckless naked ascetic." The Blessed One, knowing the topic of their conversation, came out from the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), sat on the Buddha's seat with a psychic power suitable for the moment, and addressed the monks: "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" They told him everything. Then the Blessed One said: "Monks, the Tathāgata does not teach the Dhamma without cause or condition. The Tathāgata's teaching of the Dhamma is stainless; no fault can be seen therein. Monks, by depending on that Dhamma teaching, Upaka has now become a Non-returner." Having said this, he uttered this verse illustrating the stainless nature of his teaching.

The meaning of that verse is: Because he is not overcome by all the aggregates, sense bases, and elements which are objects of the taints (āsava) through the abandoning of desire and lust, and because he himself exists having overcome all those things, he is called 'Conqueror of All' (Sabbābhibhū). Because he has known those things and all other things in every aspect, he is called 'All-knower' (Sabbavidū). Because he is endowed with the beautiful wisdom called 'medhā' which is capable of teaching all Dhammas, he is called 'One of Good Wisdom' (Sumedha). By whatever smears of craving and views one is smeared in all things such as the aggregates accompanied by taints, because those smears do not exist, he is 'Unstained' (Anupalitta) in all those things. Because he stands having abandoned all those things through the absence of desire and lust, he is 'Abandoner of All' (Sabbañjaha). Because he is specially liberated in Nibbāna, the destruction of craving, with a mind inclined towards seclusion from the substrates (upadhi), he is called 'Liberated in the Destruction of Craving' (Taṇhakkhaye vimutta); this also means 'Adhimutta' (intent on). The wise also know such a person as a Sage (Muni). Behold how extraordinary this Sage is; where could there be any stain in his teaching? Thus he showed himself.
250:
In this word, the particle 'vā' clarifies the meaning. Some teachers, however, explain: "At that time, even though Upaka saw the Tathāgata, he did not believe 'This is the Buddha-Sage.'" How did the monks raise this matter? Then the Blessed One, wishing to show "Whether Upaka believes or not, the wise know that Sage," uttered this verse.

What is the origin of the verse 'Paññābalaṃ'? This verse was spoken concerning the Elder Revata. In the same manner as stated in the verse "Gāme vā yadi vā raññe", one should understand the Elder Revata's ordination from the beginning, his dwelling in the Acacia forest (Khadiravana) after ordaining, his attainment of distinction while living there, and the Blessed One's journey there and back. When the Blessed One returned, an elderly monk who had forgotten his sandals went back and saw them hanging on an Acacia tree. Upon reaching Sāvatthī, when the laywoman Visākhā asked the monks, "Venerable sirs, is the dwelling place of the Elder Revata pleasant?", that monk, wishing to discourage her from the praise of other monks, said, "Laywoman, those monks speak in vain; that ground is not good, it is merely a very parched and rough Acacia forest." After eating the meal for guests provided by Visākhā, in the afternoon when the monks were assembled in the pavilion, he said, wishing to disparage them, "Friends, what did you see that was pleasant in the Elder Revata's monastery?" The Blessed One, knowing that talk, came out from the Fragrant Chamber, reached the midst of the assembly with a psychic power suitable for the moment, sat on the Buddha's seat, and addressed the monks: "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" They replied, "Venerable Sir, a discussion has arisen concerning Revata: 'When will one who is thus occupied with new work (navakammika) practice the recluse's Dhamma?'" "Monks, Revata is not one occupied with new work; Revata is an Arahant whose taints are destroyed." Having said this, he uttered this verse for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to those monks.

The meaning of that verse is: Because he is endowed with the power of wisdom that accomplishes the abandoning of the weak defilements, or with the power of wisdom consisting of various psychic transformations (vikubbana) and resolutions (adhiṭṭhāna), he is called 'Power of Wisdom' (Paññābala). Because he is endowed with the fourfold purification of virtue and the ascetic practices (dhutanga), he is called 'Endowed with Virtue and Vows' (Sīlavatūpapanna). Because he is composed through the concentration of the path, the concentration of fruition, and the concentration of postures, he is called 'Concentrated' (Samāhita).
