'Those who go to darkness' (tamaṃ vajanti ye) refers to those who go to the darkness known as the interval between worlds (lokantarika) or to the darkness of being born into low families and so forth. 'Beings who fall head-first into hell' (patanti sattā nirayaṃ avaṃsirā) refers to those beings who fall into hells such as Avīci with their heads downward. The three types of āmagandha consisting of greed, opposition, and killing, which are the cause of those beings going to darkness and falling into hell, and which are the root of all āmagandha, are the only true āmagandha. The eating of meat, however, is not āmagandha.

Thus, the Blessed One, having explained āmagandha in the ultimate sense and having revealed it as the path to the states of misery (duggati), now, in order to show that the ascetic—who perceives the eating of fish and meat as āmagandha and as the path to misery, and who, desiring purity by not eating it, abstains from it—is unable to purify himself or others of that kind, spoke the six verses beginning with 'Na macchamaṃsaṃ.' In those verses:
307:
All phrases should be connected with the final phrase: 'Abstaining from fish and meat does not purify a mortal who has not crossed over doubt; performing sacrifices and seasonal observances do not purify a mortal who has not crossed over doubt'—this is how they should be connected. In this verse, 'na macchamaṃsaṃ' means that the non-eating of fish and meat does not purify a mortal. Similarly, the ancient teachers explain that the state of being one who does not eat fish and meat does not purify. However, it would be even better to interpret it thus: 'It is not the state of not eating fish and meat, nor is it the state of not not eating fish and meat; rather, the state of not eating fish and meat does not purify a mortal'—this is the meaning. If this is the case, one might ask: 'Will the state of not eating fish and meat then be diminished?' It cannot be diminished, because it is included within the practice of 'amaratapa' (asceticism for immortality). In the passage 'There are many amaratapa practices in the world,' it should be understood that all remaining forms of self-mortification (attakilamatha) mentioned are included. 

'Naggiyaṃ' means nakedness (acelakattaṃ). 'Muṇḍiyaṃ' means the state of having a shaven head (muṇḍabhāvo). 'Jaṭājallaṃ' means matted hair and the smearing of dust and dirt. 'Kharājināni' means rough antelope skins. 'Aggihuttassūpasevanā' means tending the sacrificial fire. 'Amarā' refers to the defilements of the body that arise from the longing for the state of immortality. 'Bahū' refers to many practices such as the practice of squatting and so forth. 'Tapā' refers to practices that torment the body. 'Mantā' refers to the Vedic scriptures. 'Āhutī' refers to the act of making fire offerings. 'Yaññamutūpasevanā' refers to sacrifices such as the Assamedha and the observance of the seasons. 'Observance of the seasons' means seeking out heat in the summer, staying at the foot of a tree in the rainy season, and entering the water in the winter. 

'Do not purify a mortal who has not crossed over doubt' means they cannot purify a mortal who is not yet free from doubt (vicikicchā), whether in terms of the purification of defilements or the purification of existence. Indeed, as long as the stain of doubt exists, one cannot be pure, and you yourself are still possessed of doubt. In this context, regarding the phrase 'one who has not crossed over doubt,' we do not hold the view that the Buddha spoke this because doubt arose in the ascetic as to whether 'the path of purification might be achieved through the non-eating of fish and meat, etc.' Rather, it should be understood that this was spoken in reference to the doubt that arose in the ascetic regarding the Buddha as soon as he heard that 'He [the Buddha] eats fish and meat.'

Having thus shown the inability of practices such as not eating fish and meat to bring about purification, the Buddha now spoke the verse beginning with 'Sotesu gutto' (Guarded in the senses) to show the qualities that are capable of bringing about purification. In that verse, 'sotesu' refers to the six sense faculties. 'Gutto' means being endowed with the protection of sense-restraint (indriyasaṃvara). By this much, He shows the virtue (sīla) that is the retinue of sense-restraint. 'Viditindriyo care' means that one should fare or dwell having known the six sense faculties through 'full understanding of the known' (ñātapariññā) and making them clear. By this much, He shows the discernment of mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa-pariccheda) of one who possesses pure virtue. 'Dhamme ṭhito' means being established in the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths which are to be realized through the Noble Path. By this, He shows the stage of Stream-entry (sotāpatti).
308:
'Ajjavamaddave rato' means delighting in uprightness and gentleness. By this, He shows the stage of the Once-returner (sakadāgāmi). Indeed, a Once-returner delights in uprightness and gentleness because of the thinning out of greed and hatred, which cause crookedness of body and so forth, and which make the mind stubborn. 'Saṅgātigo' means one who has transcended the attachments of greed and hatred. By this, He shows the stage of the Non-returner (anāgāmi). 'Sabbadukkhappahīno' means one who has abandoned all suffering by abandoning the causes of the entire round of suffering (vaṭṭadukkha). By this, He shows the stage of Arahantship (arahatta). 'Na lippati diṭṭhasutesu dhīro' means that the wise one, having thus reached Arahantship in due order and being endowed with steadfastness, is no longer smeared by any defilement in things seen or heard. Not only is he not smeared by things seen and heard, but he is also not smeared by things sensed or cognized. On the contrary, he is one who has reached supreme purity—thus the Buddha concluded the teaching with Arahantship as its peak.

## 254-5. From here on, the two verses beginning with 'Iccetamattaṃ' were spoken by the Elders who conducted the Recital (Saṅgītikāras). The meaning of those verses is: Thus, the Blessed Kassapa Buddha explained, declared, and elaborated that matter again and again through many verses, using both teachings based on principles (dhammādhiṭṭhāna) and teachings based on persons (puggalādhiṭṭhāna), until that ascetic understood. 'Naṃ vedayi mantapāragū' means that Tissa the Brahmin ascetic, who had reached the end of the mantras and the end of the Vedas, also understood that meaning. For what reason? Because the Sage (Muni) revealed it through verses that were beautiful in meaning, in phrasing, and in the method of teaching. 

What kind of Dhamma was it? It is called 'nirāmagandha' (free from raw stench) because of the absence of the defilements known as 'āmagandha'. It is called 'asita' (unattached) because of the absence of dependence on craving and views. It is called 'durannaya' (difficult to track) because no one is able to lead him away by the power of external views, saying 'This is better, this is superior.' Having heard the well-spoken words of the Buddha who thus revealed it—having heard the Dhamma teaching that is free from raw stench, unyoked from defilements, and the dispeller of all suffering, the dispeller of all the suffering of the round—Tissa the Brahmin, with a humble mind, paid homage to the Tathāgata; he paid homage at the feet of the Tathāgata by performing the five-point prostration. 'Tattheva pabbajjamarocayittha' means that right there, the ascetic Tissa requested the going-forth (pabbajjā) from the Blessed Kassapa who was seated on his seat; he begged for it. The Blessed One said to him, 'Ehi bhikkhu' (Come, monk). At that very moment, he became endowed with the eight requisites and, descending from the sky like an elder of a hundred years, he paid homage to the Blessed One. Within a few days, having penetrated the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvakapāramīñāṇa), he became the Chief Disciple named Tissa. Later, the second [Chief Disciple] was named Bhāradvāja. Thus, that Blessed One had the pair of disciples named Tissa and Bhāradvāja.
309: Our Buddha brought together all fourteen verses—the three verses spoken first by the Brahmin Tissa, the nine verses spoken in the middle by the Blessed One Kassapa, and the two verses spoken at the end by the Reciters (Saṅgītikārakas) at that time—and, making them complete, he explained the Āmagandha Sutta, the teaching on 'inner stench,' to the five hundred ascetics led by their teacher. Having heard that discourse, the Brahmin became humble in mind, paid homage at the feet of the Blessed One, and requested ordination along with his followers. The Blessed One said, 'Come, monks (Ehi bhikkhavo).' They immediately attained the status of 'Ehi Bhikkhu' monks, came through the air, paid homage to the Blessed One, and within a few days, all of them were established in the highest fruit, Arahantship. ## The Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya named Paramatthajotikā ## The Explanation of the Āmagandha Sutta in the Commentary on the Suttanipāta is finished. ## 3. Explanation of the Hiri Sutta 'Hiriṃ tarantaṃ' and so forth is the Hiri Sutta. What is the occasion for its arising? Before the Buddha had appeared, there was a certain wealthy Great Brahmin (Brāhmaṇa-mahāsāla) in Sāvatthī with a fortune of eighty crores. He had a beloved and dear only son. Although he raised the boy like a divine prince with various comforts and services, the Brahmin passed away along with his wife before he could hand over the wealth to his son. Then, after the death of the youth's parents, the treasurer opened the storehouse and, wishing to hand over the inheritance, said: 'Master, this is the property from your parents' time; this is the property of your grandfathers and great-grandfathers; this has come down through seven generations of the family.' When the youth saw the wealth, he thought: 'Only this wealth is seen; those who accumulated it are no longer seen; all have come under the power of death. And when they went, they could not take anything from here. Indeed, one must go to the next world having abandoned these enjoyments; it is not possible to take anything except for good conduct (sucarita). What if I were to give up this wealth and take the wealth of good conduct, which can be taken along?' Every day he spent a hundred thousand, and again he thought: 'This wealth is vast; how can it be fulfilled with such a small renunciation? ...'
310: 'What if I were to give a great almsgiving?' he thought. He informed the King: 'Great King, there is this much wealth in my house; I wish to give a great almsgiving with it. It would be good, Great King, if you would have a proclamation made in the city.' The King had it done as requested. Filling the vessels of all who came, he gave away all his wealth for seven days. After giving, he thought: 'After making such a great renunciation, it is not proper to live in a house; what if I were to go forth?' Then he informed his servants of this matter. They said, 'Master, do not think "My wealth is exhausted"; we will accumulate wealth again in a short time through various means,' and they pleaded with him in many ways. Without heeding their plea, he went forth as an ascetic (tāpasa). In that ascetic life, there are eight kinds of ascetics: (1) Saputtabhariya, (2) Uñchācārika, (3) Sampattakālika, (4) Anaggipakkika, (5) Asmamuṭṭhika, (6) Dantaluyyaka, (7) Pavattafalika, and (8) Vaṇṭamuttika. Among these eight, the Saputtabhariya are those like the matted-hair ascetic Keṇiya, who go forth with their wives and children and make a living through farming, trade, and so forth. The Uñchācārika are those who have a hermitage built at the city gate, teach arts and sciences to princes and Brahmin youths there, reject gold and silver, and accept only allowable items (kappiya-bhaṇḍa) such as sesame and rice. These are superior to the Saputtabhariya ascetics. The Sampattakālika are those who sustain themselves by taking whatever food is obtained at the time of eating. These are superior to the Uñchācārika ascetics. The Anaggipakkika are those who sustain themselves by eating leaves and fruits that are not cooked by fire. These are superior to the Sampattakālika ascetics. The Asmamuṭṭhika are those who wander carrying a stone hammer or other small knives, and when hungry, take bark from a tree they reach, eat it, undertake the factors of the Uposatha, and develop the four Brahma-vihāras. These are superior to the Anaggipakkika ascetics. The Dantaluyyaka are those who wander without even carrying stone hammers and so forth, and when hungry, peel off bark with their teeth from a tree they reach, eat it, undertake the factors of the Uposatha, and develop the Brahma-vihāras. These are superior to the Asmamuṭṭhika ascetics. The Pavattafalika are those who live depending on a lake or a forest grove, eating whatever lotus stalks or roots are in the lake, or flowers when it is flowering season, or fruits when it is fruiting season in the forest grove. When there are no flowers or fruits, they live by eating at least the tree bark there; they do not go elsewhere for the sake of food.
311:
They observe the factors of the Uposatha and practice the development of the Brahma-vihāras; these (Pavattaphalika) ascetics are superior to the Dantaluyyaka ascetics. Those called Vaṇṭamuttika eat only leaves that have fallen from their stalks to the ground; the rest of their practice is the same as before; these ascetics are the most excellent of all.

This young man of a Brahmin family thought, "I will undertake the highest form of renunciation among the ascetic renunciations," and having become a Vaṇṭamuttika ascetic, he crossed two or three mountains in the Himavanta and built a hermitage where he resided. At that time, the Blessed One had appeared in the world, set in motion the noble Wheel of Dhamma, and in due course arrived at Sāvatthī, staying at the Jetavana monastery, the park of Anāthapiṇḍika in Sāvatthī. At that time, a man living in Sāvatthī, while searching for sandalwood heartwood and such on the mountains, reached the ascetic's hermitage, paid homage, and stood at a respectful distance. Seeing him, the ascetic asked, "Where have you come from?" "From Sāvatthī, venerable sir," he replied. "What news is there from there?" he asked. "Venerable sir, the people there are diligent and perform meritorious deeds such as giving (dāna)," he replied. "Whose instruction do they follow in doing so?" he asked. "They follow the instruction of the Blessed Buddha," he replied. Hearing the word "Buddha," the ascetic was amazed and asked three times, in the manner described in the Āmagandha Sutta, "O man, did you say 'Buddha'?" Thinking, "Even this sound is rare in the world," he became joyful and, wishing to go to the Blessed One, thought, "It is not proper to go to the Buddha empty-handed; what should I take with me?" Then he thought, "Buddhas do not care for material gifts; I will take a gift of the Dhamma," and he prepared four questions:

What kind of friend should not be associated with? What kind of friend should be associated with?
What kind of effort (payoga) should be exerted? Among tastes, which taste is the most excellent?

Taking those questions, he set out towards the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa) and in due course reached Sāvatthī and entered the Jetavana monastery. At that time, the Blessed One was seated on his designated seat to teach the Dhamma. Seeing the Blessed One, the ascetic stood at a respectful distance without paying homage. The Blessed One greeted him, saying, "Ascetic, is it bearable for you?" and so on. The ascetic also replied, "Venerable Gotama, it is bearable," and so on, and then thought, "If he is truly the Buddha, he will answer with speech the questions I ask in my mind." He then asked those questions to the Blessed One only in his mind. When the Blessed One was thus questioned by the Brahmin (ascetic)...
312: To answer the first question first, starting with the words 'Hiriṃ tarantaṃ,' he spoke two and a half verses (gāthās). The meaning of those verses is: 'Hiriṃ tarantaṃ' means one who transgresses the sense of shame, who is shameless, who lacks shame regarding evil deeds. 'Vijigucchamānaṃ' means one who views [shame] with disgust, like excrement. A shameless person is disgusted by shame and views it like excrement; therefore, he does not associate with or cling to it. Thus it is said, 'vijigucchamānaṃ.' 'Tavāhamasmi' means one who speaks only with words, saying, 'Friend, I am your companion, I wish for your welfare and happiness, I have even sacrificed my life for your sake,' and so on. 'Sayhāni kammāni anādiyantaṃ' means one who, despite saying such things, does not undertake or commit to performing the tasks of a friend that he is capable of. Or, it refers to one who does not pay serious attention in his heart and, when tasks arise, shows only ruin. A wise man should know, 'This person is not my good friend, but only a false friend.' 'Ananvayaṃ' means that although he says, 'I will give, I will do,' it does not happen according to what he says. He is one who speaks pleasant words to friends only with a mere appearance of affection, using useless words about the past and future. Wise men distinguish and know, 'This person is a false friend called vacīparama (one who excels only in speech),' who does not do what he says, but speaks only with words. 'One who is always looking for ruin, staying close with sweet words, and without being negligent, watches for faults, thinking, "When will he blame me? Then I will accuse him back with this point," is not a friend to be associated with.' Thus, the Blessed One answered the first question, 'What kind of friend should not be associated with?' and to answer the second question, he spoke the half-verse starting with 'Yasmiñca seti'.
313:
The meaning of that verse is: In whichever friend a friend enters the heart and sleeps, just as a son sleeps on his father's breast, without hesitation or suspicion, thinking, "While I sleep on this breast, will there be suffering or displeasure for this father?" and so forth; even so, placing trust in wife, wealth, life, and so on, he sleeps (lives) without suspicion in the state of friendship. Whichever friend cannot be divided (broken) by others even if they speak a hundred or a thousand reasons, that person should indeed be known as a friend to be associated with.

Thus the Blessed One, having answered the second question, "What kind of friend should be associated with?", spoke the verse beginning with "Pāmuzzakaraṇaṃ" to answer the third question. The meaning of that verse is: It is called "pāmuzzakaraṇa" because it causes joy (pāmuzza). "Ṭhāna" means cause. What is that cause? It is energy (vīriya). Indeed, that energy is called "pāmuzzakaraṇa" because it produces joy, gladness, and happiness associated with the Dhamma. As the Blessed One said: "Monks, in this well-expounded Dhamma-Vinaya, whichever monk has aroused energy, he dwells happily." It is called "pasaṃsāvahana" because it brings praise. It is called "sukha" (happiness) by way of metonymy (phalūpacāra), because it brings the happiness of devas and humans in the beginning, and the happiness of Nibbāna in the end. It is called "phalānisaṃsa" because it longs for the fruit. "Bhāveti" means to develop (increase). "Vahanto porisaṃ dhuraṃ" means while dwelling by carrying the burden suitable for men, he develops this state called right exertion (sammappadhāna-vīriya); such an application (payoga) should be practiced.

Thus the Blessed One, having answered the third question, "What kind of effort should be practiced?", spoke the verse beginning with "Pavivekarasaṃ" to answer the fourth question. In that verse, "paviveka" (seclusion) refers to the noble fruit of Arahatship (arahattaphala) because it arises from seclusion from defilements. Its "rasa" (taste) is the happiness (sukha) associated with that fruit in the sense of being enjoyed. "Upasama" (peace) is also that same fruit of Arahatship, either because it arises when defilements are stilled or because it has the peace called Nibbāna as its object. "Dhammapītirasa" (the taste of joy in the Dhamma) is also that same fruit of Arahatship, because it is not separate from the noble Dhamma and because it is the taste of joy arisen in the Dhamma called Nibbāna. Having drunk that taste of seclusion and the taste of peace, and drinking that very taste of joy in the Dhamma, one becomes free from distress and sinless. Even after drinking, one is free from distress because of the absence of the fever of defilements; even while drinking, one is sinless because of having abandoned evil (pāpa). Therefore, this taste is the supreme among tastes. However, some teachers say: "By virtue of jhāna, Nibbāna, and reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā), or by virtue of seclusion of body (kāya-viveka), seclusion of mind (citta-viveka), and seclusion from substrata (upadhi-viveka), these three states such as the taste of seclusion are only three."
314:
Some teachers connect [it] (with the three: jhāna, nibbāna, and viveka); however, the previously mentioned meaning is indeed better. In this way, the Blessed One, while answering the fourth question, concluded the teaching with Arahantship as its culmination. At the conclusion of the teaching, that brahmin went forth in the presence of the Blessed One, and within just a few days, he became an Arahant attained to the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
